With an effort Sonya sat up and began wiping her eyes and trying to explain.

"Nicholas is going away in a week, his... papers... have come... he told me himself... but still I shouldn't cry," and she showed a sheet of paper she was holding—the verses Nicholas had written—"still, I shouldn't cry, but you can't... no one can understand... what a soul he has!"
And she started crying again because he had such a noble soul.

"It's easy for you... I'm not jealous... I love you and Boris too," she went on, gaining a little strength. "He's nice... there are no obstacles in your way... But Nicholas is my cousin... one would have to... the Metropolitan himself... and even then it can't be done. And besides, if she tells Mama"—Sonya considered the countess her mother and called her that—"that I'm ruining Nicholas's career and that I'm heartless and ungrateful, when truly... God is my witness"—she crossed herself—"I love her so much, and all of you, only Vera... And what for? What have I done to her? I'm so grateful to you that I'd willingly sacrifice everything, only I have nothing..."
Sonya couldn't go on and hid her face again in her hands and in the feather bed. Natasha tried to comfort her, but her face showed she understood the full weight of her friend's trouble.
"Sonya," she burst out suddenly, as if she'd guessed the real reason for her friend's grief, "I'm sure Vera said something to you after dinner. Didn't she?"

"Yes—these are the verses Nicholas wrote himself, and I copied some others, and she found them on my table and said she'd show them to Mama. She said I was ungrateful, and that Mama would never let him marry me, and that he'd marry Julie. You saw how he's been with her all day... Natasha, what have I done to deserve this?"
And she began to sob again, more bitterly than before. Natasha pulled her up, hugged her, and, smiling through her own tears, started to comfort her.

"Sonya, don't believe her, darling! Don't believe her! Remember how we all talked—you and Nicholas and me—in the sitting room after supper? We worked out how everything would be arranged. I don't remember exactly how, but don't you remember that it could all work out and how wonderful it would be? There's Uncle Shinshin's brother who married his first cousin. And we're only second cousins, you know. And Boris says it's perfectly possible. You know I've told him all about it. And he's so clever and so good!" said Natasha. "Don't cry, Sonya, dear love, darling Sonya!" And she kissed her and laughed. "Vera is spiteful—never mind her! Everything will be all right, and she won't say anything to Mama. Nicholas will tell her himself, and he doesn't care about Julie at all."
Natasha kissed her on the hair.
Sonya sat up. The little kitten brightened, its eyes shone, and it seemed ready to raise its tail, hop down on its soft paws, and start playing with a ball of yarn the way a kitten should.
"Do you think so?... Really? Truly?" she asked, quickly smoothing her dress and hair.
"Really, truly!" Natasha answered, tucking a wayward curl back under her friend's braid.
Both girls laughed.
"Well, let's go sing 'The Brook.'"
"Let's go!"
"You know, that fat Pierre who sat across from me is so funny!" said Natasha, stopping suddenly. "I feel so happy!"
And she took off running down the hallway.

Sonya, brushing off bits of down that clung to her and tucking the verses into the front of her dress against her thin little chest, ran after Natasha down the hallway into the sitting room, her face flushed, her steps light and joyful. At the guests' request the young people sang the quartet "The Brook," which delighted everyone. Then Nicholas sang a song he had just learned:
In the moonlight's gentle glow, How sweet, as fancies wander free, To know that in this world below There's one who's thinking still of thee!
That as her fingers touch the harp, Sending sweet music o'er the lea, It is for thee her heart beats sharp, Breathing its message out to thee...
A day or two, then joy unspoiled— But oh, till then I cannot live!...
He hadn't finished the last verse before the young people began getting ready to dance in the great hall, and the sound of feet and musicians coughing drifted down from the gallery.

Pierre was sitting in the drawing room where Shinshin had drawn him into a political conversation—as someone recently returned from abroad—in which several others had joined but which bored Pierre. When the music started, Natasha came in and walked straight up to Pierre, laughing and blushing.
"Mama told me to ask you to join the dancing."
"I'm afraid I'll mix up the figures," Pierre replied, "but if you'll be my teacher..." And lowering his big arm, he offered it to the slender little girl.

While the couples were arranging themselves and the musicians tuning up, Pierre sat down with his small partner. Natasha was perfectly happy—she was dancing with a grown-up man who had been abroad. She was sitting in a prominent spot, talking to him like a proper lady. She had a fan in her hand that one of the women had given her to hold. Striking quite the pose of a society woman—heaven knows when or where she'd learned it—she chatted with her partner, fanning herself and smiling over the fan.
"Dear, dear! Just look at her!" exclaimed the countess as she crossed the ballroom, pointing at Natasha.
Natasha blushed and laughed.
"Well, really, Mama! Why not? What's so surprising?"

In the middle of the third ecossaise there was a clatter of chairs being pushed back in the sitting room, where the count and Marya Dmitrievna had been playing cards with most of the older, more distinguished guests. Now they stood up, stretching after sitting so long, put away their purses and wallets, and came into the ballroom. First came Marya Dmitrievna and the count, both looking very pleased with themselves. The count, with a playful ceremony that was almost balletic, offered his bent arm to Marya Dmitrievna. He drew himself up, a smile of debonair gallantry lit up his face, and as soon as the last figure of the ecossaise ended, he clapped his hands at the musicians and called up to their gallery, addressing the first violin:
"Semen! Do you know the Daniel Cooper?"
This was the count's favorite dance, one he had danced in his youth. (Strictly speaking, the Daniel Cooper was a single figure of the anglaise.)
"Look at Papa!" Natasha shouted to the whole room, and completely forgetting that she was dancing with a grown-up partner, she bent her curly head to her knees and filled the room with her laughter.

And indeed everyone in the room watched with amused delight as the jolly old gentleman took his place beside his tall, stout partner Marya Dmitrievna—curved his arms, beat time, straightened his shoulders, turned out his toes, tapped his foot lightly, and with a smile that kept spreading across his round face, prepared the audience for what was coming. The moment the provocatively cheerful strains of the Daniel Cooper began—a tune that sounded rather like a merry peasant dance—every doorway of the ballroom was suddenly filled with household servants, the men on one side and the women on the other, who had come with beaming faces to watch their master enjoy himself.
"Just look at the master! A real eagle!" the nurse declared loudly from one of the doorways.

The count danced well and knew it. But his partner could not dance well and had no desire to. Her enormous figure stood rigid, her powerful arms hanging at her sides (she had given her handbag to the countess), and only her stern but handsome face truly joined in the dance. Everything that the count's plump body expressed through movement, Marya Dmitrievna conveyed solely through her increasingly radiant face and quivering nose. But if the count charmed the spectators with the surprise of his nimble footwork and the agility with which he sprang about on his light feet, Marya Dmitrievna made no less of an impression through the slightest effort—a small shift of her shoulders, a bend of her arms while turning, a stamp of her foot—all of which everyone appreciated given her size and usual severity. The dance grew livelier and livelier. The other couples couldn't draw a moment's attention to themselves and didn't even try. Everyone was watching the count and Marya Dmitrievna. Natasha kept tugging at everyone's sleeves and dresses, urging them to "look at Papa!"—though they were already unable to tear their eyes away. In the pauses between steps the count, breathing hard, waved at the musicians and shouted for them to play faster. Faster, faster, and faster—more lightly, still more lightly—the count whirled around Marya Dmitrievna, now on his toes, now on his heels, until, spinning his partner back to her seat, he executed the final step, kicking his soft foot up behind him, bowing his sweating head, smiling, and sweeping his arm wide—to a thunder of applause and laughter, led by Natasha. Both dancers stood still, breathing heavily and mopping their faces with their handkerchiefs.
[Speaking in French] "That's how we used to dance in our day, my dear," said the count.
"Now that was a Daniel Cooper!" exclaimed Marya Dmitrievna, rolling up her sleeves and puffing hard.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: While the sixth anglaise was being danced at the Rostovs' ball, with the exhausted musicians stumbling through the tune and the tired footmen and cooks preparing supper, Count Bezukhov suffered his sixth stroke. The doctors declared there was no hope of recovery. After a silent confession, the dying man received communion, and preparations began for the sacrament of last rites. The house was filled with the nervous energy that always accompanies such moments. Outside the gates, a group of undertakers lurked in the shadows, hiding whenever a carriage pulled up, waiting for the lucrative order for an expensive funeral. The Military Governor of Moscow, who had been diligently sending aides to check on the count's condition, came in person that evening to pay his final respects to this celebrated nobleman from Catherine the Great's court, Count Bezukhov.

The grand reception room was packed. Everyone rose respectfully as the Military Governor emerged after spending about half an hour alone with the dying man. He gave a slight nod to acknowledge their bows and tried to get out as quickly as possible, avoiding the stares of the doctors, clergy, and family members. Prince Vasili, who had grown thinner and paler over the past few days, walked him to the door, repeating something to him several times in a low voice.

After the Military Governor left, Prince Vasili sat alone on a chair in the ballroom, crossing one leg high over the other, resting his elbow on his knee, and covering his face with his hand. He sat like that for a while, then stood up and, looking around with frightened eyes, hurried with unusually quick steps down the long corridor that led to the back of the house, toward the eldest princess's room.

The people in the dimly lit reception room spoke in nervous whispers, and whenever anyone entered or left the dying man's room, they fell silent and watched the door—which gave a slight creak when opened—with eyes full of curiosity or anticipation.
"The limits of human life are fixed and cannot be exceeded," an old priest was telling a lady who had sat down beside him and was listening with naive attention.
"I wonder if it's too late to administer last rites?" the lady asked, adding the priest's proper title, as though she had no opinion of her own on the matter.
"Ah, madam, it is a great sacrament," the priest replied, running his hand over the thin gray strands of hair combed across his bald head.
"Who was that? The Military Governor himself?" people were asking on the other side of the room. "How young he looks!"
"Yes, and he's over sixty. I hear the count no longer recognizes anyone. They wanted to administer last rites."
"I knew someone who received that sacrament seven times."

The second princess had just come from the sickroom with red, tear-swollen eyes and sat down next to Dr. Lorrain, who was seated in an elegant pose beneath a portrait of Catherine the Great, leaning his elbow on a table.
"Beautiful," the doctor said in response to a comment about the weather. "The weather is beautiful, Princess. And besides, in Moscow one feels almost as if one were in the country."
"Yes, indeed," the princess replied with a sigh. "So he may have something to drink?"
Lorrain considered this.
"Has he taken his medicine?"
"Yes."
The doctor glanced at his watch.
"Take a glass of boiled water and add a pinch of cream of tartar," he said, indicating with his delicate fingers what he meant by a pinch.
"There has never been a case," a German doctor was saying to an aide-de-camp, "where anyone survives the third stroke."
"And what a healthy man he was!" the aide-de-camp remarked. "And who will inherit his wealth?" he added in a whisper.
"It won't go begging," the German replied with a smile.
Everyone looked toward the door again as it creaked open and the second princess went in with the drink she had prepared according to Lorrain's instructions. The German doctor approached Lorrain.
[Speaking in French] "Do you think he can last until morning?" the German asked, addressing Lorrain in poorly pronounced French.
Lorrain pursed his lips and waved a firmly negative finger in front of his nose.
"Tonight, no later," he said quietly, then moved away with a composed smile of satisfaction at having been able to clearly assess and state the patient's condition.
Meanwhile, Prince Vasili had opened the door to the princess's room.

The room was almost dark, lit only by two small lamps burning before the icons, and filled with a pleasant scent of flowers and incense. It was crowded with small pieces of furniture—whatnots, cupboards, and little tables. Behind a screen, the white quilt of a high feather bed was just visible. A small dog began to bark.
"Ah, is that you, cousin?"
She rose and smoothed her hair, which was, as always, so impossibly smooth that it looked as though it were made of one piece with her head and coated in varnish.
"Has something happened?" she asked. "I'm so frightened."

"No, nothing has changed. I just came to talk business, Catiche," the prince muttered wearily, sinking into the chair she had just vacated. "You've certainly made it warm in here, I'll say that. Well, sit down. Let's talk."
*Catherine.
"I thought something might have happened," she said, her face set in its usual expression of stony severity. She sat down across from the prince and prepared to listen.
"I was trying to get some sleep, my dear cousin, but I can't."
"Well, my dear?" said Prince Vasili, taking her hand and bending it downward, as was his habit.
It was clear that this "well?" referred to much that they both understood without having to say it.

The princess, whose body was straight and rigid, disproportionately long for her legs, looked directly at Prince Vasili with no trace of emotion in her prominent gray eyes. Then she shook her head and glanced up at the icons with a sigh. This could have been taken as an expression of sorrow and devotion, or of weariness and a wish to rest soon. Prince Vasili took it as weariness.
"And what about me?" he said. "Do you think this is any easier for me? I'm worn out like a post horse, but I still need to talk with you, Catiche. A very serious talk."

Prince Vasili fell silent, and his cheeks began to twitch nervously—first one side, then the other—giving his face an unpleasant expression that would never have appeared in a drawing room. His eyes, too, seemed strange: at one moment they looked brazenly cunning, and at the next they darted around in alarm.

The princess, holding her little dog on her lap with her thin, bony hands, stared attentively into Prince Vasili's eyes, clearly resolved not to be the first to break the silence, even if she had to wait until morning.

"Well, you see, my dear princess and cousin, Catherine Semenovna," Prince Vasili continued, returning to his subject with what seemed like an inner struggle, "at a moment like this, one must think of everything. One must think of the future, of all of you... I love you all like my own children, as you know."
The princess continued to look at him without moving, her expression unchanged.

"And then, of course, my own family must also be considered," Prince Vasili went on, testily pushing a small table aside without looking at her. "You know, Catiche, that we—you three sisters, Mamontov, and my wife—are the count's only direct heirs. I know how difficult it is for you to talk or think about such things. It's no easier for me. But, my dear, I'm getting on toward sixty and must be prepared for anything. Did you know I've sent for Pierre? The count"—he pointed to the portrait on the wall—"specifically asked that he be called."
Prince Vasili looked questioningly at the princess, but couldn't tell whether she was weighing what he had said or simply staring at him.
"There is one thing I constantly pray God to grant, my dear cousin," she replied, "and that is that He would be merciful to him and allow his noble soul to peacefully depart this—"

"Yes, yes, of course," Prince Vasili interrupted impatiently, rubbing his bald head and angrily pulling back the little table he had just pushed away. "But... in short, the fact is... you know yourself that last winter the count made a will leaving all his property not to us, his direct heirs, but to Pierre."
"He's made plenty of wills!" the princess remarked quietly. "But he can't leave the estate to Pierre. Pierre is illegitimate."

"But my dear," said Prince Vasili suddenly, gripping the little table and becoming more animated, speaking more rapidly, "what if a letter has been written to the Emperor asking for Pierre's legitimation? You must understand that given the count's services, such a request would certainly be granted..."
The princess smiled the way people do when they think they know more about the subject than the person they're talking to.

"I can tell you even more," Prince Vasili continued, seizing her hand. "That letter was written, though never sent, and the Emperor knew about it. The only question is whether it has been destroyed. If it hasn't, then as soon as it's all over"—Prince Vasili sighed to make clear what he meant by 'all over'—"and the count's papers are opened, the will and the letter will be delivered to the Emperor, and the petition will certainly be granted. Pierre will get everything as the legitimate son."
"And what about our share?" asked the princess with an ironic smile, as though anything might happen except that.

"But my poor Catiche, it's as clear as daylight! He'll be the legal heir to everything, and you won't get a thing. You must know, my dear, whether the will and letter were written and whether they've been destroyed. And if by some chance they've been overlooked, you need to know where they are, and you must find them, because..."

"What next?" the princess interrupted with a sardonic smile, her eyes unchanged. "I am a woman, and you think we're all stupid. But I know this: an illegitimate son cannot inherit... [Speaking in French] a bastard!" she added, as though this French translation would conclusively prove the invalidity of his argument.
* A bastard.

"Really, Catiche! Can't you understand? You're so intelligent—how can you not see that if the count has written to the Emperor asking him to recognize Pierre as legitimate, then Pierre will no longer be plain Pierre but Count Bezukhov, and he'll inherit everything under the will? And if the will and letter haven't been destroyed, you'll have nothing but the consolation of having been dutiful, [Speaking in French] and all that follows from that! That's certain."
* And all that follows therefrom.

"I know the will was made, but I also know it's invalid. And you, my dear cousin, seem to take me for a complete fool," said the princess with the expression women wear when they think they're being witty and cutting.

"My dear Princess Catherine Semenovna," Prince Vasili began impatiently, "I didn't come here to argue with you, but to discuss your interests as a kinsman—a good, kind, loyal relative. I'm telling you for the tenth time: if the letter to the Emperor and the will in Pierre's favor are among the count's papers, then, my dear girl, you and your sisters are not heirs! If you don't believe me, believe the experts. I've just spoken with Dmitri Onufrich"—the family lawyer—"and he says the same thing."

At this, something suddenly shifted in the princess's manner. Her thin lips went white, though her eyes remained unchanged, and when she spoke, her voice passed through such transitions that she herself was clearly surprised by them.
"That would be wonderful!" she said. "I never wanted anything, and I don't now."
She pushed the little dog off her lap and straightened her dress.
"And this is the gratitude—this is the recognition for those who sacrificed everything for him!" she cried. "Splendid! Just fine! I don't want anything, Prince."
"Yes, but you're not the only one. There are your sisters..." Prince Vasili replied.
But the princess wasn't listening.
"Yes, I knew it long ago but had forgotten. I knew I could expect nothing but meanness, deceit, envy, and intrigue in this house—the blackest ingratitude..."
"Do you or do you not know where that will is?" Prince Vasili insisted, his cheeks twitching more violently than ever.
"Yes, I was a fool! I still believed in people, loved them, sacrificed myself for them. But only the base and the vile succeed! I know who's been scheming!"
The princess tried to stand, but the prince held her by the hand. She looked like someone who had suddenly lost all faith in the human race. She shot her companion an angry glance.

"There's still time, my dear. You must remember, Catiche, that it was all done hastily, in a moment of anger and illness, and was forgotten afterward. Our duty, my dear, is to correct his mistake—to ease his last moments by preventing this injustice, and not to let him die feeling he has made miserable those who..."

"Who sacrificed everything for him," the princess chimed in, and she would have stood again if the prince hadn't still been holding her. "Though he never knew how to appreciate it. No, my dear cousin," she added with a sigh, "I shall always remember that in this world one must expect no reward—that in this world there is neither honor nor justice. In this world one has to be cunning and cruel."
"Now, now! Be reasonable. I know your excellent heart."
"No, I have a wicked heart."

"I know your heart," the prince repeated. "I value your friendship and want you to think well of me. Don't upset yourself, and let us talk sensibly while there's still time—whether it's a day or only an hour. Tell me everything you know about the will, and above all, where it is. You must know. We'll take it to the count immediately. No doubt he's forgotten all about it and will want to destroy it. You understand that my only desire is to faithfully carry out his wishes—that's my sole reason for being here. I came simply to help him and you."
"Now I see it all! I know who's been scheming—I know!" the princess cried.
"That's not the point, my dear."
"It's that protégée of yours, that sweet Princess Drubetskaya, that Anna Mikhaylovna whom I wouldn't hire as a housemaid... the infamous, vile woman!"
"Let's not waste any time..."

"Oh, don't talk to me about it! Last winter she wormed her way in here and told the count such vile, disgraceful things about us—especially about Sophie—I can't even repeat them. It made the count so ill that he refused to see us for two whole weeks. I know that was when he wrote that vile, infamous document, but I thought it was invalid."
"So we've finally gotten to it—why didn't you tell me about this sooner?"

"It's in the inlaid portfolio he keeps under his pillow," said the princess, ignoring his question. "Now I know! Yes—if I have a sin, a great sin, it is hatred of that vile woman!" she nearly shrieked, now completely transformed. "And what is she doing here, worming her way in? But I'll give her a piece of my mind. The time will come!"

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: While these conversations were taking place in the reception room and the princess's room, a carriage carrying Pierre—who had been sent for—and Anna Mikhaylovna, who felt it necessary to accompany him, was pulling into the courtyard of Count Bezukhov's house. As the wheels rolled softly over the straw that had been laid beneath the windows, Anna Mikhaylovna turned to offer some comforting words to her companion—and realized he was asleep in his corner. She woke him up. Pierre roused himself and followed Anna Mikhaylovna out of the carriage, only then beginning to think about the visit with his dying father that lay ahead. He noticed they hadn't come to the front entrance but to a back door. As he was climbing down from the carriage, two men who looked like tradesmen darted away from the entrance and hid in the shadows along the wall. Pausing, Pierre spotted several other men of the same type lurking in the shadows on both sides of the house. But neither Anna Mikhaylovna nor the footman nor the coachman—who couldn't have missed seeing them—paid any attention. "It must be all right," Pierre told himself, and followed Anna Mikhaylovna. She hurried up a narrow, dimly lit stone staircase, calling back to Pierre, who was falling behind, to keep up. Though he couldn't see why it was necessary for him to visit the count at all, much less why they had to use the back stairs, Anna Mikhaylovna's air of confidence and urgency made Pierre conclude that it was all absolutely essential. Halfway up, they were nearly knocked over by some men carrying pails who came clattering down the stairs in heavy boots. These men pressed themselves against the wall to let Pierre and Anna Mikhaylovna pass, showing not the slightest surprise at seeing them there.
"Is this the way to the princesses' apartments?" Anna Mikhaylovna asked one of them.
"Yes," a footman answered in a bold, loud voice, as though anything were now permissible. "The door on the left, ma'am."
"Perhaps the count didn't ask for me," Pierre said when they reached the landing. "I'd better go to my own room."
Anna Mikhaylovna stopped and waited for him to catch up.
"Oh, my friend!" she said, touching his arm just as she had touched her son's that afternoon. "Believe me, I'm suffering no less than you are, but be a man!"
"But really, shouldn't I just go?" he asked, looking at her kindly over his spectacles.

"Oh, my dear friend! Forget whatever wrongs may have been done to you. Remember—he is your father... perhaps in the agony of death." She sighed. "I've loved you like a son from the very beginning. Trust me, Pierre. I won't forget your interests."
Pierre didn't understand a word of this, but his growing conviction that all of it was necessary only strengthened, and he meekly followed Anna Mikhaylovna, who was already opening a door.

The door led into a back anteroom. In one corner, an old servant of the princesses sat knitting a stocking. Pierre had never been in this part of the house and didn't even know these rooms existed. Anna Mikhaylovna addressed a maid hurrying past with a decanter on a tray as "my dear" and "my sweet," asked about the princess's health, and then led Pierre down a stone passage. The first door on the left opened into the princesses' apartments. The maid with the decanter, in her haste, had left the door open—everything in the house was being done in haste just then—and as Pierre and Anna Mikhaylovna passed, they instinctively glanced inside. There sat Prince Vasili and the eldest princess, close together, talking intensely. Seeing them pass, Prince Vasili drew back with obvious irritation, while the princess leaped up and, in a gesture of desperation, slammed the door shut with all her strength.

This was so unlike the princess's usual composure, and the fear on Prince Vasili's face so out of keeping with his dignity, that Pierre stopped and looked questioningly over his spectacles at his guide. Anna Mikhaylovna showed no surprise. She only gave a faint smile and sighed, as if to say this was no more than she had expected.
"Be a man, my friend. I'll look after your interests," she said in response to his look, and walked even faster down the corridor.

Pierre couldn't make sense of any of it, least of all what "looking after his interests" meant, but he decided that all these things simply had to happen. From the corridor they entered a large, dimly lit room next to the count's reception room. It was one of those grand but cold apartments Pierre knew only from approaching through the front entrance, but now even this room had an empty bathtub standing in it, and water had been spilled on the carpet. A deacon with a censer and a servant passed them on tiptoe without so much as a glance. They continued into the reception room that Pierre knew well, with its two Italian windows facing the conservatory, its large bust, and its full-length portrait of Catherine the Great. The same people sat there in nearly the same positions as before, whispering among themselves. They all fell silent and turned to look at Anna Mikhaylovna—pale and tear-stained—as she entered, and at Pierre's large, heavy figure following meekly behind her with his head bowed.

Anna Mikhaylovna's expression conveyed her awareness that the decisive moment had arrived. With the manner of a practical Petersburg lady, she entered the room even more boldly than she had that afternoon, keeping Pierre close beside her. She knew that by bringing the person the dying man had asked to see, her own presence was assured. Scanning the room with a quick glance and noticing the count's confessor, she glided over to him in a kind of half-bow—seeming to grow suddenly smaller—and respectfully received the blessing first of one priest, then another.
"Thank God you've come in time," she said to one of the priests. "We relatives have all been so worried. This young man is the count's son," she added more softly. "What a terrible moment!"
Then she went up to the doctor.
"Dear doctor," she said, "this young man is the count's son. Is there any hope?"

The doctor glanced upward quickly and gave a silent shrug. Anna Mikhaylovna mirrored the exact same movement—raising her shoulders and eyes, nearly closing them—sighed, and turned away from the doctor to Pierre. In a particularly respectful and tenderly sorrowful voice, she said:
"Trust in His mercy!" Then, pointing him to a small sofa where he could sit and wait, she moved silently toward the door everyone was watching. It gave a faint creak as she disappeared behind it.

Pierre, having resolved to obey his guide in everything, moved toward the sofa she had indicated. The moment Anna Mikhaylovna vanished, he noticed that every pair of eyes in the room was fixed on him with something more than curiosity and sympathy. People whispered to one another, casting meaningful glances his way with a kind of awe—even deference. He had never been treated like this before. A strange lady, the one who had been talking with the priests, stood up and offered him her seat. An aide-de-camp picked up a glove Pierre had dropped and returned it to him. The doctors fell respectfully silent as he passed and moved aside for him. At first Pierre wanted to take a different seat so as not to inconvenience the lady, and to pick up the glove himself, and to walk around the doctors who weren't even in his way. But all at once he sensed that this wouldn't do—that tonight he was a person expected to perform some kind of solemn ritual, and therefore obliged to accept their attentions. He took the glove from the aide-de-camp in silence, sat down in the lady's chair, and placed his large hands symmetrically on his knees in the naive pose of an Egyptian statue. He had decided that in order not to lose his head and do something foolish, he must not act on his own judgment tonight but surrender himself entirely to the will of those guiding him.

Less than two minutes later, Prince Vasili entered the room with his head held high, looking majestic. He wore his long coat with three stars on his chest. He seemed even thinner than he had that morning; his eyes appeared larger than usual as he surveyed the room and spotted Pierre. He walked over, took Pierre's hand—something he had never done before—and pulled it downward, as if testing whether it was firmly attached.
"Courage, courage, my friend! He's asked to see you. That's good!" And he turned to go.
But Pierre felt he should ask: "How is..." He hesitated, unsure whether it was proper to call the dying man "the count," yet embarrassed to call him "father."
"He had another stroke about half an hour ago. Courage, my friend..."

Pierre's mind was in such a fog that the word "stroke" made him think of a physical blow. He stared at Prince Vasili in confusion, and only later grasped that a stroke meant an attack of illness. Prince Vasili murmured something to Lorrain in passing and went through the door on tiptoe. He wasn't good at walking on tiptoe, and his whole body lurched with each step. The eldest princess followed him, and the priests, deacons, and some servants also went through the door. Behind it came the sound of things being moved around, and finally Anna Mikhaylovna—still wearing the same expression, pale but resolute in the performance of duty—hurried out, lightly touched Pierre's arm, and said:
"God's mercy is boundless! They are about to administer last rites. Come."

Pierre went through the door, stepping onto the soft carpet, and noticed that the strange lady, the aide-de-camp, and several servants all followed him in, as though there were no longer any need for permission to enter that room.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 23
paragraphs: Pierre knew this large room well—divided by columns and an arch, its walls hung with Persian carpets. The area behind the columns, with a tall silk-curtained mahogany bed on one side and an enormous icon case on the other, was bathed in red light like a Russian church during evening services. Beneath the gleaming icons stood a long reclining chair, and in it, propped on smooth white pillows that had obviously just been changed, Pierre saw the familiar, majestic figure of his father, Count Bezukhov—covered to the waist by a bright green quilt, with that gray mane of hair above his broad forehead that always made one think of a lion, and the deep, noble wrinkles of his handsome, ruddy face. He lay directly beneath the icons, his large, thick hands resting on top of the quilt. A wax taper had been placed between the forefinger and thumb of his right hand, which lay palm-down, and an old servant standing behind the chair held it in place. By the chair stood the priests, their long hair falling over magnificent, glittering vestments, holding lighted tapers and slowly, solemnly conducting the service. A little behind them stood the two younger princesses, holding handkerchiefs to their eyes. In front of them their eldest sister, Catiche, stood with a fierce and resolute expression fixed on the icons, as if declaring to everyone that she could not be held responsible for what might happen if she looked away. Anna Mikhaylovna stood by the door with a meek, sorrowful, all-forgiving expression, near the unfamiliar lady. Prince Vasili stood at the front, near the reclining chair, a wax taper in his left hand, his left arm resting on the carved back of a velvet chair he had turned around for the purpose, crossing himself with his right hand and raising his eyes heavenward each time his fingers touched his forehead. His face wore a look of calm piety and submission to God's will. "If you don't understand these feelings," his expression seemed to say, "so much the worse for you."

Behind him stood the aide-de-camp, the doctors, and the manservants. The men and women had separated as in a church. Everyone crossed themselves silently, and the only sounds were the reading of the service, the muffled chanting of deep bass voices, and in the pauses, sighs and the shuffling of feet. Anna Mikhaylovna, with an air of importance showing she knew exactly what she was doing, crossed the room to Pierre and handed him a taper. He lit it and, distracted by watching those around him, began crossing himself with the hand that held the candle.

Sophie, the rosy, youngest princess with the mole—the one who was always laughing—watched him. She smiled, buried her face in her handkerchief, and kept it hidden for a moment. Then she looked up, saw Pierre again, and couldn't help laughing once more. She clearly couldn't look at him without laughing, yet couldn't resist looking. To remove herself from temptation, she slipped quietly behind one of the columns. In the middle of the service, the priests' voices suddenly stopped. They whispered to each other, and the old servant holding the count's hand stood up and said something to the ladies. Anna Mikhaylovna stepped forward and, bending over the dying man, beckoned to Lorrain from behind her back. The French doctor had no taper; he was leaning against one of the columns in a respectful posture that showed he—a foreigner—despite all differences of faith, fully understood the significance of the rite being performed and even approved of it. He now approached the sick man with the noiseless step of a person in full health, lifted the hand that lay free from the green quilt with his delicate white fingers, turned slightly to one side, and felt the pulse, reflecting for a moment. The sick man was given something to drink. There was a brief commotion around him, then everyone returned to their places and the service continued. During this pause, Pierre noticed that Prince Vasili left the chair he had been leaning on and—with an air suggesting that he knew what he was doing, and if others didn't understand, that was their problem—walked past the dying man without stopping, joined the eldest princess, and moved with her to the side of the room where the tall bed stood with its silk hangings. They both slipped out through a back door, then returned to their places one after the other before the service concluded. Pierre paid no more attention to this than to anything else going on around him, having decided once and for all that whatever was happening that evening was somehow essential.

The chanting stopped, and the priest's voice was heard respectfully congratulating the dying man on having received the sacrament. The dying man lay as lifeless and motionless as before. People began to stir around him—footsteps, whispers—among which Anna Mikhaylovna's voice was the most audible.
Pierre heard her say:
"He really must be moved to the bed. It's impossible here..."

The sick man was so surrounded by doctors, princesses, and servants that Pierre could no longer see the ruddy, yellowish face with its gray mane—though he hadn't lost sight of it for a single moment during the entire service, even while watching other faces. He could tell from the careful movements of those crowded around the reclining chair that they were lifting the dying man and carrying him.

"Hold onto my arm or you'll drop him!" one of the servants said in a frightened whisper. "Get a grip from underneath. Here!" voices called out, and the heavy breathing of the bearers and the scraping of their feet grew more urgent, as though the weight they carried was too much for them.

As the bearers—among them Anna Mikhaylovna—passed the young man, he caught a momentary glimpse between their heads and shoulders of the dying man's broad, uncovered chest and powerful shoulders, raised by those gripping him under the arms, and of his gray, curly, lion-like head. That head, with its remarkably wide brow and cheekbones, its handsome, sensual mouth, and its cold, majestic expression, was not disfigured by the approach of death. It looked just as Pierre remembered it from three months earlier, when the count had sent him to Petersburg. But now the head swayed helplessly with the uneven movements of the bearers, and those cold, indifferent eyes were fixed on nothing.

After a few minutes of commotion around the tall bed, the bearers dispersed. Anna Mikhaylovna touched Pierre's hand and said, "Come." Pierre went with her to the bed where the sick man had been laid in a stately pose befitting the ceremony just completed. He lay with his head propped high on the pillows, his hands placed symmetrically on the green silk quilt, palms down. When Pierre approached, the count was gazing straight at him—but with an expression whose meaning no living person could decipher. Either the look meant nothing at all, just that eyes must look somewhere as long as they exist, or it meant far too much. Pierre hesitated, unsure what to do, and glanced at his guide. Anna Mikhaylovna made a quick gesture with her eyes toward the sick man's hand, moving her lips as if sending it a kiss. Pierre carefully craned his neck, trying not to touch the quilt, and pressed his lips to the large, fleshy hand with its heavy bones. Neither the hand nor a single muscle of the count's face moved. Pierre looked again at Anna Mikhaylovna, asking what to do next. She indicated a chair beside the bed with her eyes. Pierre sat down obediently, his expression silently asking whether he was doing the right thing. Anna Mikhaylovna nodded her approval. Once again Pierre assumed the naively symmetrical pose of an Egyptian statue, clearly distressed that his large, clumsy body took up so much space, doing his best to appear as small as possible. He looked at the count, who still stared at the spot where Pierre's face had been before he sat down. Anna Mikhaylovna's manner conveyed her awareness of the solemn importance of these final moments between father and son. This lasted about two minutes, though to Pierre it felt like an hour. Suddenly the broad muscles of the count's face began to twitch. The twitching grew stronger, the handsome mouth was pulled to one side—and only now did Pierre grasp how close his father was to death—and from that distorted mouth came a faint, hoarse sound. Anna Mikhaylovna watched the sick man's eyes intently, trying to read what he wanted. She pointed first to Pierre, then to a drink, then whispered Prince Vasili's name inquiringly, then pointed to the quilt. The dying man's eyes and face showed impatience. He made an effort to look at the servant who stood at the head of the bed.
"He wants to be turned onto his other side," the servant whispered, and rose to turn the count's heavy body toward the wall.
Pierre got up to help.

As the count was being turned, one of his arms fell back limply, and he made a futile effort to pull it forward. Whether he noticed the look of horror with which Pierre stared at that lifeless arm, or whether some other thought crossed his dying mind, he glanced at the disobedient arm, then at Pierre's terrified face, then back at the arm, and a faint, pitiful smile appeared on his face—completely at odds with his features—as though mocking his own helplessness. At the sight of that smile, Pierre felt an unexpected tremor in his chest and a prickling in his nose, and tears blurred his eyes. The sick man was turned onto his side, facing the wall. He sighed.
"He's dozing," said Anna Mikhaylovna, noticing one of the princesses coming to take her turn at the bedside watch. "Let's go."
Pierre went out.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: By now, no one remained in the reception room except Prince Vasili and the eldest princess, who sat beneath the portrait of Catherine the Great, talking urgently. The moment they saw Pierre and his companion, they fell silent. Pierre thought he caught the princess hiding something as she whispered:
"I can't stand the sight of that woman."
"Catiche has had tea set up in the small drawing room," Prince Vasili told Anna Mikhaylovna. "Go and have something, my poor Anna Mikhaylovna, or you won't hold up."
To Pierre he said nothing, only gave his arm a sympathetic squeeze below the shoulder. Pierre followed Anna Mikhaylovna into the small drawing room.

"There is nothing quite so refreshing after a sleepless night as a cup of this delicious Russian tea," Lorrain was saying with restrained animation, standing and sipping from a delicate Chinese handleless cup before a table set with tea things and a cold supper in the small circular room. Everyone who was at Count Bezukhov's house that night had gathered here to fortify themselves. Pierre remembered this circular drawing room with its mirrors and small tables well. During balls at the house, Pierre—who didn't know how to dance—used to like sitting here, watching the ladies pass through in their ball gowns with diamonds and pearls on bare shoulders, admiring themselves in the brilliantly lit mirrors that multiplied their reflections. Now the same room was dimly lit by only two candles. On a small table, the tea things and supper dishes stood in disarray, and in the middle of the night a mixed group of people sat there—not celebrating but whispering somberly, every word and gesture showing that none of them could forget what was happening, and was about to happen, in the bedroom. Pierre ate nothing, though he very much wanted to. He looked inquiringly at his guide and saw that she was once again tiptoeing toward the reception room where they had left Prince Vasili and the eldest princess. Pierre decided this too must be essential, and after a short pause, followed her. Anna Mikhaylovna was standing beside the princess, and the two women were speaking in agitated whispers.
"Let me be the judge, Princess, of what is necessary and what is not," said the younger of the two, clearly in the same state of agitation as when she had slammed her door.

"But my dear princess," Anna Mikhaylovna answered calmly but firmly, positioning herself to block the way to the bedroom and prevent the other woman from passing, "won't this be too much for poor Uncle at a moment when he needs rest? Worldly matters at a time when his soul is already prepared..."

Prince Vasili sat in an armchair in his usual pose, one leg crossed high over the other. His flabby cheeks—which looked heavier at the bottom—were twitching violently, but he wore the air of a man unconcerned with what the two ladies were saying.
"Come now, my dear Anna Mikhaylovna, let Catiche do as she wishes. You know how fond the count is of her."

"I don't even know what's in this document," said the younger woman, turning to Prince Vasili and pointing at the inlaid portfolio in her hand. "All I know is that his real will is in his writing desk, and this is just a paper he's forgotten about...."
She tried to get past Anna Mikhaylovna, but Anna Mikhaylovna sprang forward to block her path.

"I know, my dear, kind princess," Anna Mikhaylovna said, gripping the portfolio so tightly it was obvious she would not let go easily. "Dear princess, I beg you, I implore you—have some pity on him! [Speaking in French] I beseech you..."

The princess said nothing. The only sounds were their struggle over the portfolio. But it was clear that if the princess did speak, her words would not be kind to Anna Mikhaylovna. Despite her tenacious grip, Anna Mikhaylovna's voice lost none of its honeyed firmness and softness.
"Pierre, my dear, come here. I think he won't be out of place in a family discussion—don't you agree, Prince?"

"Why don't you speak, cousin?" the princess suddenly shrieked, so loudly that the people in the drawing room heard and were startled. "Why are you standing there in silence while heaven knows who takes it upon herself to interfere—making a scene on the very threshold of a dying man's room? You schemer!" she hissed viciously, and yanked the portfolio with all her might.
But Anna Mikhaylovna stepped forward to maintain her grip and adjusted her hold.
Prince Vasili rose from his chair. "Oh!" he said with reproach and surprise. "This is absurd! Come, let go, I tell you."
The princess released her grip.
"And you too!"
But Anna Mikhaylovna did not obey.
"Let go, I tell you! I'll take responsibility. I'll go in and ask him myself. I!... Is that good enough for you?"

"But, Prince," said Anna Mikhaylovna, "after such a solemn sacrament, give him a moment's peace! Here, Pierre, tell them what you think," she said, turning to the young man, who had come close and was staring in astonishment at the princess's furious face—stripped of all dignity—and at Prince Vasili's twitching cheeks.
"Remember, you will answer for the consequences," Prince Vasili said severely. "You don't know what you're doing."
"Vile woman!" the princess shouted, lunging unexpectedly at Anna Mikhaylovna and snatching the portfolio from her hands.
Prince Vasili bowed his head and spread his hands in a helpless gesture.

At that moment, the terrible door—which Pierre had watched for so long, and which had always opened so quietly—burst open with a bang against the wall, and the second of the three sisters rushed out, wringing her hands.
"What are you doing!" she cried desperately. "He's dying, and you leave me alone with him!"

The eldest sister dropped the portfolio. Anna Mikhaylovna swooped down, snatched up the contested object, and ran into the bedroom. The eldest princess and Prince Vasili, recovering their composure, hurried after her. A few minutes later, the eldest sister emerged with a pale, rigid face, biting her lower lip again. When she caught sight of Pierre, her expression showed undisguised hatred.
"Yes, now you can celebrate!" she said. "This is what you've been waiting for." Then she burst into tears, covered her face with her handkerchief, and rushed from the room.

Prince Vasili came out next. He staggered to the sofa where Pierre was sitting and collapsed onto it, covering his face with his hand. Pierre noticed he was pale, and that his jaw was trembling and shaking as though he had a fever.

"Oh, my friend!" he said, gripping Pierre by the elbow. There was a sincerity and vulnerability in his voice that Pierre had never heard before. "How often we sin, how much we deceive—and for what? I'm nearly sixty, my dear friend... I too... It all ends in death. Death is terrible..." And he burst into tears.
Anna Mikhaylovna was the last to come out. She approached Pierre with slow, quiet steps.
"Pierre!" she said.
Pierre looked at her questioningly. She leaned forward and kissed the young man on his forehead, wetting him with her tears. After a pause, she said:
"He is gone...."
Pierre stared at her over his spectacles.
"Come, I'll go with you. Try to cry—nothing brings such relief as tears."

She led him into the dark drawing room, and Pierre was grateful that no one could see his face. Anna Mikhaylovna left him there, and when she returned, he had fallen asleep with his head resting on his arm.
The next morning, Anna Mikhaylovna said to Pierre:

"Yes, my dear, this is a great loss for all of us—to say nothing of you. But God will sustain you. You are young, and now, I hope, the master of an immense fortune. The will hasn't been opened yet. I know you well enough to be certain this won't go to your head, but it does impose responsibilities on you, and you must be a man."
Pierre said nothing.

"Perhaps I'll tell you someday, my dear boy, that if I hadn't been there, God only knows what would have happened. You know, your uncle promised me just the day before yesterday not to forget Boris. But he didn't have time. I hope, my dear friend, that you'll carry out your father's wishes?"

Pierre understood none of this and, blushing with embarrassment, looked at Princess Anna Mikhaylovna in silence. After her conversation with Pierre, Anna Mikhaylovna returned to the Rostovs' and went to bed. When she woke up the next morning, she told the Rostovs and all her acquaintances the details of Count Bezukhov's death. She said the count had died just as she herself would wish to die—that his end was not only moving but spiritually uplifting. As for the final meeting between father and son, it was so touching she could hardly think of it without tears, and she couldn't say who had shown more grace in those terrible moments—the father, who had remembered everyone at the last and spoken such tender words to his son, or Pierre, whose grief was heartbreaking to witness, though he had tried so hard to hide it to spare his dying father. "It's painful, but it does the soul good. It elevates you to see men like the old count and his worthy son," she said. About the eldest princess and Prince Vasili, she spoke disapprovingly—but only in whispers, and as a great secret.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: At Bald Hills, the estate of Prince Nikolai Andreevich Bolkonsky, the arrival of young Prince Andrei and his wife was expected any day, but this didn't disrupt the old prince's rigid household routine. General-in-Chief Prince Nikolai Andreevich—nicknamed "the King of Prussia" in society—had been living at his country estate continuously since Emperor Paul had exiled him there, together with his daughter, Princess Mary, and her companion, Mademoiselle Bourienne. Though the new reign had made him free to return to the capitals, he continued to live in the country, remarking that anyone who wanted to see him could make the hundred-mile trip from Moscow to Bald Hills, while he himself needed nobody and nothing. He liked to say there are only two sources of human vice—idleness and superstition—and only two virtues—activity and intelligence. He personally oversaw his daughter's education, and to develop these two virtues in her, gave her lessons in algebra and geometry until she was twenty and organized her life so that every hour was accounted for. He himself was perpetually busy: writing his memoirs, solving problems in higher mathematics, turning snuffboxes on a lathe, working in the garden, or supervising the construction that was always underway on his estate. Since regularity is the first condition of productivity, regularity in his household was maintained to the highest degree of precision. He always came to meals not just at the same hour but at the same minute. With everyone around him, from his daughter down to the servants, the prince was sharp and unfailingly demanding—not out of cruelty, but with a severity that inspired the kind of fear and respect that few genuinely cruel men could have commanded. Although he was retired and no longer wielded political influence, every senior official appointed to the province felt duty-bound to pay him a visit, and they waited in his lofty antechamber—alongside the architect, the gardener, and Princess Mary—until the prince appeared at precisely the appointed time. Everyone in that waiting room experienced the same mix of respect and dread when the enormously tall study door swung open to reveal the small figure of the old man: powdered wig, small withered hands, and bushy gray eyebrows that, when he frowned, could hide the sharp gleam of his youthful, piercing eyes.

On the morning of the day the young couple was expected, Princess Mary entered the antechamber at the usual time for the morning greeting, crossing herself nervously and repeating a silent prayer. She came in like this every morning, and every morning she prayed the encounter would go smoothly.
An old powdered manservant sitting in the antechamber stood quietly and said in a whisper: "Please go in."

Through the door came the steady hum of a lathe. The princess timidly pushed open the door, which moved silently on its hinges. She paused at the threshold. The prince was working at the lathe and, after a quick glance, went on with what he was doing.

The enormous study was full of objects clearly in constant use. A large table strewn with books and plans, tall glass-fronted bookcases with keys in their locks, a high standing desk with an open exercise book on it, the lathe with tools at the ready and shavings scattered around—everything spoke of continuous, varied, disciplined activity. The rhythmic motion of his small foot in a silver-embroidered Tartar boot, and the firm pressure of his lean, sinewy hand, showed that the prince still possessed all the endurance and energy of a hardy old age. After a few more turns of the lathe, he removed his foot from the pedal, wiped his chisel, dropped it into a leather pouch attached to the lathe, and walked to the table to greet his daughter. He never gave his children a blessing, so he simply offered his bristly, unshaven cheek and, looking at her with tender attention, said sternly:
"Feeling well? Good. Sit down." He took the exercise book of geometry lessons he had written himself and pulled up a chair with his foot.
"For tomorrow!" he said, quickly finding the right page and marking a section with a hard fingernail, scratching from one paragraph to the next.
The princess bent over the exercise book on the table.
"Wait—here's a letter for you," the old man said suddenly, pulling a letter in a woman's handwriting from a bag hanging above the table and tossing it to her.
Red blotches appeared on the princess's face at the sight of the letter. She snatched it up quickly and bent her head over it.
"From Heloise?" the prince asked with a cold smile that revealed his still-sound, yellowish teeth.
"Yes, it's from Julie," the princess replied with a timid glance and a shy smile.
"I'll let two more letters pass, but the third one I'm reading," the prince said sternly. "I'm afraid you write a lot of nonsense. I'll read the third!"
"Read this one if you like, Father," said the princess, blushing even more and holding out the letter.
"The third, I said the third!" the prince snapped, pushing the letter away. He leaned his elbows on the table and drew the geometry exercise book toward him.

"Now then, young lady," he began, bending over the book close to his daughter and resting his arm on the back of her chair, so that she found herself enveloped on all sides by the sharp scent of old age and tobacco that she had known all her life. "Now then—these triangles are equal. Please observe that the angle ABC..."

The princess stared with frightened eyes at her father's face, which glittered with intensity right next to hers. The red patches came and went on her cheeks, and it was obvious she understood nothing and was so terrified that her fear would block any comprehension of his explanations, no matter how clear. Whether the fault lay with the teacher or the student, the same thing happened every day: the princess's eyes glazed over, she could neither see nor hear, conscious only of her stern father's withered face close to hers, his breath and his smell, able to think of nothing but escaping to her own room to work out the problem in peace. The old man would lose his composure, noisily shoving his chair back and forth, struggling to hold his temper—and nearly always failing. He would scold her, and sometimes hurl the exercise book across the room.
The princess gave a wrong answer.
"Now, isn't she a fool!" the prince shouted, shoving the book aside and turning sharply away. But he immediately stood up, paced the room, gently touched his daughter's hair, and sat down again.
He pulled his chair closer and resumed his explanation.

"This won't do, Princess, it won't do," he said as Princess Mary closed the exercise book with tomorrow's lesson and prepared to leave. "Mathematics is essential, young lady! I don't want you turning out like those silly society women. Stick with it and you'll come to enjoy it." He patted her cheek. "It'll drive all the foolishness out of your head."
She turned to go, but he stopped her with a gesture and took an uncut book from the high desk.
"Here's some sort of Key to the Mysteries that your Heloise sent you. Religion! I don't interfere with anyone's beliefs... I've had a look at it. Take it. Well—go on, go."
He patted her on the shoulder and personally closed the door behind her.

Princess Mary returned to her room wearing the sad, anxious expression that rarely left her face and that made her plain, sickly features seem even plainer. She sat down at her writing desk, which was surrounded by miniature portraits and cluttered with books and papers. The princess was as messy as her father was orderly. She set down the geometry book and eagerly broke the seal on her letter. It was from her closest childhood friend—the very same Julie Karagina who had been at the Rostovs' name-day party.
Julie wrote in French:

Dear and precious Friend, How terrible and frightening it is to be separated! Though I tell myself that half my life and half my happiness are wrapped up in you, and that despite the distance between us our hearts are joined by unbreakable bonds, my heart rebels against fate, and despite all the pleasures and distractions around me, I cannot shake a certain secret sorrow that has lived in my heart ever since we parted. Why can't we be together as we were last summer, in your big study, on the blue sofa—the sofa where we shared our secrets? Why can't I draw fresh moral strength from your gaze, as I did three months ago—that gaze so gentle, calm, and searching, which I loved so much and seem to see before me now as I write?

Having read this far, Princess Mary sighed and glanced at the mirror on her right. It reflected a thin, graceless figure and a gaunt face. Her eyes, always sad, now looked with particular hopelessness at her own reflection. "She flatters me," the princess thought, looking away and continuing to read. But Julie was not flattering her friend. The princess's eyes—large, deep, and luminous, as though warm shafts of light sometimes radiated from them—were so beautiful that despite the plainness of her face, they often lent her a magnetism more powerful than conventional beauty. But the princess never saw the beautiful expression of her own eyes—the look they had when she wasn't thinking about herself. Like everyone, her face took on a forced, unnatural expression as soon as she looked in a mirror. She continued reading:

All Moscow talks of nothing but war. One of my two brothers is already abroad; the other is with the Guards, who are about to march for the frontier. Our dear Emperor has left Petersburg, and it's believed he intends to expose his precious person to the dangers of war. God grant that the Corsican monster who is destroying the peace of Europe may be overthrown by the angel whom the Almighty, in His goodness, has given us as our sovereign! To say nothing of my brothers, this war has robbed me of one of the bonds dearest to my heart. I mean young Nikolai Rostov, who was so passionately enthusiastic that he couldn't bear to remain idle and has left the university to join the army. I will confess to you, dear Mary, that despite his extreme youth, his departure for the army was a great sorrow for me. This young man, of whom I told you last summer, is so noble-spirited and full of that genuine youthfulness one so rarely finds anymore among our old men of twenty—and above all, he is so honest and has so much heart. He is so pure and poetic that my relationship with him, brief as it was, has been one of the sweetest comforts to my poor heart, which has already suffered so much. Someday I'll tell you about our parting and everything that was said. It's all still too fresh. Ah, dear friend, you're lucky not to know these sharp joys and sorrows. You are fortunate, because the sorrows are usually stronger! I know perfectly well that Count Nikolai is too young ever to be more than a friend to me, but this sweet friendship, this poetic, pure bond, was exactly what my heart needed. But enough of this! The main news, the talk of all Moscow, is the death of old Count Bezukhov and his inheritance. Can you imagine! The three princesses received almost nothing, Prince Vasili got nothing at all, and it's Monsieur Pierre who has inherited everything and has been officially recognized as legitimate—so he is now Count Bezukhov and the owner of the greatest fortune in Russia. People say Prince Vasili played a thoroughly contemptible role in the whole affair and went back to Petersburg completely humiliated.

I'll admit I don't understand much about wills and inheritance, but I do know that ever since this young man—whom we all used to know as plain Monsieur Pierre—became Count Bezukhov and owner of one of the largest fortunes in Russia, I've been greatly entertained watching how the tone and manners of mothers with marriageable daughters, and of the young ladies themselves, have changed toward him. Though, between you and me, he always struck me as a rather unremarkable fellow. Since for the past two years people have amused themselves finding husbands for me—most of whom I don't even know—the Moscow matchmaking rumor mill now speaks of me as the future Countess Bezukhova. But you'll understand I have no interest in that title. Speaking of marriages: did you know that a while ago that universal busybody Anna Mikhaylovna told me, in the strictest confidence, about a marriage plan for you? It involves none other than Prince Vasili's son Anatole, whom they hope to reform through marriage to someone wealthy and distinguished—and you are the one his family has chosen. I don't know how you'll feel about it, but I thought it my duty to tell you. He's said to be very handsome and an absolute rogue. That's all I've been able to find out about him.

But enough gossip. I'm at the bottom of my second sheet of paper, and Mama has sent for me to go dine at the Apraksins'. Read the mystical book I'm sending you—it's an enormous success here. Though there are things in it that are hard for our feeble human minds to grasp, it is a wonderful book that calms and elevates the soul. Farewell! Give my respects to your father and my regards to Mademoiselle Bourienne. I embrace you as I love you.
JULIE
P.S. Send me news of your brother and his charming little wife.

The princess sat thinking for a while, a thoughtful smile on her face, her luminous eyes lighting up until her expression was completely transformed. Then she rose abruptly and, with her heavy step, went to the writing table. She took out a sheet of paper and her hand flew rapidly across it. This was her reply, also in French:

Dear and precious Friend, Your letter of the 13th brought me great joy. So you still love me, my romantic Julie? The separation you complain about so bitterly seems not to have had its usual effect on you. You speak of your loneliness—but what should I say, I who am cut off from everyone dear to me? Ah, if we didn't have religion to comfort us, life would be so bleak. Why do you think I would judge your feelings for that young man harshly? In such matters I am strict only with myself. I understand such feelings in others, and though I've never experienced them, I can neither approve nor condemn them. It only seems to me that Christian love—love of neighbor, love of one's enemy—is worthier, sweeter, and more beautiful than the feelings that a handsome young man's eyes can awaken in a romantic and loving young girl like you.

The news of Count Bezukhov's death reached us before your letter, and my father was deeply affected. He says the count was the last representative but one of the great century, and that his own turn is next—though he'll do everything he can to postpone it as long as possible. God spare us from that terrible misfortune!

I can't agree with you about Pierre, whom I've known since he was a child. He always seemed to me to have an excellent heart, and that is the quality I value most in people. As for his inheritance and Prince Vasili's role in it—how sad for both of them. Ah, my dear friend, how terribly true are our divine Savior's words: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of God. I pity Prince Vasili, but I feel even sorrier for Pierre. So young, and weighed down with such wealth—what temptations lie ahead of him! If anyone asked me what I desire most on earth, it would be to be poorer than the poorest beggar. A thousand thanks, dear friend, for the book you've sent, which is enjoying such success in Moscow. But since you tell me it contains things our weak minds cannot understand alongside its good things, it seems rather pointless to spend time on what is incomprehensible and therefore fruitless. I have never understood why some people enjoy confusing their minds with mystical books that only awaken doubt and inflame the imagination, giving them a tendency toward exaggeration entirely contrary to Christian simplicity. Let us read the Epistles and the Gospels instead. Let us not try to penetrate their mysteries, for how can we—wretched sinners that we are—presume to understand the terrible, holy secrets of Providence while we remain in this flesh, which is an impenetrable veil between us and the Eternal? Let us confine ourselves to the sublime rules our divine Savior left for our guidance here on earth. Let us try to follow them, and let us trust that the less we allow our feeble human minds to wander, the more we shall please God, who rejects all knowledge not from Him; and the less we try to fathom what He has chosen to conceal from us, the sooner He will reveal it through His divine Spirit.

My father has not spoken to me of a suitor, but has only mentioned that he received a letter and is expecting a visit from Prince Vasili. Regarding this marriage proposal, I will tell you, dear sweet friend, that I consider marriage a divine institution to which we must submit. However painful it may be, should the Almighty place upon me the duties of wife and mother, I will try to fulfill them as faithfully as I can, without troubling myself to examine my feelings toward whomever He may give me as a husband.

I've had a letter from my brother announcing his imminent arrival at Bald Hills with his wife. This pleasure will be short-lived, however, as he will be leaving again to take part in this terrible war into which we have been drawn—God knows how or why. Not only where you are, at the heart of affairs and society, but even here, amid farmwork and the tranquility of nature that city people think defines the countryside—here too the rumors of war are heard and felt painfully. My father talks of nothing but marches and countermarches, things I understand nothing about. And the day before yesterday, during my daily walk through the village, I witnessed a heartbreaking scene.... It was a column of conscripts drafted from our people, setting off to join the army. You should have seen the state of the mothers, wives, and children of the men who were leaving. You should have heard the weeping. It seems as if humanity has forgotten the laws of our divine Savior, who preached love and the forgiveness of wrongs—and that people now believe the highest merit lies in the skill of killing one another.
Farewell, dear and kind friend. May our divine Savior and His most Holy Mother keep you in Their holy and all-powerful care!
MARY

"Ah, so you're sending a letter, Princess? I've already sent mine. I wrote to my poor mother," said Mademoiselle Bourienne with a smile, speaking quickly in her pleasant, melodious voice with its rolling r's. She brought into Princess Mary's earnest, sorrowful world a completely different atmosphere—carefree, lighthearted, and self-satisfied.

"Princess, I should warn you," she added, lowering her voice and clearly enjoying the sound of it, speaking with exaggerated affectation, "the prince has been scolding Mikhail Ivanovich. He's in a terrible mood—very grim. Be prepared."
"Ah, dear friend," Princess Mary replied, "I've asked you never to tell me what mood my father is in. I don't allow myself to judge him, and I wouldn't want others to either."

The princess glanced at her watch and, seeing that she was five minutes late starting her practice on the clavichord, hurried into the sitting room with an anxious expression. Between twelve and two o'clock, according to the day's fixed schedule, the prince rested and the princess played the clavichord.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 26
paragraphs: The gray-haired valet sat drowsily listening to the prince snoring in his large study. From the far side of the house, through closed doors, came the sound of a difficult passage from a Dussek sonata—repeated twenty times over.

Just then, a closed carriage and a hooded cart pulled up to the front porch. Prince Andrei stepped out, helped his small wife down, and let her enter the house ahead of him. Old Tikhon, wearing a wig, poked his head out of the antechamber door, whispered that the prince was sleeping, and quickly shut it again. Tikhon knew that neither the son's arrival nor any other unusual event was allowed to disturb the appointed order of the day. Prince Andrei apparently knew this just as well as Tikhon. He checked his watch, as if to confirm whether his father's habits had changed since his last visit, and, satisfied that they hadn't, turned to his wife.
"He won't be up for twenty minutes. Let's go see Mary," he said.
The little princess had put on weight since they'd last been here, but her eyes and her short, downy upper lip—which lifted when she began to speak—were as merry and charming as ever.

"Why, this is a palace!" she said to her husband, looking around with the expression people use when complimenting their host at a ball. "Come on, quick, quick!" And she flashed a smile at Tikhon, at her husband, and at the footman escorting them.
"Is that Mary practicing? Let's sneak up and surprise her."
Prince Andrei followed her with a courteous but melancholy expression.
"You've gotten older, Tikhon," he said in passing to the old man, who kissed his hand.
Before they reached the room from which the clavichord music was coming, the pretty, fair-haired Frenchwoman, Mademoiselle Bourienne, burst out, apparently beside herself with excitement.
"Oh, what joy for the princess!" she cried. "At last! I must go tell her!"
"No, no, please don't... You're Mademoiselle Bourienne," said the little princess, kissing her. "I feel like I already know you through my sister-in-law's friendship. She wasn't expecting us?"
They approached the sitting room door, from which the same passage of the sonata could be heard repeating. Prince Andrei stopped and made a pained face, as if bracing for something unpleasant.

The little princess walked in. The music broke off mid-phrase, a cry rang out, followed by Princess Mary's heavy footsteps and the sound of kissing. When Prince Andrei entered, the two princesses—who had met only once before, briefly, at his wedding—were locked in each other's arms, pressing their lips to whatever part of each other's face they could reach. Mademoiselle Bourienne stood nearby with her hand pressed to her heart, wearing a blissful smile and looking equally prepared to burst into tears or laughter. Prince Andrei shrugged and frowned, the way music lovers do when they hear a wrong note. The two women released each other, then immediately seized each other's hands again, kissing them, pulling them away, and kissing each other's faces once more. To Prince Andrei's bewilderment, they both began to cry, then kissed again. Mademoiselle Bourienne started crying too. Prince Andrei was clearly uncomfortable, but to the two women it all felt perfectly natural—it apparently never crossed their minds that their meeting could have gone any other way.

"Oh, my dear!... Oh, Mary!..." they exclaimed simultaneously, then laughed. "I dreamed about you last night..." "You weren't expecting us?..." "Oh, Mary, you've gotten thinner!..." "And you've gotten heavier!..."
"I recognized the princess right away," Mademoiselle Bourienne put in.
"And I had no idea!..." Princess Mary exclaimed. "Oh, Andrei—I didn't even see you."

Prince Andrei and his sister took each other's hands and kissed, and he told her she was still the same crybaby she had always been. Princess Mary turned toward her brother, and through her tears the warm, loving, gentle light of her large, luminous eyes—extraordinarily beautiful in that moment—rested on Prince Andrei's face.

The little princess chattered nonstop. Her short, downy upper lip kept dipping to meet her rosy lower lip, then lifting again as her face broke into a smile of gleaming teeth and sparkling eyes. She told them about an accident they'd had on Spassky Hill that could have been serious in her condition, then immediately reported that she'd left all her clothes in Petersburg and heaven knew what she would wear here, and that Andrei had completely changed, and that Kitty Odyntsova had married an old man, and that there was a real suitor for Mary—but they'd discuss that later. Princess Mary watched her brother in silence, her beautiful eyes full of love and sadness. She was clearly following her own train of thought, independent of her sister-in-law's stream of words. In the middle of a description of the latest Petersburg party, she turned to her brother:
"So you're really going to the war, Andrei?" she asked with a sigh.
Lise sighed too.
"Yes—tomorrow, in fact," her brother replied.
"He's leaving me here, God knows why, when he could have had a promotion..."
Princess Mary didn't hear the rest. Following her own thoughts, she turned to her sister-in-law with a tender glance at her figure.
"Is it definite?" she asked.
The little princess's face changed. She sighed and said: "Yes, quite definite. Oh, it's so frightening..."
Her lip dropped. She brought her face close to her sister-in-law's and suddenly began to cry again.
"She needs to rest," Prince Andrei said with a frown. "Don't you, Lise? Take her to your room, and I'll go see Father. How is he? The same as ever?"
"Yes, exactly the same. Though I don't know what you'll make of it," the princess answered cheerfully.

"Same hours? Same walks along the avenues? And the lathe?" Prince Andrei asked with a barely perceptible smile, showing that despite all his love and respect for his father, he was well aware of his quirks.
"The same hours, and the lathe, and the mathematics, and my geometry lessons," Princess Mary said happily, as though geometry were among the greatest pleasures of her life.

When the twenty minutes were up and it was time for the old prince to rise, Tikhon came to summon the young prince. In honor of his son's arrival, the old man made an exception to his routine: he gave orders for Prince Andrei to be admitted to his rooms while he dressed for dinner. The old prince always dressed in the old-fashioned way—an antique-style coat and powdered hair. When Prince Andrei entered his father's dressing room—not wearing the contemptuous expression he put on in drawing rooms, but the lively face he showed when talking with Pierre—the old man was sitting in a large leather armchair, wrapped in a powdering cape, offering his head to Tikhon's ministrations.
"Ah, the warrior! Come to conquer Bonaparte?" the old man said, shaking his powdered head as much as the braid Tikhon was plaiting would allow.
"You'd better deal with him properly, or he'll have us all as his subjects before long! How are you?" And he offered his cheek.

The old man was in high spirits after his pre-dinner nap. (He used to say that a nap after dinner was silver, but before dinner was gold.) He cast fond, sidelong glances at his son from beneath those thick, bushy brows. Prince Andrei went over and kissed his father on the indicated spot. He made no comment on his father's favorite hobby—ridiculing modern-day military leaders, and Bonaparte in particular.
