The Emperor, surrounded by his officers and courtiers, was riding a bob-tailed chestnut mare — a different horse from the one at the review — and leaning to one side, he gracefully held a gold lorgnette to his eyes and looked down at a soldier lying face-down, blood on his bare head. The wounded man was so dirty, rough, and disfigured that his closeness to the Emperor shocked Rostov. Rostov saw how the Emperor's rounded shoulders shuddered as though a chill ran through them, how his left foot began involuntarily tapping the horse's side with the spur, and how the well-trained horse glanced around unconcerned and didn't move. An adjutant dismounted and lifted the soldier under the arms to place him on a stretcher that had been brought up. The soldier groaned.
"Gently, gently! Can't you do it more carefully?" said the Emperor, apparently suffering more than the dying soldier himself, and he rode away.
Rostov saw tears filling the Emperor's eyes and heard him say to Czartoryski as he rode off: "What a terrible thing war is — what a terrible thing!"

The vanguard troops were positioned in front of Wischau, within sight of the enemy's lines, which had given ground all day at the slightest exchange of fire. The Emperor's gratitude was announced to the vanguard, rewards were promised, and the men received a double ration of vodka. The campfires crackled and the soldiers' songs rang out even louder than the night before. Denisov was celebrating his promotion to major, and Rostov, who had already drunk plenty, proposed a toast to the Emperor at the end of the feast. "Not 'our Sovereign, the Emperor,' the way they say it at official dinners," he said, "but to the health of our Sovereign — that good, wonderful, and great man! Let's drink to his health and to the certain defeat of the French!"

"If we fought the way we did before," he continued, "not letting the French through, like at Schon Grabern — what won't we do now that he himself is leading us? We'll all gladly die for him! Isn't that right, gentlemen? Maybe I'm not saying this perfectly — I've had a lot to drink — but that's how I feel, and I know you feel the same! To the health of Alexander the First! Hurrah!"
"Hurrah!" rang out the enthusiastic voices of the officers.
And the old cavalry captain Kirsten shouted just as enthusiastically and just as sincerely as the twenty-year-old Rostov.

When the officers had drained and smashed their glasses, Kirsten filled new ones and, in his shirtsleeves and breeches, walked glass in hand to the soldiers' bonfires. With his long gray mustache and his white chest showing through his open shirt, he stood in a grand pose by the firelight, waving his raised arm.
"Boys! To our Sovereign, the Emperor, and victory over our enemies! Hurrah!" he bellowed in his bold, old hussar's baritone.
The hussars crowded around and responded with hearty, loud cheers.
Late that night, after everyone had gone their separate ways, Denisov patted his favorite, Rostov, on the shoulder with his short hand.
"Since there's no one to fall in love with on campaign, he's gone and fallen in love with the Tsar," he said.
"Denisov, don't joke about it!" cried Rostov. "It's such an elevated, beautiful feeling, such a..."
"I believe you, I believe you, my friend, and I share it and approve..."
"No, you don't understand!"

And Rostov got up and wandered among the campfires, dreaming of what happiness it would be to die — not saving the Emperor's life (he didn't even dare dream of that), but simply to die before his eyes. He truly was in love with the Tsar, with the glory of Russian arms, and with the hope of future victory. And he wasn't the only one who felt this way during those memorable days before the battle of Austerlitz: nine-tenths of the men in the Russian army were then in love, though less ecstatically, with their Tsar and the glory of Russian arms.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The next day the Emperor stayed in Wischau, and his physician Villier was called in repeatedly. At headquarters and among the nearby troops, word spread that the Emperor was unwell. He had eaten nothing and slept badly, according to those around him. The cause of his illness was the powerful impression the sight of the dead and wounded had made on his sensitive nature.

At dawn on the seventeenth, a French officer carrying a flag of truce and requesting an audience with the Russian Emperor was brought into Wischau from the outposts. The officer was Savary. The Emperor had only just fallen asleep, so Savary had to wait. At noon he was admitted to see the Emperor, and an hour later he rode off with Prince Dolgorukov toward the French army's forward positions.

It was rumored that Savary had been sent to propose a meeting between Alexander and Napoleon. To the joy and pride of the entire army, a personal meeting was refused, and instead of the Emperor himself, Prince Dolgorukov — the victor at Wischau — was sent with Savary to negotiate with Napoleon, in case these negotiations reflected a genuine desire for peace.
Toward evening Dolgorukov returned, went straight to the Tsar, and remained alone with him for a long time.

On November 18th and 19th, the army advanced two days' march, and the enemy's outposts retreated after brief exchanges of fire. In the highest military circles, from midday on the 19th, a frantic, excited flurry of activity began that lasted until the morning of the 20th, when the famous battle of Austerlitz was fought.

Until midday on the 19th, the activity — the urgent conversations, the rushing back and forth, the dispatching of adjutants — was confined to the Emperor's headquarters. But that afternoon it reached Kutuzov's headquarters and the staffs of the column commanders. By evening the adjutants had carried it to every corner of the army, and during the night of the 19th-20th, the entire force of eighty thousand allied troops rose from their bivouacs to a hum of voices, and the army surged and set off in one enormous mass six miles long.

The concentrated activity that had begun at the Emperor's headquarters that morning and set the whole movement in motion was like the first turn of the main wheel in a great tower clock. One wheel slowly began to move, then another, then a third, and soon wheels were spinning faster and faster, levers and gears engaged, chimes began to play, figures popped out, and the hands advanced with steady regularity — all as a result of that initial motion.

Just as in a clock's mechanism, so in the mechanism of the military machine: once an impulse is given, it leads inevitably to the final result. And just as the untouched parts of a clock sit completely still until the motion reaches them — wheels that could remain idle for a hundred years — so it is in an army. But the moment comes when the lever catches, and that dormant wheel begins to creak and joins the common motion, the ultimate result and purpose of which are beyond its comprehension.

Just as in a clock the result of the complicated motion of countless wheels and pulleys is simply the slow, steady movement of the hands showing the time, so the result of all the complicated human activities of 160,000 Russians and French — all their passions, desires, remorse, humiliation, suffering, bursts of pride, fear, and enthusiasm — was nothing more than the loss of the battle of Austerlitz, the so-called Battle of the Three Emperors — that is, a slow movement of the hand on the dial of human history.
Prince Andrew was on duty that day and in constant attendance on the commander in chief.
At six in the evening, Kutuzov went to the Emperor's headquarters, and after spending only a short time with the Tsar, went to see the grand marshal of the court, Count Tolstoy.

Bolkonsky seized the opportunity to visit Dolgorukov and get some details about the coming battle. He sensed that Kutuzov was upset and dissatisfied about something, and also that the people at the Emperor's headquarters were dissatisfied with Kutuzov — and that everyone there spoke with the air of people who know something others don't. So he wanted to talk to Dolgorukov.
"Well, how are you, my dear fellow?" said Dolgorukov, who was sitting having tea with Bilibin. "The celebration is tomorrow. How's your old man? Out of sorts?"
"I wouldn't say out of sorts, but I get the feeling he'd like to be heard."
"But they did hear him at the council of war, and they'll hear him again when he talks sense. But to hesitate and wait when Bonaparte fears nothing more than a full-scale battle — that's impossible."
"Yes, you've seen him?" said Prince Andrew. "So what is Bonaparte like? What impression did he make on you?"

"Yes, I saw him, and I'm convinced he fears nothing more than a general engagement," Dolgorukov repeated, clearly prizing this conclusion he'd drawn from his meeting with Napoleon. "If he weren't afraid of battle, why would he have requested that meeting? Why negotiate? And above all, why retreat — when retreating goes completely against his usual way of making war? Believe me, he's afraid. Afraid of a full battle. His time has come! Mark my words!"
"But tell me, what is he actually like?" Prince Andrew asked again.

"He's a man in a gray overcoat who very much wanted me to call him 'Your Majesty' but was annoyed to get no such title from me. That's what he is, nothing more," replied Dolgorukov, glancing at Bilibin with a smile.

"Despite my great respect for old Kutuzov," he went on, "we'd be fools to sit around waiting and give Napoleon a chance to escape or trick us, now that we clearly have him in our grasp! No, we must remember Suvorov's rule: don't put yourself in a position to be attacked — attack first. Believe me, in war the energy of young men often shows the way better than all the experience of old procrastinators."
"But in what position are we going to attack him? I was at the outposts today and it's impossible to determine where his main forces are," said Prince Andrew.
He wanted to explain to Dolgorukov a plan of attack he had worked out himself.
"Oh, that doesn't matter at all," Dolgorukov said quickly, and standing up he spread a map on the table. "Every possibility has been anticipated. If he's positioned in front of Brunn..."
And Prince Dolgorukov rapidly but unclearly explained Weyrother's plan for a flanking maneuver.

Prince Andrew began to respond and present his own plan, which might have been just as good as Weyrother's, except that Weyrother's had the disadvantage of already being approved. As soon as Prince Andrew started pointing out the flaws in Weyrother's plan and the strengths of his own, Dolgorukov stopped listening and stared absently — not at the map, but at Prince Andrew's face.
"There'll be a council of war at Kutuzov's tonight — you can present all this there," Dolgorukov remarked.
"I will," said Prince Andrew, stepping back from the map.

"Whatever are you two getting worked up about, gentlemen?" said Bilibin, who had been listening to their conversation with an amused smile and was now clearly ready with a witticism. "Whether tomorrow brings victory or defeat, the glory of Russian arms is assured. Aside from your Kutuzov, there isn't a single Russian commanding a column! The commanders are: Herr General Wimpfen, Count Langeron, Prince Lichtenstein, Prince Hohenlohe, and finally Prshprsh — and so on, all those Polish names."
"Quiet, you troublemaker!" said Dolgorukov. "That's not true. There are now two Russians: Miloradovich and Dokhturov. And there'd be a third — Count Arakcheev — if his nerves weren't too fragile."
"Anyway, I think General Kutuzov has come out," said Prince Andrew. "I wish you good luck and success, gentlemen!" he added, and left after shaking hands with Dolgorukov and Bilibin.
On the way back, Prince Andrew couldn't stop himself from asking Kutuzov, who was sitting silently beside him, what he thought about tomorrow's battle.

Kutuzov looked sternly at his adjutant and, after a pause, replied: "I think the battle will be lost, and I said as much to Count Tolstoy. I asked him to tell the Emperor. And do you know what he answered? 'My dear general, I'm busy with rice and cutlets — you look after military matters yourself!' Yes... That was the answer I got!"

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Shortly after nine that evening, Weyrother arrived at Kutuzov's quarters with his plans for the council of war. All the column commanders had been summoned, and all except Prince Bagration, who declined to attend, were there at the appointed time.

Weyrother, who was fully in charge of the planned battle, presented a sharp contrast in his eagerness and energy to the dissatisfied and drowsy Kutuzov, who reluctantly played the role of chairman. Weyrother was clearly aware he was driving a movement that had already become unstoppable. He was like a horse harnessed to a heavy cart running downhill — whether he was pulling it or being pushed by it, he couldn't tell, but he rushed forward at breakneck speed with no time to think about where this was all heading. He had been to the enemy's picket line twice that evening to scout in person, twice to the Russian and Austrian Emperors to report and explain, and to his own headquarters where he had dictated the battle plan in German. Now, thoroughly exhausted, he arrived at Kutuzov's.

He was so preoccupied that he forgot even basic courtesy toward the commander in chief. He interrupted him, spoke rapidly and indistinctly without looking at the person he was addressing, and ignored questions put to him. He was spattered with mud and had a harried, exhausted, distracted look about him, though at the same time he was arrogant and self-assured.

Kutuzov was occupying a modest nobleman's manor near Ostralitz. In the large drawing room that had become the commander in chief's office, Kutuzov himself, Weyrother, and the other council members had gathered. They were drinking tea and waiting only for Prince Bagration to begin. Finally Bagration's orderly arrived with the news that the prince could not attend. Prince Andrew came in to report this to the commander in chief and, having previously received Kutuzov's permission to attend the council, remained in the room.
"Since Prince Bagration isn't coming, we may as well begin," said Weyrother, hurriedly rising and going to the table where an enormous map of the area around Brunn was spread out.

Kutuzov, his uniform unbuttoned so that his thick neck bulged over his collar as though trying to escape, sat almost asleep in a low chair, his pudgy old hands resting symmetrically on the armrests. At the sound of Weyrother's voice, he opened one eye with effort.
"Yes, yes, go ahead. It's already late," he said, and nodding his head he let it droop and closed his eye again.

If at first the council members thought Kutuzov was only pretending to sleep, the sounds that soon came from his nose proved that the commander in chief was absorbed by something far more pressing than any desire to show his contempt for the battle plan or anything else — he was satisfying the irresistible human need for sleep. He was genuinely asleep. Weyrother, with the manner of a man too busy to waste a single moment, glanced at Kutuzov, confirmed he was asleep, picked up a paper, and in a loud, monotonous voice began reading out the battle plan, starting with its title:
"Dispositions for an attack on the enemy position behind Kobelnitz and Sokolnitz, November 30, 1805."
The dispositions were extremely complicated and difficult to follow. They began:

"Since the enemy's left wing rests on wooded hills and his right extends along Kobelnitz and Sokolnitz behind the ponds there, while we on the other hand far outflank his right with our left wing, it is advantageous to attack the enemy's right wing, especially if we occupy the villages of Sokolnitz and Kobelnitz, whereby we can both strike his flank and pursue him across the plain between Schlappanitz and the Thuerassa forest, avoiding the defiles of Schlappanitz and Bellowitz that cover the enemy's front. To this end it is necessary that... The first column marches... The second column marches... The third column marches..." and so on, Weyrother read.

The generals appeared to listen reluctantly to the complicated orders. The tall, fair-haired General Buxhowden stood leaning against the wall, his eyes fixed on a burning candle, seeming not to listen — or even wanting to be thought to listen. Directly opposite Weyrother sat the ruddy-faced Miloradovich, holding a military pose with his elbows out, hands on his knees, and shoulders raised, his glistening wide eyes fixed on Weyrother and his mustache twisted upward. He remained stubbornly silent, staring at Weyrother's face, and only looked away when the Austrian chief of staff finished reading. Then Miloradovich glanced around meaningfully at the other generals, though it was impossible to tell from that look whether he agreed or disagreed, was satisfied or not. Beside Weyrother sat Count Langeron, who wore the subtle smile that never left his typically southern French face throughout the entire reading, as he gazed at his slender fingers rapidly spinning a gold snuffbox adorned with a portrait. Midway through one of the longest sentences, he stopped spinning the snuffbox, raised his head, and with a thin-lipped smile of hostile politeness tried to interrupt Weyrother to make a point. But the Austrian general, still reading, frowned angrily and jerked his elbows, as if to say: "You can share your views later — for now, kindly look at the map and listen." Langeron raised his eyebrows in confusion, glanced at Miloradovich as if seeking support, but meeting the latter's impressive yet meaningless gaze, he dropped his eyes sadly and went back to spinning his snuffbox.
"A geography lesson!" he muttered, seemingly to himself but loud enough for everyone to hear.

Przhebyshevsky, with respectful but dignified politeness, cupped his hand to his ear toward Weyrother, with the air of a man deeply absorbed in concentration. Dokhturov, a small man sitting opposite Weyrother, leaned over the spread-out map with a conscientious and modest expression, earnestly studying the battle plan and the unfamiliar terrain. He asked Weyrother several times to repeat words he hadn't caught clearly and the difficult names of villages. Weyrother obliged, and Dokhturov noted them down.

When the reading — which lasted more than an hour — was over, Langeron set down his snuffbox again and, without looking at Weyrother or anyone in particular, began explaining how difficult it would be to carry out such a plan when the enemy's position was only assumed and not actually known, since the enemy might well be on the move. Langeron's objections were valid, but it was clear that his main purpose was to show General Weyrother — who had read his plan with the self-assurance of a teacher lecturing schoolchildren — that he was not dealing with fools, but with men who could teach him a thing or two about military affairs.

When the monotonous drone of Weyrother's voice stopped, Kutuzov opened his eye the way a miller wakes up when the soothing hum of the mill wheel suddenly stops. He listened to Langeron's remarks as if to say, "So you're still going on with this nonsense!" then quickly closed his eye again and let his head sink even lower.

Langeron, trying as sharply as possible to wound Weyrother's pride as the plan's author, argued that Bonaparte might easily attack rather than be attacked, which would make the entire plan worthless. Weyrother met every objection with a firm, contemptuous smile, clearly having prepared responses to any possible criticism.
"If he could have attacked us, he would have done so today," he said.
"So you think he's powerless?" said Langeron.
"He has forty thousand men at most," Weyrother replied, with the smile of a doctor whose elderly patient is trying to tell him how to treat the case.
"In that case he's practically inviting his own destruction by waiting for our attack," said Langeron with a subtly mocking smile, again glancing around at Miloradovich for support.
But Miloradovich was obviously thinking about anything other than what the generals were arguing about.
"Well!" he said. "Tomorrow we'll see it all on the battlefield."

Weyrother again gave that smile that seemed to say he found it both strange and absurd to face objections from Russian generals and to have to prove things he had already convinced not just himself of, but the Emperors as well.

"The enemy has put out his fires and there's a constant noise coming from his camp," he said. "What does that mean? Either he's retreating — which is the only thing we need to worry about — or he's changing position." He smiled knowingly. "But even if he also takes up a position in the Thuerassa, he merely saves us a great deal of trouble, and all our plans down to the smallest detail remain the same."
"How is that..." Prince Andrew began. He had been waiting a long time for a chance to voice his doubts.
But at that moment Kutuzov woke up, coughed heavily, and looked around at the generals.

"Gentlemen, the plans for tomorrow — or rather for today, since it is past midnight — can no longer be changed," he said. "You have heard them, and we shall all do our duty. But before a battle, there is nothing more important..." He paused. "...than a good night's sleep."
He moved as if to stand. The generals bowed and withdrew. It was past midnight. Prince Andrew went out.

The council of war, at which Prince Andrew had not managed to express the opinion he'd hoped to share, left him with a vague, uneasy feeling. Whether Dolgorukov and Weyrother were right, or Kutuzov, Langeron, and the others who opposed the plan of attack — he couldn't tell. "But was it really impossible for Kutuzov to speak plainly to the Emperor? Is it possible that because of court politics and personal considerations, tens of thousands of lives — and my life, my life," he thought, "must be put at risk?"

"Yes, it's very likely that I'll be killed tomorrow," he thought. And suddenly, at this thought of death, a whole series of distant, deeply personal memories rose in his mind: he remembered his last farewell to his father and his wife; he remembered the early days when he first loved her. He thought about her pregnancy and felt sorry for her, and for himself, and in this nervously emotional, tender mood he walked out of the cabin where he was quartered with Nesvitsky and began pacing back and forth outside it.

The night was foggy, and through the mist the moonlight shimmered eerily. "Yes, tomorrow, tomorrow!" he thought. "Tomorrow everything may be over for me! All these memories will mean nothing — none of them will matter anymore. Tomorrow perhaps — almost certainly — I have a feeling that for the first time I'll have a chance to show everything I'm capable of." And in his imagination the battle unfolded: the defeat, the fighting concentrated at one crucial point, the hesitation of all the commanders. And then that glorious moment — that Toulon he had waited for so long — finally arrives. He states his views firmly and clearly to Kutuzov, to Weyrother, and to the Emperors. Everyone is struck by the brilliance of his analysis, but no one dares to carry it out, so he takes a regiment, a division — on the condition that no one interferes with his command — leads his division to the decisive point, and wins the victory single-handedly. "But death and suffering?" suggested another voice. Prince Andrew, however, did not answer that voice and continued dreaming of his triumphs. The plans for the next battle are drawn up by him alone. Officially he is still just an adjutant on Kutuzov's staff, but he does everything himself. The next battle is won by him alone. Kutuzov is removed, and he is appointed... "And then what?" asked the other voice. "If before that you're not wounded ten times over, or killed, or betrayed — then what?" "Well then," Prince Andrew answered himself, "I don't know what will happen and don't want to know, and can't know. But if I want this — want glory, want to be known, want to be loved — it's not my fault that I want it and want nothing else and live for nothing else. Yes, for that alone! I will never tell anyone this, but oh God! What am I supposed to do if I love nothing but glory and the esteem of others? Death, wounds, the loss of family — none of it frightens me. And dear as so many people are to me — my father, my sister, my wife — the people closest to me — yet terrible and unnatural as it seems, I would give them all up in an instant for one moment of glory, of triumph, of love from people I don't know and never will know — for the love of these men here," he thought, listening to voices in Kutuzov's courtyard. It was the orderlies packing up; one voice, probably a coachman's, was teasing Kutuzov's old cook, whom Prince Andrew knew — a man called Tit. "Tit, hey, Tit!" he was saying.
"What?" the old man replied.
"Go on, Tit, go thresh a bit!" said the joker.
"Oh, go to hell!" called out a voice, drowned by the laughter of the orderlies and servants.
"All the same, I love and value nothing but victory over them all — this mysterious power and glory that hovers here above me in the mist!"

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: That same night, Rostov was on skirmish duty with a platoon, positioned ahead of Bagration's detachment. His hussars were stationed along the line in pairs, and he rode back and forth trying to fight off the drowsiness that kept overcoming him. Behind him stretched an enormous space where the army's campfires glowed dimly through the fog; ahead was nothing but misty darkness. Rostov strained to see into that foggy distance but could make out nothing: now something seemed to gleam gray, now something looked black, now tiny lights appeared to flicker where the enemy should be, then he thought it might just be his own eyes playing tricks. His eyelids kept drooping, and in his half-dreams he saw the Emperor, then Denisov, then memories of Moscow — and then he'd jerk his eyes open again to see the head and ears of his horse right in front of him, and sometimes, when he rode within six paces, the dark shapes of hussars nearby. But in the distance, the same misty darkness remained. "Why not?" thought Rostov. "It could easily happen. The Emperor might come across me and give me an order, just like he would any other officer. He'd say: 'Go find out what's out there.' There are plenty of stories about him noticing an officer by chance and taking him onto his personal staff. What if he gave me a place at his side? Oh, how I would protect him, how I would tell him the truth, how I would expose the people deceiving him!" And to make his devoted love for the sovereign feel more vivid, Rostov imagined an enemy or a treacherous German whom he would not only kill with pleasure but slap across the face right in front of the Emperor. Suddenly a distant shout jerked him awake. He started and opened his eyes.

"Where am I? Oh, right — the skirmish line. Password and countersign: shaft, Olmutz. What a shame our squadron's in reserve tomorrow," he thought. "I'll ask for leave to go to the front. This might be my only chance to see the Emperor. It won't be long until my duty's over. I'll make one more round, and when I get back I'll go to the general and ask." He adjusted himself in the saddle and urged his horse forward to ride another circuit past his hussars. It seemed to him that the sky was growing lighter. To the left he could see an illuminated slope, and facing it a dark hill that looked steep as a wall. On this hill there was a white patch that Rostov couldn't identify — was it a moonlit clearing in the woods, unmelted snow, or some white buildings? He even thought he saw something move on that white spot. "Probably snow... a spot... a patch — une tache," he thought. "Wait... it's not a patch... Natasha... my sister, those dark eyes... Na-tasha... (Won't she be amazed when I tell her I saw the Emperor?) Natasha... take my sabretache..." — "Keep to the right, your honor, there are bushes here," came the voice of a hussar he was riding past, already half asleep. Rostov lifted his head, which had drooped almost to his horse's mane, and pulled up beside the hussar. He was surrendering to an irresistible, youthful, childlike drowsiness. "But what was I thinking about? I mustn't forget. How am I going to speak to the Emperor? No, that's not it — that's tomorrow. Oh yes! Natasha... sabretache... saber them... Whom? The hussars... Ah, the hussars with their mustaches. Down Tverskaya Street rode the hussar with the mustache... I was thinking about him too, right across from Guryev's house... Old Guryev... Oh, but Denisov's a wonderful fellow. But that's all nonsense. The main thing is that the Emperor is here. The way he looked at me and wanted to say something but didn't dare... No, it was I who didn't dare. But that's all nonsense — the main thing is not to forget the important thought I was having. Yes, Na-tasha, sabretache, oh yes, yes! That's right!" And his head sank to his horse's neck once more. Suddenly he thought he was being shot at. "What? What? What?... Cut them down! What?" said Rostov, jolting awake. The moment he opened his eyes, he heard from ahead — from the enemy's direction — the long, drawn-out shouts of thousands of voices. His horse and the hussar's horse beside him pricked up their ears at the sound. Over where the shouting came from, a fire flared up and then went out, then another, and then all along the French line on the hill, fires blazed up one after another and the shouting grew louder and louder. Rostov could hear French words but couldn't make them out. The roar of so many voices was too great; all he could distinguish was "ahahah!" and "rrrr!"
"What's going on? What do you think that is?" said Rostov to the hussar beside him. "That must be the enemy's camp!"
The hussar didn't reply.
"Well? Don't you hear it?" Rostov asked again, after waiting for an answer.
"Who can say, your honor?" the hussar replied reluctantly.
"From the direction, it has to be the enemy," Rostov repeated.
"Maybe it is, maybe it's nothing," the hussar muttered. "It's dark... Steady!" he called to his restless horse.

Rostov's horse was getting agitated too, pawing at the frozen ground, pricking its ears at the noise, and staring toward the lights. The shouting grew even louder, merging into a roar that only an army of several thousand men could produce. The lights spread farther along what was probably the French camp's line. Rostov no longer felt sleepy. The jubilant, triumphant shouting from the enemy camp had an electrifying effect on him. "Long live the Emperor! The Emperor!" — he could now hear the words distinctly.
"They can't be far away — probably just beyond the stream," he said to the hussar beside him.

The hussar only sighed, said nothing, and coughed irritably. The sound of hooves approaching at a trot along the line of hussars reached them, and out of the foggy darkness the figure of a hussar sergeant appeared, looming as large as an elephant.
"Your honor, the generals!" said the sergeant, riding up to Rostov.

Rostov, still glancing back toward the fires and the shouting, rode with the sergeant to meet some mounted men coming along the line. One of them was on a white horse. It was Prince Bagration and Prince Dolgorukov, with their adjutants, who had come to see the strange spectacle of lights and shouts from the enemy camp for themselves. Rostov rode up to Bagration, made his report, and then joined the adjutants listening to the generals' conversation.
"Believe me," said Prince Dolgorukov, turning to Bagration, "it's nothing but a ruse. He's retreated and left fires and noise behind to fool us."

"I doubt it," said Bagration. "I saw them on that hill this evening. If they'd retreated, they would have pulled out from there too... Officer!" he said to Rostov. "Are the enemy's skirmishers still in position?"
"They were there this evening, but I can't say for certain now, your excellency. Shall I ride out with some of my hussars to check?" Rostov replied.
Bagration stopped and tried to make out Rostov's face through the mist before answering.
"Well, go and see," he said after a pause.
"Yes, sir."

Rostov spurred his horse, called Sergeant Fedchenko and two other hussars, told them to follow, and trotted downhill toward the source of the shouting. He felt both scared and excited to be riding alone with three hussars into that mysterious, dangerous, misty unknown where no one had gone before him. Bagration called after him from the hilltop not to cross the stream, but Rostov pretended not to hear and kept riding on, continually mistaking bushes for trees and ditches for men, and continually realizing his mistakes. After descending the hill at a trot, he could no longer see either the Russian or the French campfires, but he heard the French shouting more loudly and clearly. In the valley ahead he saw what looked like a river, but when he reached it, he found it was a road. Coming out onto the road, he reined in his horse, hesitating whether to follow it or cross it and ride up the black hillside. Staying on the road, which gleamed white through the mist, would have been safer — easier to spot people coming. "Follow me!" he said. He crossed the road and began galloping uphill toward where the French pickets had been posted that evening.

"Your honor, there he is!" cried one of the hussars behind him. And before Rostov could make out what the dark shape in the fog was, there was a flash, a report, and a bullet whizzed high overhead through the mist with a mournful whine and passed out of hearing. Another musket misfired but flashed in the pan. Rostov wheeled his horse around and galloped back. Four more shots rang out at intervals, the bullets whistling past somewhere in the fog, each with a different pitch. Rostov eased his horse to a walk — the animal's spirits had risen with the firing, just like his own — and headed back at a leisurely pace. "More! Come on, more!" a happy voice said inside him. But no more shots came.
Only when he was close to Bagration did Rostov let his horse gallop again, and he rode up to the general with his hand at the salute.
Dolgorukov was still insisting that the French had retreated and had only left fires behind to trick them.
"What does that prove?" he was saying as Rostov rode up. "They could retreat and leave the pickets."
"It's clear they haven't all gone, Prince," said Bagration. "Let's wait until tomorrow morning — we'll find out everything then."

"The picket is still on the hill, your excellency — right where it was this evening," Rostov reported, leaning forward with his hand at the salute, unable to suppress the smile of exhilaration that his ride and especially the sound of the bullets had produced.
"Very good, very good," said Bagration. "Thank you, officer."
"Your excellency," said Rostov, "may I ask a favor?"
"What is it?"
"Our squadron is supposed to be in reserve tomorrow. May I request to be attached to the first squadron?"
"What's your name?"
"Count Rostov."
"Oh, very well — you may remain in my personal retinue."
"Count Ilya Rostov's son?" asked Dolgorukov.
But Rostov didn't reply.
"Then I can count on it, your excellency?"
"I'll give the order."
"Tomorrow I might even be sent with a message to the Emperor," Rostov thought.
"Thank God!"

The fires and shouting in the enemy camp were caused by the fact that Napoleon's proclamation was being read to the troops, and the Emperor himself was riding through his bivouacs. The soldiers, catching sight of him, lit bundles of straw and ran after him shouting, "Long live the Emperor!" Napoleon's proclamation read as follows:

Soldiers! The Russian army is advancing against you to avenge the Austrian army of Ulm. These are the same battalions you crushed at Hollabrunn and have been chasing ever since. The position we hold is a strong one, and while they march to outflank me on the right, they will expose their flank. Soldiers! I will personally direct your battalions. I will stay out of the firing line if, with your customary bravery, you carry chaos and confusion into the enemy's ranks. But should victory be in doubt even for a moment, you will see your Emperor expose himself to the enemy's first blows, for there must be no uncertainty about victory — especially on this day, when the honor of the French infantry is at stake, so vital to the honor of our nation.

Do not break ranks on the excuse of helping the wounded! Let every man be filled with the conviction that we must defeat these mercenaries of England, who harbor such hatred for our nation! This victory will end our campaign, and we can return to winter quarters where fresh French troops being raised in France will join us. The peace I will then make will be worthy of my people, of you, and of myself.
NAPOLEON

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: At five in the morning it was still completely dark. The troops at the center, the reserves, and Bagration's right flank had not yet moved, but on the left flank the columns of infantry, cavalry, and artillery — the ones designated to descend the heights first, attack the French right flank, and drive it into the Bohemian mountains according to plan — were already up and stirring. The smoke from campfires, into which the soldiers were tossing everything they couldn't carry, stung their eyes. It was cold and dark. Officers were hurriedly drinking tea and eating breakfast; soldiers were munching on biscuits and stamping their feet to keep warm, gathered around the fires and feeding the flames with the remains of sheds, chairs, tables, wheels, barrels, and anything else they didn't need or couldn't take. Austrian column guides moved back and forth among the Russian troops, serving as harbingers of the advance. As soon as an Austrian officer appeared near a commanding officer's quarters, the regiment began to move: soldiers ran from the fires, shoved their pipes into their boots, stuffed their bags into carts, grabbed their muskets, and fell into rank. Officers buttoned their coats, buckled on their swords and pouches, and walked along the ranks shouting orders. The wagon drivers and orderlies harnessed the horses and loaded the carts. The adjutants, battalion commanders, and regimental commanders mounted up, crossed themselves, gave last instructions to the baggage handlers staying behind, and the monotonous thud of thousands of marching feet echoed into the darkness. The column moved forward without knowing where it was headed, unable — because of the dense crowds around them, the smoke, and the thickening fog — to see either the place they were leaving or the place they were going.

A soldier on the march is hemmed in and carried along by his regiment just as a sailor is by his ship. No matter how far he walks, no matter what strange, unknown, or dangerous places he reaches, the soldier is always surrounded by the same familiar things — the same comrades, the same formation, the same Sergeant Major Ivan Mitrich, the same company dog Jack, the same commanding officers — just as a sailor always sees the same decks, masts, and rigging. A sailor rarely cares about the latitude his ship is crossing, but on the day of battle — who knows how or from where — a solemn, grave note sounds through the moral atmosphere of an army, one that everyone can feel. It awakens an unusual curiosity in the men. On battle day, soldiers strain to look beyond the concerns of their own regiment; they listen hard, look around eagerly, and press each other for news of what's happening.

The fog had grown so thick that even as dawn approached, they couldn't see ten paces ahead. Bushes looked like enormous trees, and flat ground appeared to be cliffs and slopes. Anywhere, on any side, an enemy invisible at ten paces might appear. But the columns marched on and on through the same fog, going downhill and uphill, past gardens and fences, across unfamiliar terrain, and nowhere did they encounter the enemy. On the contrary, the soldiers gradually became aware that in front, behind, and on every side, other Russian columns were moving in the same direction. Every soldier felt reassured to know that wherever he was headed, many more of his own were going there too.
"Look — the Kursk regiment's gone past too," voices said in the ranks.
"It's amazing how many of our troops are here, lads! Last night I looked at the campfires — there was no end to them. Like Moscow!"

Although none of the column commanders rode along the ranks or spoke to the men (the commanders, as we saw at the council of war, were in a bad mood and unhappy with the whole affair, so they simply followed orders without trying to boost morale), the troops marched cheerfully, as they always do when heading into action, especially an attack. But after about an hour of marching through the dense fog, most of the men had to stop, and an uncomfortable sense that something had gone wrong began spreading through the ranks. It's very hard to explain how such an awareness spreads, but it does — surely, imperceptibly, and unstoppably, the way water seeps into a creek bed. If the Russian army had been fighting alone without allies, it might have taken much longer for this sense of mismanagement to become a general conviction. But since there were allies, the disorder was naturally blamed on the stupid Germans, and everyone became convinced that a dangerous mix-up had been caused by the sausage-eaters.
"Why have we stopped? Is the way blocked? Or have we already run into the French?"
"No, you can't hear them. They'd be shooting if we had."
"They were in such a rush to get us started, and now here we stand in the middle of a field for no reason. It's all those damned Germans and their bungling! Stupid idiots!"
"I'd have sent them out in front, but no — they're all crowded up behind us. And now we're standing here hungry."
"Any idea when we'll get clear? They say the cavalry is blocking the way," said an officer.
"Ah, those damned Germans! Don't even know their own country!" said another.
"What division are you?" shouted an adjutant, riding up.
"The Eighteenth."
"Then what are you doing here? You should have moved on long ago — now you won't get there before evening."
"What idiotic orders! They don't even know what they're doing themselves!" said the officer, and rode off.
Then a general rode past, shouting something angrily in a language that wasn't Russian.
"Tafa-lafa! No one can understand a word he's saying," said a soldier, imitating the general who had ridden away. "I'd shoot every one of them, the bastards!"
"We were ordered to be in position by nine, and we haven't even gotten halfway. Fine orders!" This complaint was being repeated all around.
And the energy with which the troops had set out began turning to frustration and anger at the stupid arrangements and at the Germans.

The cause of the confusion was this: while the Austrian cavalry was moving toward the left flank, the high command realized the center was too far separated from the right flank, and all the cavalry was ordered to turn back to the right. Several thousand horsemen had to cross in front of the infantry, which had no choice but to wait.

At the head of the column, an argument broke out between an Austrian guide and a Russian general. The general shouted that the cavalry must be halted; the Austrian protested that it wasn't his fault — the blame lay with the higher command. Meanwhile the troops stood around, growing listless and disheartened. After an hour's delay they finally moved forward again, descending the hill. The fog that was lifting on the heights was even thicker in the valley below. Up ahead in the fog, a shot rang out, then another — first at irregular intervals, trata... tat — then faster and more steadily, and the fighting at the Goldbach Stream began.

Having stumbled on the enemy unexpectedly down by the stream in the fog, hearing no words of encouragement from their commanders, with the sense of being late spreading through the ranks, and above all unable to see anything in front or around them in the dense mist, the Russians exchanged shots with the enemy halfheartedly, advancing and then halting, receiving no clear orders from officers or adjutants who were wandering around the fog in unfamiliar terrain, unable to find their own units. This was how the fighting began for the first, second, and third columns, which had descended into the valley. The fourth column, with Kutuzov, remained on the Pratzen Heights.

Below, where the battle was unfolding, the fog was still thick; on the higher ground it was clearing, but nothing could be seen of what was happening in front. Whether the entire enemy force was six miles away as assumed, or right there in that sea of mist, no one knew until after eight o'clock.

It was nine in the morning. The fog lay unbroken like an ocean below, but higher up at the village of Schlappanitz, where Napoleon stood surrounded by his marshals, it was completely clear. Above them stretched a pure blue sky, and the sun's enormous disk trembled like a vast, hollow, crimson buoy floating on the surface of that milky sea of mist. The whole French army — and Napoleon himself with his staff — was not on the far side of the streams and ravines of Sokolnitz and Schlappanitz, beyond which the allies had planned to take up position and begin the battle. They were on the near side, so close to the Russian forces that Napoleon could distinguish mounted men from those on foot with the naked eye. Napoleon, wearing the blue cloak from his Italian campaign, sat on his small gray Arab horse slightly ahead of his marshals. He gazed in silence at the hills that seemed to rise from the sea of mist, on which the Russian troops were moving in the distance, and he listened to the sounds of gunfire from the valley. Not a single muscle moved in his face — which in those days was still thin. His gleaming eyes were fixed intently on one point. His predictions were being confirmed. Part of the Russian force had already descended into the valley toward the ponds and lakes, and another part was leaving the Pratzen Heights — which he intended to attack and considered the key to the whole position. Through the mist he could see that in a hollow between two hills near the village of Pratzen, the Russian columns, their bayonets glinting, were streaming continuously in one direction toward the valley and disappearing into the fog one after another. From the intelligence he'd received the night before, from the sounds of wheels and footsteps his outposts had heard during the night, from the disorderly movement of the Russian columns, and from every other indication, he could see clearly that the allies believed him to be far off in front of them, that the columns moving near Pratzen were the center of the Russian army, and that this center was already weakened enough to be successfully attacked. But still he did not begin the engagement.

This was a momentous day for him — the anniversary of his coronation. Before dawn he had slept a few hours, and now refreshed, vigorous, and in high spirits, he had mounted and ridden out onto the field in that happy mood where everything seems possible and everything goes right. He sat motionless, looking at the heights visible above the mist, and his cold face wore that particular look of assured, self-satisfied happiness you see on the face of a boy who is deeply and happily in love. His marshals stood behind him, not daring to interrupt his thoughts. He looked from the Pratzen Heights to the sun emerging from the fog.

When the sun had fully risen above the mist and the fields and vapor glowed with dazzling light — as though he had been waiting for exactly this moment to begin — he drew the glove from his elegant white hand, made a signal to the marshals, and gave the order to attack. The marshals, accompanied by adjutants, galloped off in every direction, and within minutes the main body of the French army was surging rapidly toward the Pratzen Heights, which were being steadily emptied as Russian troops marched down into the valley on their left.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: At eight o'clock, Kutuzov rode toward Pratzen at the head of the fourth column — Miloradovich's — which was supposed to replace the columns of Przhebyshevsky and Langeron, both of which had already descended into the valley. He greeted the soldiers of the lead regiment and gave the order to march, signaling that he intended to lead this column himself. When they reached the village of Pratzen, he halted. Prince Andrei rode behind, lost among the enormous crowd that made up the commander in chief's retinue. He was in a state of suppressed excitement and agitation, though outwardly calm — the way a person gets when a long-anticipated moment is finally at hand. He was firmly convinced that this would be his Toulon, his bridge of Arcole. He didn't know exactly how it would happen, but he was certain it would. He knew the terrain and the positions of the troops as well as anyone in the army could. His own strategic plan, now clearly impossible to carry out, had been set aside. Instead, working within Weyrother's plan, Prince Andrei considered possible developments and formed new projects that might call for his quick thinking and decisive action.

Down to the left, through the mist, the crackle of musket fire from unseen forces could be heard. That was where Prince Andrei expected the fighting to intensify. "That's where the difficulties will come," he thought, "and that's where I'll be sent with a brigade or a division. There, with the standard in my hand, I'll charge forward and break through whatever stands in my way."
He couldn't look calmly at the regimental standards as the battalions passed by. Each time he saw one, he kept thinking: "That might be the very standard I'll carry when I lead the army."

By morning, all that remained of the night's fog on the heights was a thin frost turning to dew, but down in the valleys it still lay like a sea of white milk. Nothing was visible in the valley to the left, where the troops had descended and where the gunfire was coming from. Above the heights stretched a dark, clear sky, and to the right hung the vast disk of the sun. In the distance, on the far shore of that misty sea, some wooded hills were just barely visible — the enemy was probably there, since something could be made out moving. To the right, the Guards were entering the mist with the sound of hooves and wheels, and now and then a glint of bayonets; to the left, beyond the village, similar masses of cavalry appeared and vanished into the white sea. In front and behind, infantry moved forward. The commander in chief stood at the edge of the village, watching the troops pass. That morning, Kutuzov seemed worn out and irritable. The infantry marching past him suddenly came to a halt without any order being given, apparently blocked by something ahead.

"Order them to form battalion columns and go around the village!" he said angrily to a general who had ridden up. "Don't you understand, your excellency, my dear sir, that you can't march through narrow village streets when we're advancing against the enemy?"
"I was planning to re-form them on the other side of the village, your excellency," the general replied.
Kutuzov gave a bitter laugh.
"That'll work out wonderfully — deploying in full view of the enemy! Just wonderful!"
"The enemy is still far away, your excellency. According to the battle plan —"
"The battle plan!" Kutuzov snapped bitterly. "Who told you that? Do as you're ordered."
"Yes, sir."
"My dear fellow," Nesvitsky whispered to Prince Andrei, "the old man is in a foul mood."
An Austrian officer in a white uniform with green plumes on his hat galloped up to Kutuzov and asked, on behalf of the Emperor, whether the fourth column had advanced into action.

Kutuzov turned away without answering, and his gaze happened to fall on Prince Andrei standing beside him. When he saw him, Kutuzov's bitter, caustic expression softened, as if acknowledging that none of this was his adjutant's fault. Still ignoring the Austrian, he addressed Bolkonsky.
"Go, my dear fellow, and see whether the third division has passed the village. Tell them to stop and wait for my orders."
Prince Andrei had barely started when Kutuzov stopped him.
"And find out if they've posted sharpshooters," he added. "What are they doing? What are they doing?" he muttered to himself, still not answering the Austrian.
Prince Andrei galloped off to carry out the order.

Riding past the advancing battalions, he stopped the third division and confirmed that there were indeed no sharpshooters deployed ahead of the columns. The colonel leading the regiment was shocked by the commander in chief's order to send out skirmishers. He had been certain there were other troops in front of him and that the enemy must be at least six miles away. In truth, nothing was visible ahead except a barren slope hidden by thick mist. After issuing orders in the commander in chief's name to correct this oversight, Prince Andrei galloped back. Kutuzov was still in the same place, his heavy body sagging wearily in the saddle, yawning with closed eyes. The troops had stopped and now stood with the butts of their muskets resting on the ground.
"All right, all right!" he said to Prince Andrei, then turned to a general who, watch in hand, was insisting it was time to move since all the left-flank columns had already gone down.
"Plenty of time, your excellency," Kutuzov muttered through a yawn. "Plenty of time," he repeated.

Just then, from somewhere behind Kutuzov, came the sound of regiments cheering, and the wave of salutes rolled rapidly closer along the whole extended line of advancing Russian columns. Clearly, whoever they were greeting was riding quickly. When the soldiers in the regiment nearest Kutuzov began to shout, he moved off to the side a little and looked back with a frown. A squadron-like group of horsemen in various uniforms came galloping along the road from Pratzen. Two of them rode ahead, side by side, at full gallop. One wore a black uniform with white plumes and rode a short-tailed chestnut horse; the other wore white and rode a black horse. These were the two Emperors, followed by their entourages. Kutuzov, putting on the manner of a grizzled old soldier at the front, called out "Attention!" and rode up to the Emperors with a salute. His entire appearance and demeanor were suddenly transformed. He adopted the air of a subordinate who obeys without question. With a show of deference that clearly struck Alexander as excessive, he rode up and saluted.

This unpleasant impression merely passed across the young and joyful face of the Emperor like a wisp of haze drifting over a clear sky, and was gone. After his illness, he looked somewhat thinner than he had on the field of Olmutz, where Bolkonsky had first seen him abroad. But there was still the same captivating blend of majesty and gentleness in his fine gray eyes, and on his delicate lips the same ability to shift expression, with the same prevailing look of warmhearted, innocent youth.

At the Olmutz review, he had seemed more majestic; here he seemed brighter and more full of energy. He was slightly flushed from galloping two miles, and as he reined in his horse, he sighed with relief and looked around at his companions — all of them as young and animated as himself. Czartoryski, Novosiltsev, Prince Volkonsky, Strogonov, and the rest — all richly dressed, cheerful young men on splendid, well-groomed, barely warm horses — had stopped behind the Emperor, exchanging remarks and smiling. Emperor Francis, a rosy, long-faced young man, sat very straight on his handsome black horse, looking about in a leisurely and preoccupied way. He beckoned to one of his white-uniformed adjutants and asked some question. "He's probably asking what time they set out," thought Prince Andrei, watching this old acquaintance with a smile he couldn't suppress as he recalled his reception at Brunn. Among the two Emperors' retinues were the finest young orderly officers from the Guard and line regiments, both Russian and Austrian. Mixed in among them were grooms leading the Tsar's beautiful reserve horses draped in embroidered cloths.

The way a gust of fresh air from the fields sweeps into a stuffy room when a window is opened — that was how a rush of youthfulness, energy, and confidence reached Kutuzov's gloomy staff as all these brilliant young men came galloping up.
"Why haven't you started, Mikhail Ilarionovich?" Emperor Alexander asked Kutuzov quickly, at the same time casting a courteous glance at Emperor Francis.
"I'm waiting, Your Majesty," Kutuzov answered, bowing forward respectfully.
The Emperor frowned slightly and leaned his ear forward as if he hadn't quite heard.
"Waiting, Your Majesty," Kutuzov repeated. (Prince Andrei noticed that Kutuzov's upper lip twitched unnaturally as he said the word "waiting.") "Not all the columns have formed up yet, Your Majesty."
The Tsar heard but clearly didn't like the reply. He shrugged his somewhat rounded shoulders and glanced at Novosiltsev, who stood nearby, as if to complain about Kutuzov.

"You know, Mikhail Ilarionovich, we're not on the parade ground, where the review doesn't begin until all the troops are assembled," the Tsar said with another glance at Emperor Francis, as if inviting him — if not to join in — at least to listen. But Emperor Francis continued to look around and didn't seem to be listening.

"That is exactly why I have not begun, sire," Kutuzov said in a loud, clear voice, evidently making sure he would not go unheard, and again something in his face twitched. "That is exactly why I have not begun, sire — because we are not on parade and not on the Empress's Field." He spoke clearly and distinctly.
Everyone in the Emperor's retinue exchanged quick glances of displeasure and reproach. "Old as he may be, he shouldn't — he absolutely shouldn't — speak like that," their looks seemed to say.

The Tsar stared intently at Kutuzov's face, waiting for him to say something more. But Kutuzov, with his head respectfully bowed, appeared to be waiting as well. The silence stretched on for about a minute.
"However, if you command it, Your Majesty," Kutuzov said at last, raising his head and resuming his former tone — that of a dull, unquestioning, obedient general.
He nudged his horse forward and, calling over Miloradovich, the column commander, gave him the order to advance.
The troops began moving again, and two battalions of the Novgorod regiment and one of the Apsheron regiment marched past the Emperor.

As the Apsheron battalion went by, the red-faced Miloradovich — without his greatcoat, medals pinned to his chest, and a huge plume in his cocked hat worn sideways with corners pointing front and back — galloped energetically forward and reined in his horse before the Emperor with a dashing salute.
"God be with you, General!" said the Emperor.
[Speaking in French] "Indeed, sire, we shall do everything in our power, sire," he answered cheerfully, though his poor French drew ironic smiles from the gentlemen in the Tsar's entourage.
Footnote: "Indeed, Sire, we shall do everything it is possible to do, Sire."

Miloradovich wheeled his horse sharply and positioned himself just behind the Emperor. The Apsheron soldiers, energized by the Tsar's presence, marched past the Emperors and their suites at a bold, brisk pace, keeping perfect step.

"Lads!" Miloradovich shouted in a loud, confident, and cheerful voice — so carried away by the sound of gunfire, the prospect of battle, and the sight of the gallant Apsherons (his old comrades from Suvorov's campaigns, now marching so splendidly past the Emperors) that he forgot the sovereigns were right there. "Lads, it's not the first village you've had to take!" he cried.
"Glad to do our best!" the soldiers shouted back.

The Emperor's horse startled at the sudden cry. This was the same horse that had carried the sovereign through reviews in Russia, and it carried him here too on the field of Austerlitz, bearing the absent-minded kicks of his left foot and pricking its ears at the sound of gunfire — just as it had done on the Empress's Field — without understanding the meaning of the shots, or the proximity of Emperor Francis's black horse, or anything that was being said, thought, and felt by its rider that day.
The Emperor turned with a smile to one of his attendants and said something, pointing at the brave Apsherons.

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Kutuzov, accompanied by his adjutants, rode at a walk behind the carabiniers.

After less than half a mile, he stopped at an isolated, abandoned building that had probably once been a roadside inn, at a fork where two roads diverged. Both roads led downhill, and troops were marching along each of them.

The fog had started to thin, and enemy forces were dimly visible about a mile and a half away on the opposite heights. Down to the left, the firing grew more distinct. Kutuzov had stopped and was speaking with an Austrian general. Prince Andrei, riding a little behind, turned to an adjutant and asked to borrow a field glass.
"Look, look!" the adjutant said, staring not at the distant troops but down the hill in front of them. "It's the French!"

The two generals and the adjutant all grabbed at the field glass, trying to snatch it from one another. The look on every face suddenly turned to horror. The French were supposed to be a mile and a half away, but had appeared just in front of them — suddenly and without warning.
"Is that the enemy? No! Yes, look — it is! For certain. But how can that be?" different voices said.
With his naked eye, Prince Andrei could see below them, to the right, not more than five hundred paces from where Kutuzov stood, a dense French column advancing toward the Apsheron regiment.
"This is it! The decisive moment has come. My turn has arrived," Prince Andrei thought, and spurring his horse, he rode up to Kutuzov.

"The Apsherons must be stopped, your excellency!" he shouted. But at that very instant a cloud of smoke billowed in every direction, gunfire erupted at close range, and a voice of raw, terrified panic — barely two steps from Prince Andrei — screamed: "Brothers! We're done for!" And at that, as if on command, everyone began to run.

Confused and swelling crowds were streaming back toward the place where, just five minutes earlier, the troops had marched past the Emperors. It would have been impossible to stop that tide — you couldn't even avoid being swept along with it. Bolkonsky could only try not to lose touch with the retreating mass as he looked around in bewilderment, unable to grasp what was happening ahead. Nesvitsky, red-faced and angry, looking nothing like himself, was shouting at Kutuzov that he would certainly be taken prisoner if he didn't ride away immediately. Kutuzov stayed where he was. Without answering, he pulled out a handkerchief. Blood was flowing from his cheek. Prince Andrei forced his way to him.
"You're wounded?" he asked, barely managing to control the trembling of his jaw.

"The wound isn't here — it's there!" Kutuzov said, pressing the handkerchief to his wounded cheek and pointing at the fleeing soldiers. "Stop them!" he shouted, and at almost the same moment — probably realizing that stopping them was impossible — he spurred his horse and rode to the right.
A fresh wave of the fleeing mob caught him and carried him along with it.

The troops were running in such a dense mass that once you were caught among them, it was nearly impossible to get free. One man was shouting, "Move! Why are you blocking us?" Another, in the same spot, spun around and fired into the air. A third was hitting the horse Kutuzov himself was riding. With great difficulty, Kutuzov managed to break away to the left of the stampede. His suite was now reduced by more than half. They rode toward the sound of nearby artillery fire. Having also fought his way out of the flood of fugitives, Prince Andrei tried to keep close to Kutuzov. Through the smoke on the hillside, he could see a Russian battery still firing, with French soldiers running toward it. Higher up stood Russian infantry that was neither advancing to protect the battery nor retreating with the fleeing crowd. A mounted general broke away from the infantry and rode up to Kutuzov. Of his original suite, only four men remained. They were all pale, exchanging silent looks.

"Stop those cowards!" Kutuzov gasped to the regimental commander, pointing at the fleeing soldiers. But at that very instant — as if to punish him for those words — bullets came whistling across the regiment and across Kutuzov's group like a flock of small birds.

The French had attacked the battery and, spotting Kutuzov, were now shooting at him. After this volley, the regimental commander grabbed his leg; several soldiers dropped; and a second lieutenant holding the flag let it slip from his hands. It swayed and fell, but caught on the muskets of the nearest soldiers. The men began firing on their own, without orders.

"Oh! Oh! Oh!" Kutuzov groaned in despair, looking around. "Bolkonsky!" he whispered, his voice trembling with the frailty of age. "Bolkonsky!" he whispered again, pointing at the shattered battalion and at the enemy. "What is that?"
But before he had finished speaking, Prince Andrei — tears of shame and fury choking him — had already leapt from his horse and was running toward the standard.
"Forward, lads!" he shouted in a piercing, almost childlike voice.
"This is it!" he thought, grabbing the staff of the standard, and he heard with pleasure the whistle of bullets that were clearly aimed at him. Several soldiers fell around him.
"Hurrah!" Prince Andrei shouted, and barely able to hold up the heavy standard, he ran forward, fully confident that the entire battalion would follow him.

And indeed, he ran only a few steps alone. First one soldier moved, then another, and soon the whole battalion charged forward with a shout of "Hurrah!" and overtook him. A sergeant ran up and grabbed the flag, which was swaying from its weight in Prince Andrei's hands, but he was killed immediately. Prince Andrei seized the standard again and, dragging it by the staff, ran on with the battalion. Ahead he could see Russian artillerymen — some still fighting, others abandoning their guns and running toward him. He could also see French infantry soldiers seizing the artillery horses and turning the cannons around. Prince Andrei and the battalion were now within twenty paces of the guns. He heard the ceaseless whistle of bullets above him, and to his right and left soldiers kept groaning and falling. But he didn't look at them — he looked only at what was happening in front of him, at the battery. He could now clearly see a red-haired gunner with his cap knocked crooked, pulling one end of a ramrod while a French soldier tugged at the other. He could distinctly see the frantic yet angry expressions on both men's faces — they clearly had no idea what they were doing.

"What are they even doing?" Prince Andrei wondered, watching them. "Why doesn't the red-haired gunner run? He's unarmed. Why doesn't the Frenchman stab him? The gunner won't get away before the Frenchman remembers his bayonet and runs him through."

And sure enough, another French soldier came running up with his musket trailing behind him, heading straight for the two struggling men. The fate of the red-haired gunner — who had triumphantly secured the ramrod and still had no idea what was about to happen to him — was about to be decided. But Prince Andrei never saw how it ended. It felt as though one of the soldiers near him struck him on the head with the full swing of a club. It hurt, but what was worse was that the pain broke his concentration and kept him from seeing what he had been watching.

"What's this? Am I falling? My legs are giving way," he thought — and fell onto his back. He opened his eyes, hoping to see how the fight between the Frenchmen and the gunners had ended, whether the red-haired gunner had been killed, whether the cannon had been captured or saved. But he saw nothing. Above him now there was only the sky — the vast sky, not clear, yet immeasurably high, with gray clouds drifting slowly across it. "How quiet, how peaceful, how solemn — nothing like the way I was running," Prince Andrei thought. "Not the way we ran, shouting and fighting — not like the gunner and the Frenchman clawing at the ramrod with their frightened, angry faces. The clouds moving across that endless sky — how completely different they are from all of that. How is it I never noticed this sky before? And how happy I am to have found it at last! Yes! Everything is empty, everything is a lie — except this infinite sky. Nothing exists, nothing at all, except this. But even the sky doesn't really exist — there is nothing but stillness and peace. Thank God!"

chapters.title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: On the right flank, commanded by Bagration, the battle had not yet begun at nine o'clock. Not wanting to agree to Dolgorukov's demand that he launch the attack, and hoping to avoid responsibility, Prince Bagration proposed sending a messenger to the commander in chief for instructions. Bagration knew perfectly well that since the distance between the two flanks was over six miles, even if the messenger wasn't killed along the way (which was very likely), and even if he managed to find the commander in chief (which would be extremely difficult), he still wouldn't make it back before evening.

Bagration let his large, expressionless, sleepy eyes wander across his staff, and the first face to catch his attention was the boyish face of Rostov, breathless with excitement and hope. He sent him.
"And if I meet His Majesty before I meet the commander in chief, your excellency?" Rostov asked, raising his hand to his cap.
"You may deliver the message to His Majesty," Dolgorukov cut in quickly, before Bagration could reply.

Having been relieved from picket duty, Rostov had managed to grab a few hours of sleep before dawn. He felt cheerful, bold, and full of purpose — his movements springy, his faith in his luck unshaken, and his overall state of mind one in which everything seems possible, pleasant, and easy.

Every one of his wishes was coming true that morning: a major battle was underway and he was part of it; better still, he was serving as orderly to the bravest general; and on top of that, he was riding off with a message for Kutuzov, and perhaps even for the sovereign himself. It was a bright morning, he had a strong horse under him, and his heart was full of joy and happiness. As soon as he received the order, he gave his horse its head and galloped along the line. At first he rode along Bagration's troops, which hadn't yet joined the fighting and stood motionless. Then he passed through the area held by Uvarov's cavalry, where he noticed preparations and a stir of activity. Beyond Uvarov's cavalry, he could clearly hear the sound of cannon and musket fire ahead of him. The firing grew louder.

In the fresh morning air, what he heard now was no longer the scattered musket shots at irregular intervals from before, followed by an occasional cannon blast. Instead, there was a continuous roll of musketry volleys from the slopes below Pratzen, broken by cannon reports so frequent that sometimes several of them merged together into a single roar.

He could see puffs of musketry smoke chasing each other down the hillsides, and clouds of cannon smoke rolling outward, spreading, and blending together. Through the smoke, he could also make out — by the glint of bayonets — moving masses of infantry and narrow lines of artillery with green ammunition wagons.

Rostov stopped his horse on a small hill to try to understand what was going on, but no matter how hard he strained his attention, he couldn't figure out or make sense of any of it. Down there in the smoke, men of some kind were moving around; lines of troops moved in the front and behind. But why, in which direction, and who they were — it was impossible to tell. Far from depressing or frightening him, the sights and sounds only heightened his energy and determination.
"Go on! Go on! Give it to them!" he cheered mentally at the sounds, and then continued galloping along the line, riding deeper and deeper into the area where the army was already engaged.
"What will happen there, I don't know, but it'll all work out!" Rostov thought.
After passing some Austrian troops, he noticed that the next section of the line — the Guards — was already in action.
"Even better! I'll get to see it up close," he thought.

He was riding almost along the front line. A cluster of men came galloping toward him — Uhlans, returning from an attack with their ranks in disarray. Rostov moved out of their way, involuntarily noticing that one of them was bleeding, and galloped on.

"That's not my concern," he thought. He hadn't gone many hundred yards when, off to his left, spanning the full width of the field, he saw an enormous body of cavalry in brilliant white uniforms mounted on black horses, trotting straight toward him and directly across his path. Rostov pushed his horse to full gallop to get clear of them, and he might have succeeded had they maintained their speed — but they kept going faster, and some of the horses were already at a full gallop. Rostov heard the pounding of hooves and the jingling of weapons, and he could see their horses, their figures, even their faces more and more clearly. These were the Horse Guards, advancing to attack the French cavalry that was riding to meet them.

The Horse Guards were galloping but still holding their horses in check. Rostov could already make out their faces and heard the command: "Charge!" shouted by an officer who was driving his thoroughbred to top speed. Fearing he would be crushed or dragged into the attack against the French, Rostov galloped along the front as fast as his horse could go, but still couldn't avoid them in time.

The last of the Horse Guards — a massive, pockmarked fellow — scowled angrily at seeing Rostov in his path, knowing a collision was inevitable. This Guardsman would certainly have knocked Rostov and his Bedouin horse flat (Rostov felt positively tiny and weak next to these enormous men and their horses), had Rostov not thought to crack his whip in front of the Guardsman's horse. The big black horse, sixteen hands high, shied and pinned back its ears. But the pockmarked Guardsman dug in his huge spurs, and the horse flicked its tail, stretched out its neck, and charged forward even faster. The Horse Guards had barely passed Rostov when he heard them shout "Hurrah!" and, looking back, he saw their front ranks tangled up with foreign cavalry wearing red shoulder pieces — probably French. He could see nothing more after that, because suddenly cannon began firing from somewhere and smoke covered everything.

At that moment, as the Horse Guards disappeared into the smoke beyond him, Rostov hesitated: should he gallop after them, or continue on to where he'd been sent? This was the brilliant charge of the Horse Guards that stunned even the French. Rostov was horrified to learn later that out of that entire mass of huge, handsome men — all those brilliant, wealthy young officers and cadets who had galloped past him on their thousand-ruble horses — only eighteen survived the charge.
"Why should I envy them? My chance hasn't passed, and maybe I'll see the Emperor any minute now!" Rostov thought, and galloped on.

When he came level with the Foot Guards, he became aware that cannonballs were flying nearby — not so much from hearing them as from seeing the anxious looks on the soldiers' faces and the forced, unnatural solemnity of the officers.
As he passed behind one of the Foot Guard regiment's lines, a voice called out his name.
"Rostov!"
"What?" he answered, not recognizing Boris.
"Guess what — we were in the front line! Our regiment attacked!" Boris said with the bright, happy smile of a young man who has been under fire for the first time.
Rostov stopped.
"Really? How did it go?"

"We drove them back!" Boris said excitedly, becoming talkative. "Can you imagine it?" And he launched into a story about how the Guards had taken up their position and spotted troops ahead, assumed they were Austrians, and then suddenly realized from the cannonballs raining down on them that they were actually on the front line and had to go into action unexpectedly. Rostov spurred his horse before Boris had finished.
"Where are you headed?" Boris asked.
"To deliver a message to His Majesty."

"There he is!" Boris said, thinking Rostov had said "His Highness," and pointing to the Grand Duke, who stood a hundred paces away in his helmet and Horse Guards jacket, his high shoulders squared and brows knitted, shouting something at a pale, white-uniformed Austrian officer.
"But that's the Grand Duke — I need the commander in chief, or the Emperor," Rostov said, about to spur his horse forward.

"Count! Count!" Berg shouted, running up from the other side, just as eager as Boris. "Count! I've been wounded in my right hand" — and he showed his bleeding hand wrapped in a handkerchief — "and I stayed at the front! I held my sword in my left hand, Count. Our whole family — the von Bergs — have always been knights!"
He said something more, but Rostov didn't wait to hear it and rode away.

Having passed the Guards and crossed an open stretch, Rostov — wanting to avoid being caught in front of the first line again, as he had been during the Horse Guards' charge — followed the line of reserves, giving a wide berth to the areas with the heaviest musket and cannon fire. Suddenly he heard musket fire very close, directly in front of him and behind the Russian positions — somewhere the enemy should not have been.

"What's going on?" he thought. "The enemy behind our army? That's impossible!" And suddenly he was seized by a wave of fear — fear for himself and for the outcome of the whole battle. "But whatever happens," he told himself, "there's no way around it now. I have to find the commander in chief right here, and if everything is lost, then I'll die with the rest."
The sense of dread that had suddenly gripped Rostov only grew stronger the farther he rode into the area behind the village of Pratzen, which was teeming with troops of every kind.
"What does it mean? What's happening? Who are they firing at? Who's doing the firing?" Rostov kept asking as he encountered Russian and Austrian soldiers running in confused crowds across his path.
"The devil only knows! Everyone's been killed! It's all over!" he was told in Russian, German, and Czech by the fleeing crowds, who understood what was happening no better than he did.
"Kill the Germans!" one man shouted.
"To hell with them — the traitors!"
"Damn these Russians!" a German muttered.
Footnote: "Hang these Russians!"

Several wounded men came along the road, and curses, screams, and groans all merged into a general uproar. Then the firing died away. Rostov later learned that Russian and Austrian soldiers had been shooting at each other.
