He remembered his honeymoon and blushed at the memory. One recollection was particularly vivid, humiliating, and shameful — how one day, shortly after his marriage, he had come out of the bedroom into his study a little before noon in his silk dressing gown, and found his head steward there. The man bowed respectfully, glanced at his face and his dressing gown, and smiled slightly, as if expressing a tactful understanding of his master's happiness.

"But how often I was proud of her — proud of her majestic beauty and social skill," he thought. "I was proud of my house, where she entertained all of Petersburg, proud of her cool composure and beauty. So this is what I was proud of! Back then I thought I didn't understand her. How often, when thinking about her character, I told myself that I was the one at fault for not understanding her, for not understanding that constant poise and self-satisfaction and complete lack of interests or desires. And the whole secret lies in the terrible truth that she is a corrupt woman. Now I've said that terrible word to myself, everything has become clear."

"Anatole used to come to borrow money from her and would kiss her bare shoulders. She didn't give him the money but let herself be kissed. Her father once tried, as a joke, to make her jealous, and she replied with a calm smile that she wasn't stupid enough to be jealous. 'Let him do what he wants,' she used to say about me. One day I asked her if she had any signs of pregnancy. She laughed scornfully and said she wasn't fool enough to want children, and that she wasn't going to have any children by me."
Then he recalled the coarseness and bluntness of her thoughts and the vulgarity of her expressions, despite her aristocratic upbringing.
"'I'm not that stupid.... Just you try.... Get lost,' she used to say. Seeing how successful she was with young and old men and women, Pierre often couldn't understand why he didn't love her.
* "Get lost."

"Yes, I never loved her," he said to himself. "I knew she was a corrupt woman," he repeated, "but I didn't dare admit it to myself. And now Dolokhov is sitting in the snow with a forced smile, perhaps dying, while I face my remorse with some kind of forced bravado!"
Pierre was one of those people who, despite appearing to have what's called a weak character, don't seek a confidant when they're in trouble. He processed his suffering alone.

"It's all her fault," he told himself. "But what does that matter? Why did I tie myself to her? Why did I say 'I love you' to her — which was a lie, and worse than a lie? I'm guilty and must endure... what? A stain on my name? A lifelong misfortune? Oh, that's nonsense," he thought. "A stain on my name and honor — that's something separate from who I really am."
* I love you.

"Louis XVI was executed because they said he was dishonorable and a criminal," the thought came to Pierre. "And from their point of view, they were right — just as those were right who made him a saint and died as martyrs for his sake. Then Robespierre was beheaded for being a tyrant. Who is right and who is wrong? No one! But if you're alive — live. Tomorrow you'll die, just as I might have died an hour ago. And is it worth tormenting yourself when you have only a moment of life compared to eternity?"

But the moment he imagined himself calmed by such thoughts, she suddenly came into his mind as she had been in those moments when he'd most strongly expressed his fake love for her, and he felt the blood rush to his heart and had to get up again and move around and smash and tear at whatever came to hand. "Why did I tell her 'I love you'?" he kept repeating to himself. And after saying it for the tenth time, Moliere's words came to him: "But what the devil was he doing in that boat?" — and he began to laugh at himself.
* "But what the devil was he doing in that boat?"

During the night he called his valet and told him to pack for Petersburg. He couldn't imagine how he could face her now. He decided to leave the next day and write her a letter informing her of his intention to separate from her forever.
The next morning, when the valet came in with coffee, Pierre was lying asleep on the ottoman with an open book in his hand.
He woke up and looked around for a while with a startled expression, unable to grasp where he was.
"The countess asked me to inquire whether your excellency was at home," said the valet.

But before Pierre could decide what answer to send, the countess herself entered the room. She wore a white satin dressing gown embroidered with silver, her hair simply arranged — two thick braids wound twice around her lovely head like a crown. She was calm and majestic, except for an angry crease on her rather prominent marble forehead. With unshakable composure she didn't speak in front of the valet. She knew about the duel and had come to discuss it. She waited until the valet had set down the coffee things and left. Pierre looked at her timidly over his spectacles, like a hare that, surrounded by hounds, flattens its ears and crouches motionless before its enemies — he tried to go on reading. But realizing this was pointless and impossible, he glanced at her timidly again. She didn't sit down but stood looking at him with a contemptuous smile, waiting for the valet to leave.
"Well, what's this about? What have you been up to now, I'd like to know?" she asked sternly.
"Me? What have I...?" Pierre stammered.
"So you're a hero now, are you? Come on, what was this duel about? What is it supposed to prove? What? I'm asking you."
Pierre rolled over heavily on the ottoman and opened his mouth but couldn't reply.

"If you won't answer, I'll tell you myself..." Helene continued. "You believe everything people tell you. You were told" — Helene laughed — "that Dolokhov was my lover," she said with her characteristic blunt directness, tossing out the word as casually as any other, "and you believed it! Well, what have you proved? What does this duel prove? That you're a fool — but everybody already knew that. What's going to happen now? I'll be the laughingstock of all Moscow. Everyone will say that you, drunk and clueless about what you were doing, challenged a man you were jealous of for no reason." Helene's voice rose and she grew more and more agitated. "A man who is better than you in every way..."
"Hmm... hmm..." Pierre growled, frowning without looking at her and not moving a muscle.
"And how could you believe he was my lover? Why? Because I enjoy his company? If you were more intelligent and more pleasant, I'd prefer yours."
"Don't talk to me... please," Pierre muttered hoarsely.
"Why shouldn't I talk? I can say whatever I want, and I'll tell you plainly that very few wives with husbands like you would have avoided taking lovers — but I haven't done that," she said.

Pierre wanted to say something. He looked at her with a strange expression she didn't understand, then lay down again. He was in physical agony at that moment — there was a weight on his chest and he couldn't breathe. He knew he had to do something to end this suffering, but what he wanted to do was too terrible.
"We should separate," he muttered in a broken voice.
"Separate? Fine, but only if you give me a fortune," said Helene. "Separate! As if that's supposed to scare me!"
Pierre leaped up from the sofa and rushed staggering toward her.
"I'll kill you!" he shouted, and seizing the marble top of a table with a strength he'd never felt before, he took a step toward her, brandishing the heavy slab.

Helene's face became terrified. She shrieked and sprang aside. His father's nature showed itself in Pierre. He felt the thrill and ecstasy of rage. He hurled down the marble slab, shattering it, and lunging toward her with outstretched hands, he roared "Get out!" in such a terrible voice that the whole house heard it with horror. God knows what he would have done if Helene hadn't fled the room.
A week later Pierre gave his wife full control over all his estates in central Russia, which made up the greater part of his wealth, and left for Petersburg alone.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Two months had passed since news of the Battle of Austerlitz and the loss of Prince Andrew had reached Bald Hills. Despite letters sent through the embassy and extensive searches, his body had not been found, nor was he on any list of prisoners. Worst of all for his family was the lingering possibility that he had been picked up on the battlefield by local people and might now be lying somewhere, recovering or dying, alone among strangers, unable to send word. The official newspapers, from which the old prince first learned of the defeat at Austerlitz, reported — as usual very briefly and vaguely — that after brilliant engagements the Russians had been forced to retreat and had done so in perfect order. The old prince understood from this report that the army had been defeated. A week after the newspaper account of the battle, a letter arrived from Kutuzov informing the prince of what had befallen his son.

"Your son," Kutuzov wrote, "fell before my eyes, a standard in his hand, at the head of a regiment — he fell as a hero, worthy of his father and his fatherland. To my great regret and that of the whole army, it is still uncertain whether he is alive or not. I take comfort, and offer it to you, in the hope that your son is alive, since otherwise he would have been listed among the officers found on the battlefield — a list which has been sent to me under a flag of truce."

After receiving this news late in the evening, when he was alone in his study, the old prince went for his walk as usual the next morning. But he was silent with his steward, the gardener, and the architect, and though he looked very stern, he said nothing to anyone.
When Princess Mary came to him at the usual hour, he was working at his lathe and, as always, didn't look up when she entered.

"Ah, Princess Mary!" he suddenly said in an unnatural voice, throwing down his chisel. The wheel continued spinning by its own momentum, and Princess Mary would always remember the dying creak of that wheel, which merged in her memory with everything that followed.

She went up to him, saw his face, and something broke inside her. Her eyes grew dim. From the expression on her father's face — not sad, not broken, but angry and working unnaturally — she could see that some terrible catastrophe was hanging over her and about to crush her. The worst thing in life, something she had never experienced — irreparable and incomprehensible — the death of someone she loved.
"Father! Andrew!" said the plain, awkward princess with such indescribable beauty of grief and selflessness that her father couldn't bear her look and turned away with a sob.
"Bad news! He's not among the prisoners or the dead! Kutuzov writes..." and he let out a piercing scream, as if trying to drive the princess away with it. "Killed!"

The princess didn't collapse or faint. She was already pale, but when she heard these words, her face changed and something lit up in her beautiful, radiant eyes. It was as if a supreme joy — a joy beyond the joys and sorrows of this world — flooded over the immense grief within her. She forgot all fear of her father, went up to him, took his hand, and drawing him down, put her arm around his thin, bony neck.
"Father," she said, "don't turn away from me. Let us cry together."
"Scoundrels! Villains!" the old man shrieked, turning his face away from her. "Destroying the army, destroying men! And for what? Go — go and tell Lise."

The princess sank helplessly into an armchair beside her father and wept. She saw her brother as he had been at the moment he said goodbye to her and to Lise — his expression tender yet proud. She saw him tender and amused as he had been when he put on the little icon. "Did he believe? Had he repented of his doubt? Was he there now? There, in the realm of eternal peace and blessedness?" she wondered.
"Father, tell me how it happened," she asked through her tears.
"Go! Go! Killed in battle, where the finest Russian men and Russia's glory were led to destruction. Go, Princess Mary. Go and tell Lise. I'll follow."

When Princess Mary returned from her father, the little princess sat doing needlework, looking up with that curious expression of inner, happy calm that is unique to pregnant women. It was clear that her eyes didn't see Princess Mary — they were looking inward, into herself, at something joyful and mysterious happening within her.
"Mary," she said, pushing away from the embroidery frame and leaning back, "give me your hand." She took her sister-in-law's hand and placed it below her waist.
Her eyes smiled with anticipation; her soft, downy lip lifted and stayed raised in childlike happiness.
Princess Mary knelt before her and buried her face in the folds of her sister-in-law's dress.
"There — there! Do you feel it? It's such a strange feeling. And you know, Mary, I'm going to love him so much," said Lise, gazing at her sister-in-law with bright, happy eyes.
Princess Mary couldn't lift her head. She was crying.
"What's the matter, Mary?"
"Nothing... it's just that I feel sad... sad about Andrew," she said, wiping her tears on her sister-in-law's knee.

Several times that morning Princess Mary tried to prepare her sister-in-law for the news, but each time she started, she began to cry. Unobservant as the little princess was, these tears, whose cause she didn't understand, unsettled her. She said nothing but glanced around uneasily, as if searching for something. Before dinner the old prince, of whom she was always afraid, came into her room with a particularly restless and hostile expression, then left again without a word. She looked at Princess Mary, then sat thinking for a while with that look of inward attention seen only in pregnant women, and suddenly began to cry.
"Has there been any word from Andrew?" she asked.
"No — you know it's too soon for news. But Father is worried, and I'm frightened."
"So there's nothing?"
"Nothing," answered Princess Mary, looking firmly at her sister-in-law with her radiant eyes.

She had resolved not to tell her and had persuaded her father to hide the terrible news until after the birth, which was expected any day. Princess Mary and the old prince each bore and concealed their grief in their own way. The old prince refused to hold out any hope. He made up his mind that Prince Andrew had been killed, and although he sent an official to Austria to search for traces of his son, he ordered a monument from Moscow that he planned to erect in his own garden as a memorial, and he told everyone that his son had been killed. He tried not to change his usual routine, but his strength was failing. He walked less, ate less, slept less, and grew weaker every day. Princess Mary held onto hope. She prayed for her brother as for a living man and was constantly waiting for news of his return.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: "Darling," said the little princess after breakfast on the morning of the nineteenth of March, and her downy little lip rose from old habit. But since sorrow now colored every smile, every word, and even every footstep in that house after the terrible news had arrived, the little princess's smile — though she didn't know the cause of the sadness around her — only served as another reminder of the general grief.
"Darling, I'm afraid this morning's breakfast — or fruschtique, as Foka the cook calls it — hasn't agreed with me."
* Fruhstuck: breakfast.
"What's wrong, sweetheart? You look pale. Oh, you're very pale!" said Princess Mary in alarm, hurrying over to her sister-in-law with her soft, heavy steps.

"Your excellency, shouldn't we send for Mary Bogdanovna?" said one of the maids who was present. Mary Bogdanovna was a midwife from the nearby town who had been staying at Bald Hills for the past two weeks.
"Oh yes," agreed Princess Mary. "Perhaps that's what it is. I'll go. Be brave, my angel." She kissed Lise and was about to leave the room.
"Oh, no, no!" And beyond the pallor and physical discomfort on the little princess's face, there appeared an expression of childlike terror at the prospect of unavoidable pain.

"No, it's just indigestion... Say it's only indigestion, say so, Mary! Say it..." And the little princess began crying like a suffering child, wringing her small hands with something almost theatrical in the gesture. Princess Mary rushed out of the room to fetch Mary Bogdanovna.
"My God! My God! Oh!" she heard as she left.
The midwife was already on her way to meet her, rubbing her small, plump white hands with an air of calm self-assurance.
"Mary Bogdanovna, I think it's starting!" said Princess Mary, her eyes wide with alarm.
"Well, the Lord be praised, Princess," said Mary Bogdanovna without hurrying. "You young ladies really don't need to know about these things."

"But why hasn't the doctor from Moscow arrived yet?" asked the princess. In keeping with Lise's and Prince Andrew's wishes, they had sent to Moscow for a doctor well in advance, and were expecting him at any moment.
"It doesn't matter, Princess. Don't be alarmed," said Mary Bogdanovna. "We'll manage perfectly well without a doctor."

Five minutes later, from her room, Princess Mary heard something heavy being carried past. She looked out. The servants were carrying the large leather sofa from Prince Andrew's study into the bedroom. Their faces wore a quiet, solemn expression.

Princess Mary sat alone in her room, listening to the sounds of the house, occasionally opening her door when someone passed and watching the activity in the corridor. Women went quietly in and out of the bedroom, glancing at the princess and turning away. She didn't dare ask any questions and closed her door again, sometimes sitting in her armchair, sometimes picking up her prayer book, sometimes kneeling before the icon stand. To her surprise and distress, she found that prayer did not calm her agitation. Suddenly her door opened softly and her old nurse, Praskovya Savishna — who almost never came to that part of the house because the old prince had forbidden it — appeared on the threshold with a shawl around her head.
"I've come to sit with you a bit, Masha," said the nurse, "and look, I've brought the prince's wedding candles to light before his icon, my angel," she added with a sigh.
"Oh, nurse, I'm so glad!"
"God is merciful, my dear."

The nurse lit the gilded candles before the icons and sat down by the door with her knitting. Princess Mary picked up a book and began to read. Only when they heard footsteps or voices did the two women look at each other — the princess anxious and questioning, the nurse reassuring. Everyone in the house felt the same thing Princess Mary was feeling in her room. But because of the old belief that the fewer people who know about it, the less a woman in labor suffers, everyone pretended to be unaware. No one spoke of it, yet beneath the usual composed and respectful manners of the prince's household, there was a shared sense of anxiety, a softening of hearts, and a feeling that something great and mysterious was taking place.

There was no laughter in the maids' large hall. In the men servants' quarters, everyone sat waiting — silent and alert. In the outer servants' lodgings, torches and candles burned and no one slept. The old prince, pacing his study on his heels, sent Tikhon to ask Mary Bogdanovna for news. "Just say 'the prince asked me to inquire' — and come tell me her answer."
"Please inform the prince that labor has begun," said Mary Bogdanovna, giving the messenger a meaningful look.
Tikhon went and told the prince.
"Very good!" said the prince, closing the door behind him. After that, Tikhon heard not the slightest sound from the study.

After a while he went back in as if to trim the candles, and seeing the prince lying on the sofa, looked at him, noticed his troubled face, shook his head, and going up to him, silently kissed him on the shoulder and left the room — without trimming the candles and without explaining why he'd come. The most sacred mystery in the world continued to unfold. Evening passed, night came, and the feeling of suspense and tenderness before the unknowable did not lessen but grew stronger. No one slept.

It was one of those March nights when winter seems determined to reclaim its hold, scattering its last snows and storms with desperate fury. A relay of fresh horses had been sent to the highway to meet the German doctor traveling from Moscow, who was expected at any moment, and men on horseback with lanterns had been dispatched to the crossroads to guide him over the country road with its ruts and snow-covered puddles.

Princess Mary had long since set aside her book. She sat in silence, her luminous eyes fixed on her nurse's wrinkled face — every line of which she knew so well — on the strand of gray hair escaping from under the kerchief, and on the loose skin hanging beneath her chin.

Nurse Savishna, knitting in hand, was telling in low tones — barely hearing or understanding her own words — the story she had told hundreds of times before: how the late princess had given birth to Princess Mary in Kishinev with only a Moldavian peasant woman to help, instead of a proper midwife.
"God is merciful — doctors are never needed," she said.

Suddenly a gust of wind slammed against the casement window, from which the inner frame had been removed — as per the prince's standing order to remove one window frame in each room as soon as the larks returned. The gust forced open the loosely fastened latch, set the damask curtain flapping, and blew out the candle with its cold, snowy draft. Princess Mary shuddered. Her nurse set down her knitting, went to the window, and leaned out to catch the swinging casement. The cold wind whipped the ends of her kerchief and her loose strands of gray hair.
"Princess, my dear — there's someone coming up the drive!" she said, still holding the casement open. "With lanterns. Most likely the doctor."
"Oh, thank God! Thank God!" said Princess Mary. "I must go meet him — he doesn't speak Russian."

Princess Mary threw a shawl over her head and ran to meet the new arrival. As she crossed the front hall, she could see through the window a carriage with lanterns standing at the entrance. She went out onto the stairs. On a banister post stood a tallow candle guttering in the draft. On the landing below, Philip the footman stood looking frightened, holding another candle. Still lower, beyond the turn of the staircase, she could hear footsteps in thick felt boots, and a voice that sounded familiar to Princess Mary was saying something.
"Thank God!" said the voice. "And Father?"
"Gone to bed," replied the voice of Demyan the house steward from below.
Then the voice said something more, Demyan answered, and the footsteps in felt boots came more rapidly up toward the unseen bend of the staircase.

"It's Andrew!" thought Princess Mary. "No, it can't be — that would be too extraordinary." And at the very moment she thought this, the face and figure of Prince Andrew appeared on the landing where the footman stood with the candle. He wore a fur cloak with a deep collar covered in snow. Yes, it was him — pale, thin, with a changed and strangely softened but agitated expression on his face. He climbed the stairs and embraced his sister.

"You didn't get my letter?" he asked, and without waiting for a reply — which he wouldn't have received anyway, since the princess was unable to speak — he turned back, quickly went down the stairs again with the doctor who had come in after him (they had met at the last post station), and then came back up and embraced his sister again.
"What a strange twist of fate, Masha darling!" And having taken off his cloak and felt boots, he went to the little princess's room.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: The little princess lay propped up on pillows, a white cap on her head — the contractions had just stopped for the moment. Strands of her black hair clung to her flushed, perspiring cheeks. Her lovely rosy mouth with its downy lip was open and she was smiling happily. Prince Andrew came in and stopped at the foot of the sofa where she lay. Her shining eyes, filled with childlike fear and excitement, rested on him without changing expression. "I love everyone and have never harmed anyone — so why must I suffer like this? Help me!" her look seemed to say. She saw her husband but didn't grasp what his appearance here and now really meant. Prince Andrew walked around the sofa and kissed her forehead.
"My darling!" he said — a word he had never used with her before. "God is merciful...."
She looked at him with an inquiring, childlike reproach.

"I was counting on you for help, and I get none — none from you either!" her eyes seemed to say. She wasn't surprised that he had come; she didn't fully register his arrival. His being there had nothing to do with her suffering or with easing it. The contractions started again and Mary Bogdanovna advised Prince Andrew to leave the room.
The doctor arrived. Prince Andrew went out and, meeting Princess Mary, joined her again. They began talking in whispers, but their conversation kept breaking off. They waited and listened.
"Go to her, dear," said Princess Mary.

Prince Andrew went back to his wife and sat waiting in the room next to hers. A woman came out of the bedroom with a frightened face and became flustered when she saw Prince Andrew. He covered his face with his hands and stayed like that for several minutes. Pitiful, helpless, animal moans came through the door. Prince Andrew stood up, went to the door, and tried to open it. Someone was holding it shut from inside.
"You can't come in! You can't!" said a terrified voice from within.

He began pacing the room. The screaming stopped, and a few more seconds passed. Then suddenly a terrible shriek — it couldn't be hers, she couldn't scream like that — came from the bedroom. Prince Andrew ran to the door; the scream cut off and he heard the wail of a newborn.
"Why have they brought a baby in there?" thought Prince Andrew in the first instant. "A baby? What baby...? Why is there a baby? Or has the baby been born?"

Then suddenly he grasped the joyful meaning of that cry. Tears choked him, and leaning his elbows on the windowsill, he began to weep, sobbing like a child. The door opened. The doctor emerged with his sleeves rolled up, without his coat, pale and with a trembling jaw. Prince Andrew turned to him, but the doctor gave him a dazed look and walked past without a word. A woman rushed out and, seeing Prince Andrew, hesitated on the threshold. He went into his wife's room. She was lying dead, in the same position he had seen her in five minutes before. Despite the fixed stare and the pallor of her cheeks, the same expression remained on her lovely, childlike face with its upper lip covered in fine dark hair.
"I love everyone, and I've never harmed anyone — and what have you done to me?" said her beautiful, pitiful, lifeless face.
In a corner of the room something red and tiny grunted and squealed in Mary Bogdanovna's trembling white hands.

Two hours later Prince Andrew, stepping softly, went into his father's room. The old man already knew everything. He was standing near the door, and as soon as it opened, his rough old arms closed like a vise around his son's neck. Without a word, he began to sob like a child.

Three days later the little princess was buried, and Prince Andrew went up the steps to where the coffin stood to give her a final kiss. There in the coffin lay the same face, though now with closed eyes. "Ah, what have you done to me?" it still seemed to say. And Prince Andrew felt something give way in his soul — he was guilty of a sin he could neither undo nor forget. He couldn't weep. The old man came up too and kissed the small waxen hands lying quietly crossed on her chest, and to him as well her face seemed to say: "Ah, what have you done to me, and why?" And at the sight, the old man turned angrily away.

Another five days passed, and then the young Prince Nikolai Andreevich was baptized. The wet nurse held the coverlet with her chin while the priest used a goose feather to anoint the baby's small red, wrinkled soles and palms.

His grandfather, who was his godfather, trembling and afraid of dropping him, carried the infant around the battered tin font and handed him over to the godmother, Princess Mary. Prince Andrew sat in another room, faint with fear that the baby might be dropped into the font, and waited for the ceremony to end. He looked up joyfully at the baby when the nurse brought him over, and nodded his approval when she told him that the wax with the baby's hair had not sunk in the font but had floated.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Rostov's involvement in Dolokhov's duel with Bezukhov was smoothed over through the efforts of old Count Rostov, and instead of being demoted to the ranks as he'd expected, Nicholas was appointed adjutant to the governor-general of Moscow. As a result, he couldn't go to the country with the rest of the family and was kept in Moscow all summer by his new duties. Dolokhov recovered, and Rostov grew very close to him during his convalescence. Dolokhov lay ill at his mother's home — she loved him passionately and tenderly — and old Mary Ivanovna, who had taken a liking to Rostov because of his friendship with her Fedya, often talked to him about her son.

"Yes, Count," she would say, "he is too noble and pure-hearted for this depraved world of ours. Nobody values virtue anymore — it seems like a reproach to everyone. Now tell me, Count — was it right, was it honorable, what Bezukhov did? And Fedya, with his noble spirit, loved him and still doesn't say a word against him. Those pranks in Petersburg when they played tricks on a policeman — didn't they do it together? And look! Bezukhov got off without a scratch while Fedya had to shoulder the whole burden. Think what he went through! Yes, he's been reinstated, but how could they not reinstate him? I doubt there were many sons of the fatherland out there as brave as he was. And now this duel! Have these people no sense of decency or honor? Knowing he's an only son, to challenge him and shoot so accurately! Thank God He had mercy on us. And what was it all about? Who doesn't have affairs these days? If he was so jealous — to my mind — he should have said something sooner, instead of letting it go on for months. And then to challenge him, counting on Fedya not fighting because he owed him money! How low! How contemptible! I know you understand Fedya, my dear Count — and believe me, that's why I'm so fond of you. Very few people truly understand him. He has such a noble, heavenly soul!"
Dolokhov himself, during his recovery, spoke to Rostov in a way no one would have expected.

"I know people think I'm a bad man!" he said. "Let them! I don't care about anyone except those I love. But the people I love, I love so fiercely I'd give my life for them — and everyone else I'd crush if they got in my way. I have a wonderful, priceless mother and two or three friends — you among them — and as for the rest, they only matter to me insofar as they're harmful or useful. And most of them are harmful, especially the women. Yes, my friend," he went on, "I've met loving, noble, high-minded men, but I've never yet met a woman — whether countess or kitchen maid — who wasn't mercenary. I haven't found that divine purity and devotion I look for in a woman. If I found someone like that, I'd give my life for her! But these..." and he made a gesture of contempt. "And believe me, if I still value my life, it's only because I still hope to find such a heavenly creature — someone who will transform, purify, and lift me up. But you don't understand that."
"Oh yes, I understand completely," answered Rostov, who was now fully under his new friend's influence.

In the autumn the Rostovs returned to Moscow. Early in the winter Denisov arrived too and stayed with them. The first half of the winter of 1806, which Nicholas Rostov spent in Moscow, was one of the happiest and most carefree times for him and the whole family. Nicholas brought many young men home to his parents' house. Vera was a striking girl of twenty; Sonya was a girl of sixteen with all the charm of a flower just opening; Natasha — half grown-up and half child — was sometimes childishly amusing, sometimes enchantingly girlish.

At that time the Rostov household was filled with the kind of romantic atmosphere typical of homes where there are very young and very charming girls. Every young man who visited — seeing those responsive, smiling young faces (smiling, no doubt, at their own happiness), feeling the eager energy around him, and hearing the bursts of song and music and the lighthearted, open chatter of girls ready for anything and full of hope — felt the same thing: a shared readiness to fall in love and an expectation that happiness was just around the corner.

Among the young men Nicholas brought to the house, one of the first was Dolokhov, whom everyone liked except Natasha. She nearly quarreled with her brother over him. She insisted that he was a bad person, that Pierre had been in the right in the duel and Dolokhov in the wrong, and furthermore that he was disagreeable and fake.

"There's nothing to understand," she declared with stubborn conviction. "He's cruel and heartless. Look — I like your Denisov, even though he's a wild one and all that — I still like him. So you see, I can judge people. But with this one, everything is calculated, and I don't like that. But Denisov..."

"Oh, Denisov is completely different," replied Nicholas, implying that even Denisov was nothing compared to Dolokhov. "You need to understand what kind of soul Dolokhov has — you should see him with his mother. What a heart!"
"Well, I don't know about all that, but I'm uncomfortable around him. And did you know he's fallen in love with Sonya?"
"That's nonsense..."
"I'm sure of it. You'll see."

Natasha's prediction turned out to be right. Dolokhov, who normally didn't seek out women's company, began visiting the house frequently, and the question of whom he was coming to see — though nobody spoke of it openly — was soon answered. He came for Sonya. And Sonya, though she would never have dared say it aloud, knew it and blushed bright red every time Dolokhov appeared.

Dolokhov often dined at the Rostovs', never missed a performance they attended, and went to Iogel's dance parties for young people, which the Rostovs always frequented. He was pointedly attentive to Sonya and looked at her in a way that made not only her blush but even the old countess and Natasha turn red when they noticed his gaze.
It was obvious that this strange, powerful man was under the irresistible spell of the dark, graceful girl who loved someone else.

Rostov noticed something new in Dolokhov's behavior toward Sonya, but he didn't try to figure out what these new dynamics meant. "They're always falling in love with somebody," he thought about Sonya and Natasha. But he wasn't as comfortable around Sonya and Dolokhov as before, and he spent less time at home.

In the autumn of 1806, talk of war with Napoleon had flared up again, even more intensely than the year before. Orders went out to raise recruits — ten men from every thousand for the regular army, plus nine from every thousand for the militia. Bonaparte was denounced everywhere, and in Moscow nothing was talked about but the coming war. For the Rostov family, the real significance of all these war preparations was that Nicholas refused to stay in Moscow and was only waiting for Denisov's leave to end after Christmas so he could return with him to their regiment. His approaching departure didn't stop him from enjoying himself — if anything, it added urgency to his pleasures. He spent most of his time away from home, at dinners, parties, and balls.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: On the third day after Christmas, Nicholas dined at home — something he'd rarely done lately. It was a grand farewell dinner, since he and Denisov were leaving to rejoin their regiment after Epiphany. About twenty people were present, including Dolokhov and Denisov.

Never had love so filled the air, and never had the romantic atmosphere been felt so strongly in the Rostov house as during this holiday season. "Seize the moments of happiness — love and be loved! That is the only reality in the world; all else is foolishness. It is the one thing we care about here," said the spirit of the place.

Nicholas, having worn out two pairs of horses as usual without managing to visit all the places he'd meant to go and had been invited to, returned home just before dinner. The moment he walked in, he noticed and felt the charged romantic atmosphere in the house, and also a peculiar awkwardness among some of those present. Sonya, Dolokhov, and the old countess were especially unsettled, and to a lesser degree Natasha. Nicholas understood that something must have happened between Sonya and Dolokhov before dinner, and with the instinctive kindness natural to him, he was very gentle and careful with both of them throughout the meal. That same evening, there was to be one of the holiday balls given by Iogel, the dancing master, for his students.
"Nicholas, will you come to Iogel's? Please do!" said Natasha. "He invited you, and Vasili Dmitrich* is coming too."
* Denisov.
"Where would I not go at the countess's command!" said Denisov, who had playfully taken on the role of Natasha's knight at the Rostovs'. "I'm even weady to dance the pas de châle."
"If I have time," Nicholas answered. "But I promised the Arkharovs — they're having a party."
"And you?" he asked Dolokhov, but as soon as the question was out, he realized he shouldn't have asked it.
"Perhaps," Dolokhov replied coldly and angrily, glancing at Sonya. Then, with a scowl, he gave Nicholas the same kind of look he had given Pierre at the club dinner.
"Something's going on," thought Nicholas, and this impression was confirmed when Dolokhov left immediately after dinner. He found Natasha and asked her what was the matter.
"I was actually looking for you," said Natasha, running out to him. "I told you, but you wouldn't believe me," she said triumphantly. "He proposed to Sonya!"

Though Nicholas hadn't paid much attention to Sonya lately, something seemed to break inside him at this news. Dolokhov was a suitable and in some ways a brilliant match for a girl who was penniless and an orphan. From the perspective of the old countess and society in general, it was unthinkable for her to refuse him. And so Nicholas's first reaction on hearing the news was anger at Sonya. He tried to say, "That's wonderful — of course she'll forget her childhood promises and accept the offer." But before he could get the words out, Natasha continued.
"And imagine — she refused him! Flat out!" she added after a pause. "She told him she loved someone else."
"Yes, my Sonya could never have done anything else!" thought Nicholas.
"No matter how much Mama pushed her, she refused. And I know she won't change her mind once she's decided..."
"And Mama pushed her!" said Nicholas reproachfully.
"Yes," said Natasha. "Do you know, Nicholas — don't be angry — but I know you won't marry her. I know it, heaven knows how, but I'm absolutely certain you won't marry her."
"You don't know anything of the sort!" said Nicholas. "But I need to talk to her. What a darling Sonya is!" he added with a smile.
"Oh, she really is a darling! I'll send her to you."
And Natasha kissed her brother and ran off.

A minute later Sonya came in looking frightened, guilty, and anxious. Nicholas went up to her and kissed her hand. This was the first time since his return that they had spoken alone about their love.

"Sophie," he began, timidly at first and then with growing confidence, "if you want to refuse someone who is not only a brilliant and advantageous match but a wonderful, noble man... he is my friend..."
Sonya interrupted him.
"I've already refused," she said quickly.
"If you're refusing because of me, I'm afraid that I..."
Sonya interrupted him again. She gave him an imploring, frightened look.
"Nicholas, don't say that!" she said.

"No, but I have to. It may seem arrogant, but it's better to be honest. If you're refusing him on my account, I have to tell you the whole truth. I love you, and I think I love you more than anyone else..."
"That is enough for me," said Sonya, blushing.

"No, but I've been in love a thousand times and will fall in love again, though I've never felt the same friendship, trust, and love for anyone as I feel for you. And I'm young. Mama doesn't approve. In short, I make no promise. And I ask you to consider Dolokhov's offer," he said, struggling to pronounce his friend's name.
"Don't say that to me! I want nothing. I love you as a brother and always will, and I want nothing more."
"You're an angel — I'm not worthy of you, but I'm afraid of misleading you."
And Nicholas kissed her hand again.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Iogel's balls were the most enjoyable in Moscow. The mothers said so as they watched their children performing the steps they'd just learned. The boys and girls themselves said so as they danced until they could barely stand. And the older young men and women who came with an air of superiority also agreed — these were the best balls around. That year, two marriages had resulted from these dances. The two pretty young Princesses Gortchakov had met their future husbands there, which only added to the reputation of these events. What set them apart from other balls was the absence of a host or hostess, replaced by the good-natured Iogel himself, fluttering about like a feather, bowing with perfect form as he collected tickets from his guests. Only people who genuinely wanted to dance came — people who still felt the pure delight that thirteen- and fourteen-year-old girls feel when wearing long dresses for the first time. With few exceptions, all the girls were — or seemed to be — pretty, their smiles so radiant and their eyes so bright. Sometimes the best students, led by the exceptionally graceful Natasha, even danced the pas de châle, but at this particular ball only the écossaise, the anglaise, and the mazurka — which was just coming into fashion — were performed. Iogel had rented a ballroom in Bezukhov's house, and everyone agreed the ball was a great success. There were many pretty girls, and the Rostov girls were among the prettiest. Both were especially happy and glowing that evening. Sonya, proud of Dolokhov's proposal, her refusal, and her conversation with Nicholas, had twirled about at home so much that the maid could barely braid her hair. She was radiant with impulsive joy.
Natasha, no less proud of wearing her first long dress and of attending a real ball, was even happier. They were both dressed in white muslin with pink ribbons.

Natasha fell in love the very moment she entered the ballroom. She wasn't in love with anyone in particular — she was in love with everyone. Whatever person she happened to look at, she was in love with them for that instant.
"Oh, how wonderful this is!" she kept saying, running up to Sonya.
Nicholas and Denisov were walking back and forth, watching the dancers with kindly approval.
"How sweet she is — she'll be a weal beauty!" said Denisov.
"Who?"
"Countess Natasha," Denisov answered.
"And how she dances! Such gwace!" he said again after a pause.
"Who are you talking about?"
"Your sister," Denisov said irritably.
Rostov smiled.

"My dear count, you were one of my best students — you must dance," said little Iogel, coming up to Nicholas. "Look at all these charming young ladies —" He made the same request to Denisov, who had also been his student.
"No, my dear fellow, I'll be a wallflower," said Denisov. "Don't you wecollect how badly I used your lessons?"
"Oh no!" said Iogel, rushing to reassure him. "You were only inattentive, but you had talent — oh yes, real talent!"

The band struck up the newly fashionable mazurka. Nicholas couldn't refuse Iogel and asked Sonya to dance. Denisov settled in with the older ladies and, leaning on his saber and tapping time with his foot, entertained them with funny stories while watching the young people dance. Iogel and Natasha — his pride and best student — were the first couple on the floor. Moving noiselessly on his little feet in low shoes, Iogel glided across the hall with Natasha, who, though shy, performed her steps with care. Denisov didn't take his eyes off her, beating time with his saber in a way that made clear: if he wasn't dancing, it was because he chose not to, not because he couldn't. In the middle of a figure, he beckoned to Rostov as he passed by:
"This is not how it's done," he said. "What sort of Polish mazuwka is this? But she does dance splendidly."
Knowing that Denisov had a reputation — even in Poland — for his masterful mazurka, Nicholas ran up to Natasha:
"Go choose Denisov. He's a real dancer — a marvel!" he said.

When Natasha's turn came to choose a partner, she stood up and, running quickly across the floor in her little bow-trimmed shoes, hurried shyly to the corner where Denisov sat. She saw that everyone was watching her, waiting. Nicholas could see Denisov refusing, though he was smiling with delight. He ran over to them.
"Please, Vasili Dmitrich," Natasha was saying, "please come!"
"Oh no, let me off, Countess," Denisov replied.
"Come on, Vaska," said Nicholas.
"They're coaxing me like I'm Vaska the cat!" Denisov said jokingly.
"I'll sing for you the whole evening," said Natasha.

"Oh, the faiwy! She can do anything with me!" said Denisov, and he unhooked his saber. He emerged from behind the chairs, clasped his partner's hand firmly, threw back his head, and positioned his foot, waiting for the beat. Only on horseback and in the mazurka was Denisov's short stature invisible — he looked like the dashing figure he felt himself to be. At the right beat, he glanced sideways at his partner with a merry, triumphant look, suddenly stamped one foot, bounced from the floor like a ball, and flew around the room with his partner. He glided silently on one foot across half the floor, and seeming not to notice the chairs, appeared about to crash straight into them when suddenly — clinking his spurs and spreading his legs wide — he stopped dead on his heels, stood still for a second, stamped in place with a clank of spurs, whirled rapidly around, and striking his left heel against his right, flew off in a circle again. Natasha guessed what he intended and, giving herself over to his lead, followed instinctively, hardly knowing how. He spun her first one way then another, holding her with his left hand, then his right. He dropped to one knee and whirled her around him, then leaped up and dashed forward so impetuously it seemed he would fly through every room in the house without taking a breath — and then he suddenly stopped and performed an entirely new and unexpected sequence of steps. When at last he smartly twirled his partner in front of her chair and drew up with a click of his spurs and a bow, Natasha didn't even curtsy in return. She stared at him in amazement, smiling as if she didn't recognize him.
"What was that?" she managed to say.

Although Iogel wouldn't officially acknowledge it as a proper mazurka, everyone was thrilled by Denisov's skill. He was asked again and again to dance, and the older guests began reminiscing with smiles about Poland and the good old days. Denisov, flushed from the mazurka and mopping himself with his handkerchief, sat down beside Natasha and didn't leave her side for the rest of the evening.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: For two days after that, Rostov didn't see Dolokhov — either at his own home or at Dolokhov's. On the third day, he received a note from him:

Since I don't intend to visit your home again for reasons you are aware of, and since I'm leaving to rejoin my regiment, I'm giving a farewell supper tonight for my friends. Come to the English Hotel.

Around ten o'clock, Rostov went to the English Hotel straight from the theater, where he'd been with his family and Denisov. He was immediately shown to the best room, which Dolokhov had reserved for the evening. About twenty men were gathered around a table where Dolokhov sat between two candles. On the table was a pile of gold coins and paper money — he was running the bank. Rostov hadn't seen him since the proposal and Sonya's refusal, and he felt uneasy at the thought of how they would meet.
Dolokhov's clear, cold gaze met Rostov the moment he walked through the door, as though he'd been waiting for him a long time.
"It's been a while since we've seen each other," he said. "Thanks for coming. I'll just finish dealing, and then Ilyushka will come with his singers."
"I stopped by your place once or twice," said Rostov, blushing.
Dolokhov said nothing in reply.
"You can play if you like," he said.
Rostov remembered a strange conversation he'd once had with Dolokhov. "Only fools trust to luck in cards," Dolokhov had said then.
"Or are you afraid to play with me?" Dolokhov asked now, as if reading Rostov's thoughts.

Beneath Dolokhov's smile, Rostov recognized the mood he'd seen at the club dinner and on other occasions — when Dolokhov, as if tired of everyday life, felt driven to break free of it through some wild and usually cruel action.

Rostov felt uneasy. He tried and failed to come up with some joke to deflect Dolokhov's words. But before he could think of anything, Dolokhov looked him straight in the face and said slowly and deliberately, loud enough for everyone to hear:
"Remember our conversation about cards? 'Only a fool trusts to luck — you should make certain.' Well, I want to put that to the test."
"Test his luck, or his certainty?" Rostov wondered to himself.
"Well, you'd better not play then," Dolokhov added, and cracking open a new pack of cards, he announced: "Bank, gentlemen!"
He pushed the money forward and began dealing. Rostov sat down beside him but didn't play at first. Dolokhov kept glancing at him.
"Why aren't you playing?" he asked.
And strangely, Nicholas felt he couldn't help himself — he picked up a card, placed a small bet on it, and began to play.
"I don't have any money on me," he said.
"I'll trust you."
Rostov bet five rubles on a card and lost. He bet again and lost again. Dolokhov "killed" — that is, beat — ten of Rostov's cards in a row.
"Gentlemen," said Dolokhov after dealing for some time, "please put your money on the cards, or I'll get confused with the accounts."
One of the players said he hoped he could be trusted.
"Of course you can, but I'm afraid of mixing up the numbers. So please put the money on your cards," Dolokhov replied. "Don't hold back — we'll settle up later," he added, turning to Rostov.
The game continued. A waiter kept circulating with champagne.

Rostov kept losing. He had eight hundred rubles marked against him. He wrote "800 rubles" on a card, but while the waiter filled his glass, he changed his mind and crossed it out to write his usual stake of twenty rubles.
"Leave it," said Dolokhov, though he didn't seem to even be looking at Rostov. "You'll win it back faster that way. I lose to the others but win from you. Or are you afraid of me?" he asked again.

Rostov gave in. He left the eight hundred and laid down a seven of hearts with a torn corner that he'd picked up from the floor. He would remember that seven for a long time afterward. He set down the seven of hearts, on which he'd written "800 rubles" in clear upright figures with a broken piece of chalk. He drained the glass of warm champagne that was handed to him, smiled at Dolokhov's words, and with a sinking heart, waiting for a seven to come up, watched Dolokhov's hands holding the deck. A great deal depended on whether Rostov won or lost on that seven of hearts. The previous Sunday, the old count had given his son two thousand rubles and, though he always hated discussing money problems, had told Nicholas that this was all he could give him until May, and asked him to be more careful this time. Nicholas had replied that it would be more than enough and had given his word of honor not to ask for anything more until spring. Now only twelve hundred rubles remained, so this seven of hearts meant not just the loss of sixteen hundred rubles, but the shame of breaking his word. With a sinking heart he watched Dolokhov's hands and thought, "Come on, hurry up and give me this card, and I'll grab my hat and drive home to supper with Denisov, Natasha, and Sonya, and I swear I'll never touch a card again." At that moment, his home life — the jokes with Petya, the conversations with Sonya, the duets with Natasha, the card games with his father, even his comfortable bed in the house on the Povarskaya — rose before him with such vividness and warmth that it felt like a lost, unappreciated paradise. He couldn't grasp that a stupid twist of chance — the seven landing to the right instead of the left — could strip him of all this happiness, which he was only now truly appreciating, and plunge him into some unknown abyss of misery. It couldn't be — and yet he waited with a sinking heart for the movement of Dolokhov's hands. Those broad, reddish hands with their hairy wrists showing below the shirt cuffs set down the deck and picked up a glass and pipe that were offered to him.
"So you're not afraid to play with me?" Dolokhov repeated, and as if about to tell a good story, he put down the cards, leaned back in his chair, and began deliberately, with a smile:
"Yes, gentlemen, I've heard there's a rumor going around Moscow that I'm a cheat, so I advise you all to be careful."
"Come on, deal!" Rostov burst out.
"Oh, those Moscow gossips!" said Dolokhov, and he picked up the cards with a smile.
"Aah!" Rostov nearly screamed, clutching his head with both hands. The seven he needed was lying on top — the first card in the deck. He had lost more than he could ever pay.
"Still, don't ruin yourself," said Dolokhov with a sidelong glance at Rostov as he continued dealing.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: An hour and a half later, most of the players had lost interest in their own games.

All attention was now focused on Rostov. Instead of sixteen hundred rubles, he had a long column of figures scored against him — he'd calculated it at around ten thousand, but it must have been closer to fifteen thousand by now, he vaguely thought. In reality, it had already passed twenty thousand rubles. Dolokhov had stopped listening to stories or telling them. He followed every movement of Rostov's hands and occasionally glanced at the running total of his debt. He had decided to keep playing until the score reached forty-three thousand. He'd chosen that number because forty-three was the sum of his own age and Sonya's. Rostov, his head propped on both hands, sat at the table, which was covered in scrawled figures, stained with spilled wine, and littered with cards. One agonizing thought wouldn't leave him: that those broad-boned, reddish hands with hairy wrists showing below the shirt sleeves — those hands he both loved and hated — held him completely in their power.

"Six hundred rubles, ace, a corner, a nine... winning it back is impossible... Oh, how good it was at home!... The jack, double or nothing... it can't be!... And why is he doing this to me?" Rostov's thoughts raced. Sometimes he staked a large sum, but Dolokhov refused to accept it and set the stake himself. Nicholas submitted, and one moment he was praying to God — as he had on the battlefield at the bridge over the Enns — and the next he was guessing that whichever card he happened to pull first from the crumpled pile under the table would save him. Then he counted the braids on his coat and bet on a card with that number, or tried to stake the full total of his losses on a single card. Then he looked around for help from the other players, or peered at Dolokhov's cold, impassive face, trying to read what was going on behind it.

"He must know what this loss means to me. He can't want to ruin me. Wasn't he my friend? Didn't I care about him? But it's not his fault — what can he do if luck runs his way?... And it's not my fault either," he told himself. "I haven't done anything wrong. Have I killed anyone? Have I insulted anyone or wished anyone harm? Then why this terrible disaster? And when did it start? Just a little while ago, I sat down at this table planning to win a hundred rubles to buy a box for Mama's name day and then go home. I was so happy, so free, so carefree! I didn't even realize how happy I was! When did that end, and when did this new, awful reality begin? What was the turning point? I've been sitting in the same place at this same table the whole time, choosing cards and placing bets, watching those same broad-boned, agile hands. When did it happen? What happened? I'm healthy and strong, still the same person in the same place. No — it can't be! Surely it will all turn out to be nothing!"
He was flushed and drenched in sweat, though the room wasn't warm. His face was terrible and pitiful to see, especially because of his helpless efforts to appear calm.

The score against him reached the fateful sum of forty-three thousand. Rostov had just prepared a card — planning to bend the corner to double the three thousand just added to his debt — when Dolokhov slammed the deck down, pushed it aside, and began rapidly tallying Rostov's total, the chalk snapping as he marked the figures in his clear, bold handwriting.
"Supper — it's time for supper! And here are the gypsies!"
A group of dark-skinned men and women were indeed coming in from the cold, saying something in their Romani accents. Nicholas understood it was all over, but he said in a casual tone:
"Well, aren't we going to continue? I had a wonderful card ready" — as if the fun of the game were all he cared about.
"It's finished! I'm ruined!" he thought. "A bullet through my brain — that's all that's left!" And at the same time, he said cheerfully:
"Come on, just one more little card!"

"All right," said Dolokhov, having finished adding up the figures. "All right — twenty-one rubles," he said, pointing to the number twenty-one that pushed the total just past the round sum of forty-three thousand. He picked up a new deck and prepared to deal. Rostov obediently straightened the bent corner of his card and, instead of the six thousand he'd planned to bet, carefully wrote "twenty-one."
"It doesn't matter to me," he said. "I just want to see whether you'll let me win this ten or beat it."
Dolokhov began dealing in earnest. Oh, how Rostov loathed those hands at that moment — those short, reddish fingers with their hairy wrists that held him in their power... The ten went to Dolokhov.
"You owe forty-three thousand, Count," said Dolokhov, and stretching, he rose from the table. "Sitting so long really does tire you out," he added.
"Yes, I'm tired too," said Rostov.
Dolokhov cut him short, as if to remind him that this was no time for casual remarks.
"When can I expect the money, Count?"
Rostov, flushing, drew Dolokhov into the next room.
"I can't pay it all at once. Will you accept a promissory note?" he said.
"Listen, Rostov," said Dolokhov clearly, smiling and looking Nicholas straight in the eyes. "You know the saying — 'Lucky in love, unlucky at cards.' Your cousin is in love with you. I know."

"Oh, how terrible to feel so completely in this man's power," thought Rostov. He knew the shock this loss would inflict on his father and mother. He knew what a relief it would be to escape it all. And he felt that Dolokhov knew he could save him from all this shame and misery — but chose instead to toy with him, the way a cat plays with a mouse.
"Your cousin..." Dolokhov began, but Nicholas interrupted him.
"My cousin has nothing to do with this, and there's no need to bring her into it!" he burst out fiercely.
"Then when will I have the money?"
"Tomorrow," Rostov replied, and left the room.

chapters.title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: Saying "tomorrow" and keeping up a dignified front wasn't difficult. But going home alone, facing his sisters, brother, mother, and father, confessing what he'd done, and asking for money he had no right to after giving his word of honor — that was terrible.

At home, they hadn't gone to bed yet. The young people had come back from the theater, had supper, and were gathered around the clavichord. The moment Nicholas walked in, he was enveloped by the romantic atmosphere that had pervaded the Rostov household all winter — and which, after Dolokhov's proposal and Iogel's ball, seemed to have grown even thicker around Sonya and Natasha, like the air before a thunderstorm. Sonya and Natasha were standing by the clavichord in the light blue dresses they'd worn to the theater, looking pretty and aware of it, happy and smiling. Vera was playing chess with Shinshin in the drawing room. The old countess, waiting for her husband and son to come home, was playing patience with the elderly gentlewoman who lived with the family. Denisov, his eyes sparkling and his hair disheveled, sat at the clavichord striking chords with his short fingers, his legs thrown back and his eyes rolling as he sang in his small, husky, but true voice some verses he'd composed called "Enchantress," for which he was trying to find the right music:
Enchantress, say, to my forsaken lyre / What magic power is this recalls me still? / What spark has set my inmost soul on fire, / What is this bliss that makes my fingers thrill?
He sang with passion, his sparkling dark eyes fixed on the frightened and happy Natasha.
"Wonderful! Brilliant!" exclaimed Natasha. "Another verse!" she said, without even noticing Nicholas.
"Everything's the same with them," thought Nicholas, glancing into the drawing room where he saw Vera and his mother with the old lady.
"Oh, Nicholas is here!" cried Natasha, running up to him.
"Is Papa home?" he asked.
"I'm so glad you've come!" said Natasha, ignoring his question. "We're having such a wonderful time! Vasili Dmitrich is staying an extra day just for me! Did you know?"
"No, Papa isn't back yet," said Sonya.
"Nicholas, is that you? Come here, darling!" called the old countess from the drawing room.
Nicholas went to her, kissed her hand, and sat down silently at her table, watching her hands arrange the cards. From the music room came laughter and cheerful voices urging Natasha to sing.
"All wight! All wight!" Denisov shouted. "No more excuses! It's your turn to sing the ba'cawolla — I beg you!"
The countess glanced at her silent son.
"What's wrong?" she asked.
"Oh, nothing," he said, as though tired of being asked the same question over and over. "Will Papa be home soon?"
"I think so."
"Everything's the same with them. They know nothing about it! Where can I go?" Nicholas thought, and he went back to the music room where the clavichord stood.
Sonya was at the clavichord, playing the prelude to Denisov's favorite barcarolle. Natasha was getting ready to sing. Denisov was watching her with adoring eyes.
Nicholas began pacing up and down the room.
"Why do they want her to sing? How can she sing? There's nothing to be happy about!" he thought.
Sonya struck the first chord of the prelude.
"My God, I'm a ruined and disgraced man! A bullet through my brain is the only thing left for me — not singing!" his thoughts ran on. "Leave? But where? It doesn't matter — let them sing!"
He continued pacing the room, looking darkly at Denisov and the girls, avoiding their eyes.
"Nikolenka, what's wrong?" Sonya's eyes seemed to ask. She noticed at once that something had happened to him.

Nicholas turned away from her. Natasha too, with her quick instincts, had instantly noticed her brother's state. But though she saw it, she was so full of joy at that moment, so far from any sorrow, sadness, or self-reproach, that she deliberately fooled herself, as young people often do. "No, I'm too happy right now to let anyone's suffering spoil it," she felt, and told herself: "No, I must be wrong — he's probably just as happy as I am."
"Ready, Sonya!" she said, walking to the very center of the room, where she believed the acoustics were best.
She lifted her head, let her arms drop limply at her sides like a ballet dancer, and, rising energetically from her heels to her toes, stepped to the middle of the room and stood still.
"Yes, this is me!" she seemed to say, responding to the rapt gaze with which Denisov followed her.
"And what is she so pleased about?" Nicholas thought, looking at his sister. "Why doesn't she feel gloomy and ashamed?"

Natasha took her first note. Her throat swelled, her chest rose, her eyes grew serious. In that moment she was oblivious to everything around her, and from her smiling lips flowed sounds that anyone can produce at the same intervals and sustain for the same duration — but which leave you cold a thousand times, and on the thousand-and-first time make you tremble and weep.

That winter, Natasha had begun singing seriously for the first time, mainly because Denisov took such delight in her voice. She no longer sang like a child — the comical, painstaking, childish quality was gone. But she didn't yet sing well, as every expert who heard her would say: "It's an untrained voice, but a beautiful one that needs proper training." Except they usually said this some time after she'd finished. While that untrained voice was actually sounding — with its imperfect breathing and labored transitions — even the critics said nothing. They simply listened with pleasure and wanted to hear more. In her voice there was a virginal freshness, an unawareness of her own gifts, and a velvety softness that had not yet been shaped by art — and these qualities blended so perfectly with her lack of technique that it seemed nothing about that voice could be changed without ruining it.

"What is this?" thought Nicholas, listening with wide eyes. "What's happened to her? How she's singing today!" And suddenly the whole world narrowed for him to the anticipation of the next note, the next phrase, and everything divided into three beats: "Oh mio crudele affetto"... One, two, three... one, two, three... One... "Oh mio crudele affetto"... One, two, three... One. "Oh, this senseless life of ours!" thought Nicholas. "All this misery, and money, and Dolokhov, and anger, and honor — it's all nonsense... but this is real... Come on, Natasha, come on, darling! Come on, sweetheart! How will she take that high note? She took it! Thank God!" And without realizing he was singing, he added a harmony — a second and then a third below the high note. "Oh God, how beautiful! Did I really hit that note? How wonderful!" he thought.

Oh, how that chord vibrated, and how deeply it stirred the finest part of Rostov's soul! And this was something apart from everything else in the world, something above everything in the world. "What are losses, and Dolokhov, and words of honor?... All nonsense! A person could kill and rob and still be happy..."

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: It had been a long time since Rostov had enjoyed music as much as he did that day. But the moment Natasha finished her barcarolle, reality came crashing back. He got up without a word and went downstairs to his own room. Fifteen minutes later the old count came home from his club, cheerful and pleased with himself. Nicholas, hearing the carriage pull up, went to meet him.
"Well — did you have a good time?" said the old count, beaming proudly at his son.
Nicholas tried to say "Yes," but could barely get the word out — he nearly burst into sobs. The count was lighting his pipe and didn't notice his son's state.

"It can't be helped!" thought Nicholas, for the first and last time. And suddenly, in the most casual tone he could manage — a tone that made him ashamed of himself — he said, as if merely asking his father for the carriage to go into town:
"Papa, I've come about a matter of business. I nearly forgot. I need some money."
"Oh dear!" said his father, who was in an especially good mood. "I told you it wouldn't be enough. How much?"

"Quite a lot," said Nicholas, flushing, and with a stupid, careless smile for which he could never forgive himself afterward. "I've lost a little — I mean a good deal, a great deal — forty-three thousand."
"What! To whom? Nonsense!" cried the count, suddenly reddening with a rush of blood to his neck and the back of his head, the way old men do.
"I promised to pay tomorrow," said Nicholas.
"Well!" said the old count, spreading out his arms and sinking helplessly onto the sofa.

"It can't be helped! It happens to everyone!" said the son in a bold, offhand tone, while deep in his soul he saw himself as a worthless scoundrel whose entire life couldn't make up for his crime. He longed to kiss his father's hands and beg forgiveness on his knees, yet he spoke in a careless, even rude voice, saying that it happens to everyone!
The old count dropped his eyes at his son's words and began frantically searching around for something.
"Yes, yes," he muttered, "it'll be hard, I'm afraid — hard to raise... happens to everybody! Yes, who hasn't done it?"
And with a furtive glance at his son's face, the count left the room. Nicholas had been prepared for resistance, but had not at all expected this.
"Papa! Papa!" he called after him, sobbing. "Forgive me!" And seizing his father's hand, he pressed it to his lips and burst into tears.
While father and son were having this conversation, the mother and daughter were having one no less important. Natasha came running to her mother, breathless with excitement.
"Mama! Mama! He's made me..."
"Made what?"
"Made me — he's proposed, Mama! Mama!" she exclaimed.
The countess couldn't believe her ears. Denisov had proposed. To whom? To this slip of a girl, Natasha, who not long ago was playing with dolls and was still having lessons.
"Don't be silly, Natasha! What nonsense!" she said, hoping it was a joke.
"Nonsense indeed! I'm telling you it's true," said Natasha indignantly. "I've come to ask you what to do, and you call it 'nonsense!'"
The countess shrugged her shoulders.
"If it's true that Monsieur Denisov has proposed to you, tell him he's a fool — that's all!"
"No, he's not a fool!" replied Natasha, indignant and serious.
"Well then, what do you want? You're all in love these days. Fine — if you're in love, marry him!" said the countess with an annoyed laugh. "Good luck to you!"
"No, Mama, I'm not in love with him. I don't think I'm in love with him."
"Well then, tell him so."
"Mama, are you angry? Don't be angry, darling! Is it my fault?"
"No, but what is all this, my dear? Do you want me to go tell him?" said the countess with a smile.

"No, I'll do it myself — just tell me what to say. It's easy for you," said Natasha, smiling back. "You should have seen how he said it! I know he didn't mean to say it — it just slipped out accidentally."
"Well, all the same, you must refuse him."
"No, I can't. I feel so sorry for him! He's so nice."
"Well then, accept his proposal. It's high time you were married," the countess answered sharply and sarcastically.
"No, Mama, but I feel so sorry for him. I don't know how to say it."
"And there's nothing for you to say. I'll speak to him myself," said the countess, indignant that anyone should dare treat this little Natasha as a grown-up.

"No, absolutely not! I'll tell him myself, and you can listen at the door," and Natasha ran through the drawing room to the ballroom, where Denisov sat on the same chair by the clavichord with his face in his hands.
He jumped up at the sound of her light step.
"Nataly," he said, rushing toward her with quick steps, "decide my fate. It is in your hands."
"Vasili Dmitrich, I feel so sorry for you! No, but you are so nice... but it won't do... not that... but as a friend, I will always love you."

Denisov bent over her hand, and she heard strange sounds she didn't understand. She kissed his rough, curly black head. At that instant they heard the quick rustle of the countess's dress. She came up to them.

"Vasili Dmitrich, I thank you for the honor," she said in an embarrassed voice that sounded severe to Denisov, "but my daughter is so young, and I would have thought that, as my son's friend, you would have spoken to me first. In that case you would not have forced me to give this refusal."
"Countess..." said Denisov, with downcast eyes and a guilty expression. He tried to say more but faltered.
Natasha could not bear seeing him in such distress. She began to sob aloud.

"Countess, I was wrong," Denisov continued in an unsteady voice, "but believe me, I adore your daughter and all your family so much that I would give my life twice over..." He looked at the countess, and seeing her stern face said: "Well, goodbye, Countess," and kissing her hand, he strode out of the room without looking at Natasha.

The next day Rostov saw Denisov off. He didn't want to stay another day in Moscow. All of Denisov's Moscow friends gave him a farewell party at the gypsies', with the result that he had no memory of how he was put in the sleigh or of the first three stages of his journey.

After Denisov's departure, Rostov spent another two weeks in Moscow without leaving the house, waiting for the money his father couldn't raise right away, and he spent most of his time in the girls' room.

Sonya was more tender and devoted to him than ever. It was as if she wanted to show him that his losses were something noble that made her love him all the more, but Nicholas now considered himself unworthy of her.

He filled the girls' albums with verses and music, and having at last sent Dolokhov the full forty-three thousand rubles and received his receipt, he left at the end of November — without taking leave of any of his acquaintances — to rejoin his regiment, which was already in Poland.

chapters.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: After his confrontation with his wife, Pierre left for Petersburg. At the Torzhok post station, either there were no horses or the postmaster refused to provide them. Pierre was forced to wait. Without undressing, he lay down on the leather sofa in front of a round table, put his big feet in their heavy boots up on the table, and began to think.
"Shall I bring in the bags? Get a bed ready? Some tea?" asked his valet.

Pierre didn't answer — he neither heard nor saw anything. He had started thinking at the last station and was still turning over the same question — one so important that he noticed nothing around him. Not only did it not matter whether he reached Petersburg sooner or later, or whether he found a room at this station, but compared to the thoughts consuming him it was all the same whether he stayed there a few hours or the rest of his life.

The postmaster, his wife, the valet, and a peasant woman selling Torzhok embroidery came into the room offering their services. Without changing his careless posture, Pierre looked at them over his spectacles, unable to understand what they wanted or how they could go on living without having solved the problems that absorbed him. He had been gripped by these same thoughts ever since the day he returned from Sokolniki after the duel and spent that first agonizing, sleepless night. But now, in the solitude of the journey, they seized him with special force. No matter what he thought about, he always came back to these same questions he could not solve yet could not stop asking himself. It was as if the thread of the main screw holding his life together had been stripped, so that the screw could neither go in nor come out, but just kept turning uselessly in the same place.

The postmaster came in and began obsequiously begging his excellency to wait only two hours, when — come what may — he would provide the courier horses. It was obvious he was lying and only wanted to squeeze more money out of the traveler.

"Is this good or bad?" Pierre asked himself. "It's good for me, bad for another traveler, and unavoidable for himself, because he needs money for food. The man told me that an officer once beat him for letting a private traveler have the courier horses. But the officer beat him because he needed to get somewhere quickly. And I," Pierre continued, "I shot Dolokhov because I felt insulted, and Louis XVI was executed because they considered him a criminal, and a year later they executed those who executed him — also for some reason. What is bad? What is good? What should one love, and what should one hate? What does one live for? And what am I? What is life, and what is death? What power governs everything?"

There was no answer to any of these questions, except one — and that was not a logical answer, not really a reply at all. The answer was: "You'll die and everything will end. You'll die and either learn everything or stop asking." But dying was terrifying too.

The Torzhok peddler woman, in a whining voice, kept offering her goods, especially a pair of goatskin slippers. "I have hundreds of rubles I don't know what to do with, and she stands there in her tattered coat, looking timidly at me," he thought. "And what does she want the money for? As if money could add even a fraction to happiness or peace of mind. Can anything in the world make her or me less vulnerable to evil and death? — death, which ends everything and must come today or tomorrow — in any case, in an instant compared to eternity." And again he twisted the stripped screw, and again it turned uselessly in the same place.

His servant handed him a half-finished epistolary novel by Madame de Souza. He began reading about the sufferings and virtuous struggles of a certain Emilie de Mansfeld. "And why did she resist her seducer when she loved him?" he thought. "God could not have placed in her heart a desire that went against His will. My wife — as she once was — did not resist, and perhaps she was right. Nothing has been found out, nothing has been discovered," Pierre told himself again. "All we can know is that we know nothing. And that's the height of human wisdom."
Everything within and around him seemed confused, senseless, and repulsive. Yet in this very disgust with all his circumstances, Pierre found a kind of bitter satisfaction.
"I must ask your excellency to move over a bit for this gentleman," said the postmaster, entering the room followed by another traveler, also stranded for lack of horses.
The newcomer was a short, large-boned, yellow-faced, wrinkled old man with bushy gray eyebrows hanging over bright eyes of an indefinite grayish color.

Pierre took his feet off the table, stood up, and lay down on a bed that had been prepared for him, glancing now and then at the newcomer. The old man, with a gloomy, tired expression, was wearily removing his wraps with his servant's help, not looking at Pierre. Wearing felt boots on his thin bony legs and keeping on his worn, nankeen-covered sheepskin coat, the traveler sat down on the sofa, leaned back his large head with its broad temples and close-cropped hair, and looked at Bezukhov. The stern, shrewd, penetrating expression of that gaze struck Pierre. He felt a desire to speak to the stranger, but by the time he had made up his mind to ask about the roads, the traveler had closed his eyes. His shriveled old hands were folded, and on one finger Pierre noticed a large cast-iron ring with a seal depicting a death's head.
