But at that moment Berg came up to Pierre and insisted that he join a debate between the general and the colonel about affairs in Spain.

Berg was satisfied and happy. The smile of pleasure never left his face. The party was a great success and exactly like other parties he had attended. Everything was just right: the ladies' subtle conversation, the cards, the general raising his voice at the card table, the samovar and the tea cakes. Only one thing was still missing — the thing he had always noticed at the evening parties he wanted to emulate. They hadn't yet had a loud, lively discussion among the men about something important and clever. Now the general had started just such a discussion, and so Berg pulled Pierre into it.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: The next day, having been invited by the count, Prince Andrew dined with the Rostovs and spent the rest of the day there.

Everyone in the house sensed for whose sake Prince Andrew kept coming, and without pretending otherwise, he tried to be near Natasha all day. Not only in the soul of the frightened yet happy and enraptured Natasha, but throughout the whole house, there was a feeling of awe — as though something important and inevitable was about to happen. The countess looked at Prince Andrew with sad, solemnly serious eyes when he talked to Natasha, and timidly launched into some artificial small talk whenever he glanced her way. Sonya was afraid to leave Natasha alone with him and equally afraid of being in the way. Natasha went pale with nervous anticipation whenever she found herself alone with him for a moment. His shyness astonished her. She felt that he wanted to say something but couldn't bring himself to do it.
That evening, when Prince Andrew had left, the countess went up to Natasha and whispered: "Well, what?"
"Mama! For heaven's sake, don't ask me anything now! One can't talk about it," said Natasha.

But all the same, that night, now agitated and now frightened, Natasha lay for a long time in her mother's bed, staring straight ahead. She told her how he had complimented her, how he'd mentioned going abroad, how he'd asked where they planned to spend the summer, and then how he'd asked about Boris.

"But such a thing... such a thing has never happened to me before!" she said. "Only I feel afraid when I'm with him. I'm always afraid. What does that mean? Does it mean it's the real thing? Yes? Mama, are you asleep?"
"No, my love; I'm frightened myself," answered her mother. "Now go to sleep!"

"I won't be able to sleep anyway. What silliness — to sleep! Mama! Mama! Nothing like this has ever happened to me before," she said, surprised and alarmed by the feeling she was aware of in herself. "And could we ever have imagined!..."

It seemed to Natasha that even the first time she had seen Prince Andrew at Otradnoe she had fallen in love with him. It was as if she feared this strange, unexpected happiness of meeting again the very man she had chosen then — she was firmly convinced she had — and finding him, it seemed, not indifferent to her.

"And it had to happen that he should come to Petersburg while we were here. And it had to happen that we should meet at that ball. It's fate. Clearly it's fate — everything was leading up to this! From the very first moment I saw him I felt something special."
"What else did he say to you? What are those poems? Read them..." said her mother, thinking it over, referring to some verses Prince Andrew had written in Natasha's album.
"Mama, does it matter that he's a widower?"
"Don't, Natasha! Pray to God. 'Marriages are made in heaven,'" said her mother.
"Darling Mama, how I love you! How happy I am!" cried Natasha, shedding tears of joy and excitement and hugging her mother.
At that very moment Prince Andrew was sitting with Pierre, telling him of his love for Natasha and his firm resolve to make her his wife.

That day Countess Helene had a reception at her house. The French ambassador was there, and a foreign prince of the blood who had recently become a frequent visitor, along with many brilliant ladies and gentlemen. Pierre, who had come downstairs, walked through the rooms and struck everyone by his preoccupied, absent-minded, and gloomy air.

Since the ball he had felt the approach of a spell of nervous depression and had been fighting desperately against it. Since the intimacy between his wife and the royal prince, Pierre had unexpectedly been made a gentleman of the bedchamber, and from that time he had begun to feel oppressed and ashamed in court society, and dark thoughts about the vanity of all things came to him more often than before. At the same time, the connection he had noticed between his protegee Natasha and Prince Andrew intensified his gloom by the contrast between his own situation and his friend's. He tried equally hard not to think about his wife, about Natasha, or about Prince Andrew; and yet everything seemed trivial compared with eternity. Again the question kept presenting itself: Why? What for? And he forced himself to work day and night at Masonic studies, hoping to drive away the dark spirit that threatened him. Toward midnight, after he had left the countess's apartments, he was sitting upstairs in a shabby dressing gown, copying out the original documents of the Scottish lodge of Freemasons at a table in his low, smoke-filled room, when someone came in. It was Prince Andrew.

"Ah, it's you!" said Pierre with a preoccupied, dissatisfied look. "And here I am, you see, hard at work." He pointed to his manuscript book with that air of seeking escape from life's troubles with which unhappy people regard their work.
Prince Andrew, with a beaming, ecstatic expression of renewed life on his face, stopped in front of Pierre and, not noticing his sad expression, smiled at him with the self-absorption of joy.
"Well, my dear friend," he said, "I wanted to tell you yesterday and I've come to do it now. I've never felt anything like this before. I am in love, my friend!"
Suddenly Pierre heaved a deep sigh and sank his heavy body down on the sofa beside Prince Andrew.
"With Natasha Rostova, yes?" he said.

"Yes, yes! Who else? I would never have believed it, but this feeling is stronger than I am. Yesterday I tortured myself, I suffered, but I wouldn't trade even that torment for anything in the world. I have not lived until now. Only now am I truly alive, but I can't live without her... But can she love me? I'm too old for her... Why don't you say something?"

"I? I? What did I tell you?" said Pierre, suddenly jumping up and pacing the room. "I always thought so... That girl is such a treasure... she is a rare girl... My dear friend, I beg you, don't analyze it, don't doubt it — marry, marry, marry!... And I'm sure there won't be a happier man on earth than you."
"But what about her?"
"She loves you."
"Don't talk nonsense..." said Prince Andrew, smiling and looking into Pierre's eyes.
"She does — I know it," Pierre declared fiercely.
"But listen," said Prince Andrew, catching him by the arm. "Do you know what state I'm in? I have to talk to someone about this."

"Well, go on, go on. I'm very glad," said Pierre, and his face really did change — his brow smoothed out and he listened to Prince Andrew with evident pleasure. Prince Andrew seemed, and truly was, a completely different, brand-new man. Where was his world-weariness, his contempt for life, his disillusionment? Pierre was the only person he had decided to confide in openly, and to him he poured out everything that was in his soul. Now he boldly and freely made plans for an expansive future, said he could not sacrifice his own happiness to his father's whims, and spoke of how he would either win his father's consent to the marriage and his love for Natasha, or manage without that consent. He marveled at the feeling that had taken hold of him, as at something strange, separate from and independent of himself.

"I wouldn't have believed anyone who told me I was capable of such love," said Prince Andrew. "It's not at all the same feeling I knew before. The whole world is now divided into two halves for me: one half is her, and there all is joy, hope, light; the other half is everything where she is not, and there all is gloom and darkness..."
"Gloom and darkness," repeated Pierre. "Yes, yes — I understand that."
"I can't help loving the light — it's not my fault. And I am very happy! You understand me? I know you're glad for my sake."
"Yes, yes," Pierre agreed, gazing at his friend with a moved and sorrowful expression. The brighter Prince Andrew's future appeared, the darker his own seemed.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 23
paragraphs: Prince Andrew needed his father's consent to the marriage, and the next day he set off for the country to obtain it.

His father received his son's news with outward calm but inner fury. He could not understand how anyone could wish to change his life or introduce anything new when his own life was already nearing its end. "If only they would let me finish my days in peace," the old man thought, "then they can do as they please." With his son, however, he employed the diplomacy he reserved for important occasions and, adopting a calm tone, discussed the whole matter.

First of all, the marriage was not a brilliant one as regards birth, wealth, or rank. Second, Prince Andrew was no longer young, and his health was poor — the old man stressed this particularly — while she was very young. Third, he had a son whom it would be a pity to entrust to a slip of a girl. "Fourth and finally," the father said, looking at his son with irony, "I ask you to put it off for a year. Go abroad, take a cure, find a German tutor for little Nicholas as you planned. Then if your love or passion or stubbornness — call it what you will — is still as strong, marry! And that's my last word on it. Remember — the last..." the prince concluded, in a tone that made clear nothing would change his mind.

Prince Andrew could see clearly that the old man hoped either his feelings or his fiancee's would not survive a year's test, or that he himself would die before then. He decided to comply with his father's wish — to propose and postpone the wedding for a year.
Three weeks after his last evening with the Rostovs, Prince Andrew returned to Petersburg.

The day after her conversation with her mother, Natasha waited for Bolkonsky all day, but he didn't come. It was the same on the second and third days. Pierre didn't come either, and Natasha, not knowing that Prince Andrew had gone to see his father, could not explain his absence.

Three weeks went by like this. Natasha had no desire to go out anywhere and drifted from room to room like a shadow, idle and listless; she cried in secret at night and no longer came to her mother in the evenings. She blushed constantly and was irritable. It seemed to her that everyone knew about her disappointment and was laughing at her and pitying her. As strong as her inner grief was, this wound to her vanity only made her misery worse.
Once she came to her mother, tried to say something, and suddenly burst into tears. Her tears were those of an offended child who doesn't understand why it's being punished.
The countess began to comfort Natasha, who at first listened to her mother's words but then suddenly cut her off:
"Stop it, Mama! I don't think about it and I don't want to think about it! He just came and then stopped, stopped..."
Her voice trembled and she nearly cried again, but she recovered and went on quietly:
"And I don't want to get married at all. And I'm afraid of him; I've become quite calm now, quite calm."

The day after this conversation Natasha put on an old dress that she knew had the special property of making her feel cheerful in the morning, and that day she returned to the old way of life she had abandoned since the ball. After morning tea she went to the ballroom, which she particularly loved for its resonant acoustics, and began singing her vocal exercises. When she finished her first exercise she stopped in the middle of the room and sang a musical phrase that especially pleased her. She listened joyfully — as though she hadn't expected it — to the charm of the notes reverberating, filling the whole empty ballroom, and slowly dying away; and all at once she felt cheerful. "What's the point of making such a fuss about it? Things are perfectly fine as they are," she told herself, and she began pacing the room — not simply walking on the resonant parquet but stepping with each step from heel to toe, in a new and favorite pair of shoes, and listening to the rhythmic tap of the heel and creak of the toe with as much pleasure as she had listened to her own singing. Passing a mirror she glanced into it. "There — that's me!" her expression seemed to say. "Well, and very nice too! I don't need anybody."

A footman tried to come in to clear something from the room, but she wouldn't let him. Having shut the door behind him, she continued her walk. That morning she had returned to her favorite mood — love of and delight in herself. "What a charming girl that Natasha is!" she said again, speaking as if she were some third, collective, male person. "Pretty, a good voice, young, and not in anyone's way if only they'd leave her alone." But however much she was left alone, she couldn't be at peace now, and she immediately sensed this.

In the hall the front door opened, and someone asked "Is the family at home?" and then there were footsteps. Natasha was looking in the mirror but didn't see herself. She was listening to the sounds in the hall. When she caught sight of her own face, it was pale. It was him. She was certain of it, though she could barely hear his voice through the closed doors.
Pale and agitated, Natasha ran into the drawing room.
"Mama! Bolkonsky is here!" she said. "Mama, this is terrible, it's unbearable! I don't want... to be tormented! What am I supposed to do?..."

Before the countess could answer, Prince Andrew entered the room with an agitated, serious face. The moment he saw Natasha his face brightened. He kissed the countess's hand and Natasha's and sat down beside the sofa.
"It's been so long since we had the pleasure..." the countess began, but Prince Andrew interrupted her by answering her intended question, clearly in a hurry to say what he had come to say.

"I haven't been to see you all this time because I was at my father's. I needed to discuss a very important matter with him. I only got back last night," he said, glancing at Natasha. "I need to speak with you, Countess," he added after a moment's pause.
The countess lowered her eyes, sighing deeply.
"I am at your disposal," she murmured.
Natasha knew she ought to leave, but couldn't. Something gripped her throat, and ignoring all propriety she stared straight at Prince Andrew with wide-open eyes.
"Now? This very instant?... No, it can't be!" she thought.
He glanced at her again, and that glance convinced her she was not mistaken. Yes — right now, this very instant, her fate would be decided.
"Go, Natasha! I'll call you," said the countess in a whisper.
Natasha looked at Prince Andrew and at her mother with frightened, imploring eyes and went out.
"I have come, Countess, to ask for your daughter's hand," said Prince Andrew.
The countess's face flushed hotly, but she said nothing.

"Your offer..." she began at last, speaking with an effort at composure. He remained silent, looking into her eyes. "Your offer..." she grew confused, "is welcome to us, and I accept your offer. I am glad. And my husband... I hope... but it will depend on her..."
"I will speak to her when I have your consent... Do you give it to me?" said Prince Andrew.

"Yes," replied the countess. She held out her hand to him, and with a mingled feeling of strangeness and tenderness pressed her lips to his forehead as he stooped to kiss her hand. She wanted to love him as a son but felt he was a stranger, a daunting man. "I'm sure my husband will agree," said the countess, "but your father..."
"My father, to whom I have told my plans, has made it an express condition that the wedding not take place for a year. And I wanted to tell you of that," said Prince Andrew.
"It's true that Natasha is still young, but — that long?..."
"It can't be helped," said Prince Andrew with a sigh.
"I will send her to you," said the countess, and left the room.
"Lord have mercy on us!" she repeated as she went to find her daughter.

Sonya said Natasha was in her bedroom. Natasha was sitting on the bed, pale and dry-eyed, staring at the icons and whispering something as she rapidly crossed herself. Seeing her mother she jumped up and flew to her.
"Well, Mama?... Well?..."
"Go, go to him. He is asking for your hand," said the countess, coldly it seemed to Natasha. "Go... go," said the mother, sadly and reproachfully, with a deep sigh, as her daughter rushed away.

Natasha never remembered how she entered the drawing room. When she walked in and saw him, she stopped. "Is it possible that this stranger has now become everything to me?" she asked herself, and immediately answered: "Yes, everything! He alone is now dearer to me than everything in the world." Prince Andrew came toward her with lowered eyes.
"I have loved you from the very first moment I saw you. May I hope?"
He looked at her and was struck by the serious, passionate expression on her face. Her face said: "Why ask? Why doubt what you cannot help but know? Why put into words what words can never express?"
She moved closer to him and stopped. He took her hand and kissed it.
"Do you love me?"
"Yes, yes!" Natasha whispered, almost crossly. Then she sighed deeply and, catching her breath faster and faster, began to sob.
"What is it? What's the matter?"
"Oh, I'm so happy!" she answered, smiled through her tears, leaned closer to him, paused for a moment as if asking herself whether she might, and then kissed him.

Prince Andrew held her hands, looked into her eyes, and did not find in his heart his former love for her. Something in him had suddenly changed; there was no longer the old poetic and mystical pull of desire, but instead pity for her feminine and childish vulnerability, awe at her devotion and trust, and a heavy yet joyful sense of the duty that now bound him to her forever. The present feeling, though not as bright and poetic as the earlier one, was stronger and more serious.
"Did your mother tell you it cannot be for a year?" asked Prince Andrew, still looking into her eyes.

"Is it possible that I — the 'little girl,' as everyone called me," thought Natasha, "is it possible that I am now to be the wife and equal of this strange, dear, clever man whom even my father looks up to? Can it be true? Can it be true that there can be no more playing at life, that now I am grown up, that I am responsible for my every word and deed? Yes, but what did he just ask me?"
"No," she replied, but she hadn't understood his question.
"Forgive me," he said. "But you are so young, and I have already been through so much. I am afraid for you — you don't yet know yourself."
Natasha listened with intense concentration, trying but failing to grasp the meaning of his words.

"Difficult as this year of delay will be — the year that postpones my happiness," continued Prince Andrew, "it will give you time to be sure of yourself. I ask you to make me happy in a year, but you are free: our engagement shall remain a secret, and should you find that you don't love me, or should you come to love..." said Prince Andrew with a forced smile.
"Why do you say that?" Natasha interrupted. "You know that from the very day you first came to Otradnoe I have loved you," she cried, completely convinced she was speaking the truth.
"In a year you will learn to know yourself..."
"A whole year!" Natasha repeated suddenly, only now grasping that the wedding was to be postponed for a year. "But why a year? Why a year?..."
Prince Andrew began to explain the reasons for the delay. Natasha didn't hear him.
"And there's no way around it?" she asked. Prince Andrew did not answer, but his face made clear that the decision could not be changed.

"It's awful! Oh, it's awful! Awful!" Natasha suddenly cried, and burst into sobs again. "I'll die waiting a year — it's impossible, it's awful!" She looked into her lover's face and saw in it an expression of sympathy and bewilderment.
"No, no! I'll do anything!" she said, suddenly stopping her tears. "I'm so happy."
The father and mother came into the room and gave the engaged couple their blessing.
From that day Prince Andrew began coming to the Rostovs' as Natasha's fiance.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: There was no formal betrothal ceremony, and Natasha's engagement to Bolkonsky was not announced; Prince Andrew insisted on this. He said that since he was responsible for the delay, he alone should bear the burden of it; that he had given his word and was bound forever, but that he didn't wish to bind Natasha and was giving her complete freedom. If after six months she felt she didn't love him, she would have every right to reject him. Naturally neither Natasha nor her parents wanted to hear of this, but Prince Andrew was firm. He came to the Rostovs' every day, but didn't behave toward Natasha as an engaged man: he didn't use the intimate "thou" but addressed her as "you," and kissed only her hand. After the engagement, completely different relations sprang up between them — intimate, natural, and sincere. It was as if they hadn't known each other before. Both loved to recall how they had thought of each other when they were still nothing to one another; they felt themselves now to be entirely different people — then they had been artificial, now they were natural and genuine. At first the family felt somewhat constrained around Prince Andrew; he seemed like a man from another world. For a long time Natasha had to train the family to get used to him, proudly assuring them all that he only seemed different but was really just like everyone else, and that she wasn't afraid of him and nobody else should be either. After a few days they grew accustomed to him and went on with their usual way of life in his presence, and he took part in it. He could talk about estate management with the count, about fashion with the countess and Natasha, and about albums and needlework with Sonya. Sometimes the household, both among themselves and in his presence, marveled at how it had all come about and at the obvious signs that had foretold it: Prince Andrew's visit to Otradnoe, their coming to Petersburg, the resemblance between Natasha and Prince Andrew that the old nurse had noticed on his first visit, and Andrew's encounter with Nicholas in 1805, and many other incidents that seemed to prove it was all meant to be.

In the house that poetic stillness and quiet reigned which always accompanies the presence of an engaged couple. Often when they were all sitting together everyone would fall silent. Sometimes the others would get up and leave, and the couple, left alone, would still remain silent. They rarely spoke of their future life. Prince Andrew was afraid and ashamed to bring it up. Natasha shared this feeling, as she did all his feelings, which she constantly intuited. Once she began asking about his son. Prince Andrew blushed, as he often did now — Natasha especially loved this in him — and said that his son would not live with them.
"Why not?" asked Natasha, alarmed.
"I can't take him away from his grandfather, and besides..."
"How I would have loved him!" said Natasha, instantly guessing his thought. "But I understand — you want to avoid giving anyone a reason to criticize us."

Sometimes the old count would come over, kiss Prince Andrew, and ask his advice about Petya's education or Nicholas's career. The old countess would sigh as she looked at them; Sonya kept getting nervous that she was in the way and tried to find excuses to leave them alone, even when they didn't want her to. When Prince Andrew spoke — and he could tell a story very well — Natasha listened with pride; when she spoke, she noticed with a mixture of fear and joy that he watched her attentively and searchingly. She asked herself in bewilderment: "What is he looking for in me? He's trying to find something by studying me! What if what he seeks isn't there?" Sometimes she fell into one of the wild, giddy moods that were so characteristic of her, and then she particularly loved to watch how Prince Andrew laughed. He laughed rarely, but when he did, he gave himself over to it completely, and after such laughter she always felt closer to him. Natasha would have been perfectly happy if the thought of the approaching separation had not terrified her, just as the mere thought of it made him turn pale and cold.

On the eve of his departure from Petersburg, Prince Andrew brought Pierre along. Pierre had not been to the Rostovs' once since the ball. He seemed distracted and embarrassed. He was talking to the countess, and Natasha sat down at a little chess table with Sonya, silently inviting Prince Andrew to come too. He did so.
"You've known Bezukhov a long time?" he asked. "Do you like him?"
"Yes, he's a dear, but very funny."
And as usual when talking about Pierre, she began telling stories of his absent-mindedness, some of which had even been made up about him.

"Do you know, I've told him our secret? I've known him since childhood. He has a heart of gold. I beg you, Natalie," Prince Andrew said with sudden seriousness, "I'm going away, and heaven knows what may happen. You may stop loving... All right, I know I'm not supposed to say that. Just this, then: whatever may happen to you when I'm not here..."
"What could happen?"

"Whatever trouble may come," Prince Andrew continued, "I beg you, Mademoiselle Sophie, whatever happens, turn to him alone for advice and help! He's the most absent-minded and absurd fellow, but he has a heart of gold."

Neither her father, nor her mother, nor Sonya, nor Prince Andrew himself could have predicted how the separation from her fiance would affect Natasha. Flushed and agitated, she went about the house all that day, dry-eyed, busying herself with the most trivial matters as if she didn't understand what was coming. She didn't even cry when, saying goodbye, he kissed her hand for the last time. "Don't go!" she said in a tone that made him wonder whether he really ought not to stay — and which he remembered long afterward. Nor did she cry when he was gone; but for several days she sat in her room, dry-eyed, taking no interest in anything, only saying now and then: "Oh, why did he go away?"

But two weeks after his departure, to the surprise of everyone around her, she recovered from her emotional illness just as suddenly, and became her old self again — though with a change in her inner character, as a child gets up after a long illness with a different expression on its face.

chapters.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: During that year after his son's departure, old Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky's health and temper grew much worse. He became still more irritable, and it was Princess Mary who usually bore the brunt of his frequent fits of unprovoked anger. He seemed to search deliberately for her most sensitive spots in order to torment her mentally as cruelly as possible. Princess Mary had two passions and therefore two sources of joy — her nephew, little Nicholas, and religion — and these were the old prince's favorite targets for mockery and attack. Whatever the topic of conversation, he would steer it around to the superstitions of old maids or the pampering and spoiling of children. "You want to turn him" — little Nicholas — "into an old maid like yourself! A pity! Prince Andrew wants a son, not an old maid," he would say. Or, turning to Mademoiselle Bourienne, he would ask her in Princess Mary's presence how she liked their village priests and icons, and would joke about them.

He continually hurt Princess Mary and tormented her, but it cost her no effort to forgive him. Could he really be to blame? Could her father, whom she knew loved her in spite of everything, truly be unjust? And what is justice? The princess never dwelt on that proud word "justice." All the complex laws of humanity were reduced for her into one clear and simple law — the law of love and self-sacrifice taught by Him who lovingly suffered for mankind though He Himself was God. What did she have to do with the justice or injustice of other people? She had to endure and love, and that is what she did.

During the winter Prince Andrew had come to Bald Hills and had been gay, gentle, and more affectionate than Princess Mary had known him in a long time. She felt that something had happened to him, but he told her nothing about his love. Before he left he had a long conversation with his father about something, and Princess Mary noticed that before his departure they were dissatisfied with one another.

Soon after Prince Andrew's departure, Princess Mary wrote to her friend Julie Karagina in Petersburg — the one she had dreamed, as all girls do, of marrying to her brother — who was at that time in mourning for her own brother, killed in Turkey.
Sorrow, it seems, is our common lot, my dear, tender friend Julie.

Your loss is so terrible that I can only explain it as a special act of God's providence — He who, loving you, wishes to try you and your excellent mother. Oh, my friend! Religion, and religion alone, can — I will not say comfort us — but save us from despair. Religion alone can explain what without its help we cannot comprehend: why kind and noble people who could find happiness in life — who harm no one and are necessary to the happiness of others — are called away to God, while cruel, useless, harmful people, or those who are a burden to themselves and to everyone around them, are left alive. The first death I ever witnessed, one I shall never forget — that of my dear sister-in-law — left that impression on me. Just as you ask fate why your wonderful brother had to die, so I asked why that angel Lise, who never wronged anyone and in whose soul there was never an unkind thought, had to die. And what do you think, dear friend? Five years have passed since then, and I, with my small understanding, am beginning to see clearly why she had to die, and in what way that death was an expression of the infinite goodness of the Creator, whose every action, though generally incomprehensible to us, is nothing but a manifestation of His infinite love for His creatures. Perhaps, I often think, she was too angelically innocent to have the strength to fulfill all a mother's duties. As a young wife she was irreproachable; perhaps she could not have been so as a mother. As it is, she has not only left us — and particularly Prince Andrew — with the purest memories and regrets, but she will likely receive there a place I dare not hope for myself. But to speak not of her alone — that early and terrible death has had the most beneficial influence on me and on my brother despite all our grief. Then, at the moment of our loss, these thoughts would never have occurred to me; I would have dismissed them with horror. But now they are very clear and certain. I write all this to you, dear friend, only to convince you of the Gospel truth which has become the guiding principle of my life: not a single hair of our heads will fall without His will. And His will is governed only by infinite love for us, and so whatever happens to us is for our good.

You ask whether we shall spend next winter in Moscow. Despite my wish to see you, I don't think so and don't want to. You will be surprised to hear that the reason is Bonaparte! Here is why: my father's health is growing noticeably worse; he cannot tolerate any contradiction and is becoming irritable. This irritability is, as you know, directed mainly at political matters. He cannot endure the idea that Bonaparte is negotiating on equal terms with all the sovereigns of Europe, and especially with ours, the grandson of the Great Catherine! As you know, I am quite indifferent to politics, but from my father's conversations and his talks with Michael Ivanovich I know everything that goes on in the world, and especially about the honors being heaped on Bonaparte — who, it seems, is accepted everywhere in the world as a great man and even Emperor of France, everywhere except at Bald Hills. And my father cannot bear it. It seems to me that it is mainly because of his political views that my father is reluctant to speak of going to Moscow; for he foresees the confrontations that would result from his habit of expressing his opinions without regard for anyone. Any benefit he might get from medical treatment he would lose in the arguments about Bonaparte that would be unavoidable. In any case the matter will be decided very soon.

Our family life goes on as before, except for my brother Andrew's absence. He, as I wrote to you before, has changed very much of late. After his grief, it was only this year that he truly recovered his spirits. He has become again as I knew him when we were children: kind, affectionate, with that heart of gold for which I know no equal. He has realized, it seems to me, that life is not over for him. But along with this inner change he has grown physically much weaker. He has become thinner and more nervous. I worry about him and am glad he is taking this trip abroad that his doctors have long recommended. I hope it will restore his health. You write that in Petersburg he is spoken of as one of the most active, cultivated, and capable of the young men. Forgive my family pride, but I never doubted it. The good he has done for everyone here, from his peasants to the gentry, is incalculable. On his arrival in Petersburg he received only his due. I am always amazed at the way rumors fly from Petersburg to Moscow, especially false ones such as the one you mention — that my brother is engaged to the little Rostova. I do not think my brother will ever marry again, and certainly not her; and this is why: first, I know that though he rarely speaks of the wife he lost, the grief of that loss has gone too deep in his heart for him ever to give her a successor and our little angel a stepmother. Second, as far as I know, that girl is not the kind who could please Prince Andrew. I do not think he would choose her for a wife, and frankly I would not wish it. But I am going on too long and am at the end of my second sheet. Goodbye, my dear friend. May God keep you in His holy and mighty care. My dear friend Mademoiselle Bourienne sends you kisses.
MARY

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 26
paragraphs: In the middle of summer Princess Mary received an unexpected letter from Prince Andrew in Switzerland, containing strange and surprising news. He wrote of his engagement to Natasha Rostova. The entire letter breathed a loving rapture for his betrothed and a tender, confiding affection for his sister. He wrote that he had never loved as he did now and that only now did he understand what life truly was. He asked his sister to forgive him for not having told her of his decision during his last visit to Bald Hills, though he had discussed it with their father. He had not told her for fear she would ask their father for his consent, angering the old man and bearing the brunt of his displeasure without achieving anything. "Besides," he wrote, "the matter was not so definite then as it is now. Our father insisted on a year's delay, and now already six months — half the time — have passed, and my resolve is firmer than ever. If the doctors did not keep me here at the spa I would be back in Russia already, but as it is I must postpone my return for three months. You know me and my relationship with Father. I want nothing from him. I have always been and always shall be independent; but to go against his will and provoke his anger, when he may remain with us only a short time longer, would destroy half my happiness. I am now writing to him about the same matter, and I beg you to choose a good moment to give him my letter and let me know how he takes it, and whether there is any hope that he may agree to shorten the waiting period by four months."
After long hesitation, doubt, and prayer, Princess Mary gave the letter to her father. The next day the old prince said to her quietly:
"Write and tell your brother to wait until I'm dead... It won't be long — I'll set him free soon enough."
The princess tried to reply, but her father wouldn't let her speak and, raising his voice higher and higher, cried:

"Marry, marry, my boy!... A fine family!... Smart people, eh? Rich, eh? Yes, a nice stepmother for little Nicholas! Write and tell him he can marry tomorrow if he likes. She'll be little Nicholas's stepmother, and I'll marry Bourienne!... Ha, ha, ha! He shouldn't be without a stepmother either! Only one thing — no more women in my house. Let him marry and live on his own. Maybe you'd like to go live with him too?" he added, turning to Princess Mary. "Go right ahead! Out into the cold... the cold... the cold!"

After this outburst the prince did not raise the subject again. But his suppressed fury at his son's weak-willed behavior found expression in his treatment of his daughter. To his former pretexts for mockery a new one was added — pointed references to stepmothers and conspicuous courtesies toward Mademoiselle Bourienne.
"Why shouldn't I marry her?" he asked his daughter. "She'll make a splendid princess!"

And lately, to her surprise and bewilderment, Princess Mary noticed that her father really was associating more and more with the Frenchwoman. She wrote to Prince Andrew about their father's reaction but tried to comfort him with hopes of a reconciliation.

Little Nicholas and his education, her brother Andrew, and religion were Princess Mary's joys and consolations; but besides these, since everyone must have personal hopes, Princess Mary had a hidden dream deep in her heart that provided the chief comfort of her life. This comforting dream and hope were given to her by God's folk — the half-witted wanderers and other pilgrims who visited her without the prince's knowledge. The longer she lived and the more she saw of life, the greater was her wonder at the shortsightedness of people who seek pleasure and happiness on this earth: toiling, suffering, struggling, and harming one another to attain an impossible, illusory, sinful happiness. Prince Andrew had loved his wife — she died, but that was not enough: he wanted to bind his happiness to another woman. Her father objected because he wanted a more distinguished and wealthy match for Andrew. And they all struggled and suffered and tormented one another and damaged their eternal souls, all for the sake of benefits that last no more than an instant. Not only do we know this ourselves, but Christ, the Son of God, came down to earth and told us that this life is but a moment, a trial; yet we cling to it and think to find happiness in it. "How is it that no one sees this?" thought Princess Mary. "No one except these despised holy wanderers who, with knapsack on their backs, come to me by the back door, afraid of being seen by the prince — not from fear of mistreatment but to save him from sin. To leave family, home, and all worldly cares, to wander in rough garments from place to place under an assumed name, doing no one any harm but praying for all — for those who drive one away as well as for those who shelter one: there is no life or truth higher than that!"

There was one pilgrim, a quiet, pockmarked little woman of about fifty named Theodosia, who for over thirty years had walked barefoot and worn heavy chains. Princess Mary was especially fond of her. Once, when they sat together in a dimly lit room before an icon, Theodosia was telling the story of her life, and the thought suddenly came to Princess Mary with overwhelming force that Theodosia alone had found the true path. She resolved then and there to become a pilgrim herself. She confided this idea to no one except her confessor, Father Akinfi the monk, who approved. Under the guise of a gift for the pilgrims, Princess Mary prepared a complete pilgrim's outfit for herself: a rough shirt, bast shoes, a coarse coat, and a black kerchief. Often, approaching the chest of drawers that held this secret treasure, Princess Mary would pause, wondering whether the time had come to put her plan into action.

Often, listening to the pilgrims' stories, she was so moved by their simple words — mechanical to them but full of deep meaning for her — that several times she was on the point of abandoning everything and running away from home. In her imagination she already saw herself beside Theodosia, dressed in coarse rags, walking with a staff and a knapsack on her back along a dusty road, making her way from one holy shrine to another, free from envy, earthly love, or desire, and reaching at last the place where there is no more sorrow or sighing, but eternal joy and bliss.

"I shall come to a place and pray there, and before I have time to get attached to it or love it, I shall move on. I will keep walking until my legs give way, and I'll lie down and die somewhere, and at last reach that eternal, peaceful haven where there is neither sorrow nor sighing..." thought Princess Mary.

But afterward, when she saw her father and especially little Koko — Nicholas — her resolve would weaken. She would weep quietly and feel that she was a sinner who loved her father and her little nephew more than she loved God.

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Bible tells us that the absence of labor — idleness — was a condition of the first man's happiness before the Fall. Fallen man has kept a love of idleness, but the curse weighs on the race not only because we must earn our bread by the sweat of our brows, but because our moral nature is such that we cannot be both idle and at ease. An inner voice tells us we are wrong if we are idle. If a man could find a state in which he felt that though idle he was fulfilling his duty, he would have found one of the conditions of that original human happiness. And such a state of obligatory and blameless idleness is the lot of an entire class — the military. The chief attraction of military service has always been and always will be this compulsory and irreproachable idleness.

Nicholas Rostov experienced this blessed condition to the full when, after 1807, he continued to serve in the Pavlograd regiment, in which he now commanded the squadron he had taken over from Denisov.

Rostov had become a bluff, good-natured fellow whom his Moscow acquaintances would have considered a bit rough around the edges, but who was liked and respected by his comrades, subordinates, and superiors, and who was well content with his life. Of late, in 1809, he found in letters from home more and more complaints from his mother that their affairs were falling into ever-greater disorder, and that it was time for him to come back and comfort his aging parents.

Reading these letters, Nicholas felt a dread of being dragged away from the surroundings where, shielded from all of life's entanglements, he was living so calmly and quietly. He sensed that sooner or later he would have to plunge back into that whirlpool of life, with its embarrassments and problems to be sorted out, its accounts with stewards, quarrels and intrigues, its obligations, the social world, and Sonya's love and his promise to her. It was all impossibly difficult and complicated, and he replied to his mother in cold, formal letters in French, beginning "My dear Mama" and ending "Your obedient son," that said nothing about when he would return. In 1810 he received letters from his parents telling him of Natasha's engagement to Bolkonsky, and that the wedding would be in a year because the old prince was making difficulties. This letter grieved and annoyed Nicholas. First, he was sorry that Natasha — for whom he cared more than for anyone else in the family — was being lost to the home; and second, from his hussar's point of view, he regretted not having been there to show that fellow Bolkonsky that a connection with his family was no such great honor, and that if he loved Natasha he could do without his doddering father's permission. For a moment he wondered whether to apply for leave to see Natasha before her wedding, but then came the maneuvers, and his thoughts about Sonya, and the confusion of family finances — and Nicholas put it off again. But in the spring of that year he received a letter from his mother, written without his father's knowledge, and that letter persuaded him to return. She wrote that if he didn't come and take charge of things, their entire property would be sold at auction and they would all be left destitute. The count was so weak, trusted Mitenka so completely, and was so good-natured, that everyone took advantage of him and things were going from bad to worse. "For God's sake, I beg you, come at once if you don't want to make me and the whole family wretched," the countess wrote.
This letter moved Nicholas. He had the practical common sense that showed him what he ought to do.

The right thing now was, if not to resign from the service, at least to go home on leave. Why he had to go he could not exactly say; but after his afternoon nap he ordered Mars saddled — an extremely vicious gray stallion that hadn't been ridden in a long time — and when he came back with the horse lathered in sweat, he informed Lavrushka (Denisov's servant who had stayed on with him) and the comrades who turned up that evening that he was applying for leave and going home. Difficult and strange as it was to contemplate leaving without finding out from headquarters — and this interested him enormously — whether he'd been promoted to captain or would receive the Order of St. Anne for the last maneuvers; strange as it was to think of going without having sold his three roan horses to the Polish Count Golukhovski, who was haggling over the horses Rostov had bet he'd sell for two thousand rubles; incomprehensible as it was that the ball the hussars were throwing in honor of the Polish Mademoiselle Przazdziecka — in rivalry with the Uhlans, who had given one for their own Polish Mademoiselle Borzozowska — would take place without him; he knew he must leave this good, bright world for somewhere where everything was stupid and confused. A week later he got his leave. His hussar comrades — not just his regiment but the whole brigade — gave Rostov a farewell dinner at fifteen rubles a head, with two bands and two choirs of singers. Rostov danced the Trepak with Major Basov; the tipsy officers tossed, hugged, and dropped Rostov; the soldiers of the third squadron tossed him too and shouted "Hurrah!"; then they bundled him into his sleigh and escorted him to the first post station.

During the first half of the journey — from Kremenchug to Kiev — all of Rostov's thoughts, as usually happens, were still with the squadron he'd left behind. But once he was more than halfway he began to forget his three roans and his quartermaster Dozhoyveyko, and instead wondered anxiously how things would be at Otradnoe and what he would find there. His thoughts of home grew stronger the closer he got — much stronger, as if this feeling obeyed the law by which gravitational force increases as the distance decreases. At the last post station before Otradnoe he gave the driver a three-ruble tip, and on arriving he ran up the steps of his home, breathless as a boy.

After the ecstasy of reunion, and after that odd feeling of unmet expectations — the sense that "everything's the same, so why did I rush?" — Nicholas began to settle into his old home world. His father and mother were much the same, only a little older. What was new about them was a certain anxiety and occasional discord that hadn't existed before, and which, as Nicholas soon discovered, was caused by the bad state of their finances. Sonya was nearly twenty; she had stopped growing prettier and promised nothing more than she already was, but that was enough. She radiated happiness and love from the moment Nicholas returned, and the faithful, unchanging love of this girl had a cheering effect on him. Petya and Natasha surprised Nicholas most. Petya was a big, handsome boy of thirteen — merry, witty, and mischievous, with a voice that was already breaking. As for Natasha, for a long time Nicholas just kept staring at her and laughing.
"You're not the same at all," he said.
"What? Am I uglier?"
"On the contrary — but such dignity! A princess!" he whispered to her.
"Yes, yes, yes!" cried Natasha joyfully.
She told him about her romance with Prince Andrew, about his visit to Otradnoe, and showed him his latest letter.
"Well, are you happy?" asked Natasha. "I feel so peaceful and content now."
"Very happy," answered Nicholas. "He's an excellent man... And are you very much in love?"

"How shall I put it?" replied Natasha. "I was in love with Boris, with my teacher, and with Denisov, but this is completely different. I feel calm and settled. I know that no better man exists, and I am at peace now. Not at all like before."

Nicholas expressed his disapproval of the year-long postponement of the marriage; but Natasha attacked her brother with exasperation, insisting it couldn't be otherwise, that it would be wrong to join a family against the father's wishes, and that she herself wanted it this way.
"You don't understand at all," she said.
Nicholas fell silent and agreed with her.

Her brother often wondered as he looked at her. She didn't seem at all like a girl in love and separated from her fiance. She was even-tempered, calm, and as cheerful as ever. This amazed Nicholas and even made him skeptical about Bolkonsky's courtship. He couldn't quite believe that her fate was sealed, especially since he hadn't seen her with Prince Andrew. It always seemed to him that there was something not quite right about this planned marriage.

"Why this delay? Why no formal engagement?" he thought. Once, when he touched on the subject with his mother, he discovered — to his surprise and a certain satisfaction — that deep down she too had doubts about the marriage.

"You see, he writes," she said, showing her son a letter from Prince Andrew with that hidden resentment a mother always harbors toward her daughter's future married happiness, "he writes that he won't come before December. What can be keeping him? His health, probably! It's very delicate. Don't tell Natasha. And don't think too much of her high spirits: that's because she's living through the last days of her girlhood, but I know what she's like every time a letter from him arrives! Still, God willing, everything will turn out well!" She always ended with these words. "He is an excellent man!"

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: After reaching home Nicholas was at first serious and even glum. He was weighed down by the looming necessity of dealing with the stupid business matters his mother had called him home for. To get the burden off his back as quickly as possible, on the third day after his arrival he went, angry and scowling and refusing to say where he was going, to Mitenka's lodge and demanded a full accounting. But what a "full accounting" might look like, Nicholas knew even less than the frightened and bewildered Mitenka. The interview and review of the books did not last long. The village elder, a peasant representative, and the village clerk, who were waiting in the corridor, heard with a mixture of fear and delight first the young count's voice roaring and snapping and rising louder and louder, and then foul words — terrible words — erupting one after another.
"Thief!... Ungrateful wretch!... I'll hack the dog to pieces! I'm not my father!... Robbing us!..." and so on.

Then with no less fear and delight they watched the young count, red-faced and with bloodshot eyes, drag Mitenka out by the scruff of his neck and apply his boot and knee to his backside with remarkable agility, timing each kick between the words and shouting: "Get out! Never let me see your face here again, you scoundrel!"

Mitenka flew headlong down the six steps and ran off into the shrubbery. (This shrubbery was a well-known refuge for wrongdoers at Otradnoe. Mitenka himself, returning drunk from town, used to hide there, and many of the residents at Otradnoe, hiding from Mitenka, knew of its protective qualities.)
Mitenka's wife and sisters-in-law poked their heads and frightened faces out the door of a room where a bright samovar was boiling and where the steward's high bed stood with its patchwork quilt.
The young count paid them no attention but, breathing hard, strode past with determination and went into the house.

The countess, who heard at once from the maids what had happened at the lodge, was reassured by the thought that their affairs would surely now improve, but at the same time worried about what the excitement might do to her son. She went several times on tiptoe to his door and listened as he lit one pipe after another.
The next day the old count took his son aside and, with an embarrassed smile, said:
"But you know, my dear boy, it's a shame you lost your temper! Mitenka has told me all about it."
"I knew it," thought Nicholas, "I'd never make sense of anything in this crazy world."
"You were angry because he hadn't entered those seven hundred rubles. But they were carried forward — and you didn't look at the other page."
"Papa, he's a crook and a thief! I know he is! And what I did, I did. But if you prefer, I won't say another word to him."

"No, my dear boy" — the count, too, felt embarrassed; he knew he had mismanaged his wife's property and was to blame toward his children, but he didn't know how to fix it — "No, I beg you to take care of the business. I'm old. I..."
"No, Papa. Forgive me if I've upset you. I understand it all even less than you do."

"To hell with all these peasants, and money matters, and carrying things forward from page to page," he thought. "I used to understand what a 'corner' and the stakes at cards meant, but I don't understand carrying forward at all," he told himself, and after that he didn't meddle in business affairs. But once the countess called her son in and told him that she held a promissory note from Anna Mikhaylovna for two thousand rubles, and asked him what he thought they should do with it.

"This," answered Nicholas. "You say it's up to me. Well, I don't like Anna Mikhaylovna and I don't like Boris, but they were our friends and they're poor. So — this!" And he tore up the note, which made the old countess weep tears of joy. After that, young Rostov took no further part in business affairs and threw himself with passionate enthusiasm into what was for him a new pursuit — hunting — for which his father maintained a large establishment.

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The weather was already turning wintry and morning frosts hardened the earth, which was saturated from autumn rains. The green of the pastures stood out sharply against the brownish strips of winter rye trampled by cattle, and against the pale yellow stubble of the spring buckwheat. The wooded ravines and copses, still green islands amid the black fields and stubble at the end of August, had turned to golden and crimson islands amid the green winter rye. The hares had already half changed their summer coats, the fox cubs were beginning to scatter, and the young wolves were bigger than dogs. It was the best time of year for the hunt. The hounds of the passionate young sportsman Rostov had not only reached peak winter condition but were so worn out that at a meeting of the huntsmen it was decided to give them three days' rest and then, on the sixteenth of September, to set out on a distant expedition to the oak grove where there was an undisturbed litter of wolf cubs.

All that day the hounds stayed home. It was frosty and the air was sharp, but toward evening the sky clouded over and it began to thaw. On the fifteenth, when young Rostov in his dressing gown looked out the window, he saw the morning was perfect for hunting: the sky seemed to be melting and sinking earthward with no wind at all. The only movement in the air was the slow fall of microscopic droplets of drizzling mist. The bare twigs in the garden were hung with transparent drops that fell on the freshly fallen leaves. The earth in the kitchen garden looked wet and black and glistened like poppy seeds, merging at a short distance into the dull, moist veil of fog. Nicholas went out onto the wet, muddy porch. There was a smell of rotting leaves and of dog. Milka, a black-spotted, broad-haunched bitch with prominent dark eyes, got up on seeing her master, stretched her hind legs, crouched like a hare, and then suddenly leaped up and licked him right on the nose and mustache. Another borzoi, catching sight of his master from the garden path, arched his back and, rushing headlong toward the porch with tail raised, began rubbing himself against his legs.

"O-hoy!" came that inimitable huntsman's call at that moment — the one that blends the deepest bass with the shrillest treble — and around the corner came Daniel, the head huntsman and chief kennelman: a gray, wrinkled old man with hair cut straight across his forehead in the Ukrainian style, a long bent whip in his hand, and that look of independence and scorn for everything that is only found in huntsmen. He doffed his Circassian cap to his master and looked at him contemptuously. This contempt was not offensive to his master. Nicholas knew that this Daniel, who looked down on everyone and considered himself above all of them, was still his serf and his huntsman.

"Daniel!" Nicholas said timidly, conscious at the sight of the weather, the hounds, and the huntsman that he was being swept away by that irresistible passion for the hunt that makes a man forget all his previous resolutions, as a lover forgets everything in the presence of his beloved.

"What are your orders, your excellency?" said the huntsman in his deep bass — deep as a deacon's and hoarse from years of halloing — as two flashing black eyes gazed from beneath his brows at his master, who was saying nothing. "Can you resist it?" those eyes seemed to ask.
"Good day for it, eh? For a hunt and a gallop, eh?" asked Nicholas, scratching Milka behind the ears.
Daniel didn't answer, but winked instead.

"I sent Uvarka out at dawn to listen," his deep voice boomed after a minute's pause. "He says she's moved them into the Otradnoe enclosure. They were howling there." This meant that the she-wolf they both knew about had moved with her cubs into the Otradnoe copse, a small wood about a mile and a half from the house.
"We ought to go, don't you think?" said Nicholas. "Come to me with Uvarka."
"As you wish."
"Then hold off feeding them."
"Yes, sir."

Five minutes later Daniel and Uvarka were standing in Nicholas's large study. Though Daniel was not a big man, seeing him in a room was like seeing a horse or a bear among the furniture and trappings of human life. Daniel felt this himself, and as usual stood just inside the door, trying to speak softly and keep still for fear of breaking something in the master's apartment. He rushed to say everything necessary so he could get out from under that ceiling, back into the open air under the sky.

Having finished his questions and extracted from Daniel the opinion that the hounds were fit — Daniel himself wanted to go — Nicholas ordered the horses saddled. But just as Daniel was about to leave, Natasha came in with quick steps, her hair not done up and her old nurse's big shawl wrapped around her. Petya ran in at the same moment.
"You're going?" asked Natasha. "I knew you would! Sonya said you wouldn't, but I knew that today was the kind of day you couldn't resist."

"Yes, we're going," replied Nicholas reluctantly, for today he planned to hunt seriously and didn't want to bring Natasha and Petya along. "We're going, but only after wolves — it would be dull for you."
"You know it's my greatest pleasure," said Natasha. "It's not fair — you're going off by yourself, having the horses saddled, and you didn't even tell us."
"'No barrier bars a Russian's path' — we're going!" shouted Petya.
"But you can't. Mama said you mustn't," said Nicholas to Natasha.
"Yes, I'll go. I'm definitely going," said Natasha firmly. "Daniel, tell them to saddle up for us, and have Michael come with my dogs," she added to the huntsman.

It seemed irksome and improper to Daniel to be in a room at all, but to deal with a young lady struck him as simply impossible. He lowered his eyes and hurried out as if it were none of his business, careful not to cause any accidental harm to the young lady.

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: The old count, who had always maintained an enormous hunting establishment but had now turned it entirely over to his son, was in very good spirits on this fifteenth of September and prepared to join the others.

Within an hour the whole hunting party was assembled at the porch. Nicholas, with a stern and serious air that showed there was no time for trifles, walked past Natasha and Petya, who were trying to tell him something. He inspected every detail of the hunt, sent a pack of hounds and huntsmen ahead to find the quarry, mounted his chestnut Donets, whistled to his own leash of borzois, and set off across the threshing ground toward a field that led to the Otradnoe wood. The old count's horse, a sorrel gelding called Viflynanka, was led by his groom, while the count himself rode in a small trap to a spot reserved for him.

They were taking fifty-four hounds, with six hunt attendants and whippers-in. Besides the family, there were eight borzoi keepers and more than forty borzois, so that — counting the borzois on leash belonging to family members — there were about a hundred and thirty dogs and twenty horsemen.

Each dog knew its master and its name. Each man in the hunt knew his job, his position, and what he had to do. As soon as they passed the fence they all spread out evenly and quietly, without noise or talk, along the road and field leading to the Otradnoe covert.

The horses stepped across the field as over a thick carpet, now and then splashing into puddles as they crossed a road. The misty sky still seemed to be descending evenly and imperceptibly toward the earth; the air was still, warm, and silent. Occasionally the whistle of a huntsman, the snort of a horse, the crack of a whip, or the whine of a straggling hound could be heard.
When they had gone just under a mile, five more riders with dogs appeared out of the mist, approaching the Rostovs. In front rode a fresh-looking, handsome old man with a large gray mustache.
"Good morning, Uncle!" said Nicholas as the old man drew near.

"That's it. Come on!... I was sure of it," began "Uncle." He was a distant relative of the Rostovs', a man of modest means and their neighbor. "I knew you wouldn't be able to resist, and it's a good thing you're going. That's it! Come on!" — this was "Uncle's" favorite expression. "Get to the covert at once — my man Girchik says the Ilagins are at Korniki with their pack. That's it! Come on! They'll snatch the cubs from right under your nose."
"That's where I'm heading. Shall we join up our packs?" asked Nicholas.

The hounds were combined into one pack, and "Uncle" and Nicholas rode on side by side. Natasha, muffled in shawls that couldn't hide her eager face and shining eyes, galloped up to them. She was followed by Petya, who always kept close to her, by Michael the huntsman, and by a groom assigned to look after her. Petya, laughing, kept whipping and tugging at his horse. Natasha sat easily and confidently on her black Arabchik, reining him in with a firm hand.
"Uncle" looked disapprovingly at Petya and Natasha. He didn't like mixing frivolity with the serious business of hunting.
"Good morning, Uncle! We're coming too!" shouted Petya.
"Good morning, good morning! But don't overrun the hounds," said "Uncle" sternly.
"Nicholas, what a wonderful dog Trunila is! He recognized me," said Natasha, referring to her favorite hound.

"First of all, Trunila is not a 'dog' but a harrier," thought Nicholas, and he gave his sister a stern look, trying to make her feel the distance that ought to separate them at this moment. Natasha understood.
"You mustn't think we'll be in anyone's way, Uncle," she said. "We'll go to our spots and won't budge."
"Good idea, little countess," said "Uncle." "Only don't fall off your horse — that's it, come on! — because you've got nothing to hold on to."

The oasis of the Otradnoe covert came into sight a few hundred yards away, and the huntsmen were already nearing it. Rostov, having finally agreed with "Uncle" where to position the hounds and having shown Natasha where to stand — a spot where nothing could possibly break out — rode around above the ravine.
"Well, nephew, you're going after a big wolf," said "Uncle." "Don't let her slip!"

"That's as may be," answered Rostov. "Karay, here!" he shouted, responding to "Uncle's" remark with a call to his borzoi. Karay was a shaggy old dog with a hanging jowl, famous for having tackled a big wolf single-handedly. They all took up their positions.

The old count, knowing his son's passion for the hunt, hurried so as not to be late, and the huntsmen had not yet reached their places when Count Ilya Rostov, cheerful, flushed, and with quivering cheeks, drove up with his black horses over the winter rye to the spot reserved for him, where a wolf might emerge. Having straightened his coat and fastened on his hunting knives and horn, he mounted his good, sleek, well-fed horse Viflynanka — which was turning gray, like himself. His carriage was sent home. Count Ilya Rostov, though not a keen sportsman at heart, knew the rules of the hunt well. He rode to the bushy edge of the road where he was to stand, settled his reins, got comfortable in the saddle, and — feeling he was ready — looked about with a smile.

Beside him was Simon Chekmar, his personal attendant, an old horseman now somewhat stiff in the saddle. Chekmar held in leash three formidable wolfhounds who had, however, grown fat like their master and his horse. Two wise old dogs lay nearby, unleashed. About a hundred paces farther along the edge of the wood stood Mitka, the count's other groom — a daring horseman and enthusiastic rider to hounds. Before the hunt, following an old tradition, the count had drunk a silver cupful of mulled brandy, had a snack, and washed it down with half a bottle of his favorite Bordeaux.

He was a bit flushed from the wine and the drive. His eyes were somewhat moist and glittered more than usual, and as he sat in the saddle wrapped in his fur coat, he looked like a child taken out for a treat.

The thin, hollow-cheeked Chekmar, having gotten everything ready, kept glancing at his master — with whom he had lived on the best of terms for thirty years — and sensing his mood, expected a pleasant chat. A third person rode up cautiously through the wood (clearly he had been taught a lesson) and stopped behind the count. This was a gray-bearded old man in a woman's cloak, with a tall peaked cap on his head. He was the buffoon, who went by a woman's name — Nastasya Ivanovna.
"Well, Nastasya Ivanovna!" the count whispered, winking at him. "If you scare off the quarry, Daniel will give you what for!"
"I know a thing or two myself!" said Nastasya Ivanovna.
"Shh!" whispered the count and turned to Simon. "Have you seen the young countess? Where is she?"
"With young Count Petya, by the Zharov tall grass," answered Simon, smiling. "Though she's a lady, she's very keen on hunting."
"And you're surprised at the way she rides, Simon, eh?" said the count. "She's as good as any man!"
"Of course! It's wonderful. So bold, so easy!"
"And Nicholas? Where is he? By the Lyadov upland, isn't he?"
"Yes, sir. He knows where to stand. He understands the sport so well that Daniel and I are often quite amazed," said Simon, knowing what would please his master.
"Rides well, eh? And how fine he looks on his horse, eh?"

"A perfect picture! The other day he chased a fox out of the tall grass by the Zavarzinsk thicket! He jumped over a terrifying obstacle — what a sight when they burst from the covert! The horse worth a thousand rubles and the rider beyond all price! Yes, you'd have to search far to find another like him."
"Far indeed..." repeated the count, evidently wishing Simon had said more. "Far indeed," he said, turning back the skirt of his coat to reach his snuffbox.

"The other day when he came from church in full uniform, Michael Sidorych..." Simon didn't finish, for on the still air he had clearly caught the sound of the hunt — just two or three hounds giving tongue. He bent his head and listened, raising a warning finger at his master. "They're on the scent of the cubs..." he whispered, "heading straight for the Lyadov uplands."

The count, forgetting to smooth the smile off his face, gazed into the distance down the narrow open space ahead, holding his snuffbox but not taking any. After the cry of the hounds came the deep tones of Daniel's hunting horn calling the wolf; the pack joined the first three hounds and could be heard in full cry, with that special lift in the note that signals they are after a wolf. The whippers-in stopped urging on the hounds and changed to the cry of ulyulyu, and above all the others rose Daniel's voice — now a deep bass, now piercingly shrill. His voice seemed to fill the whole forest and carried far out into the open field.

After listening in silence for a few moments, the count and his attendant could tell that the hounds had split into two packs: the larger pack, giving eager tongue, began to fade in the distance; the other rushed past through the wood near the count, and it was with this second pack that Daniel's voice could be heard calling ulyulyu. The sounds of both packs mingled and broke apart, but both were growing more distant.

Simon sighed and bent down to straighten a leash that a young borzoi had tangled; the count sighed too and, noticing the snuffbox in his hand, opened it and took a pinch. "Back!" cried Simon to a borzoi that was pushing forward out of the wood. The count flinched and dropped the snuffbox. Nastasya Ivanovna dismounted to pick it up. The count and Simon were looking at him.
Then, unexpectedly — as often happens — the sound of the hunt suddenly seemed to rush toward them, as if the hounds in full cry and Daniel calling ulyulyu were right in front of them.
The count turned and saw, on his right, Mitka staring at him with eyes popping out of his head, raising his cap and pointing urgently to the other side.
"Look out!" Mitka shouted, in a voice that showed he had been straining to let that word loose for some time, and releasing the borzois he galloped toward the count.

The count and Simon burst out of the wood and saw to their left a wolf trotting at an easy lope, swaying gently from side to side, heading toward the very spot where they were standing. The angry borzois whined, tore free of their leashes, and dashed past the horses' feet at the wolf.

The wolf paused, turned its heavy head toward the dogs with an awkward motion — like a man with a sore throat — and, still swaying slightly, gave a couple of leaps and, with a swish of its tail, vanished into the edge of the wood. At the same instant, with a cry like a wail, first one hound, then another, then another, came flying helter-skelter from the wood on the opposite side, and the whole pack raced across the field toward the very spot where the wolf had disappeared. The hazel bushes parted behind the hounds, and Daniel's chestnut horse appeared, dark with sweat. On its long back Daniel sat hunched forward, capless, his disheveled gray hair hanging over his flushed, sweating face.
"Ulyulyulyu! Ulyulyu!" he cried. When he spotted the count, his eyes flashed like lightning.
"Damn you!" he shouted, raising his whip threateningly at the count.

"You let the wolf go!... Call yourselves sportsmen!" And as if scorning to waste further words on the frightened and shamefaced count, he lashed the heaving flanks of his sweating chestnut with all the fury the count had provoked and flew off after the hounds. The count, like a punished schoolboy, looked around, trying to win Simon's sympathy with a smile. But Simon was already gone — galloping around through the bushes while the rest of the field closed in from both sides, all trying to head off the wolf. But it vanished into the woods before they could reach it.

chapters.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: Nicholas Rostov meanwhile stayed at his post, waiting for the wolf. From the way the hunt approached and receded, from the cries of the dogs whose voices he knew well, from how the voices of the huntsmen rose and fell, he could tell what was happening at the copse. He knew that young and old wolves were there, that the hounds had split into two packs, that somewhere a wolf was being chased, and that something had gone wrong. He expected the wolf to come his way at any moment. He made a thousand guesses about where and from which side the animal would appear and how he would set upon it. Hope alternated with despair. Several times he found himself praying to God to let the wolf come his way. He prayed with that intense, embarrassed feeling people have when they pray in moments of great excitement over trivial things. "What would it cost You to do this for me?" he said to God. "I know You are great and that it's a sin to ask, but for God's sake let the old wolf come my way, and let Karay spring at its throat — right in front of Uncle, who's watching from over there — and seize it in a death grip!" A thousand times during that half hour Rostov cast eager, restless glances at the edge of the wood with its two scrawny oaks rising above the aspen undergrowth, and the gully with its eroded bank, and Uncle's cap just visible above a bush to his right.

"No, I won't have that luck," thought Rostov. "And yet, what wouldn't it be worth! It's not meant to be! Everywhere — at cards, in war — I'm always unlucky." Memories of Austerlitz and of Dolokhov flashed rapidly through his mind. "Just once in my life to get an old wolf — that's all I ask!" he thought, straining his eyes and ears, looking left and then right, listening for the slightest change in the hounds' cries.

Again he looked to the right and saw something running toward him across the empty field. "No, it can't be!" thought Rostov, drawing a deep breath like someone witnessing the arrival of something long hoped for. The peak of happiness was reached — and so simply, without warning, or noise, or fanfare, that Rostov couldn't believe his eyes and remained in doubt for a full second. The wolf ran forward and jumped heavily over a gully in its path. It was an old animal with a gray back and a big reddish belly. It ran without haste, clearly confident no one had spotted it. Rostov, holding his breath, glanced at the borzois. They stood or lay there, not seeing the wolf, not grasping the situation. Old Karay had turned his head and was angrily snapping at fleas, baring his yellow teeth and nipping at his hind legs.

"Ulyulyulyu!" Rostov whispered, pursing his lips. The borzois jumped up, jerking their leash-rings and pricking their ears. Karay finished scratching, cocked his ears, and stood up with quivering tail, tufts of matted hair hanging from his thigh.

"Should I release them or not?" Nicholas asked himself as the wolf approached from the copse. Suddenly the wolf's whole expression changed: it shuddered, seeing what it had probably never seen before — human eyes fixed upon it — and, turning its head slightly toward Rostov, it paused.
"Forward or back? No matter — forward..." the wolf seemed to decide, and it moved on without another backward glance, in a quiet, long, easy but resolute lope.

"Ulyulyu!" cried Nicholas in a voice not his own, and of its own accord his good horse plunged headlong downhill, leaping over gullies to cut off the wolf, and the borzois raced past even faster. Nicholas didn't hear his own shout, didn't feel himself galloping, didn't see the borzois or the ground beneath him — he saw only the wolf, which quickened its pace and bounded in the same direction along the hollow. The first to come into view was Milka, with her black markings and powerful hindquarters, gaining on the wolf. Closer and closer... now she was alongside. But the wolf turned its head to face her, and instead of putting on speed as she usually did, Milka suddenly raised her tail and braced her front legs.
"Ulyulyulyulyu!" shouted Nicholas.

The reddish Lyubim rushed forward from behind Milka, sprang boldly at the wolf, and seized it by the haunches — but instantly jumped away in terror. The wolf crouched, snapped its jaws, and rose again, bounding forward. All the borzois followed at a distance of a couple of feet but couldn't close the gap.
"She'll get away! No, it's impossible!" thought Nicholas, still shouting in a hoarse voice.

"Karay, ulyulyu!" he called, looking around for the old borzoi who was now his only hope. Karay, with all the strength his age still allowed, stretched himself to the utmost and, watching the wolf, galloped heavily at an angle to cut it off. But the wolf's speed and the borzoi's slower pace made it clear that Karay had misjudged the angle. Nicholas could already see the woods not far ahead — the wolf would certainly escape if it reached them. But coming toward him from that direction he saw hounds and a huntsman galloping almost straight at the wolf. There was still hope. A long, yellowish young borzoi that Nicholas didn't recognize — from another leash — rushed at the wolf from the front and nearly knocked it over. But the wolf recovered faster than anyone could have expected and, snapping its jaws, flew at the yellowish borzoi, which fell with a piercing yelp, its head hitting the ground, blood pouring from a gash in its side.
"Karay! Old boy!..." wailed Nicholas.

Thanks to the delay caused by the young borzoi's charge, old Karay, with his matted hair hanging from his thigh, had closed to within five paces. As if sensing its danger, the wolf glanced at Karay, tucked its tail even tighter between its legs, and ran faster. But at that moment Nicholas saw something happen to Karay — the borzoi was suddenly on top of the wolf, and together they tumbled into a gully just ahead.

That instant — when Nicholas saw the wolf struggling in the gully with the dogs while from beneath them he could make out its gray fur and outstretched hind leg and its frightened, choking head with ears laid back, Karay pinning it by the throat — was the happiest moment of his life. With his hand on the saddlebow, he was ready to dismount and stab the wolf when it suddenly thrust its head up from the mass of dogs and got its front paws onto the edge of the gully. It clicked its teeth — Karay no longer had it by the throat — and with a movement of its hind legs leaped out of the gully. Having shaken off the dogs, it tucked its tail in again and loped forward. Karay, his fur bristling and probably bruised or hurt, climbed with difficulty out of the gully.
"Oh my God! Why?" Nicholas cried in despair.
"Uncle's" huntsman was galloping from the other side to block the wolf's path, and his borzois once more stopped its advance. It was hemmed in again.
