"Yes, I was much criticized," he said, "both for that war and the peace... but everything came at the right time. Everything comes to him who knows how to wait. And there were just as many advisers there as here..." he went on, returning to the topic of "advisers" that clearly preoccupied him. "Ah, those advisers!" he said. "If we had listened to them all, we'd never have made peace with Turkey and would never have finished that war. Everything in haste, but the more haste, the less speed. Kamensky would have been ruined if he hadn't died. He stormed fortresses with thirty thousand men. It's not hard to capture a fortress, but it's hard to win a campaign. For that, you don't need storming and attacking—you need patience and time. Kamensky sent soldiers against Rushchuk, but I used only those two things—patience and time—and I took more fortresses than Kamensky, and made the Turks eat horseflesh!" He swayed his head. "And the French will too, believe me," he went on, growing more animated and striking his chest, "I'll make them eat horseflesh!" And tears again dimmed his eyes.
* "Everything comes in time to him who knows how to wait."
"But won't we have to accept battle?" asked Prince Andrew.

"We will if everyone wants it; it can't be helped... But believe me, my dear boy, there is nothing stronger than those two: patience and time—they will do everything. But the advisers don't see it that way, and that's the trouble. Some want one thing, others want something else. What's one to do?" he asked, evidently expecting an answer. "Well, what do you want us to do?" he repeated, and his eye shone with a deep, shrewd look. "I'll tell you what to do," he continued, since Prince Andrew still didn't reply: "I'll tell you what to do, and what I do. When in doubt, my dear fellow"—he paused—"do nothing." He articulated the French proverb deliberately.
* "Don't see it that way—that's the trouble."
* "When in doubt, my dear fellow, do nothing."

"Well, goodbye, my dear fellow; remember that with all my heart I share your sorrow, and that for you I am not a Serene Highness, nor a prince, nor a commander in chief, but a father! If you need anything, come straight to me. Goodbye, my dear boy."
Again he embraced and kissed Prince Andrew, but before the latter had left the room Kutuzov gave a sigh of relief and went back to his unfinished novel, The Knights of the Swan by Madame de Genlis.

Prince Andrew could not have explained how or why, but after that interview with Kutuzov he returned to his regiment reassured about the general course of affairs and about the man to whom they had been entrusted. The more he recognized the absence of all personal ambition in the old man—in whom there seemed to remain only the habit of old passions, and in place of an intellect that groups events and draws conclusions, only the ability to calmly observe the course of events—the more reassured he was that everything would be as it should. "He won't introduce any plan of his own. He won't devise or initiate anything," thought Prince Andrew, "but he will listen to everything, remember everything, and put everything in its proper place. He will not obstruct anything useful or permit anything harmful. He understands that there is something stronger and more important than his own will—the inevitable course of events—and he can see them and grasp their significance, and seeing that significance, can refrain from meddling and renounce his personal desires. And above all," thought Prince Andrew, "one believes in him because he's Russian, despite the novel by Genlis and the French proverbs, and because his voice shook when he said: 'What they have brought us to!' and there was a sob in it when he said he would 'make them eat horseflesh!'"

On such feelings—more or less dimly shared by all—were founded the unanimity and general approval with which, despite the court's influence, Kutuzov's popular appointment as commander in chief was received.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: After the Emperor left Moscow, life flowed on there in its usual course, and that course was so ordinary that it was hard to remember the recent days of patriotic fervor, hard to believe that Russia was really in danger and that the members of the English Club were also sons of the Fatherland, ready to sacrifice everything for it. The one thing that recalled the patriotic enthusiasm everyone had shown during the Emperor's stay was the call for contributions of men and money—a demand that, once the promises had been made, assumed a legal, official form and became unavoidable.

With the enemy's approach to Moscow, the Muscovites' view of their situation did not grow more serious but actually became more frivolous, as always happens with people who see a great danger approaching. At the approach of danger, two voices always speak with equal power in the human soul: one very reasonably tells a person to consider the nature of the danger and the means of escaping it; the other, still more reasonably, says that it is too depressing and painful to think about the danger since it is not in our power to foresee everything and avert the general course of events, and that it is therefore better to ignore what is painful until it arrives, and to think about what is pleasant. In solitude, a person generally listens to the first voice; in society, to the second. So it was now with the people of Moscow. It had been a long time since people had been as merry in Moscow as that year.

Rostopchin's broadsheets, headed by woodcuts of a tavern, a barkeeper, and a Moscow citizen named Karpushka Chigirin "who—having been a militiaman and having had a bit too much at the pub—heard that Napoleon wanted to come to Moscow, got angry, cursed the French in terrible language, came out of the tavern, and under the sign of the eagle began to address the crowd" were read and discussed, alongside the latest witty verses by Vasili Lvovich Pushkin.

In the Club's corner room, members gathered to read these broadsheets, and some enjoyed the way Karpushka mocked the French, saying: "They'll swell up on Russian cabbage, burst on our buckwheat porridge, and choke on cabbage soup. They're all dwarfs, and one peasant woman could toss three of them with a pitchfork." Others disliked the tone and called it stupid and vulgar. It was said that Rostopchin had expelled all Frenchmen and even all foreigners from Moscow, and that there had been spies and agents of Napoleon among them; but this was mainly told so as to introduce Rostopchin's witty remark on the occasion. The foreigners were deported to Nizhny by boat, and Rostopchin had told them in French: "Look inside yourselves; get into the boat, and don't turn it into the boat of Charon." There was talk of all the government offices having already been moved from Moscow, and to this Shinshin's quip was added—that for that alone, Moscow ought to be grateful to Napoleon. It was said that Mamonov's regiment would cost him eight hundred thousand rubles, and that Bezukhov had spent even more on his, but that the best thing about Bezukhov's gesture was that he himself was going to put on a uniform and ride at the head of his regiment without charging anything for the show.
* "Look inside yourselves; get into the boat, and take care not to make it the boat of Charon."
"You don't spare anyone," said Julie Drubetskaya as she gathered and pressed together a bunch of shredded lint with her thin, ringed fingers.
Julie was preparing to leave Moscow the next day and was hosting a farewell party.
"Bezukhov is ridiculous, but he is so kind and good-natured. What pleasure is there in being so caustic?"
"A forfeit!" cried a young man in militia uniform whom Julie called "my knight" and who was traveling with her to Nizhny.

In Julie's circle, as in many other circles in Moscow, it had been agreed that they would speak nothing but Russian, and anyone who slipped into French would pay a fine to the Committee of Voluntary Contributions.
"Another forfeit for a Gallicism," said a Russian writer who was present. "'What pleasure is there in being' is not Russian!"
"You don't spare anyone," Julie continued to the young man, ignoring the writer's remark.

"For 'caustic'—I'm guilty and I'll pay, and I'm prepared to pay again for the pleasure of telling you the truth. For Gallicisms I won't take responsibility," she said, turning to the writer. "I have neither the money nor the time, like Prince Galitsyn, to hire a tutor to teach me Russian!"

"Ah, here he is!" she added. "When one— No, no," she said to the militia officer, "you won't catch me. Speak of the sun and you see its rays!" and she smiled charmingly at Pierre. "We were just talking about you," she said with the easy dishonesty natural to a society woman. "We were saying your regiment would certainly be better than Mamonov's."
"Oh, don't talk to me about my regiment," replied Pierre, kissing his hostess's hand and taking a seat beside her. "I'm so sick of it."
"You will, of course, command it yourself?" said Julie, directing a sly, sarcastic glance at the militia officer.

The latter, in Pierre's presence, had stopped being sarcastic, and his face expressed confusion about what Julie's smile might mean. Despite his absentmindedness and good nature, Pierre's personality immediately checked any attempt to ridicule him to his face.
"No," said Pierre, with a laughing glance at his large, stout body. "I'd make too easy a target for the French. Besides, I doubt I could even climb onto a horse."
Among the people Julie's guests happened to gossip about were the Rostovs.

"I hear their affairs are in very bad shape," said Julie. "And he is so unreasonable, the count himself, I mean. The Razumovskis wanted to buy his house and his estate near Moscow, but it just drags on and on. He asks too much."
"No, I think the sale will go through in a few days," said someone. "Though it's madness to buy anything in Moscow now."
"Why?" asked Julie. "You don't think Moscow is in danger?"
"Then why are you leaving?"
"Me? What a question! I'm leaving because... well, because everyone is leaving; and besides, I'm not Joan of Arc or an Amazon."
"Well, of course, of course! Let me have some more strips of linen."
"If he manages the business properly, he should be able to pay off all his debts," said the militia officer, speaking of Rostov.

"A kindly old man but not very capable. And why are they staying on so long in Moscow? They meant to leave for the country ages ago. Natalie is quite well again now, isn't she?" Julie asked Pierre with a knowing smile.

"They're waiting for their younger son," Pierre replied. "He joined Obolensky's Cossacks and was sent to Belaya Tserkov where the regiment is being formed. But now they've had him transferred to my regiment and they're expecting him any day. The count wanted to leave long ago, but the countess absolutely won't leave Moscow until her son arrives."
"I saw them the day before yesterday at the Arkharovs'. Natalie has gotten her looks back and is more cheerful. She sang a song. How easily some people get over things!"
"Get over what?" asked Pierre, looking displeased.
Julie smiled.
"You know, Count, knights like you are only found in Madame de Souza's novels."
"What knights? What do you mean?" demanded Pierre, blushing.
"Oh, come, my dear count! It's the talk of all Moscow. I admire you, I truly do!"
* "It's the talk of all Moscow. My word, I admire you!"
"Forfeit, forfeit!" cried the militia officer.
"All right, one can't say anything—how tiresome!"
"What is 'the talk of all Moscow'?" Pierre asked angrily, rising to his feet.
"Come now, Count, you know!"
"I don't know anything about it," said Pierre.
"I know you were friends with Natalie, and so... but I was always closer to Vera—that dear Vera."

"No, madame!" Pierre continued in a tone of displeasure. "I have not taken on the role of Natalie Rostova's knight at all, and haven't visited them for nearly a month. But I cannot understand the cruelty..."

"He who excuses himself, accuses himself," said Julie, smiling and waving the lint triumphantly, and to have the last word she quickly changed the subject. "Do you know what I heard today? Poor Mary Bolkonskaya arrived in Moscow yesterday. Did you know she lost her father?"
* "He who excuses himself, accuses himself."
"Really? Where is she? I would very much like to see her," said Pierre.
"I spent the evening with her yesterday. She's going to their estate near Moscow either today or tomorrow morning, with her nephew."
"Well, how is she?" asked Pierre.

"She's all right, but sad. But do you know who rescued her? It's quite a romance. Nicholas Rostov! She was surrounded, they wanted to kill her and had wounded some of her people. He rushed in and saved her..."
"Another romance," said the militia officer. "Really, this general exodus has been arranged to get all the old maids married off. Catiche is one and Princess Bolkonskaya another."
"Do you know, I actually think she's a tiny bit in love with the young man."
* "A little bit in love with the young man."
"Forfeit, forfeit, forfeit!"
"But how would you say that in Russian?"

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: When Pierre returned home, he was handed two of Rostopchin's broadsheets that had been delivered that day.

The first declared that the report of Count Rostopchin forbidding people to leave Moscow was false; on the contrary, he was glad that ladies and merchants' wives were leaving the city. "There will be less panic and less gossip," the broadsheet read, "but I will stake my life that that scoundrel will not enter Moscow." These words showed Pierre clearly, for the first time, that the French would enter Moscow. The second broadsheet stated that Russian headquarters were at Vyazma, that Count Wittgenstein had defeated the French, but that since many Moscow residents wished to be armed, weapons were available at the arsenal: sabers, pistols, and muskets at a low price. The tone of the proclamation was not as playful as the earlier Chigirin bulletins. Pierre pondered these broadsheets. Clearly, the terrible storm he had longed for with his whole soul—yet which filled him with involuntary dread—was drawing near.
"Should I join the army and enlist, or wait?" he asked himself for the hundredth time. He took a pack of cards from the table and began laying them out for a game of patience.
"If this patience works out," he said to himself after shuffling the cards, holding them in his hand and looking up, "if it works out, it means... what does it mean?"
He hadn't decided what it would mean when he heard the eldest princess's voice at the door, asking whether she might come in.
"Then it will mean I must go to the army," Pierre said to himself. "Come in, come in!" he called to the princess.
Only the eldest princess—the one with the stony face and long waist—was still living in Pierre's house. The two younger ones had both married.

"Excuse me for disturbing you, cousin," she said in a reproachful, agitated voice. "But you know some decision must be made. What is going to happen? Everyone has left Moscow and the people are rioting. Why are we still here?"
"On the contrary, everything seems satisfactory, dear cousin," said Pierre in the bantering tone he habitually used with her, always feeling uncomfortable in the role of her benefactor.

"Satisfactory? Very satisfactory! Barbara Ivanovna was telling me today how our troops are distinguishing themselves. That is certainly to their credit! And the people too are getting quite unruly—even my maid has started being rude. At this rate they'll soon be beating us. One can't walk in the streets. But above all, the French will be here any day now, so what are we waiting for? I ask just one thing of you, cousin," she went on, "arrange for me to be taken to Petersburg. Whatever I may be, I can't live under Bonaparte's rule."
"Oh come, dear cousin! Where do you get your information? On the contrary..."
"I won't submit to your Napoleon! Others can if they wish... If you don't want to do this..."
"But I will, I'll arrange it right away."
The princess was clearly annoyed at having no one to be angry with. Muttering to herself, she sat down in a chair.

"But you've been misinformed," said Pierre. "Everything is quiet in the city and there's not the slightest danger. See—I was just reading..." He showed her the broadsheet. "Count Rostopchin writes that he'll stake his life that the enemy won't enter Moscow."

"Oh, that count of yours!" said the princess spitefully. "He's a hypocrite, a scoundrel who stirred up the people to riot himself. Didn't he write in those idiotic broadsheets that anyone, 'whoever it might be, should be dragged to the lockup by his hair'? How silly! 'And honor and glory to whoever catches him,' he says. That's what his flattery has led to! Barbara Ivanovna told me the crowd nearly killed her because she said something in French."
"Oh, but that's so... You take everything too much to heart," said Pierre, and began laying out his cards for patience.

Although the patience did come out, Pierre did not join the army but remained in the deserted city, still in the same state of agitation, indecision, and anxiety, yet at the same time joyfully awaiting something terrible.

The next day toward evening, the princess departed, and Pierre's chief steward came to inform him that the money needed to equip his regiment could not be found without selling one of the estates. The steward's general message was that Pierre's project of raising a regiment would ruin him. Pierre listened, barely suppressing a smile.
"Well then, sell it," he said. "What's to be done? I can't back out now!"

The worse everything became—especially his own affairs—the more pleased Pierre was, and the more evident it seemed that the catastrophe he expected was approaching. Almost no one he knew was left in town. Julie had gone, and Princess Mary too. Of his close friends, only the Rostovs remained, but he didn't go to see them.

To distract himself, he drove that day to the village of Vorontsovo to see the great balloon Leppich was building to destroy the enemy, and a trial balloon that was to go up the next day. The balloon wasn't ready yet, but Pierre learned it was being built by the Emperor's order. The Emperor had written to Count Rostopchin as follows:
As soon as Leppich is ready, assemble a crew of reliable and intelligent men for his gondola and send a courier to General Kutuzov to inform him. I have already told him about it.

Please impress upon Leppich that he must be very careful where he makes his first descent, so he doesn't make a mistake and fall into enemy hands. It is essential that he coordinate his movements with the commander in chief.

On his way home from Vorontsovo, passing through Bolotnaya Square, Pierre saw a large crowd around the Lobnoe Place and stopped to get out of his carriage. A French cook accused of being a spy was being flogged. The flogging had just ended, and the executioner was releasing from the flogging bench a stout man with red whiskers, wearing blue stockings and a green jacket, who was moaning piteously. Another man, thin and pale, stood nearby. Judging by their faces, both were French. With a frightened, suffering expression like the one on the thin Frenchman's face, Pierre pushed his way through the crowd.
"What is it? Who is it? What's it for?" he kept asking.

But the crowd—officials, townspeople, shopkeepers, peasants, and women in shawls and fur coats—was so absorbed in what was happening at the Lobnoe Place that no one answered him. The stout man got up, frowned, shrugged his shoulders, and clearly trying to look composed, began pulling on his jacket without looking around; but suddenly his lips trembled and he began to cry, the way full-blooded grown men cry, angry with themselves for doing so. People in the crowd began talking loudly, apparently to drown out their own feelings of pity, or so it seemed to Pierre.
"He's the cook to some prince."
"Well now, mister, seems Russian sauce is a bit sour for a Frenchman... sets his teeth on edge!" said a wrinkled clerk standing behind Pierre, as the Frenchman began to cry.
The clerk looked around, obviously hoping his joke would be appreciated. Some people laughed; others continued to watch in dismay as the executioner was undressing the other man.

Pierre choked, his face contorted, and he turned hastily away, went back to his carriage muttering something to himself, and climbed in. As they drove, he shuddered and cried out several times so loudly that the coachman asked:
"What is your pleasure?"
"Where are you going?" shouted Pierre to the coachman, who was heading toward Lubyanka Street.
"To the Governor's, as you ordered," answered the coachman.
"Fool! Idiot!" shouted Pierre, abusing his coachman—something he rarely did. "Home, I told you! And drive faster, you blockhead!" "I must get away this very day," he muttered to himself.

The sight of the tortured Frenchman and the crowd around the Lobnoe Place had so firmly decided Pierre that he could no longer stay in Moscow and would leave for the army that very day, that it seemed either he had already told the coachman this or that the man should have known it on his own.

On reaching home, Pierre ordered Evstafey—his head coachman, who knew everything, could do anything, and was known to all Moscow—to set out that night for the army at Mozhaysk, and to send his saddle horses ahead. This couldn't all be arranged that day, so on Evstafey's advice Pierre had to postpone his departure until the next day to allow time for the relay horses to go on ahead.

On the twenty-fourth, the weather cleared after a spell of rain, and after dinner Pierre left Moscow. When changing horses that night at Perkhushkovo, he learned that there had been a great battle that evening. (This was the battle of Shevardino.) He was told that there in Perkhushkovo the earth trembled from the gunfire, but nobody could answer his questions about who had won. At dawn the next day Pierre was approaching Mozhaysk.
Every house in Mozhaysk had soldiers quartered in it, and at the inn where Pierre was met by his groom and coachman there was no room to be had. It was full of officers.

Everywhere in Mozhaysk and beyond it, troops were stationed or on the march. Cossacks, infantry, cavalry, wagons, ammunition carts, and cannons were everywhere. Pierre pushed forward as fast as he could, and the farther he left Moscow behind and the deeper he plunged into that sea of troops, the more he was overcome by restless excitement and a new, joyful feeling he had never experienced before. It was a feeling similar to what he had felt at the Sloboda Palace during the Emperor's visit—a sense that he must undertake something and sacrifice something. He now experienced a glad awareness that everything that makes up human happiness—the comforts of life, wealth, even life itself—is rubbish that it is pleasant to throw away, compared with something... With what? Pierre could not say, and he didn't try to determine for whom or for what he felt such particular joy in sacrificing everything. He wasn't concerned with the question of what to sacrifice for; the very act of sacrificing brought him a new and joyful sensation.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: On the twenty-fourth of August the battle of the Shevardino Redoubt was fought; on the twenty-fifth not a shot was fired by either side; and on the twenty-sixth the battle of Borodino itself took place.

Why and how were the battles of Shevardino and Borodino fought and accepted? Why was the battle of Borodino fought? There was not the slightest sense in it for either the French or the Russians. Its immediate result for the Russians was, and was bound to be, that we were brought closer to the destruction of Moscow—which we feared more than anything in the world; and for the French, its immediate result was that they were brought closer to the destruction of their whole army—which they feared more than anything in the world. The outcome was completely obvious, and yet Napoleon offered and Kutuzov accepted the battle.

If the commanders had been guided by reason, it would seem obvious to Napoleon that by advancing thirteen hundred miles and fighting with a probability of losing a quarter of his army, he was marching toward certain destruction; and it would have been equally clear to Kutuzov that by accepting battle and risking the loss of a quarter of his army, he would certainly lose Moscow. For Kutuzov this was mathematically clear, just as it is clear in checkers that if I have one piece less and keep trading, I will certainly lose—and therefore should not trade. When my opponent has sixteen pieces and I have fourteen, I am only one-eighth weaker; but when I have traded away thirteen more, he will be three times as strong as I am.

Before the battle of Borodino our strength relative to the French was about five to six, but after the battle it was little more than one to two: before the battle we had a hundred thousand against a hundred and twenty thousand; afterward, barely fifty thousand against a hundred thousand. Yet the shrewd and experienced Kutuzov accepted the battle, while Napoleon, supposedly a commander of genius, offered it—losing a quarter of his army and stretching his supply lines even further. If we are told he expected to end the campaign by capturing Moscow, as he had ended a previous campaign by capturing Vienna, there is much evidence to the contrary. Napoleon's own historians tell us that from Smolensk onward he wanted to stop, that he knew the danger of his extended position, and that he knew the occupation of Moscow would not end the campaign, for he had seen at Smolensk the state in which Russian towns were being left to him, and had received not a single reply to his repeated proposals to negotiate.

In giving and accepting battle at Borodino, Kutuzov acted involuntarily and irrationally. But later, to fit what had occurred, historians provided cleverly crafted evidence of the foresight and genius of the generals who, of all the blind tools of history, were the most enslaved and involuntary.

The ancients left us model heroic poems in which the heroes supply the entire interest of the story, and we are still unable to accustom ourselves to the fact that for our era, such histories are meaningless.

On the other question—how the battles of Borodino and Shevardino were actually fought—there also exists a definite, well-known, but quite false account. All the historians describe the affair as follows:
The Russian army, they say, in its retreat from Smolensk, sought the best position for a general battle and found it at Borodino.

The Russians, they say, fortified this position in advance on the left of the highway (from Moscow to Smolensk) and almost at right angles to it, from Borodino to Utitsa, at the very place where the battle was fought.

In front of this position, they say, a fortified outpost was established on the Shevardino mound to observe the enemy. On the twenty-fourth, we are told, Napoleon attacked this advanced post and took it, and on the twenty-sixth attacked the whole Russian army, which was in position on the field of Borodino.
So the histories say, and it is all quite wrong, as anyone who cares to examine the matter can easily see.

The Russians did not seek the best position; on the contrary, during the retreat they passed many positions better than Borodino. They did not stop at any of them because Kutuzov did not wish to occupy a position he had not chosen himself, because the popular demand for battle had not yet been expressed strongly enough, because Miloradovich had not yet arrived with the militia, and for many other reasons. The fact is that other positions they had passed were stronger, and the position at Borodino (where the battle was fought), far from being strong, was no more of a position than any other random spot in the Russian Empire.

Not only did the Russians not fortify the position on the field of Borodino to the left of and at right angles to the highway (the position where the battle took place), but never until the twenty-fifth of August, 1812, did they even consider that a battle might be fought there. This is shown, first, by the fact that there were no entrenchments there by the twenty-fifth, and those begun on the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth were never completed; and second, by the position of the Shevardino Redoubt. That redoubt was quite senseless as an outpost of the position where the battle was actually accepted. Why was it more heavily fortified than any other point? And why were all efforts exhausted and six thousand men sacrificed defending it until late at night on the twenty-fourth? A Cossack patrol would have sufficed to observe the enemy. Third, as proof that the position where the battle was fought had not been planned, and that the Shevardino Redoubt was not an advanced post of that position, we have the fact that until the twenty-fifth, both Barclay de Tolly and Bagration believed the Shevardino Redoubt was the left flank of the position, and that Kutuzov himself, in his report written hastily after the battle, calls the Shevardino Redoubt the left flank of the position. It was only much later, when reports on the battle of Borodino were written at leisure, that the incorrect and extraordinary claim was invented (probably to justify the mistakes of a commander in chief who had to be portrayed as infallible) that the Shevardino Redoubt was an advanced post—whereas in reality it was simply a fortified point on the left flank—and that the battle of Borodino was fought on a pre-selected, entrenched position, whereas it was actually fought on a nearly unexpected and almost unfortified spot.

The situation was clearly this: a position was selected along the river Kolocha—which crosses the highway not at a right angle but at an acute angle—so that the left flank was at Shevardino, the right flank near the village of Novoe, and the center at Borodino at the confluence of the Kolocha and Voyna rivers.

To anyone looking at the field of Borodino without considering how the battle was actually fought, this position, protected by the river Kolocha, seems the obvious one for an army trying to prevent an enemy from advancing along the Smolensk road to Moscow.

Napoleon, riding to Valuevo on the twenty-fourth, did not see (as the history books claim) the Russian position from Utitsa to Borodino (he could not have seen that position because it did not exist), nor did he see an advanced post of the Russian army. Instead, while pursuing the Russian rearguard, he came upon the left flank of the Russian position—at the Shevardino Redoubt—and unexpectedly moved his army across the Kolocha. The Russians, not having time to begin a general battle, pulled back their left wing from the position they had intended to hold and took up a new position that had not been planned and was not fortified. By crossing the Kolocha to the left of the highway, Napoleon shifted the entire coming battle from right to left (from the Russian perspective) and transferred it to the plain between Utitsa, Semenovsk, and Borodino—a plain no more advantageous than any other in Russia—and there the entire battle of the twenty-sixth of August took place.

Had Napoleon not ridden out on the evening of the twenty-fourth to the Kolocha, and had he not then ordered an immediate attack on the redoubt but instead begun the attack the next morning, no one would have doubted that the Shevardino Redoubt was the left flank of our position, and the battle would have taken place where we expected. In that case, we would probably have defended the Shevardino Redoubt—our left flank—even more stubbornly. We would have attacked Napoleon in the center or on the right, and the battle would have been fought on the twenty-fifth in the position we had intended and fortified. But since the attack on our left flank came in the evening after the retreat of our rearguard (that is, immediately after the fight at Gridneva), and since the Russian commanders could not or would not begin a general engagement on the evening of the twenty-fourth, the first and decisive action of the battle of Borodino was already lost on the twenty-fourth, and this obviously led to the loss of the one fought on the twenty-sixth.

After the loss of the Shevardino Redoubt, we found ourselves on the morning of the twenty-fifth without a position for our left flank, and were forced to bend it back and hastily entrench it wherever it happened to be.

Not only was the Russian army on the twenty-sixth defended by weak, unfinished entrenchments, but the disadvantage of that position was increased by the fact that the Russian commanders—not having fully grasped what had happened, namely the loss of our position on the left flank and the shifting of the entire battlefield from right to left—maintained their extended position from the village of Novoe to Utitsa, and consequently had to shift their forces from right to left during the battle. So throughout the entire battle, the Russians opposed the entire French army launched against our left flank with only half as many men. (Poniatowski's action against Utitsa and Uvarov's on the right flank against the French were separate actions from the main battle.) So the battle of Borodino was not fought at all as it has been described (in an effort to conceal the commanders' mistakes, even at the cost of diminishing the glory due to the Russian army and people). The battle of Borodino was not fought on a pre-chosen, entrenched position with forces only slightly weaker than the enemy's. Rather, as a result of the loss of the Shevardino Redoubt, the Russians fought the battle of Borodino on an open and almost unfortified position, with forces only half as numerous as the French—that is, under conditions in which it was not merely unthinkable to fight for ten hours and achieve an indecisive result, but unthinkable to keep an army from complete collapse and rout.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: On the morning of the twenty-fifth, Pierre was leaving Mozhaysk. At the descent of the high, steep hill where a winding road led out of town past the cathedral on the right—where a service was being held and the bells were ringing—Pierre got out of his carriage and continued on foot. Behind him a cavalry regiment was coming down the hill, preceded by its singers. Coming up toward him was a train of carts carrying men wounded in the previous day's engagement. The peasant drivers, shouting and lashing their horses, kept crossing from side to side. The carts, each holding three or four wounded soldiers lying or sitting, jolted over the stones thrown on the steep slope to form something like a road. The wounded, bandaged with rags, with pale cheeks, compressed lips, and knitted brows, gripped the sides of the carts as they jolted against one another. Almost all of them stared with naive, childlike curiosity at Pierre's white hat and green tailcoat.

Pierre's coachman shouted angrily at the convoy of wounded to keep to one side of the road. The cavalry regiment, descending the hill with its singers, surrounded Pierre's carriage and blocked the road. Pierre stopped, pressed against the side of the road cut into the hillside. The sunshine from behind the hill didn't reach into the cut, and there it was cold and damp, but above Pierre's head was the bright August sun and the bells rang merrily. One of the carts of wounded stopped by the roadside close to Pierre. The driver in his bast shoes ran panting up to it, placed a stone under one of the rear wheels, and began adjusting the harness on his small horse.
One of the wounded, an old soldier with a bandaged arm who was walking alongside the cart, caught hold of it with his good hand and turned to look at Pierre.
"I say, countryman! Will they set us down here or take us on to Moscow?" he asked.

Pierre was so deep in thought that he didn't hear the question. He was looking now at the cavalry regiment that had met the convoy of wounded, now at the cart beside him, in which two wounded men were sitting and one was lying. One of those sitting up had probably been hit in the cheek. His whole head was wrapped in bandages and one cheek was swollen to the size of a baby's head. His nose and mouth were twisted to one side. This soldier was looking at the cathedral and crossing himself. Another, a young recruit as pale as if there were no blood in his thin face, looked at Pierre kindly with a fixed smile. The third lay face down so that his face was hidden. The cavalry singers were passing close by:
Ah lost, quite lost... is my head so keen, Living in a foreign land...
they sang their soldiers' marching song.

As if in response to them, but with a different kind of merriment, the metallic sound of the bells rang out high above, and the hot rays of the sun bathed the top of the opposite slope with yet another sort of joy. But below the slope, by the cart with the wounded and the panting little horse where Pierre stood, it was damp, somber, and sad.
The soldier with the swollen cheek looked angrily at the cavalry singers.
"Oh, the show-offs!" he muttered reproachfully.

"It's not just the soldiers—I've seen peasants today too... The peasants—even they have to go," said the soldier behind the cart, addressing Pierre with a sad smile. "No distinctions nowadays... They want the whole nation to attack them—in a word, it's Moscow! They want to make an end of it."
Despite the vagueness of the soldier's words, Pierre understood what he meant and nodded in agreement.
The road cleared again; Pierre descended the hill and drove on.

He kept looking to either side of the road for familiar faces but saw only the unfamiliar faces of soldiers from various branches of the service, all of whom stared with astonishment at his white hat and green tailcoat.

Having gone nearly three miles, he at last met an acquaintance and eagerly called out to him. This was one of the senior army doctors. He was driving toward Pierre in a covered gig, sitting beside a young surgeon, and on recognizing Pierre told the Cossack in the driver's seat to stop.
"Count! Your excellency, what brings you here?" asked the doctor.
"Well, you know, I wanted to see..."
"Yes, yes, there will be something to see..."
Pierre got out and talked to the doctor, explaining his intention of being present at the battle.
The doctor advised him to apply directly to Kutuzov.

"Why should you be God knows where, out of sight, during the battle?" he said, exchanging glances with his young companion. "In any case, his Serene Highness knows you and will receive you graciously. That's what you must do."
The doctor seemed tired and in a hurry.
"You think so?... I also wanted to ask—where exactly is our position?" said Pierre.
"The position?" the doctor repeated. "Well, that's not my area. Drive past Tatarinova; there's a lot of digging going on there. Go up the hill and you'll see."
"You can see from there?... If you would..."
But the doctor interrupted him and moved toward his gig.

"I'd go with you, but honestly I'm up to here"—he pointed to his throat. "I'm racing to the corps commander. How do things stand?... You know, Count, there'll be a battle tomorrow. Out of a hundred thousand, we must expect at least twenty thousand wounded, and we haven't enough stretchers, beds, medics, or doctors for six thousand. We have ten thousand carts, but we need other things too—we'll just have to manage."

The strange thought that of the thousands of men—young and old—who had stared with cheerful surprise at his hat (perhaps the very men he had noticed), twenty thousand were doomed to wounds and death, struck Pierre forcefully.

"They may die tomorrow; why are they thinking about anything but death?" And by some hidden chain of thought, the descent of the Mozhaysk hill, the carts with the wounded, the ringing bells, the slanting rays of the sun, and the cavalrymen's songs vividly recurred to him.

"The cavalry ride to battle and meet the wounded and don't give a moment's thought to what awaits them, but ride past winking at the wounded. Yet from among these men, twenty thousand are doomed to die—and they wonder at my hat! Strange!" thought Pierre, continuing toward Tatarinova.

In front of a landowner's house to the left of the road stood carriages, wagons, and crowds of orderlies and sentries. The commander in chief was staying there, but when Pierre arrived he was not in, and hardly any of the staff were present—they had gone to the church service. Pierre drove on toward Gorki.

When he had climbed the hill and reached the little village street, he saw for the first time peasant militiamen in their white shirts and with crosses on their caps, who, talking and laughing loudly, lively and sweating, were at work on a huge knoll overgrown with grass to the right of the road.
Some of them were digging, others wheeling barrowloads of earth along planks, while others stood around doing nothing.

Two officers stood on the knoll directing the men. Seeing these peasants, who were clearly still amused by the novelty of their position as soldiers, Pierre once again thought of the wounded at Mozhaysk and understood what the soldier had meant when he said: "They want the whole nation to attack them." The sight of these bearded peasants working on the battlefield, with their clumsy boots, sweating necks, and shirts open from the left to the middle, exposing their sunburned collarbones, impressed Pierre more powerfully with the solemnity and importance of the moment than anything he had yet seen or heard.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: Pierre got out of his carriage and, passing the toiling militiamen, climbed the knoll from which, according to the doctor, the battlefield could be seen.
It was about eleven o'clock. The sun was somewhat to the left and behind him, and brightly illuminated the enormous panorama that rose like an amphitheater before him in the clear, thin air.

From the upper left, cutting through that amphitheater, wound the Smolensk highway, passing through a village with a white church about five hundred paces ahead of the knoll and below it. This was Borodino. Below the village the road crossed the river by a bridge and, winding down and up, rose higher and higher to the village of Valuevo, visible about four miles away, where Napoleon was then stationed. Beyond Valuevo the road vanished into a yellowing forest on the horizon. Far in the distance in that birch and fir forest to the right of the road, the cross and belfry of the Kolocha Monastery gleamed in the sun. Scattered over the whole blue expanse, to right and left of the forest and the road, smoking campfires could be seen and indistinct masses of troops—ours and the enemy's. The ground to the right—along the course of the Kolocha and Moskva rivers—was broken and hilly. Between the hollows, the villages of Bezubova and Zakharino were visible in the distance. On the left the ground was more level; there were grain fields, and the smoking ruins of Semenovsk, which had been burned, could be seen.

Everything Pierre saw was so indistinct that neither the left nor the right side of the field matched what he had expected. Nowhere could he see the battlefield he had imagined—only fields, meadows, troops, woods, campfire smoke, villages, hills, and streams; and try as he might, he could make out no military "position" in this place teeming with life, nor could he even tell our troops from the enemy's.
"I need to ask someone who knows," he thought, and approached an officer who was looking with curiosity at his huge, unmilitary figure.
"May I ask," said Pierre, "what village that is ahead?"
"Burdino, isn't it?" said the officer, turning to his companion.
"Borodino," the other corrected him.
The officer, clearly glad of a chance to talk, moved up to Pierre.
"Are those our men there?" Pierre asked.
"Yes, and farther on are the French," said the officer. "There they are, there... you can see them."
"Where? Where?" asked Pierre.
"You can see them with the naked eye... Look, there!"
The officer pointed toward the smoke visible to the left beyond the river, and the same stern and serious expression Pierre had noticed on many faces that day came over his own.
"Ah, those are the French! And over there?" Pierre pointed to a knoll on the left, near which some troops were visible.
"Those are ours."
"And there?" Pierre pointed to another knoll in the distance with a big tree on it, near a village in a hollow where campfires were smoking and something dark could be seen.
"That's his again," said the officer. (It was the Shevardino Redoubt.) "It was ours yesterday, but now it's his."
"Then where's our position?"

"Our position?" replied the officer with a satisfied smile. "I can tell you quite clearly, because I built nearly all our fortifications. There, you see? There's our center, at Borodino, right there," and he pointed to the village with the white church ahead. "That's where you cross the Kolocha. You see down there where the rows of hay are in the hollow? That's the bridge. That's our center. Our right flank is over there"—he pointed sharply to the right, far away in the broken ground—"that's where the Moskva River is, and we've built three very strong redoubts there. The left flank..." Here the officer paused. "Well, you see, that's harder to explain... Yesterday our left flank was there at Shevardino, you see, where the oak is, but now we've pulled our left wing back—now it's over there, do you see that village and the smoke? That's Semenovsk, yes, there," he pointed to Raevsky's knoll. "But the battle probably won't be there. His having moved his troops there is just a feint; he'll probably swing around to the right of the Moskva. But wherever it may be, many a man won't be here tomorrow!" he added.
An elderly sergeant who had come up while the officer was speaking had waited silently for him to finish, but at this point, evidently not liking the officer's remark, interrupted him.
"Gabions need to be sent for," he said sternly.
The officer looked embarrassed, as though he understood one might think about how many men would be missing tomorrow but shouldn't say it aloud.
"Well, send third company again," the officer said quickly.
"And you—are you one of the doctors?"
"No, I've come on my own," answered Pierre, and he went back down the hill, passing the militiamen.
"Oh, those damned fellows!" muttered the officer, following him and holding his nose as he ran past the working men.
"There they are... bringing her, coming... There they are... They'll be here in a minute..." voices were suddenly heard, and officers, soldiers, and militiamen began running forward along the road.
A church procession was coming up the hill from Borodino. First along the dusty road came infantry in ranks, bareheaded and with arms reversed. From behind them came the sound of church singing.
Soldiers and militiamen ran bareheaded past Pierre toward the procession.
"They're bringing her—our Protectress!... The Iberian Mother of God!" someone cried.
"The Smolensk Mother of God," another corrected him.

The militiamen—both those who had been in the village and those who had been working on the battery—threw down their shovels and ran to meet the church procession. Following the battalion that marched along the dusty road came priests in their vestments—one little old man in a hood with attendants and singers. Behind them, soldiers and officers carried a large, dark-faced icon in an embossed metal cover. This was the icon that had been brought from Smolensk and had since accompanied the army. Behind, before, and on both sides, crowds of militiamen with bared heads walked, ran, and bowed to the ground.

At the top of the hill they stopped with the icon; the men who had been holding it up by the linen bands were relieved by others, the chanters relit their censers, and the service began. The hot rays of the sun beat straight down, and a fresh soft wind played with the hair of the bared heads and with the ribbons decorating the icon. The singing didn't sound loud under the open sky. An immense crowd of bareheaded officers, soldiers, and militiamen surrounded the icon. Behind the priest and chanter stood the dignitaries in a reserved spot. A bald general with a Saint George's Cross on his neck stood just behind the priest, and without crossing himself (he was evidently a German) patiently waited for the service to end, which he considered it necessary to attend, probably to arouse the Russian people's patriotism. Another general stood in a martial pose, crossing himself with a quick motion of his hand before his chest while looking about him. Standing among the crowd of peasants, Pierre recognized several acquaintances among these notables but didn't look at them—his whole attention was absorbed by the serious expression on the faces of the soldiers and militiamen, who were all gazing intently at the icon. As soon as the tired chanters, who were singing the service for the twentieth time that day, began lazily and mechanically to sing, "Save from calamity Your servants, O Mother of God," and the priest and deacon chimed in, "For to You under God we all flee as to an unbreakable wall and protection," there again kindled in all those faces the same expression of awareness of the solemnity of the approaching moment that Pierre had seen at the foot of the hill at Mozhaysk and fleetingly on the many faces he had met that morning; and heads bowed more often, hair was tossed back, and sighs and the sound of men crossing themselves were heard.
The crowd around the icon suddenly parted and pressed against Pierre. Someone—a very important person, judging by the haste with which way was made—was approaching the icon.
It was Kutuzov, who had been riding around the position and on his way back to Tatarinova had stopped where the service was being held. Pierre recognized him at once by his distinctive figure.

With a long overcoat on his extremely stout, round-shouldered body, with his uncovered white head and puffy face showing the white ball of the eye he had lost, Kutuzov walked with a plunging, swaying gait into the crowd and stopped behind the priest. He crossed himself with a practiced movement, reached down and touched the ground with his hand, and bowed his white head with a deep sigh. Behind Kutuzov was Bennigsen and the suite. Despite the commander in chief's presence, which attracted the attention of all the senior officers, the militiamen and soldiers continued their prayers without looking at him.

When the service was over, Kutuzov stepped up to the icon, sank heavily to his knees, bowed to the ground, and for a long time tried in vain to rise but could not because of his weakness and weight. His white head twitched with the effort. At last he rose, kissed the icon as a child does with naively pouting lips, and again bowed until he touched the ground with his hand. The other generals followed his example, then the officers, and after them, with excited faces, pressing on one another, crowding, panting, and pushing, came the soldiers and militiamen.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: Staggering amid the crush, Pierre looked around.
"Count Peter Kirilych! How did you get here?" said a voice.

Pierre looked round. Boris Drubetskoy, brushing his knees with his hand (he had probably dirtied them kneeling before the icon), came up to him smiling. Boris was elegantly dressed with a slightly military flair appropriate to a campaign. He wore a long coat and, like Kutuzov, had a whip slung across his shoulder.

Meanwhile Kutuzov had reached the village and seated himself in the shade of the nearest house, on a bench that one Cossack had run to fetch and another had hastily covered with a rug. An immense and brilliant suite surrounded him.
The icon was carried farther, accompanied by the crowd. Pierre stopped some thirty paces from Kutuzov, talking to Boris.
He explained his wish to be present at the battle and see the position.

"This is what you must do," said Boris. "I'll show you around the camp. You'll see everything best from where Count Bennigsen will be. I'm in attendance on him, you know; I'll mention it to him. But if you want to ride around the position, come with us. We're just going to the left flank. Then when we get back, please spend the night with me and we'll arrange a game of cards. Of course you know Dmitri Sergeevich? Those are his quarters," and he pointed to the third house in the village of Gorki.
"But I'd like to see the right flank. They say it's very strong," said Pierre. "I'd like to start from the Moskva River and ride around the whole position."
"Well, you can do that later, but the main thing is the left flank."
"Yes, yes. But where is Prince Bolkonsky's regiment? Can you show me?"
"Prince Andrew's? We'll pass it, and I'll take you to him."
"What about the left flank?" asked Pierre.

"To tell you the truth, between us, God only knows what shape our left flank is in," said Boris confidentially, lowering his voice. "It's not at all what Count Bennigsen intended. He meant to fortify that knoll quite differently, but..." Boris shrugged. "His Serene Highness wouldn't have it, or someone talked him out of it. You see..." But Boris didn't finish, because at that moment Kaisarov, Kutuzov's adjutant, came up to Pierre. "Ah, Kaisarov!" said Boris, addressing him with an easy smile. "I was just trying to explain our position to the count. It's amazing how his Serene Highness foresaw the French intentions!"
"You mean the left flank?" asked Kaisarov.
"Yes, exactly; the left flank is now extremely strong."

Though Kutuzov had dismissed all unnecessary people from the staff, Boris had managed to stay on at headquarters after the changes. He had attached himself to Count Bennigsen, who, like everyone Boris had ever attended, considered young Prince Drubetskoy an invaluable man.

In the higher command there were two sharply defined parties: Kutuzov's and Bennigsen's. Boris belonged to the latter, and while showing servile respect to Kutuzov, he skillfully created the impression that the old man wasn't up to much and that Bennigsen was running everything. Now the decisive moment of battle had come, when Kutuzov would either be discredited and power would pass to Bennigsen, or even if Kutuzov won, it would be felt that everything was Bennigsen's doing. In either case, many great rewards would be given for the next day's action, and new men would come to the fore. So Boris was full of nervous energy all day.

After Kaisarov, other people Pierre knew came up to him, and he hadn't time to answer all the questions about Moscow showered on him or to listen to everything they told him. All faces expressed excitement and apprehension, but it seemed to Pierre that the excitement in some of these faces was mainly about questions of personal advancement; his own mind, however, was occupied by the different expression he saw on other faces—an expression that spoke not of personal matters but of the universal questions of life and death. Kutuzov noticed Pierre's figure and the group gathered around him.
"Call him to me," said Kutuzov.
An aide told Pierre of his Serene Highness's wish, and Pierre went toward Kutuzov's bench. But a militiaman got there before him. It was Dolokhov.
"How did that fellow get here?" asked Pierre.

"He's a creature that worms his way in everywhere!" was the answer. "He was demoted, you know. Now he wants to claw his way back. He's been proposing some scheme or other and has crawled into the enemy's picket line at night... He's a brave fellow, though."
Pierre took off his hat and bowed respectfully to Kutuzov.
"I concluded that if I reported to your Serene Highness, you might send me away or say that you already knew what I was reporting, but then I wouldn't lose anything..." Dolokhov was saying.
"Yes, yes."
"But if I were right, I'd be rendering a service to my Fatherland, for which I'm ready to die."
"Yes, yes."
"And should your Serene Highness need a man who won't spare his skin, please think of me... Perhaps I may prove useful to your Serene Highness."
"Yes... yes..." Kutuzov repeated, his laughing eye narrowing more and more as he looked at Pierre.

Just then Boris, with his courtier's skill, stepped up to Pierre near Kutuzov and in the most natural manner, without raising his voice, said to Pierre as though continuing an interrupted conversation:
"The militia have put on clean white shirts to be ready to die. What heroism, Count!"
Boris clearly said this to Pierre intending to be overheard by his Serene Highness. He knew Kutuzov's attention would be caught by those words, and it was.
"What are you saying about the militia?" he asked Boris.
"Preparing for tomorrow, your Serene Highness—for death—they've put on clean shirts."
"Ah... a wonderful, a matchless people!" said Kutuzov; and he closed his eyes and swayed his head. "A matchless people!" he repeated with a sigh.
"So you want to smell gunpowder?" he said to Pierre. "Yes, it's a pleasant smell. I have the honor of being one of your wife's admirers. Is she well? My quarters are at your service."
And as often happens with old people, Kutuzov began looking around absent-mindedly, as if forgetting everything he wanted to say or do.
Then, evidently remembering what he wanted, he beckoned to Andrei Kaisarov, his adjutant's brother.
"Those verses... those verses of Marin's... how do they go? The ones he wrote about Gerakov: 'Lectures for the corps inditing'... Recite them!" said he, clearly preparing to laugh.
Kaisarov recited... Kutuzov nodded his head, smiling, to the rhythm of the verses.
When Pierre had left Kutuzov, Dolokhov came up to him and took his hand.

"I am very glad to meet you here, Count," he said aloud, regardless of strangers present, in a particularly resolute and solemn tone. "On the eve of a day when God alone knows who of us is destined to survive, I'm glad of this chance to tell you that I regret the misunderstandings between us and would wish you not to hold any ill feelings toward me. I beg you to forgive me."
Pierre looked at Dolokhov with a smile, not knowing what to say. With tears in his eyes, Dolokhov embraced Pierre and kissed him.
Boris said a few words to his general, and Count Bennigsen turned to Pierre and proposed that he ride with him along the line.
"It will interest you," he said.
"Yes, very much," replied Pierre.
Half an hour later Kutuzov left for Tatarinova, and Bennigsen and his suite, with Pierre among them, set out on their ride along the line.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 23
paragraphs: From Gorki, Bennigsen descended the highway to the bridge which, when they had looked at it from the hill, the officer had pointed out as the center of our position, and where rows of sweet-smelling new-mown hay lay by the riverside. They rode across that bridge into the village of Borodino and then turned to the left, passing a huge number of troops and guns, and came to a high knoll where militiamen were digging. This was the redoubt, as yet unnamed, which would later be known as the Raevsky Redoubt or the Knoll Battery, but Pierre paid no special attention to it. He didn't know it would become more memorable to him than any other spot on the plain of Borodino.

They then crossed the hollow to Semenovsk, where the soldiers were pulling the last logs from the huts and barns. Then they rode downhill and uphill, across a rye field trampled and beaten down as if by hail, following a track freshly made by the artillery over the furrows of plowed land, and reached some fleches that were still being dug.
* A type of entrenchment.

At the fleches, Bennigsen stopped and began studying the Shevardino Redoubt opposite, which had been ours the day before and where several horsemen could be seen. The officers said that either Napoleon or Murat was there, and they all gazed eagerly at this small group of riders. Pierre also looked at them, trying to guess which of the barely discernible figures was Napoleon. At last those mounted men rode away from the mound and disappeared.

Bennigsen spoke to a general who approached him and began explaining our entire troop positions. Pierre listened, straining every faculty to understand the essential points of the coming battle, but was dismayed to find that his mental capacity was inadequate for the task. He couldn't make sense of it. Bennigsen stopped speaking and, noticing that Pierre was listening, suddenly said to him:
"I don't think this interests you?"
"On the contrary, it's very interesting!" replied Pierre, not quite truthfully.

From the fleches they rode still further to the left, along a road winding through a thick, low-growing birch wood. In the middle of the wood, a brown hare with white feet sprang out and, frightened by the tramping of so many horses, grew so confused that it ran along the road in front of them for some time, attracting general attention and laughter. Only when several voices shouted at it did it dart to one side and disappear in the thicket. After going through the wood for about a mile and a half, they came out on a clearing where troops of Tuchkov's corps were stationed to defend the left flank.

Here, on the extreme left flank, Bennigsen talked at length and with great heat, and, as it seemed to Pierre, gave orders of great military importance. In front of Tuchkov's troops there was a high ground not occupied by troops. Bennigsen loudly criticized this mistake, saying it was madness to leave a height that commanded the surrounding country unoccupied, and to place troops below it. Some of the generals expressed the same opinion. One in particular declared with military passion that they had been placed there to be slaughtered. Bennigsen, on his own authority, ordered the troops to occupy the high ground. This decision on the left flank deepened Pierre's doubts about his own ability to understand military matters. Listening to Bennigsen and the generals criticize the position of the troops behind the hill, he fully understood them and shared their view—but for that very reason couldn't understand how the person who had placed them there behind the hill could have made so obvious a blunder.

Pierre didn't know that these troops were not, as Bennigsen supposed, placed there to defend the position, but were in concealment as an ambush—not meant to be seen—so they could strike an approaching enemy unexpectedly. Bennigsen didn't know this, and moved the troops forward according to his own ideas without consulting the commander in chief.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: On that bright evening of August 25, Prince Andrew lay propped on his elbow in a broken-down shed in the village of Knyazkovo at the far end of his regiment's camp. Through a gap in the broken wall he could see, beside the wooden fence, a row of thirty-year-old birches with their lower branches trimmed off, a field with sheaves of oats standing in it, and some bushes near which rose the smoke of campfires—the soldiers' kitchens.
Narrow and burdensome and useless to anyone as his life now seemed to him, Prince Andrew on the eve of battle felt as agitated and irritable as he had seven years before at Austerlitz.

He had received and given the orders for the next day's battle and had nothing more to do. But his thoughts—the simplest, clearest, and therefore most terrible thoughts—would give him no peace. He knew that tomorrow's battle would be the most terrible he had ever been in, and for the first time in his life, the possibility of death presented itself not in relation to any worldly matter or its effect on others, but simply in relation to himself, to his own soul—vividly, plainly, terribly, and almost as a certainty. And from the height of this awareness, all that had previously tormented and preoccupied him was suddenly illuminated by a cold white light without shadows, without perspective, without distinction. All of life appeared to him like magic-lantern pictures he had long been gazing at through a glass by artificial light. Now he suddenly saw those badly painted images in the clear daylight, without the glass. "Yes, yes! There they are, those false images that excited, enchanted, and tormented me," he said to himself, reviewing the principal pictures of the magic lantern of life and seeing them now in the cold white light of his clear perception of death. "There they are, those crudely painted figures that once seemed splendid and mysterious. Glory, the good of society, love of a woman, the Fatherland itself—how important these pictures seemed, with what profound meaning they appeared to be filled! And it is all so simple, pale, and crude in the cold white light of this morning I feel dawning for me." The three great sorrows of his life held his attention in particular: his love for a woman, his father's death, and the French invasion that had overrun half of Russia. "Love... that little girl who seemed to me overflowing with mysterious power! Yes, I loved her. I made romantic plans of love and happiness with her! Oh, what a fool I was!" he said aloud bitterly. "I believed in some ideal love that was to keep her faithful for the whole year of my absence! Like the gentle dove in the fable, she was to pine apart from me... But it was much simpler than that... It was all very simple and horrible."

"When my father built Bald Hills, he thought the place was his: his land, his air, his peasants. But Napoleon came and swept him aside, unconscious of his existence, as he might brush a chip from his path, and his Bald Hills and his whole life fell to pieces. Princess Mary says it is a trial sent from above. What is the trial for, when he is gone and will never return? He is gone! For whom then is the trial intended? The Fatherland, the destruction of Moscow! And tomorrow I shall be killed—perhaps not even by a Frenchman but by one of our own men, by a soldier firing a musket close to my ear, as one of them did yesterday—and the French will come and take me by the head and feet and fling me into a ditch so I won't stink under their noses, and new conditions of life will arise that will seem perfectly ordinary to others but about which I shall know nothing. I shall not exist..."

He looked at the row of birches shining in the sunshine, with their motionless green and yellow foliage and white bark. "To die... to be killed tomorrow... That I should not exist... That all this should still be, but not me..."

And the birches with their light and shade, the curly clouds, the smoke of the campfires, and everything around him changed and seemed terrible and menacing. A cold shiver ran down his spine. He rose quickly, went out of the shed, and began pacing.
When he returned, voices were heard outside the shed. "Who's that?" he called.

The red-nosed Captain Timokhin, formerly Dolokhov's company commander but now, due to the shortage of officers, a battalion commander, shyly entered the shed followed by an adjutant and the regimental paymaster.
Prince Andrew rose quickly, listened to the business they had come about, gave them additional instructions, and was about to dismiss them when he heard a familiar, lisping voice behind the shed.
"Devil take it!" said the voice of a man stumbling over something.

Prince Andrew looked out of the shed and saw Pierre, who had tripped over a pole on the ground and nearly fallen, coming his way. It was unpleasant to Prince Andrew to meet people from his own circle in general, and Pierre especially, for Pierre reminded him of all the painful moments of his last visit to Moscow.
"You? What a surprise!" he said. "What brings you here? This is unexpected!"

As he said this, his eyes and face expressed more than coldness—they expressed hostility, which Pierre noticed at once. He had approached the shed full of animation, but seeing Prince Andrew's face, he felt constrained and uncomfortable.
"I've come... simply... you know... come... it interests me," said Pierre, who had so often that day senselessly repeated the word "interesting." "I wanted to see the battle."

"Oh yes, and what do the Masonic brothers say about war? How would they stop it?" said Prince Andrew sarcastically. "Well, and how's Moscow? And my family? Have they reached Moscow at last?" he asked more seriously.
"Yes, they have. Julie Drubetskaya told me. I went to see them but missed them. They've gone to your estate near Moscow."

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: The officers were about to leave, but Prince Andrew, apparently reluctant to be left alone with his friend, asked them to stay and have tea. Seats were brought and tea was served. The officers gazed with surprise at Pierre's huge, stout figure and listened to his talk about Moscow and the position of their army, around which he had ridden. Prince Andrew remained silent, and his expression was so forbidding that Pierre directed his remarks mainly to the good-natured battalion commander.
"So you understand the whole layout of our troops?" Prince Andrew interrupted him.
"Yes—that is, how do you mean?" said Pierre. "Not being a military man, I can't say I've fully understood it, but I get the general picture."
"Well then, you know more than anyone else, whoever that may be," said Prince Andrew.
"Oh!" said Pierre, looking over his spectacles in perplexity at Prince Andrew. "Well, and what do you think about Kutuzov's appointment?" he asked.
"I was very glad of his appointment, that's all I know," replied Prince Andrew.
"And tell me your opinion of Barclay de Tolly. In Moscow they're saying all sorts of things about him... What do you think of him?"
"Ask them," replied Prince Andrew, indicating the officers.
Pierre looked at Timokhin with the condescendingly inquiring smile that everyone involuntarily used when addressing that officer.
"We can see the light again since his Serenity's been appointed, your excellency," said Timokhin timidly, continually glancing at his colonel.
"Why so?" asked Pierre.

"Well, take just firewood and fodder, for example. Why, when we were retreating from Sventsyani, we didn't dare touch a stick or a wisp of hay or anything. You see, we were leaving, so he'd get it all; isn't that right, your excellency?" and Timokhin again looked at the prince. "But we didn't dare. In our regiment two officers were court-martialed for that kind of thing. But once his Serenity took command, everything became straightforward. Now we can see the light..."
"Then why was it forbidden?"
Timokhin looked about in confusion, not knowing how to answer. Pierre put the same question to Prince Andrew.

"So as not to lay waste the country we were leaving to the enemy," said Prince Andrew with bitter irony. "It's very sound: you can't allow the land to be pillaged or accustom the troops to looting. At Smolensk too he calculated correctly that the French might outflank us since they had larger forces. But he couldn't understand this," cried Prince Andrew in a shrill voice that seemed to escape him involuntarily: "he couldn't understand that there, for the first time, we were fighting for Russian soil, and that there was a spirit in the men such as I had never seen before, and that we had held the French for two days, and that that success had increased our strength tenfold. He ordered us to retreat, and all our efforts and losses went for nothing. He didn't intend to betray us; he tried to do his best; he thought out everything carefully—and that is exactly why he's unfit. He's unfit now precisely because he plans everything very thoroughly and precisely, as every German must. How can I explain it?... Well, say your father has a German valet, and the valet is excellent and satisfies your father's needs better than you could—then it's fine to let him serve. But if your father is mortally ill, you'll send the valet away and attend to your father with your own clumsy, unpracticed hands, and will comfort him better than a skilled stranger could. That's how it's been with Barclay. While Russia was healthy, a foreigner could serve her and be a splendid minister; but the moment she's in danger, she needs one of her own. But in your Club they've been calling him a traitor! They've slandered him as a traitor, and the only result will be that later, ashamed of their false accusations, they'll suddenly make him out to be a hero or genius instead—and that will be even more unjust. He is an honest and very meticulous German."
"And they say he's a skillful commander," Pierre remarked.
"I don't understand what 'a skillful commander' means," replied Prince Andrew ironically.
"A skillful commander?" said Pierre. "Well, one who foresees all possibilities... and anticipates the enemy's intentions."
"But that's impossible," said Prince Andrew, as if it were a long-settled matter.
Pierre looked at him in surprise.
"And yet they say war is like a game of chess?" he remarked.

"Yes," replied Prince Andrew, "but with this little difference: in chess you can think over each move as long as you like and aren't limited by time, and with this further difference, that a knight is always stronger than a pawn and two pawns are always stronger than one—while in war a battalion is sometimes stronger than a division and sometimes weaker than a company. The relative strength of bodies of troops can never be known to anyone. Believe me," he continued, "if things depended on plans made by the staff, I would be there making plans. But instead I have the honor of serving here in the regiment with these gentlemen, and I believe that on us—not on those others—tomorrow's battle will depend... Success never has depended, and never will depend, on position, equipment, or even numbers—and least of all on position."
"But on what then?"
"On the feeling that is in me and in him," he pointed to Timokhin, "and in every soldier."

Prince Andrew glanced at Timokhin, who looked at his commander in alarm and confusion. In contrast to his former reserved taciturnity, Prince Andrew now seemed stirred up. He apparently couldn't stop himself from expressing the thoughts that had suddenly taken hold of him.

"A battle is won by those who firmly resolve to win it! Why did we lose the battle of Austerlitz? Our losses were nearly equal to the French, but very early we told ourselves we were losing the battle—and we lost it. And we said so because we had nothing to fight for there, we wanted to get away from the battlefield as fast as possible. 'We've lost, so let's run,' and we ran. If we hadn't said that till evening, God knows what might have happened. But tomorrow we won't say it! You talk about our position—the left flank weak, the right flank overextended," he went on. "That's all nonsense, none of it matters. But what awaits us tomorrow? A hundred million totally unpredictable circumstances that will be decided in an instant by whether our men or theirs run or don't run, and whether this man or that man is killed. Everything being done now is just play. The fact is that those men you've been riding around with don't just fail to help—they actually hinder. They're only concerned with their own petty interests."
"At such a moment?" said Pierre reproachfully.

"At such a moment!" Prince Andrew repeated. "To them it's only an opportunity to undermine a rival and earn an extra medal or ribbon. For me, tomorrow means this: a Russian army of a hundred thousand and a French army of a hundred thousand have met to fight, and the point is that these two hundred thousand men will fight, and whichever side fights more fiercely and spares itself less will win. And if you want to know: whatever happens, whatever blunders those at the top may make, we will win tomorrow's battle. Tomorrow, happen what may, we will win!"

"That's right, your excellency! That's the truth, the real truth," said Timokhin. "Who would spare himself now? The soldiers in my battalion—believe me—won't touch their vodka! 'It's not the day for that!' they say."

Everyone fell silent. The officers rose. Prince Andrew went out of the shed with them, giving final orders to the adjutant. After they had gone, Pierre approached Prince Andrew and was about to start talking when they heard the clatter of three horses on the road nearby. Looking in that direction, Prince Andrew recognized Wolzogen and Clausewitz accompanied by a Cossack. They rode close by, still talking, and Prince Andrew involuntarily caught these words:
"The war must be extended across a wide area. I cannot praise that view highly enough," said one of them.
* "The war must be extended widely. I cannot sufficiently commend that view."
"Oh yes," said the other, "the only objective is to weaken the enemy, so of course one cannot take into account the loss of private individuals."
* "Oh yes, the only aim is to weaken the enemy, so of course one cannot consider the loss of private individuals."
"Oh, no," agreed the other.

"Extend widely!" said Prince Andrew with an angry snort when they had ridden past. "In that 'extend' were my father, son, and sister at Bald Hills. That's all the same to him! That's what I was telling you—those German gentlemen won't win the battle tomorrow, they'll only make as big a mess as they can, because they have nothing in their German heads but theories not worth an empty eggshell, and haven't in their hearts the one thing needed tomorrow—the thing Timokhin has. They've surrendered all of Europe to him, and now they've come to teach us. Fine teachers!" and again his voice went shrill.
"So you think we'll win tomorrow's battle?" asked Pierre.

"Yes, yes," answered Prince Andrew absently. "One thing I would do if I had the power," he began again, "I would not take prisoners. Why take prisoners? It's playing at chivalry! The French have destroyed my home and are on their way to destroy Moscow; they have outraged and continue to outrage me every moment. They are my enemies. In my view they are all criminals. And Timokhin thinks so too, and the whole army. They should be executed! Since they are my enemies, they cannot be my friends, whatever may have been said at Tilsit."
"Yes, yes," muttered Pierre, looking with shining eyes at Prince Andrew. "I completely agree with you!"

The question that had troubled Pierre on the Mozhaysk hill and throughout the day now seemed perfectly clear and fully resolved. He now understood the whole meaning and importance of this war and of the coming battle. Everything he had seen that day, all the significant and serious expressions on the faces he had passed, were illuminated for him by a new light. He understood that latent heat (as they say in physics) of patriotism which was present in all these men he had seen, and this explained why they all prepared for death calmly and almost lightheartedly.

"Not take prisoners," Prince Andrew continued. "That alone would completely change the whole war and make it less cruel. As it is, we've been playing at war—that's what's vile! We play at magnanimity and all that stuff. Such magnanimity and sensitivity are like a lady who faints at the sight of a calf being slaughtered: she is so tenderhearted she can't look at blood, but she enjoys eating the calf served up with sauce. They talk to us about the rules of war, about chivalry, about flags of truce, about mercy to the unfortunate, and so on. It's all rubbish! I saw chivalry and flags of truce in 1805; they deceived us and we deceived them. They plunder other people's homes, circulate counterfeit money, and worst of all they kill my children and my father—and then talk about rules of war and magnanimity to the enemy!
