When the pit had been filled up, a command was given. Pierre was taken back to his place, and the rows of troops on both sides of the post made a half turn and marched past it at a measured pace. The twenty-four sharpshooters with discharged muskets, standing in the center of the circle, ran back to their places as the companies passed by.

Pierre gazed now with dazed eyes at these sharpshooters who ran in pairs out of the circle. All but one rejoined their companies. This one, a young soldier, his face deathly pale, his cap pushed back, and his musket resting on the ground, still stood near the pit at the spot from which he had fired. He swayed like a drunken man, taking some steps forward and back to keep himself from falling. An old noncommissioned officer ran out of the ranks and, taking him by the elbow, dragged him to his company. The crowd of Russians and Frenchmen began to disperse. They all went away silently and with drooping heads.
"That will teach them to start fires," said one of the Frenchmen.

Pierre glanced at the speaker and saw that it was a soldier who was trying to find some comfort after what had been done, but could not. Without finishing what he had begun to say, he made a hopeless gesture with his arm and went away.

chapters.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: After the execution, Pierre was separated from the rest of the prisoners and placed alone in a small, ruined, and filthy church.

Toward evening a noncommissioned officer entered with two soldiers and told him that he had been pardoned and would now go to the barracks for prisoners of war. Without understanding what was said to him, Pierre got up and went with the soldiers. They took him to the upper end of the field, where there were some sheds built of charred planks, beams, and scraps of wood, and led him into one of them. In the darkness some twenty different men surrounded Pierre. He looked at them without understanding who they were, why they were there, or what they wanted. He heard what they said but did not grasp the meaning of the words and drew no kind of conclusions from them. He replied to questions they put to him but did not consider who was listening or how they would understand his replies. He looked at their faces and figures, but they all seemed equally meaningless to him.

From the moment Pierre had witnessed those terrible murders committed by men who did not wish to commit them, it was as if the mainspring of his life, on which everything depended and which made everything appear alive, had suddenly been wrenched out and everything had collapsed into a heap of meaningless debris. Though he did not acknowledge it to himself, his faith in the right ordering of the universe, in humanity, in his own soul, and in God had been destroyed. He had experienced this before, but never so powerfully. Previously, when similar doubts had assailed him, they had been the result of his own wrongdoing, and at the bottom of his heart he had felt that relief from despair and doubt was to be found within himself. But now he felt that the universe had crumbled before his eyes and only meaningless ruins remained—and this through no fault of his own. He felt that it was not in his power to regain faith in the meaning of life.

Around him in the darkness men were standing, and evidently something about him interested them greatly. They were telling him something and asking him something. Then they led him away somewhere, and at last he found himself in a corner of the shed among men who were laughing and talking on all sides.
"Well, then, mates... that very prince who..." some voice at the other end of the shed was saying, with a strong emphasis on the word who.

Sitting silent and motionless on a heap of straw against the wall, Pierre sometimes opened and sometimes closed his eyes. But as soon as he closed them he saw before him the dreadful face of the factory boy—especially dreadful because of its simplicity—and the faces of the murderers, even more dreadful because of their unease. And he opened his eyes again and stared blankly into the darkness around him.

Beside him, in a stooping position, sat a small man whose presence Pierre first became aware of through a strong smell of sweat that came from him every time he moved. This man was doing something to his legs in the darkness, and though Pierre could not see his face, he sensed that the man kept glancing at him. Growing accustomed to the darkness, Pierre saw that the man was taking off his leg wrappings, and the way he did it aroused Pierre's interest.

Having unwound the string that tied the wrapping on one leg, he carefully coiled it up and immediately set to work on the other leg, glancing up at Pierre. While one hand hung up the first string, the other was already unwinding the wrapping on the second leg. In this way, having carefully removed the leg wrappings with deft circular motions of his arm following one another without interruption, the man hung them up on some pegs fixed above his head. Then he took out a knife, cut something, closed the knife, placed it under the head of his bed, and seating himself comfortably, clasped his arms around his raised knees and fixed his eyes on Pierre. Pierre was conscious of something pleasant, comforting, and well-rounded in these deft movements, in the man's well-ordered arrangements in his corner, and even in his very smell, and he looked at the man without taking his eyes off him.
"You've seen a lot of trouble, sir, haven't you?" the little man suddenly said.

And there was so much kindness and simplicity in his singsong voice that Pierre tried to reply, but his jaw trembled and he felt tears rising to his eyes. The little fellow, giving Pierre no time to show his emotion, instantly continued in the same pleasant tones:

"Eh, lad, don't fret!" said he, in the tender, singsong, caressing voice old Russian peasant women use. "Don't fret, friend—'suffer an hour, live for a lifetime!' That's how it is, my dear fellow. And here we live, thank God, without offense. Among these folk too there are good men as well as bad," said he, and still speaking, he turned on his knees with a supple movement, got up, coughed, and went off to another part of the shed.
"Hey, you rascal!" Pierre heard the same kind voice saying at the other end of the shed. "So you've come back, you rascal? She remembers... Now, now, that'll do!"
And the soldier, pushing away a little dog that was jumping up at him, returned to his place and sat down. In his hands he had something wrapped in a rag.
"Here, have a bite, sir," said he, resuming his former respectful tone as he unwrapped and offered Pierre some baked potatoes. "We had soup for dinner and the potatoes are wonderful!"
Pierre had not eaten all day, and the smell of the potatoes seemed extremely pleasant. He thanked the soldier and began to eat.
"Well, are they all right?" said the soldier with a smile. "You should try it this way."
He took a potato, drew out his clasp knife, cut it into two equal halves on the palm of his hand, sprinkled some salt on it from the rag, and handed it to Pierre.
"The potatoes are wonderful!" he said once more. "Try some like that!"
Pierre thought he had never eaten anything that tasted better.
"Oh, I'm all right," said he, "but why did they shoot those poor men? The last one was barely twenty."

"Tsk, tsk..." said the little man. "Ah, what a sin... what a sin!" he added quickly, and as if his words were always waiting ready in his mouth and flew out of their own accord, he went on: "How is it, sir, that you stayed in Moscow?"
"I didn't think they would come so soon. I stayed by accident," replied Pierre.
"And how did they arrest you, dear fellow? At your house?"
"No, I went to look at the fire, and they arrested me there and tried me as an arsonist."
"Where there's law, there's injustice," put in the little man.
"And have you been here long?" Pierre asked, munching the last of the potato.
"Me? It was last Sunday they took me, out of a hospital in Moscow."
"Why, are you a soldier then?"
"Yes, we are soldiers of the Apsheron regiment. I was dying of fever. We weren't told anything. There were some twenty of us lying there. We had no idea, never guessed at all."
"And do you feel sad here?" Pierre asked.

"How can one not feel sad, lad? My name is Platon, and the surname is Karataev," he added, evidently wanting to make it easier for Pierre to address him. "They call me 'little falcon' in the regiment. How can one not feel sad? Moscow—she's the mother of cities. How can one see all this and not feel sad? But 'the worm gnaws the cabbage, yet dies first'; that's what the old folks used to tell us," he added quickly.
"What? What did you say?" asked Pierre.
"Who? Me?" said Karataev. "I say things happen not as we plan but as God decides," he replied, thinking he was repeating what he had said before, and immediately continued:
"Well, and you, sir, do you have an estate? And a house? So you're well-off, then? And a wife? And are your old parents still living?" he asked.

And though it was too dark for Pierre to see, he felt that a suppressed smile of kindliness puckered the soldier's lips as he asked these questions. He seemed saddened that Pierre had no parents, especially no mother.
"A wife for counsel, a mother-in-law for welcome, but there's none so dear as one's own mother!" said he. "Well, and do you have little ones?" he went on asking.
Again Pierre's negative answer seemed to distress him, and he hastened to add:
"Never mind! You're young folks yet, and God willing you may still have some. The main thing is to live in harmony..."
"But it's all the same now," Pierre could not help saying.
"Ah, my dear fellow!" replied Karataev. "Never refuse a prison cell or a beggar's sack!"
He settled himself more comfortably and coughed, evidently preparing to tell a long story.

"Well, my dear fellow, I was still living at home," he began. "We had a prosperous homestead, plenty of land; we peasants lived well and our house was one to thank God for. When Father and we went out mowing, there were seven of us. We lived well. We were real peasants. It so happened..."
And Platon Karataev told a long story of how he had gone into someone's woods to take firewood, how he had been caught by the gamekeeper, was tried, flogged, and sent to serve as a soldier.

"Well, lad," and a smile changed the tone of his voice, "we thought it was a misfortune but it turned out a blessing! If it hadn't been for my sin, my brother would have had to go as a soldier. But he, my younger brother, had five little ones, while I, you see, only left a wife behind. We had a little girl, but God took her before I went as a soldier. I came home on leave and I'll tell you how it was—I look and see that they're living better than before. The yard full of livestock, the women at home, two brothers away earning wages, and only Mikhail, the youngest, at home. Father said, 'All my children are the same to me: it hurts the same whichever finger gets bitten. But if Platon hadn't been shaved for a soldier, Mikhail would have had to go.' He called us all before the icons. 'Mikhail,' he says, 'come here and bow at his feet; and you, young woman, bow down too; and you, grandchildren, also bow before him! Do you understand?' he says. That's how it is, dear fellow. Fate looks for a head. But we are always judging, 'that's not right, this isn't fair!' Our luck is like water in a net: you pull and it bulges, but when you've drawn it out, it's empty! That's how it is."
And Platon shifted his seat on the straw.
After a short silence he rose.
"Well, I think you must be sleepy," said he, and began rapidly crossing himself, repeating:

"Lord Jesus Christ, holy Saint Nicholas, Frola and Lavra! Lord Jesus Christ, holy Saint Nicholas, Frola and Lavra! Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on us and save us!" he concluded, then bowed to the ground, got up, sighed, and sat down again on his heap of straw. "That's the way. Lay me down like a stone, O God, and raise me up like a loaf," he muttered as he lay down, pulling his coat over himself.
"What prayer was that you were saying?" asked Pierre.
"Eh?" murmured Platon, who had almost fallen asleep. "What was I saying? I was praying. Don't you pray?"
"Yes, I do," said Pierre. "But what was that you said: Frola and Lavra?"

"Well, of course," replied Platon quickly, "the horses' saints. One must have pity on the animals too. Hey, you rascal! Now you've curled up and got warm, you daughter of a..." said Karataev, touching the dog that lay at his feet, and again turning over, he fell asleep immediately.

Sounds of crying and screaming came from somewhere in the distance outside, and flames were visible through the cracks of the shed, but inside it was quiet and dark. For a long time Pierre did not sleep but lay with eyes open in the darkness, listening to the steady snoring of Platon beside him, and he felt that the world that had been shattered was once more stirring in his soul with a new beauty and on new and unshakable foundations.

chapters.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: Twenty-three soldiers, three officers, and two officials were confined in the shed where Pierre had been placed and where he remained for four weeks.

When Pierre remembered them afterward, they all seemed misty figures to him except Platon Karataev, who always remained in his mind the most vivid and precious memory and the embodiment of everything Russian, kindly, and round. When Pierre saw his neighbor the next morning at dawn, the first impression of him—as of something round—was fully confirmed: Platon's whole figure—in a French overcoat belted with a cord, a soldier's cap, and bast shoes—was round. His head was perfectly round, his back, chest, shoulders, and even his arms, which he held as if ever ready to embrace something, were rounded; his pleasant smile and his large, gentle brown eyes were round too.

Platon Karataev must have been about fifty, judging by his stories of campaigns he had been in, told like an old soldier. He did not know his own age and was quite unable to determine it. But his brilliantly white, strong teeth—which showed in two unbroken semicircles when he laughed, as he often did—were all sound and good. There was not a gray hair in his beard or on his head, and his whole body gave an impression of suppleness and especially of firmness and endurance.

His face, despite its fine, rounded wrinkles, had an expression of innocence and youth; his voice was pleasant and musical. But the chief peculiarity of his speech was its directness and aptness. It was evident that he never considered what he had said or was going to say, and consequently the speed and rightness of his delivery had an irresistible persuasiveness.

His physical strength and agility during the first days of his imprisonment were such that he seemed not to know what fatigue and sickness meant. Every night before lying down he said: "Lord, lay me down as a stone and raise me up as a loaf!" And every morning on getting up he said: "I lay down and curled up, I get up and shake myself." And indeed he only had to lie down to fall asleep like a stone, and he only had to shake himself to be ready without a moment's delay for any work, just as children are ready to play the instant they wake. He could do everything—not very well but not badly. He baked, cooked, sewed, planed, and mended boots. He was always busy, and only at night allowed himself conversation—which he loved—and songs. He did not sing like a trained singer who knows he is being listened to, but like the birds, evidently giving vent to the sounds in the same way that one stretches or walks about to relieve stiffness. The sounds were always high-pitched, mournful, delicate, and almost feminine, and his face at such times was very serious.

Having been taken prisoner and allowed his beard to grow, he seemed to have thrown off everything that had been forced upon him—everything military and foreign to his nature—and had returned to his former peasant ways.
"A soldier on leave—a shirt worn outside the trousers," he would say.

He did not like talking about his life as a soldier, though he did not complain, and often mentioned that he had never once been flogged during his whole army service. When he told stories it was generally from old and evidently treasured memories of his "Christian" life, as he called his peasant existence. The proverbs that filled his speech were not the coarse and crude ones soldiers use, but those folk sayings which, taken out of context, seem so insignificant, but which used at the right moment suddenly acquire a significance of profound wisdom.

He would often say the exact opposite of what he had said on a previous occasion, yet both would be right. He liked to talk and he talked well, adorning his speech with terms of endearment and folk sayings which Pierre thought he invented himself. But the chief charm of his talk lay in the fact that the most common events—sometimes just such as Pierre had witnessed without taking notice of them—assumed in Karataev's telling a character of solemn meaning. He liked to hear the folk tales one of the soldiers told in the evenings (they were always the same), but most of all he liked to hear stories of real life. He would smile joyfully while listening to such stories, now and then putting in a word or asking a question to make the moral beauty of what he was told clear to himself. Karataev had no attachments, friendships, or love as Pierre understood them, but loved and lived warmly with everything life brought him into contact with, particularly with people—not any particular person, but those with whom he happened to be. He loved his dog, his comrades, the French, and Pierre who was his neighbor; but Pierre felt that despite Karataev's affectionate tenderness for him (by which he unconsciously gave Pierre's spiritual life its due), he would not have grieved for a moment at parting from him. And Pierre began to feel the same way toward Karataev.

To all the other prisoners, Platon Karataev seemed a most ordinary soldier. They called him "little falcon" or "Platosha," teased him good-naturedly, and sent him on errands. But to Pierre he always remained what he had seemed that first night: an unfathomable, rounded, eternal personification of the spirit of simplicity and truth.
Platon Karataev knew nothing by heart except his prayers. When he began to speak he seemed not to know how he would finish.

Sometimes Pierre, struck by the meaning of his words, would ask him to repeat them, but Platon could never recall what he had said a moment before, just as he could never repeat to Pierre the words of his favorite song: native and birch tree and my heart is sick came up in it, but when spoken rather than sung, no meaning could be extracted. He did not, and could not, understand the meaning of words apart from their context. Every word and action of his was the expression of an activity unknown to him, which was his life. But his life, as he saw it, had no meaning as a separate thing. It had meaning only as part of a whole of which he was always conscious. His words and actions flowed from him as evenly, inevitably, and spontaneously as fragrance from a flower. He could not understand the value or significance of any word or deed taken separately.

chapters.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: When Princess Mary heard from Nicholas that her brother was with the Rostovs at Yaroslavl, she at once prepared to go there, despite her aunt's efforts to dissuade her—and not merely to go herself but to take her nephew with her. Whether it was difficult or easy, possible or impossible, she did not ask and did not want to know: it was her duty, not only to herself, to be near her brother who was perhaps dying, but to do everything possible to bring his son to him, and so she prepared to set off. That she had not heard from Prince Andrew himself, Princess Mary attributed to his being too weak to write, or to his considering the long journey too hard and too dangerous for her and his son.

In a few days Princess Mary was ready to start. Her vehicles were the huge family coach in which she had traveled to Voronezh, a half-open carriage, and a baggage cart. With her traveled Mademoiselle Bourienne, little Nicholas and his tutor, her old nurse, three maids, Tikhon, and a young footman and courier her aunt had sent to accompany her.

The usual route through Moscow was out of the question, and the roundabout way Princess Mary was obliged to take through Lipetsk, Ryazan, Vladimir, and Shuya was very long and, since post horses were not available everywhere, very difficult, and near Ryazan—where the French were said to have appeared—even dangerous.

During this difficult journey, Mademoiselle Bourienne, Dessalles, and Princess Mary's servants were astonished at her energy and strength of spirit. She went to bed later and rose earlier than any of them, and no difficulties daunted her. Thanks to her activity and energy, which inspired her fellow travelers, they approached Yaroslavl by the end of the second week.

The last days of her stay in Voronezh had been the happiest of her life. Her love for Rostov no longer tormented or agitated her. It filled her whole soul, had become an integral part of herself, and she no longer fought against it. She had become convinced that she loved and was loved, though she never said this to herself in words. She had become convinced of it at her last meeting with Nicholas, when he had come to tell her that her brother was with the Rostovs. Not by a single word had Nicholas alluded to the fact that Prince Andrew's relationship with Natasha might, if he recovered, be renewed; but Princess Mary saw from his face that he knew and thought of this.

Yet despite that, his attitude toward her—considerate, delicate, and loving—not only remained unchanged, but it sometimes seemed to Princess Mary that he was even glad that the family connection between them allowed him to express his friendship more freely. She knew that she loved for the first and only time in her life, and felt that she was loved, and was happy in that knowledge.

But this happiness on one side of her spiritual nature did not prevent her from feeling grief for her brother with full force; on the contrary, that spiritual peace on one side made it all the more possible for her to give full expression to her feeling for her brother. That feeling was so strong at the moment of leaving Voronezh that those who saw her off, looking at her careworn, despairing face, felt certain she would fall ill on the journey. But the very difficulties and demands of the journey, which she took so actively in hand, saved her for a while from her grief and gave her strength.

As always happens when traveling, Princess Mary thought only of the journey itself, forgetting its purpose. But as she approached Yaroslavl, the thought of what might await her there—not after many days but that very evening—again presented itself, and her agitation reached its peak.

The courier who had been sent ahead to find out where the Rostovs were staying in Yaroslavl and in what condition Prince Andrew was, met the big coach just entering the town gates and was appalled by the terrible pallor of the princess's face looking out at him from the window.
"I have found out everything, your excellency: the Rostovs are staying at the merchant Bronnikov's house, in the square not far from here, right above the Volga," said the courier.
Princess Mary looked at him with frightened inquiry, not understanding why he did not reply to what she most wanted to know: how was her brother? Mademoiselle Bourienne asked that question for her.
"How is the prince?" she asked.
"His excellency is staying in the same house with them."
"Then he is alive," thought Princess Mary, and asked in a low voice: "How is he?"
"The servants say he is still the same."

What "still the same" might mean, Princess Mary did not ask, but with an unnoticed glance at little seven-year-old Nicholas—who was sitting in front of her looking with pleasure at the town—she bowed her head and did not raise it again until the heavy coach, rumbling, shaking, and swaying, came to a stop. The carriage steps clattered as they were let down.

The carriage door opened. On the left there was water—a great river—and on the right a porch. There were people at the entrance: servants, and a rosy girl with a large plait of black hair, smiling in a way that seemed to Princess Mary unpleasantly artificial. (This was Sonya.) Princess Mary ran up the steps. "This way, this way!" said the girl with the same artificial smile, and the princess found herself in the hall facing an elderly woman of Eastern appearance, who came quickly toward her with a look of emotion. This was the countess. She embraced Princess Mary and kissed her.
"My child!" she murmured, "I love you and have known you a long time."
* "My child! I love you and have known you a long time."

Despite her emotion, Princess Mary realized that this was the countess and that she must say something to her. Hardly knowing how she managed it, she spoke a few polite phrases in French in the same tone as those addressed to her, and asked: "How is he?"
"The doctor says he is not in danger," said the countess, but as she spoke she raised her eyes with a sigh, and her gesture conveyed a contradiction of her words.
"Where is he? Can I see him—can I?" asked the princess.

"One moment, Princess, one moment, my dear! Is this his son?" said the countess, turning to little Nicholas who was coming in with Dessalles. "There will be room for everybody; this is a big house. Oh, what a lovely boy!"

The countess took Princess Mary into the drawing room, where Sonya was talking to Mademoiselle Bourienne. The countess caressed the boy, and the old count came in and welcomed the princess. He had changed very much since she had last seen him. Then he had been a brisk, cheerful, self-assured old man; now he seemed a pitiful, bewildered person. While talking to Princess Mary he kept looking around as if asking everyone whether he was doing the right thing. After the destruction of Moscow and of his property, thrown out of his accustomed groove, he seemed to have lost his sense of his own importance and to feel that there was no longer a place for him in life.

Despite her one desire to see her brother as soon as possible, and her irritation that at the moment when all she wanted was to see him they were trying to entertain her and pretending to admire her nephew, the princess noticed all that was going on around her and felt the necessity of submitting for a time to this new order of things she had entered. She knew it was necessary, and though it was hard for her, she was not angry with these people.
"This is my niece," said the count, introducing Sonya. "You don't know her, Princess?"

Princess Mary turned to Sonya and, trying to suppress the hostile feeling that arose in her toward the girl, she kissed her. But she felt oppressed by the fact that the mood of everyone around her was so far from what was in her own heart.
"Where is he?" she asked again, addressing them all.
"He is downstairs. Natasha is with him," answered Sonya, flushing. "We have sent to ask. I think you must be tired, Princess."

Tears of frustration showed in Princess Mary's eyes. She turned away and was about to ask the countess again how to go to him, when light, eager, and seemingly buoyant steps were heard at the door. The princess looked around and saw Natasha coming in, almost running—that Natasha whom she had liked so little at their meeting in Moscow long before.

But hardly had the princess looked at Natasha's face before she realized that here was a true companion in her grief, and therefore a friend. She ran to meet her, embraced her, and began to cry on her shoulder.

As soon as Natasha, sitting at the head of Prince Andrew's bed, heard of Princess Mary's arrival, she softly left his room and hurried to her with those swift steps that had sounded buoyant to Princess Mary.

There was only one expression on her agitated face when she ran into the drawing room—that of love: boundless love for him, for her, and for all that was close to the man she loved; and of pity, suffering for others, and a passionate desire to give herself entirely to helping them. It was plain that at that moment there was in Natasha's heart no thought of herself or of her own relationship with Prince Andrew.
Princess Mary, with her acute sensitivity, understood all this at the first glance at Natasha's face, and wept on her shoulder with sorrowful joy.
"Come, come to him, Mary," said Natasha, leading her into the other room.
Princess Mary raised her head, dried her eyes, and turned to Natasha. She felt that from her she would be able to understand and learn everything.
"How..." she began her question but stopped short.
She felt that it was impossible to ask, or to answer, in words. Natasha's face and eyes would have to tell her everything more clearly and deeply.

Natasha was gazing at her but seemed afraid and in doubt whether to say all she knew or not; she seemed to feel that before those luminous eyes that penetrated into the very depths of her heart, it was impossible not to tell the whole truth as she saw it. And suddenly Natasha's lips twitched, ugly wrinkles gathered round her mouth, and covering her face with her hands, she burst into sobs.
Princess Mary understood.
But she still hoped, and asked in words she herself did not trust:
"But how is his wound? What is his general condition?"
"You, you... will see," was all Natasha could say.
They sat a little while downstairs near his room until they had stopped crying and were able to go to him with calm faces.
"How has his whole illness gone? Is it long since he grew worse? When did this happen?" Princess Mary asked.

Natasha told her that at first there had been danger from his feverish condition and the pain he suffered, but at Troitsa that had passed and the doctor had only been afraid of gangrene. That danger had also passed. When they reached Yaroslavl, the wound had begun to fester (Natasha knew all about such things as festering), and the doctor had said the festering might take a normal course. Then fever set in, but the doctor had said the fever was not very serious.
"But two days ago this suddenly happened," said Natasha, struggling with her sobs. "I don't know why, but you will see what he is like."
"Is he weaker? Thinner?" asked the princess.
"No, it's not that, but worse. You will see. Oh, Mary, he is too good, he cannot, cannot live, because..."

chapters.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: When Natasha opened Prince Andrew's door with a familiar movement and let Princess Mary pass into the room before her, the princess felt the sobs in her throat. Hard as she had tried to prepare herself and now tried to remain calm, she knew she would be unable to look at him without tears.

The princess understood what Natasha had meant by the words: "two days ago this suddenly happened." She understood those words to mean that he had suddenly softened, and that this softening and gentleness were signs of approaching death. As she stepped toward the door she already saw in her imagination Andrew's face as she remembered it in childhood—a gentle, mild, compassionate face which he had rarely shown, and which therefore affected her deeply. She was sure he would speak soft, tender words to her such as her father had said before his death, and that she would not be able to bear it and would burst into sobs in his presence. Yet sooner or later it had to be, and she went in. The sobs rose higher and higher in her throat as she more and more clearly made out his form, and her nearsighted eyes tried to distinguish his features—and then she saw his face and met his gaze.

He was lying in a squirrel-fur dressing gown on a divan, surrounded by pillows. He was thin and pale. In one thin, translucently white hand he held a handkerchief, while with the other he slowly stroked the delicate mustache he had grown, moving his fingers slowly. His eyes gazed at them as they entered.

On seeing his face and meeting his eyes, Princess Mary's pace suddenly slackened; she felt her tears dry up and her sobs cease. She suddenly felt guilty and grew timid, catching the expression of his face and eyes.
"But what am I guilty of?" she asked herself. And his cold, stern look replied: "Because you are alive and thinking of the living, while I..."
In the deep gaze that seemed to look not outward but inward, there was an almost hostile expression as he slowly regarded his sister and Natasha.
He kissed his sister, holding her hand in his as was their custom.
"How are you, Mary? How did you manage to get here?" said he in a voice as calm and detached as his look.
Had he screamed in agony, that scream would not have struck such horror into Princess Mary's heart as the tone of his voice.
"And have you brought little Nicholas?" he asked in the same slow, quiet manner, with an obvious effort to remember.
"How are you now?" said Princess Mary, herself surprised at what she was saying.
"That, my dear, you must ask the doctor," he replied, and again making an evident effort to be warm, he said with his lips only (his words clearly did not match his thoughts):
"Thank you for coming, my dear."
* "Thank you for coming, my dear."

Princess Mary pressed his hand. The pressure made him wince just perceptibly. He was silent, and she did not know what to say. She now understood what had happened to him two days before. In his words, his tone, and especially in that calm, almost hostile look could be felt an estrangement from everything belonging to this world—terrible in one who is alive. Evidently only with an effort did he understand anything living; but it was clear that he failed to understand not because he lacked the ability, but because he understood something else—something the living did not and could not understand—and which wholly occupied his mind.
"There, you see how strangely fate has brought us together," said he, breaking the silence and pointing to Natasha. "She looks after me all the time."

Princess Mary heard him and did not understand how he could say such a thing. He, the sensitive, tender Prince Andrew—how could he say that, in front of the woman he loved and who loved him? Had he expected to live, he could not have spoken those words in that offensively cold tone. If he had not known he was dying, how could he have failed to pity her, and how could he speak like that in her presence? The only explanation was that he was indifferent, because something else, much more important, had been revealed to him.
The conversation was cold and disconnected and continually broke off.
"Mary came by way of Ryazan," said Natasha.
Prince Andrew did not notice that she called his sister Mary; and only after calling her so in his presence did Natasha notice it herself.
"Really?" he asked.
"They told her that all Moscow has been burned down, and that..."
Natasha stopped. It was impossible to talk. It was plain that he was making an effort to listen but could not.
"Yes, they say it's burned," he said. "It's a great pity," and he gazed straight before him, absently stroking his mustache with his fingers.

"And so you have met Count Nicholas, Mary?" Prince Andrew suddenly said, evidently wishing to speak pleasantly to them. "He wrote here that he took a great liking to you," he went on simply and calmly, evidently unable to understand all the complex significance his words had for living people. "If you liked him too, it would be a good thing for you to get married," he added rather more quickly, as if pleased at finding words he had long been seeking.
Princess Mary heard his words but they had no meaning for her except as proof of how far away he now was from everything living.
"Why talk of me?" she said quietly and glanced at Natasha.
Natasha, who felt her glance, did not look at her. All three were again silent.
"Andrew, would you like..." Princess Mary suddenly said in a trembling voice, "would you like to see little Nicholas? He is always talking about you!"

Prince Andrew smiled just perceptibly and for the first time, but Princess Mary, who knew his face so well, saw with horror that he did not smile with pleasure or affection for his son, but with quiet, gentle irony—because he thought she was trying what she believed to be the last means of rousing him.
"Yes, I shall be very glad to see him. Is he quite well?"

When little Nicholas was brought into Prince Andrew's room, he looked at his father with frightened eyes but did not cry, because no one else was crying. Prince Andrew kissed him and evidently did not know what to say to him.
When Nicholas had been led away, Princess Mary again went up to her brother, kissed him, and unable to hold back her tears any longer, began to cry.
He looked at her attentively.
"Is it about Nicholas?" he asked.
Princess Mary nodded her head, weeping.
"Mary, you know the Gosp..." but he broke off.
"What did you say?"
"Nothing. You mustn't cry here," he said, looking at her with the same cold expression.

When Princess Mary began to cry, he understood that she was crying at the thought that little Nicholas would be left without a father. With a great effort he tried to return to life and to see things from their point of view.
"Yes, to them it must seem sad!" he thought. "But how simple it is.

"The birds of the air neither sow nor reap, yet your Father feeds them," he said to himself, and wished to say to Princess Mary; "but no, they will take it their own way. They won't understand! They can't understand that all those feelings they prize so—all our feelings, all those ideas that seem so important to us—are unnecessary. We cannot understand one another." And he remained silent.

Prince Andrew's little son was seven. He could scarcely read and knew nothing. After that day he lived through many things, gaining knowledge, observation, and experience; but had he possessed all the faculties he later acquired, he could not have had a better or more profound understanding of the meaning of the scene he had witnessed between his father, Mary, and Natasha than he had then. He understood it completely, and leaving the room without crying, went silently up to Natasha—who had come out with him—and looked shyly at her with his beautiful, thoughtful eyes. Then his upturned, rosy upper lip trembled, and leaning his head against her, he began to cry.

After that he avoided Dessalles and the countess who caressed him, and either sat alone or came timidly to Princess Mary or to Natasha, of whom he seemed even fonder than of his aunt, and clung to them quietly and shyly.

When Princess Mary had left Prince Andrew she fully understood what Natasha's face had told her. She did not speak any more to Natasha about hopes of saving his life. She took turns with her beside his sofa, and did not cry anymore, but prayed continually, turning in her soul to that Eternal and Unfathomable, whose presence above the dying man was now so clearly felt.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Prince Andrew didn't just know he was going to die—he felt himself dying, already half gone. He was aware of a detachment from everything earthly, and a strange, joyful lightness filled him. Without hurry or anxiety, he waited for what was coming. That inexorable, eternal, distant, and unknown presence he had sensed throughout his entire life was now close to him, and through the strange lightness he felt, it had become almost understandable, almost something he could touch.
He had feared death before. Twice he had experienced that terrible, tormenting fear of the end—but now he no longer understood that fear.

The first time had been when the shell spun like a top in front of him, and he looked at the field, the bushes, and the sky, knowing he was face to face with death. When he came to himself after being wounded, a flower of eternal, unbound love had instantly opened in his soul, as if freed from the chains of life that had held it back. After that, he no longer feared death and stopped thinking about it.

During the hours of solitude, suffering, and partial delirium after his wound, the deeper he penetrated into this new principle of eternal love, the more he unconsciously detached himself from earthly life. To love everything and everyone, to always sacrifice oneself for love—that meant not loving anyone in particular, not living this earthly life. And the more he embraced that principle, the more he let go of life, and the more completely he dissolved the terrible barrier that—without such love—stands between life and death. When he first remembered he would have to die, he said to himself: 'Well, so what? So much the better!'

But after that night in Mytishchi, when, half delirious, he had seen the woman he longed for appear before him, and pressing her hand to his lips had shed gentle, happy tears—love for one particular woman crept back unnoticed into his heart and bound him to life once more. Joyful, agitating thoughts began to fill his mind. Remembering the moment at the field hospital when he had seen Kuragin, he could no longer recapture what he had felt then, but was tormented by the question of whether Kuragin was still alive. And he didn't dare ask.

His illness followed its normal physical course, but what Natasha meant when she said 'This suddenly happened' had occurred two days before Princess Mary arrived. It was the last spiritual struggle between life and death, in which death won. It was the unexpected realization that he still valued life—life as embodied in his love for Natasha—and a final, though ultimately defeated, attack of terror before the unknown.

It was evening. As usual after dinner, he was slightly feverish, and his thoughts were unusually clear. Sonya was sitting by the table. He began to doze off. Suddenly a feeling of happiness washed over him.
'Ah, she's here!' he thought.
And so she was: Natasha had come in silently and taken Sonya's place.

Ever since she had begun looking after him, he had always felt this physical awareness of her nearness. She sat in an armchair turned sideways, screening the candlelight from him, knitting a stocking. She had learned to knit after Prince Andrew casually mentioned that no one nurses the sick as well as old women who knit stockings, and that there's something soothing about it. The needles clicked lightly in her slender, quickly moving hands, and he could clearly see the thoughtful profile of her bowed face. She shifted, and the ball of yarn rolled off her knees. She started, glanced at him, and shielding the candle with her hand, stooped carefully with a smooth, precise movement, picked up the ball, and settled back into her former position.
He watched her without moving and saw that after bending down she wanted to take a deep breath but held back, breathing cautiously instead.

At the Troitsa monastery they had spoken of the past, and he had told her that if he survived, he would always thank God for his wound, which had brought them together again. But after that, they never spoke of the future.

'Can it be, or can it not?' he thought now, watching her and listening to the light click of the steel needles. 'Could fate really have brought me to her so strangely only for me to die? Is it possible that the truth of life has been revealed to me only to show me that I've wasted my life in falsehood? I love her more than anything in the world! But what can I do if I love her?' He groaned involuntarily—a habit from his suffering.
Hearing that sound, Natasha put down the stocking, leaned closer, and suddenly noticing his shining eyes, stepped lightly to his side and bent over him.
'You're not asleep?'
'No, I've been watching you for a long time. I felt you come in. No one else gives me that sense of soft peace that you do... that light. I want to cry from joy.'
Natasha moved closer to him. Her face shone with radiant happiness.
'Natasha, I love you too much! More than anything in the world.'
'And I love you!'—she turned away for a moment. 'Why too much?' she asked.
'Why too much?... Well, tell me—what do you feel in your soul, your whole soul—will I live? What do you think?'
'I'm sure of it, sure!' Natasha almost shouted, seizing both his hands with a passionate movement.
He was silent for a while.
'How wonderful that would be!' And taking her hand, he kissed it.
Natasha felt happy and stirred up, but immediately remembered that this wouldn't do—he needed to stay calm.
'But you haven't slept,' she said, holding back her joy. 'Try to sleep... please!'

He pressed her hand and let it go, and she went back to the candle and sat down again in her former position. Twice she turned to look at him, and her eyes met his, beaming at her. She set herself a goal on her stocking and resolved not to look around until she finished it.
Soon he really did close his eyes and fall asleep. He didn't sleep long and suddenly woke with a start, drenched in cold sweat.
As he fell asleep, he had still been thinking about the subject that now always occupied his mind—life and death, and mainly death. He felt himself closer to it.
'Love? What is love?' he thought.

'Love holds death back. Love is life. Everything I understand, I understand only because I love. Everything exists only because I love. Everything is united by love alone. Love is God, and to die means that I, a particle of love, will return to the universal, eternal source.' These thoughts seemed comforting. But they were only thoughts. Something was missing—they weren't clear, they were too personal, too cerebral. And the old agitation and confusion remained. He fell asleep.

He dreamed he was lying in the room where he actually was, but perfectly well and unwounded. Various unimportant people appeared before him. He talked to them, discussed trivial things. They were getting ready to go somewhere. Prince Andrew vaguely realized that all this was trivial and that he had more important concerns, but he kept talking, surprising them with empty jokes. Gradually, unnoticed, all these people disappeared, and a single question—about the closed door—replaced everything else. He got up and went to bolt and lock the door. Everything depended on whether he could lock it in time. He tried to hurry, but his legs wouldn't move, and he knew he wouldn't make it. He was seized by an agonizing fear. That fear was the fear of death. It stood behind the door. But just as he was clumsily creeping toward it, that dreadful something on the other side was already pressing against it, forcing its way in. Something inhuman—death—was breaking through that door, and it had to be kept out. He grabbed the door, making a final effort to hold it back—locking it was no longer possible—but his efforts were weak and clumsy, and the door, pushed from behind by that terror, opened and closed again.
Once more it pushed from outside. His last superhuman efforts were useless, and both halves of the door swung silently open. It entered. It was death. And Prince Andrew died.
But at the very instant he died, Prince Andrew remembered that he was asleep, and at the very instant he died, making an effort, he woke up.

'Yes, that was death! I died—and woke up. Yes, death is an awakening!' And suddenly everything grew light in his soul, and the veil that had hidden the unknown was lifted from his inner vision. He felt as though powers that had been trapped within him were now released, and that strange lightness never left him again.
When he woke in a cold sweat and stirred on the couch, Natasha came to him and asked what was wrong. He didn't answer and looked at her strangely, without understanding.

That was what had happened two days before Princess Mary's arrival. From that day, as the doctor put it, the wasting fever turned malignant. But what the doctor said didn't concern Natasha—she could see the terrible spiritual symptoms that were far more convincing to her.

From that day onward, an awakening from life came to Prince Andrew alongside his awakening from sleep. And compared to the length of life, it didn't seem any slower to him than waking from sleep compared to the length of a dream.
There was nothing terrible or violent in this comparatively slow awakening.

His last days and hours passed in an ordinary, simple way. Both Princess Mary and Natasha, who never left him, felt this. They didn't weep or shudder, and during those final days they felt they were no longer tending to him—he was already gone—but to what most closely reminded them of him: his body. Both felt this so strongly that the outward, terrible side of death didn't touch them, and they didn't feel the need to feed their grief. They didn't cry in his presence or out of it, and they never talked to each other about him. They felt that no words could express what they understood.
They both watched him sinking slowly and quietly, deeper and deeper away from them, and they both knew it had to be this way, and that it was right.

He made his confession and received communion. Everyone came to say goodbye. When they brought his son to him, he pressed his lips to the boy's face and turned away—not because it was hard or sad (Princess Mary and Natasha understood that), but simply because he thought it was all that was required of him. When they told him to bless the boy, he did what was asked and looked around as if wondering whether there was anything else he should do.
When the last convulsions of the body, which the spirit was leaving, came, Princess Mary and Natasha were there.

'Is it over?' said Princess Mary, after his body had lain motionless for a few minutes, growing cold before them. Natasha went up, looked at the dead eyes, and hurried to close them. She closed them but didn't kiss them—instead she pressed herself against what reminded her most of him: his body.
'Where has he gone? Where is he now?...'
When the body, washed and dressed, lay in the coffin on a table, everyone came to say goodbye, and they all wept.

Little Nikolai cried because his heart was torn by painful confusion. The countess and Sonya cried from pity for Natasha and because he was gone. The old count cried because he felt that before long, he too would have to take that same terrible step.

Natasha and Princess Mary wept too, but not from personal grief. They wept with a reverent, softening emotion that had taken hold of their souls at the awareness of the simple, solemn mystery of death that had been accomplished in their presence.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: The human mind cannot grasp the causes of events in their totality, but the desire to find those causes is planted deep in the human soul. Without considering the countless complexity of conditions—any one of which, taken alone, might seem to be the cause—a person seizes on the first explanation that seems intelligible and says: 'This is the cause!' In historical events, the first and most primitive explanation was the will of the gods, and after that, the will of those who stood in the most prominent positions—the heroes of history. But we need only look beneath the surface of any historical event—which really lies in the activity of the masses who take part in it—to see that the will of the historical hero doesn't control the actions of the masses, but is itself constantly controlled. It may seem unimportant whether we understand historical events one way or another. Yet there is the same difference between someone who says 'the peoples of the West moved eastward because Napoleon wished it' and someone who says 'this happened because it had to happen,' as between those who believed the earth was stationary and the planets revolved around it, and those who admitted they didn't know what held the earth in place but knew there were laws governing its motion. There is, and can be, no cause of a historical event except the one cause of all causes. But there are laws directing events, and some of these laws we know while others we cannot yet comprehend. Discovering these laws becomes possible only when we completely abandon the attempt to find the cause in the will of any single individual, just as the laws of planetary motion were discovered only when people abandoned the idea that the earth was fixed.

Historians consider that, next to the Battle of Borodino and the occupation and burning of Moscow, the most important episode of the 1812 war was the movement of the Russian army from the Ryazan to the Kaluga road and to the Tarutino camp—the so-called flank march across the Krasnaya Pakhra River. They attribute this stroke of genius to various individuals and debate who deserves the credit. Even foreign historians, including the French, acknowledge the genius of the Russian commanders when they discuss this flank march. But it's hard to understand why military writers, and others following them, consider this maneuver to be some brilliant conception by a single man who saved Russia and destroyed Napoleon. First, it's hard to see where the genius lay, because it didn't take much brainpower to see that the best position for an army not under attack is where supplies are most plentiful—even a dull thirteen-year-old could have guessed that the best position after the retreat from Moscow was on the Kaluga road. So it's impossible to understand how historians conclude this was a profound maneuver. And it's even harder to understand why they think it saved Russia and destroyed the French, since this flank march—had it been preceded, accompanied, or followed by other circumstances—might have proved ruinous for the Russians. If the Russian army's position did begin to improve after this march, it doesn't follow at all that the march was the cause.

That flank march might not only have failed to benefit the Russian army but, under other circumstances, could have led to its destruction. What would have happened if Moscow hadn't burned down? If Murat hadn't lost sight of the Russians? If Napoleon hadn't remained inactive? If the Russian army at Krasnaya Pakhra had given battle, as Bennigsen and Barclay advised? What if the French had attacked the Russians while they were marching beyond the Pakhra? What if Napoleon had attacked the Russians approaching Tarutino with even a tenth of the energy he showed at Smolensk? What if the French had marched on Petersburg? In any of these scenarios, the flank march that supposedly brought salvation might have proved disastrous.

The third and most baffling thing is that historians studying this period deliberately avoid acknowledging that this flank march cannot be attributed to any single person, that no one foresaw it, and that in reality—like the retreat from Fili—it never occurred to anyone as a complete plan. It emerged moment by moment, step by step, event by event, from an endless number of diverse circumstances, and was only seen as a whole after it was accomplished and belonged to the past.

At the council at Fili, the prevailing idea among the Russian commanders was the most natural one: a direct retreat along the Nizhni road. Proof of this lies in the fact that the majority voted for such a retreat, and especially in the well-known conversation after the council between the commander in chief and Lanskoy, who was in charge of supplies. Lanskoy informed the commander in chief that army provisions were mostly stored along the Oka River in the Tula and Ryazan provinces, and that retreating toward Nizhni would separate the army from its supplies by the broad Oka, which can't be crossed early in winter. This was the first indication that they needed to deviate from the most natural course—a direct retreat toward Nizhni-Novgorod. The army turned more to the south, along the Ryazan road and closer to its supplies. Later, the French inactivity (they even lost sight of the Russian army), concern for the arsenal at Tula, and the advantage of moving closer to provisions caused the army to turn still further south onto the Tula road. After crossing to the Tula road beyond the Pakhra by a forced march, the Russian commanders planned to stay at Podolsk and had no thought of the Tarutino position. But countless circumstances—the reappearance of French troops, plans for giving battle, and above all the abundance of food in Kaluga province—forced the army to turn even further south, crossing from the Tula to the Kaluga road and proceeding to Tarutino, which lay between the supply routes. Just as it's impossible to say when the decision was made to abandon Moscow, it's impossible to say precisely when, or by whom, the decision was made to move to Tarutino. Only when the army had arrived there, as the result of innumerable and varying forces, did people begin assuring themselves that they had planned this movement all along and had foreseen its outcome.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: The famous flank movement was really quite simple: after the French advance had stopped, the Russian army—which had been retreating straight back from the invaders—veered away from that direct line and, finding it wasn't being pursued, naturally drifted toward the region where supplies were most plentiful.

If instead of imagining genius commanders leading the Russian army, we picture that army without any leaders at all, it couldn't have done anything but swing back toward Moscow in an arc toward the areas where food was most abundant and the land was richest.

This shift from the Nizhni toward the Ryazan, Tula, and Kaluga roads was so natural that even Russian stragglers moved in that direction, and orders were sent from Petersburg for Kutuzov to take this very route. At Tarutino, Kutuzov received what amounted to a reprimand from the Emperor for moving along the Ryazan road, with the Emperor's letter pointing him toward the very position near Kaluga that he had already occupied.

Having rolled like a ball in the direction given by the momentum of the whole campaign and the Battle of Borodino, the Russian army—when that momentum was spent and no fresh push came—settled into its natural position.

Kutuzov's merit lay not in any so-called strategic masterstroke but in the fact that he alone understood the significance of what had happened. He alone grasped the meaning of the French army's inactivity. He alone continued to insist that the Battle of Borodino had been a victory. He alone—though as commander in chief he might have been expected to be eager to attack—used all his strength to hold the Russian army back from pointless engagements.

The beast wounded at Borodino was lying where the fleeing hunter had left it. Whether it was still alive, whether it was strong and merely lying low—the hunter didn't know. Suddenly the beast was heard to moan.
The moan of that wounded beast—the French army—which revealed its desperate condition, was the sending of Lauriston to Kutuzov's camp with peace proposals.
Napoleon, with his usual certainty that whatever entered his head was right, wrote to Kutuzov the first words that came to mind, though they meant nothing.

'My Prince Kutuzov: I am sending one of my adjutants-general to discuss several interesting questions with you. I beg Your Highness to believe what he says, especially when he expresses the sentiments of esteem and special regard I have long held for your person. This letter having no other purpose, I pray God to keep you in His holy and gracious protection!'
NAPOLEON
Moscow, October 30, 1812

Kutuzov replied: 'I would be cursed by future generations if I were seen as the one who initiated any kind of settlement. Such is the spirit of my nation.' But he continued to use all his powers to keep his troops from attacking.

During the month the French troops spent looting Moscow while the Russian troops rested quietly at Tarutino, a shift had taken place in the relative strength of the two armies—both in spirit and in numbers—so that the advantage had passed to the Russian side. Although the Russians didn't know the exact condition and numbers of the French army, as soon as this shift occurred, the need to attack became obvious through countless signs: Lauriston's mission, the abundance of supplies at Tarutino, the reports pouring in from all sides about French disorder and inactivity, the flow of recruits into Russian regiments, the fine weather, the long rest the Russian soldiers had enjoyed, the natural impatience to do what they'd been assembled for, curiosity about what the French army was doing, the boldness of Russian outposts scouting close to the French positions at Tarutino, news of easy victories by peasants and guerrillas, the envy this aroused, the desire for revenge that burned in every Russian heart while the French remained in Moscow, and above all a dim awareness in every soldier's mind that the balance of power had shifted and the advantage was now theirs. A real change had occurred, and an advance had become inevitable. And at once—just as a clock begins to strike and chime when the minute hand completes its circle—this change showed itself through increased activity, buzzing, and ringing in the higher command.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The Russian army was being commanded by Kutuzov and his staff, and also by the Emperor from Petersburg. Before news of the abandonment of Moscow had reached Petersburg, a detailed plan for the entire campaign had been drawn up and sent to Kutuzov for guidance. Though this plan assumed Moscow was still in Russian hands, it was approved by the staff and accepted as the basis for action. Kutuzov replied only that plans made at a distance were always difficult to execute. So fresh instructions were sent for handling difficulties that might arise, along with new people to watch Kutuzov's actions and report on them.

Beyond this, the entire Russian army staff was being reorganized. The positions left vacant by Bagration, who had been killed, and by Barclay, who had departed in a huff, had to be filled. Very serious thought was given to whether it would be better to put A in B's place and B in D's, or the reverse—as if anything beyond A's or B's personal satisfaction depended on these decisions.

As a result of the hostility between Kutuzov and Bennigsen (his chief of staff), the presence of the Emperor's confidential representatives, and all these personnel changes, an unusually complicated web of political maneuvering was underway among the staff. A was undermining B, D was undermining C, and so on in every possible combination. In all these intrigues, the subject was supposedly the conduct of the war, which everyone believed they were directing. But the war went on independently of them all, following its own course—never the way people planned it, but flowing always from the essential attitude of the masses. Only in the highest circles did all these schemes and machinations appear to reflect what actually had to happen.

'Prince Mikhail Ilarionovich!' wrote the Emperor on the second of October, in a letter that reached Kutuzov after the battle of Tarutino. 'Since September 2, Moscow has been in enemy hands. Your last reports were dated the twentieth, and since then no action has been taken against the enemy or to relieve the ancient capital. According to your latest dispatch, you have even retreated further. Serpukhov is already occupied by an enemy detachment, and Tula with its famous arsenal, so vital to the army, is in danger. From General Wintzingerode's reports, I see that an enemy corps of ten thousand is moving on the Petersburg road. Another of several thousand moves on Dmitrov. A third has advanced along the Vladimir road, and a fourth, quite sizable, is stationed between Ruza and Mozhaysk. Napoleon himself was in Moscow as late as the twenty-fifth. Given all this, when the enemy has scattered his forces into large detachments and Napoleon sits in Moscow with his Guards, is it really possible that the forces facing you are too strong for you to take the offensive? On the contrary, he is probably only chasing you with detachments, or at most with a corps far weaker than your army. It would seem you could advantageously attack a weaker force and destroy it, or at least force it to retreat, holding an important part of the provinces now under enemy control and averting the danger to Tula and other interior towns. You will be held responsible if the enemy manages to direct a significant force against Petersburg, where we have been unable to keep many troops. With the army entrusted to you, acting with resolution and energy, you have ample means to prevent this fresh disaster. Remember that you still must answer to our offended country for the loss of Moscow. You have seen my readiness to reward you. That readiness will not weaken, but I and Russia have a right to expect from you all the zeal, firmness, and success that your intellect, military talent, and the courage of your troops justify us in expecting.'

But by the time this letter—which showed that the real balance of forces had already made itself felt even in Petersburg—was sent, Kutuzov had found himself unable to hold back his army any longer, and a battle had already taken place.

On October second, a Cossack named Shapovalov, who was out scouting, killed one hare and wounded another. Following the wounded hare, he wandered deep into the forest and stumbled upon the left flank of Murat's army, camped there without any precautions. The Cossack laughingly told his comrades how he'd nearly fallen into French hands. A junior officer, hearing the story, passed it to his commander.

The Cossack was brought in and questioned. The Cossack officers wanted to seize the chance to capture some horses, but one of the senior officers, who had connections to the higher authorities, reported the incident to a general on the staff. Things at staff headquarters had been extremely tense lately. Ermolov had recently visited Bennigsen and begged him to use his influence to persuade the commander in chief to take the offensive.
'If I didn't know you, I'd think you didn't actually want what you're asking for. I only have to suggest something for His Highness to do the opposite,' Bennigsen replied.

The Cossack's report, confirmed by cavalry patrols sent out afterward, was the final proof that events had ripened. The tightly coiled spring was released, the clock began to whir and the chimes to play. Despite all his supposed power, his intellect, his experience, and his knowledge of men, Kutuzov—taking into account the Cossack's report, Bennigsen's note to the Emperor, the wishes he assumed the Emperor held, and the unanimous desire of all his generals—could no longer hold back the inevitable. He gave the order to do what he considered useless and harmful—he approved, that is, the accomplished fact.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Bennigsen's note and the Cossack's report about the unguarded French left flank were merely the final signs that an attack was necessary. It was set for October fifth.
On the morning of the fourth, Kutuzov signed the battle orders. Toll read them to Ermolov, asking him to handle the further arrangements.
'Fine, fine. I don't have time right now,' Ermolov replied, and left the hut.
The orders drawn up by Toll were quite good. Just as with the Austerlitz orders, though not in German this time, it was written:

'The First Column will march here and here,' 'the Second Column will march there and there,' and so on. On paper, all these columns arrived at their positions on time and destroyed the enemy. Everything had been admirably planned, as is always the case with battle orders—and as is always the case, not a single column reached its position on time.

When enough copies of the orders had been prepared, an officer was called to deliver them to Ermolov. A young officer of the Horse Guards, Kutuzov's orderly, was pleased with the importance of his mission and set off for Ermolov's quarters.
'He's gone out,' said Ermolov's orderly.
The Horse Guards officer went to a general with whom Ermolov was often found.
'No, and the general's out too.'
The officer mounted his horse and rode to someone else.
'No, he's gone out.'

'If they blame me for this delay! What a nuisance!' thought the officer, and he rode around the entire camp. One person said he'd seen Ermolov ride by with other generals; others said he must have gone home. The officer searched until six in the evening without stopping to eat. Ermolov was nowhere to be found, and no one knew where he was. The officer grabbed a quick meal at a comrade's place and rode to the vanguard to find Miloradovich. Miloradovich was also away, but there they told him he'd gone to a ball at General Kikin's, and that Ermolov was probably there too.
'But where is it?'
'Over there, at Echkino,' said a Cossack officer, pointing to a country house in the far distance.
'What—outside our lines?'
'They've posted two regiments as outposts, and they're having quite a party in there. It's something else! Two bands and three groups of singers!'
The officer rode beyond the Russian lines to Echkino. While still far off, he could hear the merry sounds of a soldier's dance song coming from the house.

'In the meadows... in the meadows!' came the singing, accompanied by whistling and the twang of a stringed instrument, drowned now and then by shouts. The sounds lifted his spirits, but at the same time he feared being blamed for not delivering his important orders sooner. It was already past eight o'clock. He dismounted and walked up to the porch of a large country house that had somehow survived intact between the Russian and French positions. In the refreshment room and the hall, servants bustled about with wine and food. Groups of singers stood outside the windows. The officer was admitted and immediately saw all the senior generals of the army gathered together, including Ermolov's big, imposing figure. They all had their coats unbuttoned and stood in a semicircle, their faces flushed and animated, laughing loudly. In the middle of the room, a short, handsome general with a red face was dancing the trepak with tremendous energy and skill.
'Ha, ha, ha! Bravo, Nikolai Ivanych! Ha, ha, ha!'

The officer felt that arriving with important orders at such a moment made him doubly guilty. He would have preferred to wait, but one of the generals spotted him and, hearing what he'd come about, informed Ermolov.
Ermolov came forward frowning and, hearing the officer's report, took the papers without a word.

'You think he went off by chance?' a comrade on the staff said to the Horse Guards officer that evening, referring to Ermolov. 'It was a trick. It was done on purpose to get Konovnitsyn in trouble. You'll see what a mess there'll be tomorrow.'

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: The next day, the aging Kutuzov got up early, said his prayers, dressed, and with the unpleasant awareness of having to direct a battle he didn't approve of, climbed into his carriage and drove from Letashovka—a village three and a half miles from Tarutino—to where the attacking columns were supposed to assemble. He sat in the carriage, dozing and waking by turns, listening for any sound of gunfire on the right that would signal the action had begun. But everything was still quiet. A damp, gray autumn morning was just dawning. Approaching Tarutino, Kutuzov noticed cavalrymen leading their horses to water across the road he was driving along. He studied them closely, stopped his carriage, and asked what regiment they belonged to. They were part of a column that should have been far ahead, already in ambush position long before. 'Maybe it's a mistake,' thought the old commander in chief. But a little farther on, he saw infantry regiments with their weapons stacked, soldiers half-dressed, eating porridge and gathering firewood. He sent for an officer. The officer reported that no order to advance had been received.

'What! Not rec—' Kutuzov began, but caught himself and sent for a senior officer. Getting out of his carriage, he stood with his head drooping, breathing heavily, pacing silently up and down. When Eykhen, the staff officer he'd summoned, appeared, Kutuzov turned purple in the face—not because Eykhen was to blame, but because he was a sufficiently important target for his fury. Trembling and gasping, the old man fell into one of those rages in which he sometimes used to roll on the ground. He fell on Eykhen, shaking his fists, shouting and heaping vile abuse on him. Another officer, Captain Brozin, who happened to appear and was not at all to blame, suffered the same fate.
'What kind of scoundrel are you? I'll have you shot! Blackguards!' Kutuzov yelled in a hoarse voice, waving his arms and staggering.

He was suffering physically. He—the commander in chief, a Serene Highness whom everyone said held powers no man in Russia had ever possessed—to be put in this position, made the laughingstock of the whole army! 'I needn't have rushed to pray this morning, or stayed up all night thinking everything through,' he thought. 'When I was a young officer, no one would have dared mock me like this... and now!' He was in a state of physical anguish, as if he'd been beaten, and couldn't help expressing it through cries of anger and distress. But his strength soon gave out. Looking around, conscious of having said too much, he climbed back into his carriage and drove away in silence.

His rage, once spent, didn't return. Blinking wearily, he listened to excuses and justifications (Ermolov didn't come to see him until the next day) and to the insistence of Bennigsen, Konovnitsyn, and Toll that the failed operation should be attempted again the following day. Once more, Kutuzov had to consent.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: The next day, the troops assembled at their positions in the evening and advanced during the night. It was an autumn night with dark purple clouds but no rain. The ground was damp but not muddy, and the troops moved forward silently—only the occasional clinking of artillery could be faintly heard. The men were forbidden to talk aloud, smoke their pipes, or strike a light, and they tried to keep their horses from neighing. The secrecy heightened the adventure's appeal, and they marched cheerfully. Some columns, thinking they'd reached their destination, halted, stacked arms, and settled on the cold ground, but the majority marched all night and ended up in the wrong places.

Only Count Orlov-Denisov with his Cossacks—the least important detachment of all—reached his appointed position on time. His detachment halted at the edge of a forest on the path from the village of Stromilova to Dmitrovsk.

Toward dawn, Count Orlov-Denisov, who had dozed off, was woken by a French deserter being brought to him. It was a Polish sergeant from Poniatowski's corps who explained in Polish that he'd deserted because he'd been overlooked for promotion: he should have been made an officer long ago, he was braver than any of them, and so he'd left to pay them back. He said Murat was spending the night less than a mile away, and if they gave him a hundred men, he'd capture him alive. Count Orlov-Denisov consulted his fellow officers.

The offer was too tempting to refuse. Everyone volunteered, and everyone advised making the attempt. After much debate, Major-General Grekov set off with two Cossack regiments and the Polish sergeant.
'Now remember,' Count Orlov-Denisov said to the sergeant as he left, 'if you've been lying, I'll hang you like a dog. But if it's true, you'll get a hundred gold coins.'

The sergeant, without a word, mounted up with a resolute air and rode off with Grekov, whose men had quickly assembled. They vanished into the forest. Count Orlov-Denisov, having seen them off, returned, shivering in the freshness of early dawn and excited by what he'd taken on. He began scanning the enemy camp, now just visible in the deceptive predawn light and the dying campfires. The Russian columns should have been appearing on the open slope to his right. He looked that way, but though the columns would have been visible from quite far off, they were nowhere to be seen. It seemed to the count that something was stirring in the French camp, and his sharp-eyed adjutant confirmed this.
'Oh, it's really too late,' said Count Orlov, looking at the camp.

As often happens when someone you trusted is no longer in front of you, it suddenly seemed perfectly clear to him that the sergeant was a fraud, that he'd lied, and that the whole Russian attack would be ruined by the absence of those two regiments he'd sent off to God knows where. How could anyone capture a commander in chief from the middle of such a mass of troops!
'I'm sure that scoundrel was lying,' said the count.
'They can still be called back,' said one of his officers, who felt the same distrust as he looked at the enemy camp.
'Well? Really... what do you think? Should we let them go on or not?'
'Should I have them called back?'
'Call them back, call them back!' said Count Orlov with sudden decisiveness, looking at his watch. 'It'll be too late. It's getting light.'

The adjutant galloped through the forest after Grekov. When Grekov returned, Count Orlov-Denisov—stirred up by the abandoned attempt, frustrated by the infantry columns that still hadn't appeared, and energized by the enemy's nearness—decided to attack anyway. All his men felt the same excitement.
'Mount!' he commanded in a whisper. The men took their positions and crossed themselves. 'Forward, with God's help!'
'Hurrah!' echoed through the forest, and the Cossack companies, lances trailing, poured out one after another like grain from a sack and dashed merrily across the stream toward the camp.

One desperate, terrified shriek from the first French soldier who spotted the Cossacks, and everyone in the camp—undressed, barely awake—scattered in all directions, abandoning cannons, muskets, and horses.

If the Cossacks had pursued the French without worrying about what was behind and around them, they could have captured Murat and everything else. That was what the officers wanted. But it was impossible to budge the Cossacks once they had their hands on loot and prisoners. None of them listened to orders. Fifteen hundred prisoners and thirty-eight guns were taken on the spot, along with standards and—what mattered most to the Cossacks—horses, saddles, horse blankets, and the like. All this had to be dealt with: the prisoners secured, the guns claimed, the booty divided—not without some shouting and even a bit of fighting among themselves—and this was what kept the Cossacks busy.
The French, no longer being pursued, began to regroup and opened fire. Orlov-Denisov, still waiting for the other columns, advanced no further.

Meanwhile, according to the orders that said 'the First Column will march' and so on, the infantry of the late-arriving columns—commanded by Bennigsen and directed by Toll—had started out properly but, as always happens, ended up somewhere, just not where they were supposed to be. As always, the men set out cheerfully, then began to halt; grumbling was heard, confusion set in, and finally they started moving backward. Adjutants and generals galloped about, shouted, grew angry, quarreled, said they'd gone completely wrong and were late, vented their frustration, and finally gave up trying to follow the plan and just marched forward.
