Strange as it may seem that a king or emperor quarrels with another, assembles an army, fights the enemy's forces, wins by killing three, five, or ten thousand men, and thereby subjugates a kingdom of several millions—all the facts of history confirm that greater or lesser military success is the cause, or at least an essential indicator, of a nation's growing or declining strength. Even though it's hard to understand why the defeat of an army—a hundredth part of a nation—should force the entire nation to submit. An army wins a victory, and at once the rights of the conquering nation increase at the expense of the defeated. An army suffers a defeat, and the people immediately lose rights in proportion to the severity of the loss. If the army is completely destroyed, the nation is fully subjugated.

According to history, this has been true since the most ancient times, right up to the present day. All of Napoleon's wars confirm this rule. As Austria's army was defeated, Austria lost its rights, and France's rights and power grew. The French victories at Jena and Auerstadt destroyed the independent existence of Prussia.

But then, in 1812, the French win a victory near Moscow. Moscow is taken, and after that—with no further battles—it isn't Russia that ceases to exist, but the French army of six hundred thousand, and then Napoleonic France itself. To bend the facts to fit the rules of history and say that the battlefield at Borodino remained in Russian hands, or that subsequent battles destroyed Napoleon's army, is simply impossible.

After the French victory at Borodino, there was no major engagement—nor any truly serious fighting—yet the French army ceased to exist. What does this mean? If it were an example from Chinese history, we might call it 'not a historical phenomenon' (which is the historians' usual dodge when something doesn't fit their theories). If the matter involved only a brief skirmish with small numbers, we might treat it as an exception. But this happened before our fathers' eyes. For them it was a matter of national survival. And it took place in the greatest of all known wars.

The 1812 campaign, from the Battle of Borodino to the expulsion of the French, proved that winning a battle doesn't necessarily lead to a conquest, and isn't even a reliable indicator of one. It proved that the force deciding the fate of nations lies not in conquerors, nor even in armies and battles, but in something else.

French historians, describing the state of the French army before it left Moscow, assert that everything was in order in the Grand Army except the cavalry, the artillery, and the transport—there was no forage for the horses or cattle. That was a misfortune no one could fix, since the peasants of the surrounding districts burned their hay rather than let the French have it.

The victory that was won brought none of the usual results, because the peasants Karp and Vlas—who after the French evacuated Moscow drove their carts in to loot the city, and who personally displayed no heroic feelings whatsoever—along with the innumerable multitude of similar peasants, did not bring their hay to Moscow for the high prices offered them. They burned it instead.

Let's imagine two men fighting a duel with rapiers, following all the rules of fencing. The match has been going on for some time when one of them, feeling himself wounded and realizing this is no joke but a matter of life and death, throws down his rapier, grabs the first cudgel he can find, and starts swinging it. Now imagine that the combatant who so sensibly chose the simplest and best means to his end was also influenced by traditions of chivalry and, wishing to conceal what actually happened, insisted he had won his victory with the rapier according to all the rules of art. Imagine the confusion and obscurity that would result from such an account of the duel.

The fencer who demanded a contest according to the rules was the French army. His opponent, who threw away the rapier and grabbed the cudgel, was the Russian people. Those who try to explain the matter according to the rules of fencing are the historians who have described the event.

After the burning of Smolensk, a war began that followed no previous traditions. The burning of towns and villages, the retreats after battles, the blow struck at Borodino and the renewed retreat, the burning of Moscow, the hunting of marauders, the seizure of supply trains, and guerrilla warfare—all were departures from the rules.

Napoleon felt this. From the time he assumed the correct fencing stance in Moscow and, instead of his opponent's rapier, saw a cudgel raised above his head, he never stopped complaining to Kutuzov and to Emperor Alexander that the war was being fought contrary to all the rules—as if there were rules for killing people. Despite French complaints about unfair play, despite the fact that some highly placed Russians felt embarrassed about fighting with a cudgel and wanted to assume elegant fencing positions and deliver artful thrusts—the cudgel of the people's war was raised with all its threatening, majestic strength and, without consulting anyone's preferences or rules, it rose and fell with brutal simplicity, over and over, hammering the French until the entire invasion had perished.

And it is well for a people who do not—as the French did in 1813—bow according to all the rules of art, gracefully present the hilt of their rapier, and politely hand it to their magnanimous conqueror. It is well for a people who, at the moment of trial, without asking what rules others have followed in similar cases, simply pick up the first cudgel at hand and swing it until the feelings of outrage and revenge in their souls give way to contempt and compassion.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: One of the most obvious and effective departures from the so-called rules of war is the action of scattered groups against massed formations. This kind of fighting always arises in wars that take on a national character. In such actions, instead of two armies facing each other in formation, men disperse, attack individually, run when confronted by stronger forces, and attack again when the opportunity presents itself. This is what the guerrillas did in Spain, what the mountain tribes did in the Caucasus, and what the Russians did in 1812.

People have called this 'guerrilla warfare' and assume that by naming it they've explained it. But this kind of war fits no established rules and directly contradicts a widely accepted tactical principle that an attacker should concentrate his forces to be stronger than his opponent at the moment of contact.
Guerrilla warfare—which has always been successful, as history shows—directly violates that rule.
This contradiction arises because military science equates an army's strength with its numbers. Military science says: more troops means more strength. 'Big battalions are always right.'
(Large battalions are always victorious.)
For military science to say this is like defining momentum in mechanics by mass alone—claiming that momenta are equal or unequal simply because the masses are equal or unequal.
Momentum—quantity of motion—is the product of mass and velocity.
In military affairs, an army's strength is the product of its mass and some unknown factor, x.

Military science, observing countless historical instances where army size doesn't correspond to actual strength—where small detachments defeat larger ones—vaguely acknowledges this unknown factor and tries to identify it: sometimes in formations, sometimes in equipment, and most often in the genius of commanders. But assigning these meanings to the factor never produces results that match the historical facts.
Yet we need only abandon the false view—adopted to flatter 'heroes'—that the orders issued by wartime commanders actually determine outcomes, and this unknown quantity reveals itself.

That unknown quantity is the spirit of the army: the greater or lesser willingness to fight and face danger felt by every man in the army, regardless of whether they serve under a genius, fight in two or three lines, or carry cudgels or rifles that fire thirty rounds a minute. Men who want to fight will always find the most advantageous conditions for fighting.
The spirit of an army is the factor which, multiplied by its mass, yields the resulting force. Defining and measuring this unknown factor—the spirit of an army—is a problem for science.

This problem can only be solved if we stop arbitrarily substituting for x the conditions under which it becomes visible—such as the general's commands, the equipment used, and so forth—mistaking these for the thing itself. We must recognize this unknown in its entirety as the greater or lesser desire to fight and to face danger. Only then, by expressing known historical facts as equations and comparing the relative significance of this factor, can we hope to define the unknown.

Ten men, battalions, or divisions fighting fifteen conquer them—that is, kill or capture them all—while themselves losing four. So on one side four were lost and on the other fifteen. Therefore the four equaled the fifteen, meaning 4x = 15y, and x/y = 15/4. This equation doesn't give us the value of the unknown, but it gives us a ratio between two unknowns. By applying various historical units—battles, campaigns, periods of war—to such equations, a series of numbers could be obtained that might reveal certain laws.

The tactical rule that an army should mass when attacking and spread out when retreating unconsciously confirms the truth that an army's strength depends on its spirit. To lead men forward under fire requires more discipline (achievable only through mass movement) than defending against an attack. But this rule, which ignores the army's spirit, proves consistently wrong—especially when the spirit of the troops rises or falls sharply, as in all national wars.

The French, retreating in 1812, should according to tactics have broken into smaller groups to defend themselves, but instead they clustered into a mass because their spirit had fallen so low that only the mass held the army together. The Russians, who according to tactics should have attacked in mass, instead split into small units, because their spirit had risen so high that individual men, without orders, struck at the French and willingly exposed themselves to hardship and danger without needing anyone to compel them.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The so-called partisan war began with the French entry into Smolensk.

Before partisan warfare was officially recognized by the government, thousands of enemy stragglers, looters, and foragers had already been killed off by Cossacks and peasants, who destroyed them as instinctively as dogs attack a stray rabid dog. Denis Davydov, with his Russian instinct, was the first to recognize the value of this terrible weapon which, heedless of military science's rules, was destroying the French. He deserves the credit for taking the first step toward organizing this method of warfare.
On August twenty-fourth, Davydov's first partisan detachment was formed, and then others were officially recognized. As the campaign progressed, these detachments grew more numerous.

The partisans destroyed the Grand Army piece by piece. They gathered the fallen leaves that dropped by themselves from that withered tree—the French army—and sometimes shook the tree itself. By October, when the French were fleeing toward Smolensk, there were hundreds of such groups, varying widely in size and character. Some adopted full military organization with infantry, artillery, staffs, and amenities. Others consisted solely of Cossack cavalry. There were also small improvised bands of foot and horse, and groups of peasants and landowners that remained unknown. A church sexton commanded one group that captured several hundred prisoners in a month. There was Vasilisa, the wife of a village elder, who killed hundreds of Frenchmen.

The partisan war blazed most fiercely in the final days of October. Its first phase had passed—when the partisans themselves, amazed at their own boldness, feared capture at every moment, hid in the forests without unsaddling, and hardly dared dismount, always expecting pursuit. By late October, this kind of warfare had taken definite shape. Everyone now understood what could and couldn't be risked against the French. Only the commanders of large detachments with staffs, operating at a distance from the French according to established rules, still thought many things impossible. The small bands that had been active from the start and had observed the French up close considered things possible that the big detachment commanders didn't dare contemplate. The Cossacks and peasants who crept in among the French believed everything was possible.

On October twenty-second, Denisov—one of the partisans—was with his band at the height of the guerrilla fervor. Since early morning, he and his men had been on the move. All day he had been watching from the forest alongside the highway a large French convoy of cavalry baggage and Russian prisoners, which—according to spies and captured Frenchmen—was heading for Smolensk under heavy escort, separated from the rest of the army. Besides Denisov and Dolokhov (who also led a small band and operated nearby), the commanders of several large detachments with staffs knew about this convoy too and, as Denisov put it, were 'sharpening their teeth for it.' Two of these commanders—a Pole and a German—sent Denisov near-simultaneous invitations to join forces for an attack on the convoy.

'No, brother, I've grown my own mustache,' said Denisov, reading their messages. He wrote to the German that despite his heartfelt wish to serve under so valiant and famous a general, he had to decline because he was already under the command of the Polish general. To the Polish general, he sent the same reply, informing him he was already under the German's command.

Having arranged things this way, Denisov and Dolokhov planned to attack and seize the convoy on their own, without reporting to the higher command. On October twenty-second, the convoy was moving from the village of Mikulino to Shamshevo. To the left of the road, between Mikulino and Shamshevo, lay large forests that in some places extended right to the road and in others stood a mile or more back. Through these forests, Denisov and his men rode all day, sometimes well inside the tree line, sometimes at the very edge, but never losing sight of the moving French. That morning, Denisov's Cossacks had seized two wagons loaded with cavalry saddles that had gotten stuck in the mud near Mikulino where the forest pressed close to the road. Since then, the party had watched the French column without attacking. They needed to let the French reach Shamshevo undisturbed, and then—after meeting Dolokhov that evening at a watchman's hut in the forest less than a mile from Shamshevo—surprise the French at dawn, falling on them from two sides like an avalanche and routing and capturing them all in one blow.
Behind them, more than a mile from Mikulino where the forest ran right up to the road, six Cossacks were posted to report if any fresh French columns appeared.

Beyond Shamshevo, Dolokhov was watching the road for the same purpose—to find out how far away other French forces were. The convoy was estimated at fifteen hundred men. Denisov had two hundred, and Dolokhov might have as many more. The numerical disadvantage didn't deter Denisov. All he needed to know now was exactly what kind of troops these were, and for that he needed to capture a 'tongue'—that is, take a man from the enemy column. That morning's attack on the wagons had been so hasty that the Frenchmen with them had all been killed. Only a little drummer boy had been taken alive, and since he was a straggler, he could tell them nothing definite about the column's composition.

Denisov thought it too dangerous to make another attack for fear of alerting the entire column. So he sent Tikhon Shcherbaty, a peasant in his band, to Shamshevo to try to grab at least one of the French quartermasters who had been sent ahead.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: It was a warm, rainy autumn day. The sky and the horizon were both the color of muddy water. At times a kind of mist descended, and then suddenly heavy, slanting rain came pouring down.

Denisov, in a felt cloak and a sheepskin cap streaming with rain, was riding a thin, thoroughbred horse with sunken sides. Like his horse, which turned its head and flattened its ears, he flinched from the driving rain and peered anxiously ahead. His thin face with its short, thick black beard looked angry.
Beside Denisov rode an esaul—a Cossack captain—his fellow commander, also in a felt cloak and sheepskin cap, mounted on a large, sleek Don horse.
(An esaul is a captain of Cossacks.)

Esaul Lovayski the Third was a tall man, straight as an arrow, pale-faced and fair-haired, with narrow light eyes and an air of calm self-satisfaction. Though it was impossible to say exactly what set this horse and rider apart, at first glance you could tell that Denisov was a wet, uncomfortable man sitting on a horse, while the esaul was as comfortable and at ease as always—not a man who had mounted a horse but a man who was one with his horse, a being with twice the normal strength.
A little ahead of them walked a peasant guide, soaked to the skin in a gray coat and a white knitted cap.
A little behind, on a poor, scrawny little Kirghiz pony with an enormous tail and mane and a bleeding mouth, rode a young officer in a blue French overcoat.

Beside him rode a hussar, with a boy in a tattered French uniform and blue cap sitting behind him on the horse's rump. The boy clung to the hussar with cold, red hands, his eyebrows raised, gazing about in surprise. This was the French drummer boy captured that morning.

Behind them, along the narrow, sodden, rutted forest road came hussars in threes and fours, and then Cossacks—some in felt cloaks, some in French greatcoats, some with horse blankets draped over their heads. The horses, drenched by the rain, all looked black whether they were chestnut or bay. Their necks, with wet manes plastered flat, looked strangely thin. Steam rose from them. Clothes, saddles, reins—everything was wet, slippery, and sodden, like the ground and the fallen leaves that covered the road. The men sat hunched, trying not to move, hoping to keep the water that had soaked through to their bodies warm and not let in fresh cold water leaking under their seats, their knees, and down the backs of their necks. Among the strung-out line of Cossacks, two wagons drawn by French horses and hitched Cossack horses rumbled over tree stumps and branches and splashed through puddles in the ruts.
Denisov's horse swerved to avoid a pool in the track and bumped his rider's knee against a tree.
'Damn it!' exclaimed Denisov angrily, and baring his teeth he struck his horse three times with his whip, splattering himself and his companions with mud.

Denisov was in a foul mood, both from the rain and from hunger (none of them had eaten since morning), and even more because he still had no news from Dolokhov, and the man sent to capture a 'tongue' hadn't returned.

'There probably won't be another chance like this to hit a convoy. It's too risky to attack alone, and if we wait another day, one of the big guerrilla detachments will snatch the prize right out from under us,' thought Denisov, constantly scanning ahead for a messenger from Dolokhov.
Coming to a path in the forest from which he could see far to the right, Denisov stopped.
'Someone's coming,' he said.
The esaul looked where Denisov pointed.
'There are two—an officer and a Cossack. But it isn't presupposable that it's the lieutenant colonel himself,' said the esaul, who liked using words the other Cossacks didn't know.

The approaching riders dipped below a slope and vanished, then reappeared a few minutes later. In front, at a weary gallop, rode an officer, disheveled and soaked, his trousers riding up above his knees, lashing his horse with a leather whip. Behind him, standing in the stirrups, trotted a Cossack. The officer—a very young lad with a broad, rosy face and bright, merry eyes—galloped up to Denisov and handed him a soaking envelope.
'From the general,' said the officer. 'Please excuse it—not quite dry.'
Denisov frowned, took the envelope, and opened it.

'There—they kept telling us: "It's dangerous, it's dangerous,"' said the officer, turning to the esaul while Denisov read. 'But Komarov and I'—he pointed to the Cossack—'were ready. We each have two pistols. But what's this?' he asked, noticing the French drummer boy. 'A prisoner? You've already been in action? May I talk to him?'
'Rostov! Petya!' exclaimed Denisov, having scanned the dispatch. 'Why didn't you say who you were?' And with a smile, he held out his hand to the boy.
The officer was Petya Rostov.

All the way, Petya had been preparing to behave with Denisov the way a grown man and officer should—without any hint of their old acquaintance. But the moment Denisov smiled at him, Petya's face lit up. He blushed with pleasure, forgot the formal manner he'd been rehearsing, and launched into telling how he'd already been in a battle near Vyazma and how a certain hussar had distinguished himself there.
'Well, I'm glad to see you,' Denisov interrupted, and his face resumed its anxious expression.
'Mikhail Feoklitych,' he said to the esaul, 'this is from that German again, you know. He'—indicating Petya—'is serving under him.'
And Denisov told the esaul that the dispatch was another demand from the German general that Denisov join forces with him for the attack on the convoy.
'If we don't grab it tomorrow, he'll snatch it right out from under our noses,' he added.

While Denisov was talking to the esaul, Petya—embarrassed by Denisov's cool tone and assuming it was because of his trousers riding up—furtively tried to pull them down under his greatcoat so no one would notice, while keeping as soldierly an air as possible.
'Will there be any orders, sir?' he asked Denisov, saluting and resuming the role of adjutant he'd been practicing. 'Or shall I remain with you?'
'Orders?' Denisov repeated, thinking. 'Can you stay until tomorrow?'
'Oh, please... May I stay with you?' cried Petya.
'But what exactly did the general tell you? To return at once?' asked Denisov.
Petya blushed.
'He didn't give me any specific instructions. I think I could stay?' he said uncertainly.
'Well, all right,' said Denisov.

And turning to his men, he sent a party ahead to the halting place near the watchman's hut in the forest. He told the officer on the Kirghiz horse (who served as his adjutant) to go find out where Dolokhov was and whether he'd come that evening. Denisov himself intended to ride with the esaul and Petya to the edge of the forest overlooking Shamshevo, to survey the part of the French bivouac they planned to attack the next day.
'Well, old fellow,' he said to the peasant guide, 'lead us to Shamshevo.'
Denisov, Petya, and the esaul, accompanied by some Cossacks and the hussar with the prisoner, rode off to the left across a ravine toward the forest's edge.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: The rain had stopped, and now only mist hung in the air with drops still falling from the trees. Denisov, the esaul, and Petya rode in silence behind the peasant in the knitted cap, who stepped lightly on his turned-out feet, moving noiselessly in his bast shoes over roots and wet leaves as he led them to the forest's edge.
He climbed a rise, stopped, looked around, and moved toward a spot where the trees were thinner. Reaching a large oak that still held its leaves, he stopped and beckoned to them mysteriously.

Denisov and Petya rode up to him. From this spot they could see the French. Directly beyond the forest, on a downward slope, lay a field of spring rye. To the right, past a steep ravine, was a small village with a landowner's house whose roof had caved in. In the village, around the house, in the garden, by the well, by the pond, across all the rising ground, and along the road uphill from the bridge—no more than five hundred yards away—crowds of men could be seen through the shimmering mist. Their decidedly non-Russian shouts at horses straining uphill with carts, and their calls to one another, carried clearly.
'Bring the prisoner here,' said Denisov in a low voice, his eyes fixed on the French.

A Cossack dismounted, lifted the boy down, and brought him to Denisov. Pointing at the French troops, Denisov asked what these and those were. The boy, his cold hands thrust into his pockets and his eyebrows raised, looked at Denisov in fright but, despite an obvious desire to tell everything he knew, gave only confused answers, agreeing with whatever Denisov asked. Denisov turned away frowning and spoke to the esaul, sharing his own conclusions.
Petya kept turning his head rapidly—looking at the drummer boy, then at Denisov, then at the esaul, then at the French in the village and on the road—trying not to miss anything important.
'Whether Dolokhov comes or not, we have to take them—right?' said Denisov, his eyes sparkling with excitement.
'It's a very good position,' said the esaul.

'We'll send the infantry through the swamps,' Denisov continued. 'They'll creep up to the garden. You'll ride in from over there with the Cossacks'—he pointed to a spot in the forest beyond the village—'and I'll come from here with my hussars. And at the signal shot...'
'The ravine is impassable—there's a swamp there,' said the esaul. 'The horses would sink. We need to go further around to the left...'

While they were talking in undertones, a gunshot cracked from the low ground by the pond, a puff of white smoke appeared, then another, and the sound of hundreds of seemingly cheerful French voices shouting together rose from the slope. For a moment Denisov and the esaul pulled back. They were so close they thought the shooting was aimed at them. But the firing and shouting had nothing to do with them. Down below, a man in something red was running through the marsh. The French were obviously shooting and yelling at him.
'Why, that's our Tikhon,' said the esaul.
'So it is!'
'The rascal!' said Denisov.
'He'll get away!' said the esaul, squinting.

The man they called Tikhon ran to the stream and plunged in, sending up a splash of water. He disappeared for a moment, then scrambled out on all fours, black and dripping, and ran on. The French who had been chasing him stopped.
'Clever!' said the esaul.
'What a brute!' said Denisov with his earlier look of irritation. 'What's he been doing all this time?'
'Who is he?' asked Petya.
'He's our scout. I sent him to grab a "tongue."'
'Oh, yes,' said Petya, nodding at Denisov's first words as if he understood everything, though he really didn't understand any of it.

Tikhon Shcherbaty was one of the most indispensable men in their band. He was a peasant from Pokrovsk, near the Gzhat River. When Denisov had first come to Pokrovsk at the start of his operations and summoned the village elder to ask what he knew about the French, the elder—as all village elders did—claimed to have seen and heard nothing of them. But when Denisov explained that his purpose was to kill the French and asked whether any had strayed their way, the elder replied that some 'marauders' had indeed visited, but that Tikhon Shcherbaty was the only man who dealt with such matters. Denisov had Tikhon brought in and, after praising him for his activity, said a few words in the elder's presence about loyalty to the Tsar, love of country, and the hatred of the French that all sons of the fatherland should feel.

'We don't do the French any harm,' said Tikhon, clearly frightened by Denisov's words. 'We just messed around with the lads for fun, you know! We killed a couple dozen marauders, but we didn't do anything else...'

The next day, after Denisov had left Pokrovsk and completely forgotten about this peasant, word came that Tikhon had attached himself to their group and was asking to stay. Denisov gave orders to let him.

Tikhon, who at first did rough work—building campfires, fetching water, skinning dead horses—soon showed a great talent and enthusiasm for partisan warfare. At night he would go out raiding and always brought back French clothing and weapons, and when told to, brought in French captives as well. Denisov then relieved him from menial work, began taking him on expeditions, and had him enrolled among the Cossacks.

Tikhon didn't like riding and always went on foot, yet he never fell behind the cavalry. He carried a musket (mostly as a joke), a pike, and an axe, which he wielded the way a wolf uses its teeth—with equal ease picking fleas from its fur or crunching thick bones. Tikhon could split logs with full-arm swings just as accurately as he could whittle thin pegs or carve spoons. In Denisov's band, he held a unique position. When something particularly difficult or unpleasant had to be done—pushing a cart out of the mud with bare shoulders, pulling a horse out of a swamp by its tail, skinning it, sneaking into a French camp, or walking thirty miles in a day—everyone pointed laughingly at Tikhon.
'It won't hurt that devil—he's strong as a horse!' they said about him.

Once, a Frenchman Tikhon was trying to capture shot him in the fleshy part of his back. That wound—which Tikhon treated only with vodka, inside and out—became the subject of the liveliest jokes in the whole detachment, and Tikhon happily played along.

'Hey mate! Had enough? Gave you a good twist, did he?' the Cossacks would tease him. And Tikhon would deliberately writhe and make faces, pretending to be furious, swearing at the French with the funniest curses. The only lasting effect of the incident was that after being wounded, he rarely bothered bringing in prisoners.

He was the bravest and most useful man in the band. No one found more opportunities for attack, no one captured or killed more Frenchmen. And as a result, he became the butt of every joke among the Cossacks and hussars, a role he accepted willingly. Now Denisov had sent him overnight to Shamshevo to capture a 'tongue.' But whether because he hadn't been satisfied with taking just one Frenchman, or because he'd slept through the night, he had crept by day into the bushes right among the French and—as Denisov had witnessed from the hilltop—been spotted by them.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: After discussing the next day's attack with the esaul for some time—an attack that now, seeing how close they were to the French, he seemed to have definitely decided on—Denisov turned his horse and rode back.
'Come on, my lad, let's go get dry,' he said to Petya.

As they approached the watchman's hut, Denisov stopped, peering into the forest. Among the trees, a man with long legs and long, swinging arms was approaching with light, loping strides. He wore a short jacket, bast shoes, and a Kazan hat, with a musket over his shoulder and an axe stuck in his belt. When he spotted Denisov, he quickly tossed something into the bushes, pulled off his soggy hat by its floppy brim, and came up to his commander. It was Tikhon. His wrinkled, pockmarked face and narrow little eyes beamed with self-satisfied amusement. He lifted his head high and looked at Denisov as if suppressing a laugh.
'Well, where did you disappear to?' asked Denisov.
'Where did I disappear to? I went to get Frenchmen,' answered Tikhon boldly, in a husky but melodious bass.
'Why did you go pushing in there in broad daylight? You fool! So why haven't you brought one?'
'Oh, I grabbed one all right,' said Tikhon.
'Where is he?'

'Well, I nabbed one first thing at dawn,' Tikhon went on, spreading out his flat feet with their turned-out toes in their bast shoes. 'I took him into the forest. Then I had a look at him and thought: he's no good. So I decided to go fetch a better one.'
'You see?... What a rogue—just as I thought,' said Denisov to the esaul. 'Why didn't you bring that one?'
'What was the good of bringing him?' Tikhon interrupted hastily and angrily. 'That one wouldn't have done for you. Don't I know what kind you need!'
'What a brute!... Well? Go on.'

'I went for another one,' Tikhon continued. 'I crept through the woods like this and lay down.' (He suddenly dropped flat on his stomach with a supple movement to demonstrate.) 'One came along and I grabbed him, like this.' (He sprang up quickly and lightly.) '"Come along to the colonel," I said. He starts yelling, and suddenly there were four of them. They went at me with their little swords. So I laid into them with my axe, like this: "What do you think you're doing?" I shouted. "In the name of Christ!"' Tikhon yelled, waving his arms with an angry scowl, puffing out his chest.
'Yes, we saw from the hill how you ran for it through the puddles!' said the esaul, squinting with amusement.
Petya badly wanted to laugh but saw that everyone else was holding back. He looked quickly from Tikhon's face to the esaul's and Denisov's, unable to figure out what it all meant.
'Don't play the fool!' said Denisov, coughing angrily. 'Why didn't you bring the first one?'

Tikhon scratched his back with one hand and his head with the other, and then suddenly his whole face broke into a beaming, foolish grin that revealed the gap where he'd lost a tooth (which was why he was called Shcherbaty—the gap-toothed). Denisov smiled, and Petya burst into a peal of delighted laughter that Tikhon himself joined.
'Oh, but he was a complete good-for-nothing,' said Tikhon. 'The clothes on him—absolute rags! How could I bring him? And so rude, your honor! "I'm a general's son," he says, "and I won't go!"'
'You're a brute!' said Denisov. 'I needed to question him...'

'But I did question him,' said Tikhon. 'He said he didn't know much. "There are a lot of us," he says, "but we're all in poor shape—soldiers in name only. Just shout loud at them," he says, "and you'll take them all."' Tikhon concluded with a cheerful, resolute look at Denisov.
'I'll give you a hundred lashes—that'll teach you to play the fool!' said Denisov severely.
'But why are you angry?' Tikhon protested. 'Just because I haven't seen your Frenchmen before? Wait till it gets dark and I'll bring you any of them you want—three if you like.'
'Well, let's go,' said Denisov, and he rode all the way to the watchman's hut in silence, frowning angrily.
Tikhon followed behind, and Petya heard the Cossacks laughing with him and at him about some pair of boots he'd thrown into the bushes.

When the fit of laughter brought on by Tikhon's words and smile had passed, and Petya realized for a moment that this Tikhon had actually killed a man, he felt uneasy. He glanced at the captive drummer boy and felt a pang in his heart. But the uneasiness lasted only a moment. He felt he needed to hold his head higher, brace himself, and question the esaul with an air of authority about the next day's operation, so as not to be unworthy of the company he was in.
The officer sent to find out about Dolokhov met Denisov on the way with news that Dolokhov would come soon and that everything was fine.
Denisov immediately cheered up and, calling Petya over, said: 'Well, tell me about yourself.'

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Petya had left his family after their departure from Moscow, joined his regiment, and soon been taken on as orderly by a general commanding a large guerrilla detachment. From the time he received his commission, and especially since joining the active army and fighting at Vyazma, Petya had been in a state of perpetual, blissful excitement at being grown up, combined with a frantic eagerness not to miss any chance for real heroism. He was thrilled by everything he saw and experienced in the army, but at the same time it always seemed to him that the truly heroic feats were happening just where he wasn't. He was always in a hurry to be somewhere else.

When on the twenty-first of October his general had wanted to send someone to Denisov's detachment, Petya had begged so desperately to go that the general couldn't refuse. But remembering Petya's reckless behavior at Vyazma—where instead of riding along the road to his assigned position, he had galloped to the front line under French fire and twice discharged his pistol—the general explicitly forbade him from taking part in any of Denisov's operations. That was why Petya had blushed and grown flustered when Denisov asked if he could stay. Before they had even ridden to the forest's edge, Petya had been telling himself he must follow his orders strictly and return immediately. But when he saw the French, and saw Tikhon, and learned there would certainly be an attack that night, he decided—with the speed at which young people reverse their views—that the general he had greatly respected until now was a worthless German, that Denisov was a hero, the esaul was a hero, Tikhon was a hero too, and that it would be shameful to leave them at a moment of difficulty.

It was already getting dark when Denisov, Petya, and the esaul rode up to the watchman's hut. In the twilight, saddled horses could be seen, and Cossacks and hussars who had set up rough shelters in the clearing were lighting fires in a hollow where the French couldn't see the smoke. In the passageway of the small hut, a Cossack with rolled-up sleeves was chopping mutton. Inside, three of Denisov's officers were turning a door into a table. Petya took off his wet clothes, gave them to be dried, and immediately pitched in helping set up the dinner table.
In ten minutes the table was ready with a cloth spread on it. On the table were vodka, a flask of rum, white bread, roast mutton, and salt.

Sitting at the table with the officers, tearing apart the savory, fatty mutton with his fingers while grease ran down his hands, Petya was in an ecstatic, childlike state of love for everyone around him, and therefore of confidence that everyone loved him back.

'So what do you think, Vasili Dmitrich?' he said to Denisov. 'It's all right if I stay with you for a day?' And without waiting for an answer, he answered himself: 'You see, I was told to find things out—well, I am finding things out. Only please let me into the very thick of it... the real action... I don't want a reward. I just want...'
Petya clenched his teeth and looked around, tossing his head back and waving his arms.
'Into the very thick of it...' Denisov repeated with a smile.

'Only, please, give me a command—some real responsibility so I can actually command something,' Petya went on. 'What would it cost you? Oh, do you need a knife?' he asked, turning to an officer who wanted to cut some mutton.
And he handed over his clasp knife. The officer admired it.

'Please keep it. I've got several like it,' said Petya, blushing. 'Heavens! I almost forgot!' he suddenly cried. 'I've got raisins—wonderful ones, seedless. We have a new sutler and he has amazing stuff. I bought ten pounds. I like having something sweet. Would you like some?' And Petya ran out to his Cossack in the passage and came back with bags containing about five pounds of raisins. 'Help yourselves, gentlemen!'

'Do you need a coffeepot?' he asked the esaul. 'I bought a wonderful one from our sutler! He has fantastic things. And he's very honest—that's the main thing. I'll make sure to send it to you. Or maybe your flints are worn out or used up—that happens sometimes, you know. I brought some along, right here'—he showed a bag—'a hundred flints. I got them very cheap. Please take as many as you want—or all of them...'
Then, suddenly afraid he'd said too much, Petya stopped and blushed.

He tried to remember if he'd done anything else foolish. Running through the day's events, he thought of the French drummer boy. 'It's fine for us here, but what about him? Where have they put him? Have they fed him? Did anyone hurt his feelings?' But having already caught himself going overboard about the flints, he was afraid to speak.

'I could ask,' he thought, 'but they'll say: "He's just a boy himself, so he feels sorry for the boy." I'll show them tomorrow whether I'm a boy! Would it seem odd if I asked?' Petya wondered. 'Oh well, never mind!' And immediately, blushing and watching the officers anxiously for any sign of mockery, he said:
'May I call in that prisoner boy and give him something to eat? Maybe...'
'Yes, he's a poor little fellow,' said Denisov, who clearly saw nothing shameful in the suggestion. 'Bring him in. His name is Vincent Bosse. Go get him.'
'I'll call him,' said Petya.
'Yes, yes, go ahead. Poor little fellow,' Denisov repeated.
Petya was at the door when Denisov said this. He slipped between the officers, came close to Denisov, and said:
'Let me kiss you, dear old fellow! Oh, how wonderful, how splendid!'
And having kissed Denisov, he ran out of the hut.
'Bosse! Vincent!' Petya called, stopping outside the door.
'Who do you want, sir?' asked a voice from the darkness.
Petya said he wanted the French boy who had been captured that day.
'Ah, Vesenny?' said a Cossack.

Vincent, the boy's name, had already been transformed by the Cossacks into Vesenny (springlike) and by the peasants and soldiers into Vesenya. In both these adaptations, the echo of spring matched the impression made by the young lad.
'He's warming himself over at the bonfire. Hey, Vesenya! Vesenya! Vesenny!' laughing voices called to one another in the darkness.
'He's a smart lad,' said a hussar standing near Petya. 'We gave him something to eat a while ago. He was terribly hungry!'
The sound of bare feet splashing through mud was heard in the darkness, and the drummer boy appeared at the door.
'Ah, it's you!' said Petya. 'Are you hungry? Don't be afraid—no one will hurt you. Come in, come in.'
('Thank you, sir.')
('Come in, come in.')
'Thank you, sir,' said the drummer boy in a trembling, almost childish voice, and he began scraping his dirty feet on the threshold.
('Thank you, sir.')
There were many things Petya wanted to say to the drummer boy but didn't dare. He stood beside him in the passage, uncertain. Then, in the darkness, he took the boy's hand and squeezed it.
'Come in, come in!' he repeated in a gentle whisper. 'Oh, what can I do for him?' he thought, and opening the door, let the boy go in first.

When the boy had entered the hut, Petya sat down at a distance from him, feeling it beneath his dignity to pay him attention. But he fingered the money in his pocket and wondered whether it would seem ridiculous to give some to the drummer boy.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Dolokhov's arrival diverted Petya's attention from the drummer boy—whom Denisov had already had fed with mutton and vodka and dressed in a Russian coat so he could be kept with their band rather than sent away with the other prisoners. Petya had heard many stories in the army about Dolokhov's extraordinary bravery and his cruelty toward the French. So from the moment Dolokhov entered the hut, Petya couldn't take his eyes off him, bracing himself and holding his head high to prove himself worthy of such company.
Dolokhov's appearance surprised Petya by its simplicity.

Denisov wore a Cossack coat, had a beard, carried an icon of St. Nicholas the Wonder-Worker on his chest, and everything about him signaled his unusual position. But Dolokhov, who had worn Persian garb in Moscow, now looked like a textbook Guards officer. He was clean-shaven and wore a padded Guards coat with a St. George medal at his buttonhole and a plain forage cap set straight on his head. He took off his wet felt cloak in a corner without greeting anyone, went straight to Denisov, and began questioning him about the situation. Denisov told him about the large detachments' designs on the convoy, the message Petya had brought, and his own responses to both generals. Then he told him everything he knew about the French column.

'That's fine. But we need to know exactly what troops they are and how many,' said Dolokhov. 'We'll need to go there ourselves. We can't start without knowing the precise numbers. I like to work accurately. Now—wouldn't one of these gentlemen like to ride with me to the French camp? I've brought a spare uniform.'
'I'll go! I'll go with you!' cried Petya.
'You absolutely don't need to go,' said Denisov, addressing Dolokhov, 'and as for him, I won't allow it under any circumstances.'
'I like that!' exclaimed Petya. 'Why shouldn't I go?'
'Because there's no point.'
'Well, excuse me, but... because... because... I'm going, and that's final. You'll take me, won't you?' he said, turning to Dolokhov.
'Why not?' Dolokhov answered absently, studying the French drummer boy's face. 'Have you had that youngster long?' he asked Denisov.
'He was captured today, but he doesn't know anything. I'm keeping him with us.'
'And where do you put the rest of them?' Dolokhov asked.

'Where? I send them away and get a receipt for them,' Denisov burst out, suddenly flushing. 'And I say plainly that I don't have a single man's life on my conscience. Would it really be so hard to send thirty or three hundred men to town under escort, instead of staining—I say it straight—staining the honor of a soldier?'
'That kind of sweet talk would be fine coming from this sixteen-year-old count here,' said Dolokhov with cold irony. 'But it's time you dropped it.'
'I haven't said anything! I only said I'm definitely going with you,' said Petya timidly.

'But for you and me, old man, it's time to drop these niceties,' Dolokhov continued, seeming to enjoy the topic that irritated Denisov. 'Why have you kept this boy?' he went on, shaking his head. 'Because you feel sorry for him! Don't we all know about your "receipts"? You send off a hundred and thirty arrive. The rest either starve or get killed. So what's the difference?'
The esaul nodded approvingly, squinting his light-colored eyes.
'That's beside the point. I'm not going to debate it. I refuse to have it on my conscience. You say they'll die. Fine. But not because of me!'
Dolokhov laughed.

'Who's told them not to capture me these twenty times over? But if they did catch me, they'd string me up on an aspen tree, and all your chivalry wouldn't make a bit of difference.' He paused. 'Anyway, we need to get moving. Tell the Cossack to fetch my kit. I've got two French uniforms in it. So—are you coming with me?' he asked Petya.
'I? Yes, yes, absolutely!' cried Petya, blushing almost to tears and glancing at Denisov.

While Dolokhov had been arguing with Denisov about what to do with prisoners, Petya had again felt awkward and restless—but once more he didn't have time to fully grasp what they were discussing. 'If grown-up, distinguished men think this way, it must be necessary and right,' he thought. 'But above all, Denisov must not dare think I'll just obey him and let him order me around. I will definitely go to the French camp with Dolokhov. If he can do it, so can I!'
And to all Denisov's attempts to dissuade him, Petya replied that he too was in the habit of doing everything precisely, not 'just anyhow,' and that he never worried about personal danger.

'Because you have to admit—if we don't know exactly how many there are, hundreds of lives could depend on it, and there are only the two of us. Besides, I really want to go, and I'm definitely going. So please don't try to stop me,' he said. 'It will only make things worse.'

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Having put on French greatcoats and shakos, Petya and Dolokhov rode to the clearing from which Denisov had surveyed the French camp. Emerging from the forest into pitch darkness, they descended into the hollow. At the bottom, Dolokhov told the Cossacks accompanying him to wait there and rode on at a quick trot toward the bridge. Petya, his heart pounding with excitement, rode beside him.
'If we're caught, I won't be taken alive! I have a pistol,' he whispered.
'Don't speak Russian,' said Dolokhov in a hurried whisper, and at that very moment came the challenge from the darkness: 'Who goes there?' and the click of a musket.
('Who goes there?')
The blood rushed to Petya's face and he gripped his pistol.
'Lancers of the Sixth!' Dolokhov replied, neither quickening nor slowing his horse's pace.
('Lancers of the Sixth Regiment.')
The black shape of a sentinel stood on the bridge.
'Password.'
('Password.')
Dolokhov reined in his horse and walked it forward.
'Tell me, is Colonel Gerard here?' he asked.
('Tell me, is Colonel Gerard here?')
'Password,' the sentinel repeated, blocking the way without answering.
'When an officer is making his rounds, sentinels don't ask for the password!' Dolokhov suddenly barked, riding straight at the sentinel. 'I'm asking you if the colonel is here!'
('When an officer is making his rounds, sentinels don't ask for the password. I'm asking you if the colonel is here.')
And without waiting for an answer from the sentinel, who had stepped aside, Dolokhov rode up the slope at a walk.

Noticing the dark outline of a man crossing the road, Dolokhov stopped him and asked where the commander and officers were. The man—a soldier with a sack over his shoulder—stopped, came close to Dolokhov's horse, touched it with his hand, and explained simply and in a friendly way that the commander and officers were up the hill to the right, in the courtyard of the farm (as he called the landowner's house).

Having ridden up the road with French conversation audible around campfires on both sides, Dolokhov turned into the courtyard of the landowner's house. He dismounted and approached a large, blazing campfire around which several men sat talking noisily. Something was boiling in a small cauldron at the fire's edge, and a soldier in a peaked cap and blue overcoat, lit up by the flames, was kneeling beside it stirring the contents with a ramrod.
'Oh, he's a tough one,' said one of the officers sitting in the shadow on the other side of the fire.
'He'll make those fellows get a move on!' said another, laughing.
Both fell silent, peering into the darkness at the sound of Dolokhov's and Petya's footsteps approaching with their horses.
'Good evening, gentlemen!' Dolokhov said loudly and clearly.
('Good evening, gentlemen.')
There was a stir among the officers in the shadows, and one tall, long-necked officer walked around the fire toward Dolokhov.
'Is that you, Clement?' he asked. 'Where the devil—?' But catching his mistake, he broke off and, with a frown, greeted Dolokhov as a stranger, asking what he could do for him.

Dolokhov said that he and his companion were trying to catch up with their regiment and, addressing the group, asked whether anyone knew anything about the Sixth Regiment. No one knew anything. Petya thought the officers were beginning to eye him and Dolokhov with hostility and suspicion. For several seconds, no one spoke.
'If you were hoping for the evening soup, you've come too late,' said a voice from behind the fire, with a suppressed laugh.
Dolokhov replied that they weren't hungry and had to keep moving through the night.

He handed the horses to the soldier stirring the pot and squatted on his heels by the fire next to the long-necked officer, who kept staring at him and again asked what regiment he belonged to. Dolokhov, as if he hadn't heard, didn't answer. Instead, lighting a short French pipe he'd taken from his pocket, he began asking the officer how safe the road ahead was from Cossack attacks.
'Those bandits are everywhere,' replied an officer from behind the fire.

Dolokhov observed that Cossacks were only dangerous to lone stragglers like himself and his companion, 'but surely they wouldn't dare attack large detachments?' he added, as if seeking confirmation. No one responded.
'Well, now he'll leave,' Petya thought every moment as he stood by the fire listening.

But Dolokhov picked up the dropped conversation and began asking direct questions: how many men in the battalion, how many battalions, how many prisoners? Asking about the Russian prisoners in their column, Dolokhov said:

'Terrible nuisance dragging those corpses around! Better to shoot that rabble,' and he burst into such loud, strange laughter that Petya was sure the French would see through their disguise at any second. He involuntarily stepped back from the fire.

No one responded to Dolokhov's laughter. A French officer they couldn't see—lying wrapped in a greatcoat—sat up and whispered something to a companion. Dolokhov stood, called for the soldier holding their horses.
'Will they bring the horses, or won't they?' thought Petya, instinctively moving closer to Dolokhov.
The horses were brought.
'Good evening, gentlemen,' said Dolokhov.

Petya wanted to say 'Good night' but couldn't get the words out. The officers were whispering together. Dolokhov took a long time mounting his horse, which wouldn't stand still, then he rode out of the yard at a walk. Petya rode beside him, longing to look back to see if the French were following but not daring to.

Coming out onto the road, Dolokhov didn't ride back across the open ground but through the village. At one spot he stopped and listened. 'Do you hear?' he asked. Petya recognized the sound of Russian voices and saw the dark shapes of Russian prisoners huddled around their campfires. When they descended to the bridge, Petya and Dolokhov rode past the sentinel, who paced silently and morosely up and down, then dropped into the hollow where the Cossacks were waiting.
'Well then, goodbye. Tell Denisov: at the first shot, at daybreak,' said Dolokhov and was about to ride off, but Petya grabbed his arm.
'Really!' he cried. 'You're such a hero! Oh, how wonderful, how splendid! How I love you!'

'All right, all right!' said Dolokhov. But Petya wouldn't let go, and through the gloom Dolokhov saw him leaning forward, wanting to kiss him. Dolokhov kissed him, laughed, wheeled his horse around, and vanished into the darkness.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Returning to the watchman's hut, Petya found Denisov waiting in the passage. He'd been pacing with agitation, anxiety, and self-reproach for having let Petya go.

'Thank God!' he exclaimed. 'Yes, thank God!' he repeated, listening to Petya's rapturous account. 'But damn you, I couldn't sleep because of you! Well, thank God. Now lie down. We can still get some rest before morning.'
'But... no,' said Petya. 'I don't want to sleep yet. Besides, I know myself—if I fall asleep, that's the end. And anyway, I'm used to not sleeping before a battle.'
He sat in the hut for a while, happily reliving the details of his adventure and vividly imagining what would happen the next day.
Then, noticing that Denisov had fallen asleep, he got up and went outside.

It was still pitch dark. The rain had stopped, but drops were still falling from the trees. Near the watchman's hut, the dark shapes of the Cossacks' shelters and tethered horses could just be made out. Behind the hut, the dark outlines of two wagons with their horses beside them were barely visible, and in the hollow, the dying campfire glowed red. Not all the Cossacks and hussars were asleep; here and there, amid the sound of falling drops and horses munching nearby, low voices could be heard, seeming to whisper.

Petya stepped out, peered into the darkness, and walked over to the wagons. Someone was snoring underneath them, and saddled horses stood around, munching oats. In the dark, Petya recognized his own horse, which he called 'Karabakh' though it was actually a Ukrainian breed, and went up to it.
'Well, Karabakh! We'll see some action tomorrow,' he said, sniffing its nostrils and kissing it.
'Why aren't you asleep, sir?' asked a Cossack sitting under one of the wagons.
'No... Likhachev—that's your name, isn't it? You know, I've only just gotten back! We went right into the French camp.'
And Petya gave the Cossack a detailed account not only of his ride but also of his reasons, and why he thought it was better to risk his life than to do things 'just anyhow.'
'Well, you should get some sleep now,' said the Cossack.
'No, I'm used to this,' said Petya. 'By the way—are the flints in your pistols worn out? I brought some with me. Don't you want any? You can have some.'
The Cossack leaned forward from under the wagon to get a better look at Petya.
'Because I'm in the habit of doing everything precisely,' said Petya. 'Some people do things carelessly, without preparation, and then they're sorry. I don't like that.'
'That's for sure,' said the Cossack.
'Oh yes, one more thing! Please, my dear fellow, will you sharpen my saber? It's gotten bl—' (Petya was afraid to lie; the saber had never been sharpened.) 'Can you do it?'
'Of course.'
Likhachev got up, rummaged in his pack, and soon Petya heard the warlike sound of steel on whetstone. He climbed onto the wagon and sat on its edge. The Cossack was sharpening the saber underneath.
'Are the lads asleep?' asked Petya.
'Some are, some aren't—same as us.'
'And what about that boy?'
'Vesenny? Oh, he threw himself down there in the passage. Fast asleep after his fright. He was so happy!'
After that, Petya sat quietly for a long time, listening to the sounds. He heard footsteps in the darkness, and a black figure appeared.
'What are you sharpening?' asked the man, coming up to the wagon.
'This gentleman's saber.'
'That's good,' said the man, whom Petya took to be a hussar. 'Was the cup left here?'
'There, by the wheel.'
The hussar took the cup.
'Must be nearly daylight,' he said, yawning, and walked away.

Petya should have known that he was in a forest with Denisov's guerrilla band, less than a mile from the road, sitting on a wagon captured from the French; that under it Likhachev was sharpening his saber; that the big dark blotch to the right was the watchman's hut and the red blotch below to the left was the dying campfire; that the man who came for the cup was a hussar who wanted a drink. But he neither knew nor cared to know any of this. He was in a fairy kingdom where nothing resembled reality. The big dark blotch might be the watchman's hut, or it might be a cavern leading to the very depths of the earth. The red spot might be a fire, or the eye of an enormous monster. Maybe he really was sitting on a wagon, but it might just as easily be a terrifyingly high tower, and if he fell he'd keep falling for a whole day or a whole month, and never reach the bottom. Maybe it was just the Cossack Likhachev sitting under the wagon, but it might be the kindest, bravest, most wonderful man in the world—someone no one knew about. Maybe the hussar really had come for water and gone back to the hollow, but maybe he had simply vanished, dissolved into nothingness.
Nothing Petya might have seen now would have surprised him. He was in a fairy kingdom where everything was possible.

He looked up at the sky. And the sky was a fairy realm too, like the earth. It was clearing, and clouds sailed swiftly over the treetops as if unveiling the stars. Sometimes it looked as if the clouds were moving and a clear black sky showed between them. Sometimes the black spaces seemed to be clouds. Sometimes the sky appeared to rise incredibly high overhead; then it seemed to drop so low you could touch it with your hand.
Petya's eyes began to close and he swayed slightly.
The trees were dripping. Quiet talk was heard. The horses neighed and jostled. Someone snored.

'Ozheg-zheg, ozheg-zheg...' hissed the saber against the whetstone, and suddenly Petya heard a harmonious orchestra playing some unknown, sweetly solemn hymn. Petya was as musical as Natasha, and more so than Nikolai, but he had never studied music or thought about it, so the melody that came unexpectedly to his mind seemed to him especially fresh and beautiful. The music grew louder and richer, the melody passing from one instrument to another. What was being played was a fugue—though Petya had no idea what a fugue was. Each instrument—now sounding like a violin, now like a horn, but better and purer than either—played its own part, and before it had finished, another instrument took up almost the same melody, then a third and a fourth joined in. They all blended into one and then separated again, now merging into solemn church music, now into something dazzlingly brilliant and triumphant.
'Oh—wait, that was a dream!' Petya said to himself, lurching forward. 'It's in my ears. But maybe it's music of my own. Well, go on, my music! Play on!...'

He closed his eyes. From all sides, as if from a distance, sounds fluttered, swelled into harmonies, separated, and blended again into the same sweet, solemn hymn. 'Oh, this is wonderful! As much as I want, and however I want!' Petya said to himself. He tried to conduct that enormous orchestra.

'Now softer, softer—die away!' And the sounds obeyed him. 'Now fuller, more joyful! Still more, more joyful!' And from some unknown depth, increasingly triumphant sounds rose. 'Now voices, join in!' Petya ordered. And from far away he heard first men's voices, then women's. The voices swelled in harmonious, triumphant power, and Petya listened in awe and joy.

With the solemn, triumphant march there mingled the song of the dripping trees, the hissing of the saber—'Ozheg-zheg-zheg...'—and again the horses jostled and neighed, not breaking the music but joining it.
Petya didn't know how long this lasted. He savored every moment, marveling at his own delight and regretting there was no one to share it. He was woken by Likhachev's kind voice.
'It's ready, your honor. You could split a Frenchman in half with it!'
Petya woke up.
'It's getting light—it's really getting light!' he exclaimed.

The horses, previously invisible, could now be seen right down to their tails, and a watery light filtered through the bare branches. Petya shook himself, jumped up, pulled a ruble from his pocket and gave it to Likhachev, then flourished the saber, tested it, and sheathed it. The Cossacks were untying their horses and tightening saddle girths.
'Here comes the commander,' said Likhachev.
Denisov came out of the watchman's hut and, calling Petya over, gave orders to get ready.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The men quickly found their horses in the half-darkness, tightened saddle girths, and formed into companies. Denisov stood by the watchman's hut, giving final orders. The detachment's infantry filed along the road and quickly vanished among the trees in the mist of early dawn, hundreds of feet splashing through the mud. The esaul gave orders to his men. Petya held his horse by the bridle, impatiently awaiting the command to mount. His face, freshly washed in cold water, was glowing, and his eyes were especially bright. Cold shivers ran down his spine and his whole body pulsed rhythmically.
'Well, is everything ready?' asked Denisov. 'Bring the horses.'

The horses were brought. Denisov scolded the Cossack because the saddle girths were too loose, then mounted. Petya put his foot in the stirrup. His horse, out of habit, made as if to nip his leg, but Petya leaped quickly into the saddle, unaware of his own weight, and turning to look at the hussars moving up in the darkness behind him, rode up to Denisov.
'Vasili Dmitrich, give me something to do! Please... for God's sake!' he said.
Denisov seemed to have forgotten Petya even existed. He turned to glance at him.
'I ask one thing of you,' he said sternly, 'obey me and don't push yourself into anything.'

He didn't say another word to Petya the entire ride. When they reached the forest's edge, it was noticeably getting lighter over the field. Denisov whispered with the esaul, and the Cossacks began riding past Petya and Denisov. When they had all gone by, Denisov spurred his horse and rode down the hill. Slipping and sliding on their haunches, the horses carried their riders down into the ravine. Petya rode beside Denisov, the pulse of excitement in his body growing constantly stronger. It was getting lighter and lighter, but the mist still hid distant objects. Reaching the valley, Denisov looked back and nodded to a Cossack beside him.
'The signal!' he said.
The Cossack raised his arm, and a shot rang out. Instantly the sound of galloping hooves was heard, shouts broke out from all sides, and more shots followed.

At the first sound of pounding hooves and shouting, Petya whipped his horse and let the reins go slack, galloping forward without heeding Denisov, who yelled after him. It seemed to Petya that at the instant the shot was fired, it suddenly became as bright as noon. He galloped toward the bridge. Cossacks were racing along the road ahead of him. On the bridge he crashed into a Cossack who had fallen behind, but galloped on. In front of him, soldiers—probably French—were running from right to left across the road. One of them fell in the mud under his horse's hooves.

Cossacks were crowding around a hut, doing something. From the middle of the crowd came terrible screams. Petya galloped up, and the first thing he saw was the pale face and trembling jaw of a Frenchman clutching the shaft of a lance aimed at him.
'Hurrah!... Boys!... Ours!' shouted Petya, and giving his excited horse free rein, he galloped forward along the village street.

He could hear gunfire ahead. Cossacks, hussars, and ragged Russian prisoners who had come running from both sides of the road were shouting something loudly and incoherently. A dashing-looking Frenchman in a blue overcoat, bareheaded and with a frowning red face, had been fighting off the hussars. By the time Petya galloped up, the Frenchman had already fallen. 'Too late again!' flashed through Petya's mind, and he galloped on toward the place where the rapid gunfire was coming from. The shots came from the yard of the landowner's house he had visited the night before with Dolokhov. The French were making a stand behind a wattle fence in a garden thick with bushes, firing at the Cossacks crowding at the gate. Through the smoke, as he approached, Petya saw Dolokhov, his face a pale greenish tint, shouting to his men. 'Go around! Wait for the infantry!' he yelled as Petya rode up.
'Wait?... Hurrah!' shouted Petya, and without pausing for an instant, he galloped toward the place where the gunfire was thickest and the smoke was densest.

A volley rang out. Some bullets whistled past; others smacked into something. The Cossacks and Dolokhov galloped after Petya through the gateway into the courtyard. In the dense, wavering smoke, some of the French threw down their weapons and ran out of the bushes to meet the Cossacks, while others fled down the hill toward the pond. Petya was galloping across the courtyard, but instead of holding the reins, he was waving both arms about rapidly and strangely, slipping further and further to one side of his saddle. His horse, having galloped up to a campfire smoldering in the morning light, stopped suddenly, and Petya fell heavily onto the wet ground. The Cossacks saw his arms and legs jerk rapidly, though his head was completely still. A bullet had pierced his skull.

After speaking to the senior French officer—who came out of the house with a white handkerchief tied to his sword, announcing their surrender—Dolokhov dismounted and went over to Petya, who lay motionless with his arms flung out.
'Done for!' he said with a frown, and walked to the gate to meet Denisov, who was riding toward him.
'Killed?' cried Denisov, recognizing from a distance the unmistakable, horribly familiar posture of Petya's lifeless body.

'Done for!' Dolokhov repeated, as if saying the words gave him a kind of grim satisfaction, and he walked quickly to the prisoners, who were surrounded by Cossacks. 'We won't be taking them!' he called out to Denisov.
Denisov didn't reply. He rode up to Petya, dismounted, and with trembling hands turned toward himself the bloodstained, mud-covered face that had already gone white.

'I like having something sweet. Raisins—wonderful ones... take them all!' The words came back to him. And the Cossacks looked around in surprise at the sound—like the yelp of a dog—with which Denisov turned away, walked to the wattle fence, and gripped it.
Among the Russian prisoners rescued by Denisov and Dolokhov was Pierre Bezukhov.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Throughout the entire march from Moscow, no new orders had been given by the French authorities regarding the group of prisoners that included Pierre. By October twenty-second, their party was no longer traveling with the same troops and supply wagons they had left Moscow with. Half the hardtack wagons that had accompanied them on the first legs of the journey had been captured by Cossacks; the other half had gone on ahead. Not one of the dismounted cavalrymen who had marched at the front of the prisoner column remained—they had all disappeared. The artillery the prisoners had seen ahead of them during the early days had been replaced by Marshal Junot's enormous baggage train, escorted by Westphalians. Behind the prisoners came a cavalry baggage train.

From Vyazma onward, the French army, which had until then been moving in three columns, continued as a single mass. The symptoms of disorder that Pierre had first noticed at their initial stopping place after leaving Moscow had now reached their ultimate extreme.

The road they traveled was bordered on both sides by dead horses. Ragged men who had fallen behind from various regiments constantly drifted in and out, sometimes joining the moving column, sometimes dropping behind again.

Several times during the march, false alarms had been raised. The escort soldiers would grab their muskets, fire, and run in a panic, trampling one another, only to reassemble afterward and curse each other for the needless fright.
These three groups traveling together—the cavalry stores, the convoy of prisoners, and Junot's baggage train—still formed a separate and unified whole, though each group was rapidly shrinking.

Of the artillery baggage train, which had originally consisted of a hundred and twenty wagons, no more than sixty remained; the rest had been captured or abandoned. Several of Junot's wagons had also been seized or left behind. Three wagons had been raided and looted by stragglers from Davout's corps. From the talk of the Germans, Pierre learned that a larger guard had been assigned to that baggage train than to the prisoners, and that one of their comrades, a German soldier, had been shot on the marshal's direct order because a silver spoon belonging to the marshal had been found in his possession.

The group of prisoners had shrunk the most. Of the three hundred and thirty men who had set out from Moscow, fewer than a hundred now remained. The prisoners were more burdensome to their escort than even the cavalry saddles or Junot's baggage. They all understood that the saddles and Junot's spoon might have some use, but that cold and hungry soldiers should have to stand guard over equally cold and hungry Russians who kept freezing and collapsing on the road—at which point the order was to shoot them—was not merely incomprehensible but revolting. And the escort, as if afraid that giving in to the pity they felt for the prisoners would only make their own situation worse, treated them with particular harshness and cruelty.

At Dorogobuzhsk, while the convoy soldiers had locked the prisoners in a stable and gone off to loot their own supply stores, several prisoner soldiers tunneled under the wall and escaped, but they were recaptured by the French and shot.

The earlier arrangement of keeping officer prisoners separate from the rest had long since been abandoned. All who could walk went together, and after the third stage Pierre had rejoined Karataev and the gray-blue, bandy-legged dog that had adopted Karataev as its master.

On the third day after leaving Moscow, Karataev fell ill again with the fever he had suffered from in the Moscow hospital, and as he grew gradually weaker, Pierre began keeping his distance. He did not know why, but ever since Karataev had begun to deteriorate, it cost Pierre an effort to go near him. When he did approach and heard the quiet moaning with which Karataev usually lay down at each stopping place, and when he smelled the odor coming from him—now stronger than before—Pierre would move farther away and try not to think about him.

While imprisoned in the shed, Pierre had learned—not through his intellect but with his whole being, through life itself—that human beings are made for happiness, that happiness lies within us in the satisfaction of simple human needs, and that all unhappiness comes not from deprivation but from excess. And now, during these last three weeks of marching, he had learned yet another new and comforting truth: that nothing in this world is truly terrible. He had learned that just as there is no condition in which a person can be completely happy and entirely free, there is no condition in which one must be completely unhappy and lack all freedom. He learned that suffering and freedom have their limits, and that those limits are very close together; that the person lying in a bed of roses with one crumpled petal suffered as keenly as he now did, sleeping on bare damp earth with one side growing cold while the other warmed; and that when he had once worn tight dancing shoes, he had suffered just as much as he did now walking with bare feet covered in sores—his footwear having long since fallen apart. He discovered that when he had married his wife—seemingly of his own free will—he had been no more free than now, when they locked him in a stable at night. Of all the things he later called his sufferings, but which at the time he barely felt, the worst was the state of his bare, raw, scab-covered feet. (The horsemeat was actually appetizing and nourishing; the saltpeter flavor of the gunpowder they used instead of salt was even pleasant; there was no great cold; it was always warm walking during the day; and at night there were campfires; the lice that devoured him actually warmed his body.) The one thing that was initially hard to bear was his feet.

After the second day's march, Pierre examined his feet by the campfire and thought it would be impossible to walk on them. But when everyone got up, he went along limping, and once he had warmed up, walked without feeling the pain, though at night his feet looked more terrible than before. But he no longer looked at them and thought of other things instead.

Only now did Pierre truly grasp the full strength of life in a person and the saving power of being able to shift one's attention from one thing to another—like the safety valve on a boiler that releases excess steam when the pressure becomes too great.

He did not see and did not hear them shooting the prisoners who fell behind, though more than a hundred died that way. He did not think of Karataev, who grew weaker every day and would clearly soon share the same fate. Still less did Pierre think about himself. The harder his situation became and the more terrible the future, the more independent of his circumstances were the joyful and comforting thoughts, memories, and imaginings that came to him.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: At midday on October twenty-second, Pierre was trudging uphill along the muddy, slippery road, looking at his feet and at the roughness of the way. Occasionally he glanced at the familiar crowd around him, then back at his feet again. Both were equally familiar and felt like part of himself. The blue-gray, bandy-legged dog ran merrily alongside the road, sometimes lifting one hind leg to hop along on three as proof of its agility and good spirits, then going on all four again and rushing off to bark at crows sitting on carrion. The dog was merrier and sleeker than it had been in Moscow. All around lay the flesh of different creatures—from humans to horses—in various stages of decay; and since wolves were kept away by the passing men, the dog could eat all it wanted.

It had been raining since morning, seeming as though it might stop any minute and the sky clear, but after a brief pause it rained harder than before. The saturated road no longer absorbed the water, which ran along the ruts in streams.
Pierre walked along looking from side to side, counting his steps in threes and ticking them off on his fingers. Mentally addressing the rain, he repeated: "Come on now, come on! Pour harder!"

He seemed to be thinking of nothing, but deep down inside him, his soul was occupied with something important and comforting. This something was a very subtle spiritual insight drawn from a conversation with Karataev the day before.

At their previous stopping place, feeling chilled by a dying campfire, Pierre had gotten up and gone to the next one, which was burning better. There Platon Karataev sat covered up—head and all—with his greatcoat as if it were a vestment, telling the soldiers in his warm and pleasant, though now weakened voice, a story Pierre already knew. It was past midnight, the hour when Karataev was usually free of his fever and especially lively. When Pierre reached the fire and heard Platon's voice, weakened by illness, and saw his thin face brightly lit by the blaze, he felt a painful stab in his heart. His feeling of pity for this man frightened him, and he wanted to leave, but there was no other fire, so Pierre sat down, trying not to look at Platon.
"Well, how are you?" he asked.
"How am I? If we complain about sickness, God won't grant us death," replied Platon, and immediately resumed the story he had begun.
"And so, brother," he continued, with a smile on his pale, wasted face and a particularly joyful light in his eyes, "you see, brother..."

Pierre had long been familiar with that story. Karataev had told it to him alone some half-dozen times, always with a special joyful emotion. But though he knew it well, Pierre now listened as though it were something new, and the quiet rapture Karataev clearly felt as he told it communicated itself to Pierre as well. The story was about an old merchant who lived a good and God-fearing life with his family, and who once went to the Nizhni fair with a companion—a rich merchant.

Having checked into an inn, they both went to sleep, and the next morning the companion was found robbed and with his throat cut. A blood-stained knife was found under the old merchant's pillow. He was tried, flogged, and his nostrils torn off, "all in proper form" as Karataev put it, and he was sent to hard labor in Siberia.

"And so, brother" (it was at this point that Pierre had come up), "ten years or more passed. The old man was living as a convict, accepting his lot as he should and doing no wrong. He only prayed to God for death. Well, one night the convicts were gathered together just as we are, with the old man among them. And they began telling what each was being punished for and how they had sinned against God. One told how he had taken a life, another had taken two, a third had set a house on fire, while another had simply been a vagrant and done nothing wrong. So they asked the old man: 'What are you being punished for, old father?' 'I, my dear brothers,' said he, 'am being punished for my own and other men's sins. But I have not killed anyone or taken anything that was not mine—I have only helped my poorer brothers. I was a merchant, dear brothers, and had much property.'
