And he went on to tell them everything in proper order. 'I don't grieve for myself,' he says, 'God, it seems, has chosen to punish me. Only I am sorry for my old wife and the children,' and the old man began to weep. Now it happened that in the group was the very man who had killed the other merchant. 'Where did it happen, old father?' he said. 'When, and in what month?' He asked about everything, and his heart began to ache. So he came up to the old man like this, and fell down at his feet! 'You are suffering because of me, old father,' he says. 'It's the absolute truth, lads, that this man,' he says, 'is being tortured innocently and for nothing! I,' he says, 'did that deed, and I slipped the knife under your head while you were asleep. Forgive me, old father,' he says, 'for Christ's sake!'"
Karataev paused, smiling joyfully as he gazed into the fire, and pushed the logs together.

"And the old man said, 'God will forgive you—we are all sinners in His sight. I suffer for my own sins,' and he wept bitter tears. Well, and what do you think, dear friends?" Karataev continued, his face brightening more and more with a radiant smile, as if what he was about to say contained the chief beauty and the whole meaning of his story: "What do you think, dear fellows? That murderer confessed to the authorities. 'I have taken six lives,' he says (he was a great sinner), 'but what I am most sorry for is this old man. Don't let him suffer because of me.' So he confessed, and it was all written down, and the papers were sent off in proper form. The place was far away, and while they were processing things, what with one thing and another, filling in all the papers in proper form—the authorities, I mean—time passed. The case reached the Tsar. Eventually the Tsar's decree came: to set the merchant free and give him the compensation that had been awarded. The paper arrived and they began looking for the old man. 'Where is the old man who has been suffering innocently?' A paper has come from the Tsar!' So they began looking for him," here Karataev's lower jaw trembled, "but God had already forgiven him—he was dead! That's how it was, dear fellows!" Karataev concluded, and sat for a long time in silence, gazing before him with a smile.

And Pierre's soul was dimly but joyfully filled—not by the story itself, but by its mysterious meaning: by the radiant joy that lit up Karataev's face as he told it, and by the profound significance of that joy.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: "To your places!" a voice suddenly cried.
"To your places!"

A pleasant feeling of excitement and an expectation of something important and grand arose among both the convoy soldiers and the prisoners. From all sides came shouts of command, and from the left came smartly dressed cavalrymen on good horses, passing the prisoners at a trot. Every face showed the tension people feel at the approach of someone in authority. The prisoners crowded together and were pushed off the road. The convoy formed up.

"The Emperor! The Emperor! The Marshal! The Duke!" And hardly had the sleek cavalry passed before a carriage drawn by six gray horses rattled by. Pierre caught a glimpse of a man in a three-cornered hat with a calm expression on his handsome, plump, white face. It was one of the marshals. His eye fell on Pierre's large and striking figure, and in the expression with which he frowned and looked away, Pierre thought he detected sympathy and a desire to hide it.

The general in charge of the stores galloped after the carriage, red-faced and frightened, whipping up his thin horse. Several officers formed a group and some soldiers crowded around them. Their faces all looked excited and worried.
"What did he say? What did he say?" Pierre heard them asking.

While the marshal was passing, the prisoners had huddled together in a crowd, and Pierre saw Karataev, whom he hadn't yet seen that morning. He sat in his short overcoat, leaning against a birch tree. On his face, besides the look of joyful emotion it had worn the night before while he told the story of the merchant who suffered innocently, there was now an expression of quiet solemnity.

Karataev looked at Pierre with his kind, round eyes, now filled with tears, clearly wanting him to come closer so he could say something. But Pierre wasn't sure enough of himself. He acted as if he hadn't noticed that look and moved quickly away.

When the prisoners started walking again, Pierre looked back. Karataev was still sitting at the side of the road under the birch tree, and two Frenchmen were talking over his head. Pierre didn't look back again, but went limping up the hill.

From behind, where Karataev had been sitting, came the sound of a shot. Pierre heard it clearly, but at that moment he remembered he hadn't yet finished calculating how many stages remained to Smolensk—a calculation he had begun before the marshal went by. And he started counting again. Two French soldiers ran past Pierre, one of them carrying a lowered and still-smoking gun. They both looked pale, and in the expression on their faces—one of them glanced nervously at Pierre—there was something resembling what he had seen on the face of the young soldier at the execution. Pierre looked at the soldier and remembered that two days earlier, that man had burned his shirt while drying it at the fire and everyone had laughed at him.
Behind him, where Karataev had been sitting, the dog began to howl. "What a stupid animal! Why is it howling?" thought Pierre.

His comrades, the prisoner soldiers walking beside him, avoided looking back at the place where the shot had been fired and the dog was howling, just as Pierre did. But there was a fixed look on all their faces.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: The stores, the prisoners, and the marshal's baggage train halted at the village of Shamshevo. The men crowded together around the campfires. Pierre went up to a fire, ate some roast horsemeat, lay down with his back to the flames, and immediately fell asleep. He slept again as he had at Mozhaysk after the battle of Borodino.
Once more real events mingled with dreams, and once more someone—he or another—gave voice to his thoughts, the same thoughts that had been expressed in his dream at Mozhaysk.

"Life is everything. Life is God. Everything changes and moves, and that movement is God. And while there is life there is joy in the awareness of the divine. To love life is to love God. The hardest and most blessed thing of all is to love this life in one's sufferings, in innocent suffering."
"Karataev!" The name came into Pierre's mind.

And suddenly he saw vividly before him a long-forgotten, kindly old man who had given him geography lessons in Switzerland. "Wait a moment," said the old man, and showed Pierre a globe. This globe was alive—a vibrating sphere without fixed dimensions. Its entire surface consisted of drops pressed tightly together, and all these drops moved and shifted places, sometimes several of them merging into one, sometimes one dividing into many. Each drop tried to spread out and take up as much space as possible, but others striving to do the same compressed it, sometimes destroyed it, and sometimes merged with it.
"That is life," said the old teacher.
"How simple and clear it is," thought Pierre. "How is it I didn't know this before?"

"God is at the center, and each drop tries to expand so as to reflect Him to the greatest extent. And it grows, merges, disappears from the surface, sinks to the depths, and emerges again. There now, Karataev has spread out and disappeared. Do you understand, my child?" said the teacher.
"Do you understand, damn you?" shouted a voice, and Pierre woke up.

He lifted himself and sat up. A Frenchman who had just shoved a Russian soldier aside was squatting by the fire, roasting a piece of meat on a ramrod. His sleeves were rolled up and his sinewy, hairy, red hands with their short fingers deftly turned the ramrod. His dark, sullen face with its frowning brows was clearly visible by the glow of the coals.
"It's all the same to him," he muttered, quickly turning to a soldier standing behind him. "Scoundrel! Get away!"

And twisting the ramrod, he looked gloomily at Pierre, who turned away and gazed into the darkness. A prisoner, the Russian soldier the Frenchman had pushed away, was sitting near the fire patting something with his hand. Looking more closely, Pierre recognized the blue-gray dog sitting beside the soldier, wagging its tail.
"Ah, he's come?" said Pierre. "And Plat—" he began, but did not finish.

Suddenly and all at once a flood of memories surged through his mind—of the look Platon had given him sitting under the tree, of the shot heard from that spot, of the dog's howl, of the guilty faces of the two Frenchmen as they ran past him, of the lowered and smoking gun, and of Karataev's absence at this halt—and he was on the verge of realizing that Karataev had been killed. But at that very instant, he knew not why, a memory came to him of a summer evening he had spent with a beautiful Polish lady on the veranda of his house in Kiev. And without connecting the events of the day or drawing any conclusions from them, Pierre closed his eyes, seeing a vision of the countryside in summer mingled with memories of swimming and of the liquid, vibrating globe, and he sank into water so that it closed over his head.
Before sunrise he was awakened by shouts and rapid, heavy gunfire. French soldiers were running past him.
"The Cossacks!" one of them shouted, and a moment later a crowd of Russians surrounded Pierre.
For a long time he could not understand what was happening. All around him he heard his comrades sobbing with joy.
"Brothers! Dear fellows! Darlings!" old soldiers cried, weeping as they embraced Cossacks and hussars.

The hussars and Cossacks crowded around the prisoners. One offered them clothes, another boots, a third bread. Pierre sat among them sobbing and could not speak a word. He hugged the first soldier who came near him and kissed him, weeping.

Dolokhov stood at the gate of the ruined house, watching a stream of disarmed Frenchmen pass by. The French, agitated by everything that had happened, were talking loudly among themselves, but as they passed Dolokhov—who gently tapped his boots with his whip and watched them with cold, glassy eyes that promised nothing good—they fell silent. On the opposite side, Dolokhov's Cossack was counting the prisoners and marking each hundred with a chalk line on the gate.
"How many?" Dolokhov asked the Cossack.
"The second hundred," the Cossack replied.
"Move along, move along!" Dolokhov kept saying, having picked up this expression from the French, and when his eyes met those of the prisoners, they flashed with a cruel light.
("Move along, move along!")
Denisov, bareheaded and with a grim face, walked behind some Cossacks who were carrying the body of Petya Rostov to a grave that had been dug in the garden.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: After October twenty-eighth, when the frosts set in, the French flight took on an even more tragic character. Men froze to death or burned themselves alive at campfires, while carriages carrying people dressed in furs continued to roll past, hauling away the property that had been stolen by the Emperor, kings, and dukes. But the essential nature of the flight and disintegration of the French army continued as before.

From Moscow to Vyazma, the French army of seventy-three thousand men—not counting the Guards, who did nothing during the entire war but loot—was reduced to thirty-six thousand, though no more than five thousand had fallen in battle. From this starting point, the terms of the progression could be calculated mathematically. The French army melted away and perished at the same rate from Moscow to Vyazma, from Vyazma to Smolensk, from Smolensk to the Berezina, and from the Berezina to Vilna—regardless of the cold's intensity, the pursuit, the blocking of their path, or any other particular conditions. Beyond Vyazma, the French army stopped moving in three columns and huddled together into one mass, continuing that way to the end. Berthier wrote to his Emperor (and we know how far commanding officers allow themselves to stray from the truth when describing their army's condition), and this is what he said:

I consider it my duty to report to Your Majesty on the condition of the various corps I have had the opportunity to observe during different stages of the last two or three days' march. They are nearly disbanded. Scarcely a quarter of the soldiers remain with the standards of their regiments; the others wander off in every direction hoping to find food and escape discipline. In general, they all look to Smolensk as the place where they hope to recover. During the last few days many soldiers have been seen throwing away their cartridges and their weapons. In such circumstances, whatever your ultimate plans may be, Your Majesty's interests require that the army be reassembled at Smolensk and, first of all, freed from noncombatants—dismounted cavalry, unnecessary baggage, and artillery equipment no longer proportionate to our present forces. The soldiers, worn out by hunger and fatigue, need these supplies as well as a few days' rest. Many have died recently on the road or at camp. This state of affairs is growing worse every day and raises the fear that, unless prompt measures are taken, the troops will be beyond control in the event of a battle.
November 9: twenty miles from Smolensk.

After staggering into Smolensk—which had seemed to them a promised land—the French searched for food, killed one another, looted their own stores, and when everything had been plundered, fled farther.

They all went without knowing where or why they were going. Still less did that supposed genius, Napoleon, know it, for no one was issuing any orders to him. But he and those around him still clung to their old habits: writing commands, letters, reports, and orders of the day; calling one another "Sire," "Mon Cousin," "Prince of Eckmuhl," "King of Naples," and so on. But these orders and reports existed only on paper. Nothing in them was carried out, because nothing could be carried out. And though they addressed one another as Majesties, Highnesses, and Cousins, they all knew they were miserable wretches who had done great evil for which they now had to pay. And though they pretended to be concerned about the army, each was thinking only of himself and how to get away as quickly as possible.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: The movements of the Russian and French armies during the retreat from Moscow to the Niemen were like a game of Russian blindman's buff, where two blindfolded players stumble about and one occasionally rings a little bell to let the catcher know where he is. At first, the one with the bell rings it fearlessly, but when he gets cornered, he runs away as quietly as he can—and often, thinking he's escaping, runs straight into his opponent's arms.

At first, while still on the Kaluga road, Napoleon's armies made their presence known. But once they reached the Smolensk road, they ran with the bell's clapper held tight—and often, thinking they were escaping, ran right into the Russians.

Because of the speed of the French flight and the Russian pursuit, and the resulting exhaustion of the horses, the main means of determining the enemy's position—cavalry scouting—was unavailable. Besides, the frequent and rapid changes of position by both armies meant that even information received couldn't be delivered in time. If news came one day that the enemy had been at a certain position the day before, by the third day when anything could have been done, that army was already two days' march farther on and in a completely different spot.

One army fled and the other pursued. Beyond Smolensk there were several different roads available to the French, and one would have thought that during their four-day halt there they might have learned where the enemy was, devised a better plan, and tried something new. But after a four-day rest, the mob—with no strategy or plans—simply started running again along the beaten track, neither turning right nor left but taking the old, worst road through Krasnoe and Orsha.

Expecting the enemy from behind rather than ahead, the French spread out over a distance of twenty-four hours' march. At the very front fled the Emperor, then the kings, then the dukes. The Russian army, expecting Napoleon to take the road to the right beyond the Dnieper—which was the only sensible thing for him to do—turned right themselves and came out on the highway at Krasnoe. And here, as in a game of blindman's buff, the French ran into the Russian vanguard. Spotting their enemy unexpectedly, the French fell into confusion and froze with sudden fright, then resumed their flight, abandoning comrades who were farther behind. For three days, separate portions of the French army—first Murat's (the Viceroy's), then Davout's, then Ney's—ran the gauntlet of the Russian army. They abandoned one another, abandoned all their heavy baggage, artillery, and half their men, fleeing past the Russians at night by making wide detours to the right.

Ney, who came last, had been busy blowing up the walls of Smolensk, which were in nobody's way—because despite their desperate plight, or perhaps because of it, the French wanted to punish the floor they had stumbled on. Ney, who had started with a corps of ten thousand men, reached Napoleon at Orsha with only a thousand left, having abandoned all the rest along with his cannon, and having crossed the Dnieper by stealth at night at a wooded spot.

From Orsha they fled farther along the road to Vilna, still playing blindman's buff with the pursuing army. At the Berezina they fell into disarray again—many drowned, many surrendered—but those who got across the river fled on. Their supreme commander put on a fur coat and, climbing into a sleigh, galloped off alone, abandoning his companions. The others who could manage it drove away too, leaving those who could not to surrender or die.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: This campaign was essentially a flight during which the French did everything possible to destroy themselves. From the moment they turned onto the Kaluga road until the day their leader abandoned the army, not one movement of the mob made any sense. One might have expected that historians—who attribute the actions of the masses to the will of one man—would find it impossible to fit the story of this retreat into their framework. But no! Mountains of books have been written about this campaign, and everywhere we find descriptions of Napoleon's strategic arrangements, his maneuvers, and the deep plans that supposedly guided the army, as well as the military genius of his marshals.

The retreat from Malo-Yaroslavets, when Napoleon had a clear road into a well-supplied region and a parallel route that Kutuzov later followed—this needless retreat along a devastated road—is explained to us as the result of deep strategic thinking. Similarly profound reasoning is offered for his retreat from Smolensk to Orsha. Then his heroism at Krasnoe is described, where he supposedly stood ready to accept battle, took personal command, walked about with a birch stick, and said:
"I have played the Emperor long enough; it is time to play the general"—but then immediately ran away again, abandoning the scattered remnants of the army he left behind.
"I have played the Emperor long enough; it is time to play the general."

Then we are told of the greatness of soul of the marshals, especially of Ney—a greatness of soul that consisted in sneaking through the forest by night, crossing the Dnieper, and escaping to Orsha while abandoning his standards, artillery, and nine-tenths of his men.

And finally, the departure of the great Emperor from his heroic army is presented to us by historians as something noble and characteristic of genius. Even that final act of running away—which in plain language is the lowest depth of cowardice that every child is taught to be ashamed of—even that act finds justification in the historians' vocabulary.

When it becomes impossible to stretch the elastic threads of historical reasoning any further, when actions clearly violate everything humanity calls right or even just, historians produce their saving concept of "greatness." "Greatness," it seems, makes the standards of right and wrong irrelevant. For the "great" man, nothing is wrong; there is no crime for which a "great" man can be blamed.

"It is grand!" say the historians, and there is no longer any good or evil, only "grand" and "not grand." Grand is good, not grand is bad. Grand is the defining trait, in their view, of certain special creatures called "heroes." And Napoleon, escaping home in a warm fur coat while leaving his comrades—men he himself had brought there—to perish, feels that this is grand, and his conscience is at peace.
("It is grand.")
("That it is grand.")

"From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step," he said. And the whole world has been repeating for fifty years: "Sublime! Grand! Napoleon the Great!" From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step.
("From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step.")
And it occurs to no one that to accept a kind of greatness that exists outside the standards of right and wrong is simply to admit one's own insignificance and boundless moral smallness.
For us, with the standard of good and evil given us by Christ, no human actions are beyond judgment. And there is no greatness where simplicity, goodness, and truth are absent.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: What Russian, reading the account of the final phase of the 1812 campaign, hasn't felt an uncomfortable sense of regret, dissatisfaction, and confusion? Who hasn't asked: how is it that the French weren't all captured or destroyed when three Russian armies had them surrounded with superior numbers, when the disorganized French were starving and freezing and surrendering in droves, and when—as historians tell us—the Russian aim was to stop the French, cut them off, and capture every last one of them?

How was it that the Russian army, which when outnumbered by the French had given battle at Borodino, failed to achieve its purpose when it had surrounded the French on three sides and its goal was to capture them? Can the French really be so enormously superior to us that when we had them surrounded with greater forces, we couldn't beat them? How could that happen?
History (or what passes for it) answers these questions by saying it happened because Kutuzov and Tormasov and Chichagov, and this man and that man, failed to carry out certain maneuvers...

But why didn't they carry out those maneuvers? And why, if they were at fault for not following a prearranged plan, weren't they tried and punished? But even if we admit that Kutuzov, Chichagov, and others were the cause of the Russian failures, it is still incomprehensible why, given the Russian army's positions at Krasnoe and the Berezina (where we had superior forces in both cases), Napoleon's army with its marshals, kings, and Emperor wasn't captured—if that was indeed what the Russians were aiming for.
The explanation offered by Russian military historians—that Kutuzov prevented an attack—is groundless, because we know he could not restrain his troops from attacking at Vyazma and Tarutino.

Why was the Russian army—which with inferior forces had held its own against the enemy at full strength at Borodino—unable to defeat the disorganized crowds of the French at Krasnoe and the Berezina, when it had numerical superiority?

If the aim of the Russians was to cut off and capture Napoleon and his marshals—and that aim was not merely frustrated but all attempts to achieve it were most shamefully foiled—then this last period of the campaign is quite rightly considered by the French to be a series of victories, and quite wrongly considered victorious by Russian historians.

Russian military historians, insofar as they submit to logic, must accept this conclusion, and despite all their lyrical praise of valor and devotion, must reluctantly admit that the French retreat from Moscow was a series of victories for Napoleon and defeats for Kutuzov.

But setting national pride entirely aside, one feels that such a conclusion involves a contradiction: the series of French "victories" brought the French complete destruction, while the series of Russian "defeats" led to the total annihilation of the enemy and the liberation of the country.

The source of this contradiction lies in the fact that historians, studying the letters of sovereigns and generals, memoirs, reports, and plans, have attributed to this final period of the 1812 war an aim that never existed—namely, the plan to cut off and capture Napoleon along with his marshals and army.
Such an aim never existed and could never have existed, because it would have been senseless and its achievement utterly impossible.

It would have been senseless, first, because Napoleon's disorganized army was already fleeing Russia at maximum speed—which was exactly what every Russian wanted. So what was the point of carrying out various operations against Frenchmen who were running away as fast as they possibly could?
Second, it would have been senseless to try to block the path of men whose every ounce of energy was directed at escape.

Third, it would have been senseless to sacrifice Russian troops in order to destroy a French army that, without any outside interference, was already destroying itself so rapidly that it couldn't carry across the border more than a hundredth part of its original strength—which is exactly what happened by December.

Fourth, it would have been senseless to want to capture the Emperor, kings, and dukes—whose capture would have been in the highest degree embarrassing for the Russians, as the most skillful diplomats of the time, including Joseph de Maistre and others, recognized. Even more senseless would have been the idea of capturing whole French army corps when the Russian army itself had shrunk by half before reaching Krasnoe, and a full division would have been needed just to guard the prisoners, while Russian soldiers weren't always getting full rations and the prisoners already taken were dying of hunger.

All the elaborate plans for cutting off and capturing Napoleon and his army were like the plan of a gardener who, when chasing a cow out of his garden after it trampled his flower beds, runs to the gate and hits the cow on the head. The only excuse for such a gardener would be that he was very angry. But not even that could be said for those who drew up this plan, since they weren't the ones whose flowers had been trampled.
But besides the fact that cutting off Napoleon and his army would have been senseless, it was also impossible.

It was impossible, first, because—as experience shows that a column's three-mile march on a battlefield never goes according to plan—the probability of Chichagov, Kutuzov, and Wittgenstein all arriving at the same place at the appointed time was so remote as to be effectively zero—as Kutuzov himself recognized when he received the plan and remarked that operations planned over great distances never produce the intended results.
Second, it was impossible because to halt the momentum with which Napoleon's army was retreating would have required forces incomparably greater than those the Russians possessed.

Third, it was impossible because the military term "to cut off" has no real meaning. You can cut off a slice of bread, but not an army. To cut off an army—to block its road—is quite impossible, because there is always plenty of room to get around, and there is the night when nothing can be seen, as the military theorists could have learned from the examples of Krasnoe and the Berezina. Prisoners can only be taken if they agree to be taken, just as you can only catch a swallow if it lands on your hand. Men can only be captured if they surrender according to the rules of strategy and tactics, as the Germans did. But the French saw no reason to comply, since death by starvation and cold awaited them equally whether they fled or surrendered.

Fourth and most importantly, it was impossible because never since the beginning of the world had a war been fought under such conditions as those of 1812, and the Russian army, in pursuing the French, had already strained itself to the breaking point and could not have done more without destroying itself.

During the movement of the Russian army from Tarutino to Krasnoe, it lost fifty thousand sick and stragglers—a number equal to the population of a large provincial city. Half the men fell out of the army without a single battle.

And it is about this period—when the army had no boots or sheepskin coats, was short of provisions and without vodka, camping in the snow at fifteen below zero for months on end, with only seven or eight hours of daylight, when men were taken into a realm of death where discipline breaks down, not just for a few hours as in battle but for months, where every moment they fought against hunger and cold, and half the army perished in a single month—it is about this period that historians tell us how Miloradovich should have flanked here and Tormasov should have marched there and Chichagov should have waded through knee-deep snow to somewhere else, and how so-and-so "routed" and "cut off" the French, and so on.

The Russians—half of whom died—did everything that could and should have been done to achieve a goal worthy of the nation. They are not to blame because other Russians, sitting in warm rooms, proposed that they should do the impossible.

All the strange contradiction between the facts and the historical accounts arises only because historians have written the history of the fine words and feelings of various generals, rather than the history of the events themselves.

To them, the speeches of Miloradovich seem fascinating, as do their own theories and the medals this or that general received. But the question of those fifty thousand men who were left in hospitals and graves doesn't even interest them, because it falls outside the scope of their investigation.

Yet one need only set aside the study of reports and staff plans and look at the movements of those hundreds of thousands of men who took a direct part in the events, and all the questions that seemed insoluble are resolved easily and simply.
The aim of cutting off Napoleon and his army never existed except in the imaginations of a dozen people. It could not exist because it was senseless and unachievable.

The people had one single aim: to free their land from invasion. That aim was achieved, first of all, on its own, as the French ran away, so it was only necessary not to stop their flight. Second, it was achieved by guerrilla warfare, which was destroying the French. And third, it was achieved by the fact that a large Russian army was following the French, ready to use force if their retreat should stop.
The Russian army had to act like a whip driving a running animal. And the experienced driver knew it was better to hold the whip raised as a threat than to strike the running animal on the head.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: When we see a dying animal, we feel a sense of horror: something made of the same substance as ourselves is perishing before our eyes. But when it is a beloved and intimate person who is dying, besides this horror at the extinguishing of life, there is a tearing apart, a spiritual wound that, like a physical wound, is sometimes fatal and sometimes heals, but always aches and flinches at any rough, irritating touch.

After Prince Andrew's death, Natasha and Princess Mary both felt this. Crushed in spirit and closing their eyes before the menacing cloud of death that hung over them, they dared not look life in the face. They carefully guarded their raw wounds from any harsh or painful contact. Everything—a carriage rattling quickly past in the street, a summons to dinner, the maid's question about what dress to prepare, or worst of all, any word of insincere or halfhearted sympathy—felt like an insult, painfully irritating the wound, interrupting the necessary silence in which they both tried to listen to the solemn and terrible chorus still echoing in their minds, and preventing them from gazing into those mysterious, infinite vistas that had for an instant opened before them.
Only when they were alone together were they free from such assaults. They spoke little even to each other, and when they did, it was about trivial things.

Both avoided any mention of the future. To acknowledge the possibility of a future seemed to them an insult to his memory. Even more carefully did they avoid anything connected with him who was dead. It seemed that what they had lived through and experienced could not be expressed in words, and that any reference to the details of his life would violate the majesty and sacredness of the mystery that had been accomplished before their eyes.

The constant restraint from speaking, the careful avoidance of everything that might lead to the forbidden subject—this halting on all sides at the boundary of what they could not mention—brought before their minds with even greater purity and clarity what they were both feeling.

But pure and complete grief is as impossible as pure and complete joy. Princess Mary, in her role as the sole and independent guardian of her own fate and of her nephew's upbringing, was the first to be called back to life from that realm of sorrow in which she had lived for the first two weeks. She received letters from relatives that required replies; the room where little Nicholas had been placed was damp and he began to cough; Alpatych came to Yaroslavl with reports on their affairs and suggestions that they return to Moscow, to the house on Vozdvizhenka Street, which had survived intact and needed only minor repairs. Life would not stand still, and it was necessary to go on living. Hard as it was for Princess Mary to emerge from her secluded world of contemplation, and sorry and almost ashamed as she felt to leave Natasha alone, the demands of daily life required her attention and she involuntarily yielded to them. She went through the accounts with Alpatych, consulted with Dessalles about her nephew, and gave orders and made preparations for the journey to Moscow.
Natasha was left alone and, from the time Princess Mary began preparing for departure, withdrew from her too.

Princess Mary asked the countess to let Natasha travel with her to Moscow, and both parents gladly accepted the offer, seeing their daughter losing strength every day and believing that a change of scene and Moscow doctors would do her good.
"I'm not going anywhere," Natasha replied when this was proposed. "Please just leave me alone!" And she ran out of the room, barely holding back tears of irritation and vexation rather than sorrow.

After feeling herself abandoned by Princess Mary and left alone in her grief, Natasha spent most of her time in her room by herself, sitting huddled up with her feet tucked under her in the corner of the sofa, tearing and twisting something with her slender, nervous fingers, staring intently at whatever her eyes happened to fall on. This solitude exhausted and tormented her, but she desperately needed it. The moment anyone came in, she would jump up quickly, change her position and expression, and pick up a book or some sewing, clearly waiting impatiently for the intruder to leave.
She felt as though at any moment she might break through to that thing on which—with a terrible questioning too great for her strength—her whole being was fixed.

One day toward the end of December, Natasha, pale and thin, dressed in a black woolen gown with her braided hair carelessly twisted into a knot, sat crouched with her feet tucked under her in the corner of the sofa, nervously crumpling and smoothing the end of her sash while staring at a corner of the door.

She was gazing in the direction he had gone—to the other side of life. And that other side of life, which she had never thought about before and which had always seemed so distant and improbable, was now nearer and more familiar and more real to her than this side, where everything was either emptiness and desolation or suffering and humiliation.
She was gazing toward where she knew him to be; but she could not picture him other than as he had been here. She saw him again as he had been at Mytishchi, at Troitsa, and at Yaroslavl.
She saw his face, heard his voice, repeated his words and her own, and sometimes invented other words they might have said.

There he is, lying back in an armchair in his velvet cloak, leaning his head on his thin, pale hand. His chest is terribly hollow and his shoulders raised. His lips are pressed firmly together, his eyes glitter, and a wrinkle comes and goes on his pale forehead. One of his legs twitches just perceptibly, but rapidly. Natasha knows he is struggling with terrible pain. "What is that pain like? Why does he have it? What does he feel? How does it hurt him?" she thought. He noticed her watching him, raised his eyes, and began to speak seriously:

"One thing would be terrible," he said, "to bind oneself forever to a suffering man. It would be continual torture." And he looked at her searchingly. Natasha, as usual, answered before she had time to think. She said: "This can't go on—it won't. You will get well—completely well."

She now replayed that scene from the beginning and relived what she had felt then. She recalled his long, sad, and severe look at those words and understood the meaning of the reproach and despair in that prolonged gaze.

"I agreed," Natasha now said to herself, "that it would be terrible if he always continued to suffer. I said it then only because it would have been terrible for him. But he understood it differently. He thought it would be terrible for me. He still wanted to live then, and he feared death. And I said it so clumsily and stupidly! I didn't say what I meant. I thought something entirely different. If I had said what I was actually thinking, I would have said: even if he had to go on dying, dying continually before my eyes, I would have been happy compared to what I am now. Now there is nothing... nobody. Did he know that? No. He didn't know and never will. And now it can never, never be put right." And now he seemed to be saying the same words to her again, but this time, in her imagination, Natasha gave him a different answer. She stopped him and said: "Terrible for you, but not for me! You know that there is nothing in life for me but you, and to suffer with you is the greatest happiness I could have." And he took her hand and pressed it as he had pressed it on that terrible evening four days before his death. And in her imagination she said other tender and loving words that she might have said then but only spoke now: "I love you!... You!... I love, love..." she whispered, clenching her hands together and gritting her teeth with desperate effort...

She was overcome by sweet sorrow and tears were already rising in her eyes; then suddenly she asked herself to whom she was saying this. Again everything was shrouded in hard, dry confusion, and again with a strained frown she peered toward the world where he was. And now—now it seemed she was about to penetrate the mystery... But at the instant when the incomprehensible seemed about to reveal itself, a loud rattle of the door handle struck painfully on her ears. Dunyasha, her maid, burst into the room quickly and abruptly, with a frightened look and no concern for her mistress.
"Come to your father at once, please!" she said with a strange, agitated look. "A misfortune... about Pyotr Ilyich... a letter," she finished with a sob.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Besides a feeling of distance from everyone, Natasha felt a particular estrangement from the members of her own family. All of them—her father, mother, and Sonya—were so near, so familiar, so ordinary, that all their words and feelings seemed an insult to the world in which she had been living lately. She felt not merely indifferent toward them but actively hostile. She heard Dunyasha's words about Pyotr Ilyich and a misfortune but did not take them in.
"What misfortune? What misfortune can happen to them? They just live their old, quiet, ordinary life," thought Natasha.

As she entered the ballroom, her father was hurrying out of her mother's room. His face was crumpled and wet with tears. He had obviously rushed out to give vent to the sobs that were choking him. When he saw Natasha, he waved his arms in despair and burst into convulsive, agonized sobs that distorted his soft, round face.
"Pe... Petya... Go, go, she... is calling..." And weeping like a child and shuffling quickly on his feeble legs to a chair, he almost collapsed into it, covering his face with his hands.

Something like an electric shock seemed to run through Natasha's entire being. A terrible anguish struck her heart; she felt a dreadful tearing inside her, as if she were dying. But the pain was immediately followed by a sense of release from the oppressive weight that had prevented her from taking part in life. The sight of her father, the terribly wild cries of her mother that she heard through the door, made her instantly forget herself and her own grief.

She ran to her father, but he weakly waved his arm, pointing toward her mother's door. Princess Mary, pale and with trembling chin, came out of that room and, taking Natasha by the arm, said something to her. Natasha neither saw nor heard her. She went in with rapid steps, pausing for an instant at the door as if struggling with herself, then ran to her mother.
The countess was lying in an armchair in a strange and awkward position, stretching out and beating her head against the wall. Sonya and the maids were holding her arms.

"Natasha! Natasha!..." cried the countess. "It's not true... it's not true... He's lying... Natasha!" she shrieked, pushing everyone away. "Go away, all of you! It's not true! Killed!... Ha, ha, ha!... It's not true!"
Natasha put one knee on the armchair, bent over her mother, and with unexpected strength lifted her, turned her face toward herself, and held her tight.
"Mama!... Darling!... I'm here, my dearest Mama," she kept whispering without pause.
She didn't let go of her mother but struggled tenderly with her, called for a pillow and hot water, unfastened and tore open her mother's dress.
"My dearest darling... Mama, my precious!..." she whispered incessantly, kissing her head, her hands, her face, feeling her own unstoppable, streaming tears tickle her nose and cheeks.

The countess pressed her daughter's hand, closed her eyes, and became still for a moment. Suddenly she sat up with unaccustomed swiftness, glanced around vacantly, and seeing Natasha began to press her daughter's head with all her strength. Then she turned toward her daughter's face, which was wincing with pain, and gazed at it for a long time.
"Natasha, you love me?" she said in a soft, trusting whisper. "Natasha, you wouldn't deceive me? You'll tell me the whole truth?"
Natasha looked at her with eyes full of tears, and in her look there was nothing but love and a plea for forgiveness.
"My darling Mama!" she repeated, straining every power of her love to find some way of taking upon herself the crushing weight of grief that was destroying her mother.

And again, in a futile struggle with reality, her mother—refusing to believe she could go on living when her beloved boy had been killed in the prime of life—escaped from reality into a world of delirium.

Natasha did not remember how that day passed, nor the night, nor the following day and night. She did not sleep and did not leave her mother's side. Her tireless, patient love seemed to completely surround the countess at every moment—not explaining or consoling, but simply calling her back to life.

During the third night, the countess was quiet for a few minutes, and Natasha rested her head on the arm of her chair and closed her eyes, but opened them again when she heard the bedstead creak. The countess was sitting up in bed and speaking softly.
"How glad I am you've come. You're tired. Won't you have some tea?" Natasha went up to her. "You've gotten prettier and more grown-up," continued the countess, taking her daughter's hand.
"Mama! What are you saying..."
"Natasha, he is no more, no more!"
And embracing her daughter, the countess began to weep for the first time.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Princess Mary postponed her departure. Sonya and the count tried to take Natasha's place but couldn't. They saw that she alone was able to keep her mother from spiraling into unreasoning despair. For three weeks Natasha stayed constantly at her mother's side, sleeping on a lounge chair in her room, making her eat and drink, and talking to her endlessly, because the mere sound of her tender, soothing voice calmed the countess.

The mother's wounded spirit could not heal. Petya's death had torn half her life away. When the news of his death arrived, she had been a fresh and vigorous woman of fifty, but a month later she emerged from her room a listless old woman with no interest in life. But the same blow that nearly killed the countess—this second blow—restored Natasha to life.

A spiritual wound caused by the rending of the spiritual body is like a physical wound, and strange as it may seem, just as a deep wound may heal and its edges join, both physical and spiritual wounds can only truly heal from within, through the vital force of life itself.

Natasha's wound healed in that way. She had believed her life was over, but her love for her mother unexpectedly showed her that the essence of life—love—was still alive within her. Love awoke, and so did life.

Prince Andrew's last days had drawn Princess Mary and Natasha together; this new sorrow brought them closer still. Princess Mary postponed her departure and for three weeks looked after Natasha as though she were a sick child. The weeks spent in her mother's bedroom had drained Natasha's physical strength.

One afternoon, noticing Natasha shivering with fever, Princess Mary took her to her own room and made her lie down on the bed. Natasha lay down, but when Princess Mary drew the blinds and turned to leave, she called her back.
"I don't want to sleep, Mary. Sit with me a little."
"You're tired—try to sleep."
"No, no. Why did you bring me away? She'll be asking for me."
"She's much better. She spoke so well today," said Princess Mary.
Natasha lay on the bed and in the semidarkness studied Princess Mary's face.

"Is she like him?" thought Natasha. "Yes, like him and yet not like him. But she is entirely her own person—strange, new, and unknown. And she loves me. What is in her heart? Everything good. But how? What does she think about? What does she think about me? Yes, she is wonderful!"
"Mary," she said timidly, drawing Princess Mary's hand toward her, "Mary, you mustn't think I'm wicked. You don't, do you? Mary darling, how I love you! Let's be the very best of friends."
And Natasha, embracing her, began kissing her face and hands, making Princess Mary feel shy but happy at this outpouring of feeling.

From that day a tender and passionate friendship—the kind that exists only between women—was established between Princess Mary and Natasha. They were constantly kissing and saying tender things to each other and spent most of their time together. When one left the room, the other grew restless and hurried to rejoin her. Together they felt more in harmony with each other than either felt when alone. A feeling stronger than friendship arose between them—an intense sense that life was only possible in each other's presence.

Sometimes they were silent for hours; other times, after they were already in bed, they would begin talking and continue until morning. They spoke mostly of the distant past. Princess Mary told of her childhood, her mother, her father, and her dreams; and Natasha, who had previously turned away from that life of devotion, submission, and the poetry of Christian self-sacrifice with passive incomprehension, now—feeling bound to Princess Mary by love—learned to appreciate her past too and to understand a side of life that had been entirely foreign to her. She did not think of applying submission and self-denial to her own life, for she was used to seeking other kinds of joy; but she understood and loved those previously incomprehensible virtues in someone else. For Princess Mary, listening to Natasha's stories of childhood and youth, an equally new and previously unknown side of life opened up: a belief in life and its pleasures.

Just as before, they never spoke of him, so as not to lower (as they felt) their exalted feelings by putting them into words. But this silence gradually—without their realizing it—caused them to begin forgetting him.

Natasha had grown thin and pale and physically so weak that everyone discussed her health, which pleased her. But sometimes she was suddenly overcome by fear—not only of death, but of sickness, weakness, and the loss of her looks—and she would involuntarily examine her bare arm, surprised at its thinness, and in the morning notice her drawn and, as it seemed to her, pitiful face in the mirror. It seemed to her that this was how things had to be, and yet it was terribly sad.

One day she ran quickly upstairs and found herself out of breath. Without thinking, she immediately invented a reason to go back down, and then, testing her strength, ran upstairs again, carefully noting the result.

Another time, when she called Dunyasha and her voice trembled, she called again—though she could hear Dunyasha coming—this time using the deep chest tones she used to sing with, and listened to herself attentively.

She did not know, and would not have believed, that beneath the layer of mud that seemed to her impenetrable, covering her soul, delicate young shoots of grass were already sprouting. They would take root and so cover with their living green the grief that weighed her down that it would soon no longer be seen or noticed. The wound had begun to heal from within.
At the end of January, Princess Mary left for Moscow, and the count insisted that Natasha go with her to see the doctors.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: After the encounter at Vyazma, where Kutuzov had been unable to hold back his troops in their eagerness to overwhelm and cut off the enemy, the further movement of the fleeing French and the Russians who pursued them continued as far as Krasnoe without a battle. The flight was so rapid that the Russian army pursuing the French could not keep up; cavalry and artillery horses broke down, and the information about French movements was never reliable.
The men in the Russian army were so worn out by this continuous marching at twenty-seven miles a day that they simply could not go any faster.

To understand the degree of exhaustion of the Russian army, you only need to grasp the meaning of one fact: while losing no more than five thousand killed and wounded after Tarutino, and fewer than a hundred prisoners, the Russian army that had left Tarutino a hundred thousand strong reached Krasnoe with only fifty thousand.

The rapid Russian pursuit was just as destructive to our army as the French flight was to theirs. The only difference was that the Russian army moved voluntarily, without facing the total annihilation that threatened the French, and that sick Frenchmen were left behind in enemy hands while sick Russians were left among their own people. The main cause of Napoleon's army wasting away was the speed of its movement, and convincing proof of this is the corresponding decline of the Russian army.

Kutuzov, as far as it was in his power—instead of trying to check the French movement as was desired in Petersburg and by the Russian generals—directed all his efforts, as he had at Tarutino and Vyazma, toward speeding it along while easing the burden on his own troops.

But besides this, since the army's exhaustion and enormous reduction from the speed of the advance had become obvious, another reason presented itself for slowing down: the aim of the Russian army was to pursue the French. The French route was unknown, so the closer the Russians followed on their heels, the greater the distance they had to cover. Only by following at some distance could they cut across the French zigzag path. All the clever maneuvers suggested by the generals meant additional marches that would further lengthen the army's journey, whereas the only sensible objective was to shorten those marches. To this end, Kutuzov directed his efforts throughout the entire campaign from Moscow to Vilna—not casually or intermittently, but so consistently that he never once deviated from it.

Kutuzov felt and knew—not through reasoning or military science, but with every fiber of his Russian being—what every Russian soldier felt: that the French were beaten, that the enemy was fleeing and must be driven out; but at the same time he, like his soldiers, understood all the hardships of this unprecedented march.

But the generals—especially the foreign ones in the Russian army—who wanted to distinguish themselves and astonish someone, and for some reason capture a king or a duke, thought that now—when any battle would be horrible and senseless—was the perfect time to fight and conquer somebody. Kutuzov merely shrugged his shoulders when one after another they presented him with maneuver plans for soldiers who were ill-shod, barely clothed, and half-starved—soldiers who within a month, without fighting a single battle, had dwindled to half their original number and who, at best, still had farther to march than they already had before reaching the border.
This desire to distinguish themselves, to maneuver, to overthrow and cut off showed itself most clearly whenever the Russians stumbled on the French army.

So it was at Krasnoe, where they expected to find one of the three French columns but instead ran into Napoleon himself with sixteen thousand men. Despite all of Kutuzov's efforts to avoid this ruinous encounter and preserve his troops, the slaughter of the broken French mob by exhausted Russians continued at Krasnoe for three days.

Toll wrote out a battle plan: "The first column will march to such and such a place," and so on. And as usual, nothing happened according to plan. Prince Eugene of Wurttemberg fired from a hilltop at the French crowds running past and demanded reinforcements that never arrived. The French, avoiding the Russians, scattered and hid in the forest by night, making their way around as best they could, and continued their flight.

Miloradovich, who said he didn't want to know anything about commissary affairs and could never be found when needed—this self-styled knight without fear and without reproach who loved to parley with the French—sent envoys demanding their surrender, wasted time, and didn't do what he was ordered to do.
(Knight without fear and without reproach.)
"I give you that column, lads," he said, riding up to his troops and pointing out the French to the cavalry.

And the cavalry, with spurs and sabers urging on horses that could barely move, trotted with great effort to the column "presented" to them—that is, to a crowd of Frenchmen frozen stiff, frostbitten, and starving—and the column that had been "presented" threw down its arms and surrendered, as it had long been desperate to do.

At Krasnoe they took twenty-six thousand prisoners, several hundred cannon, and a stick called a "marshal's staff," and they argued about who had distinguished himself and congratulated themselves on their achievement—while deeply regretting that they hadn't captured Napoleon, or at least a marshal or some kind of hero, and blaming one another and especially Kutuzov for having failed to do so.

These men, carried away by their passions, were nothing more than blind tools of the most tragic law of necessity, yet they considered themselves heroes and imagined they were accomplishing a most noble and honorable deed. They blamed Kutuzov, saying that from the very start of the campaign he had prevented them from defeating Napoleon, that he only cared about his own comfort, that he had stopped the advance at Krasnoe because he lost his nerve on learning Napoleon was there, and that he probably had a secret agreement with Napoleon and had been bribed, and so on and so on.

Not only his contemporaries, carried away by their passions, but posterity and history itself have proclaimed Napoleon as "grand," while Kutuzov is described by foreigners as a crafty, dissolute, weak old courtier, and by Russians as something vague and indefinite—a sort of puppet useful only because he had a Russian name.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: In 1812 and 1813, Kutuzov was openly accused of blundering. The Emperor was dissatisfied with him. And in a history recently written by official command, it is stated that Kutuzov was a cunning court liar, terrified of Napoleon's name, and that by his blunders at Krasnoe and the Berezina he deprived the Russian army of the glory of a complete victory over the French.
(History of the Year 1812. The character of Kutuzov and reflections on the unsatisfactory results of the battles at Krasnoe, by Bogdanovich.)

Such is the fate—not of great men ("grands hommes") as the Russian mind does not acknowledge them—but of those rare and always solitary individuals who, perceiving the will of Providence, submit their personal will to it. The hatred and contempt of the crowd is the punishment for those who discern a higher law.

For Russian historians, strange and terrible to say, Napoleon—that most insignificant tool of history, who never anywhere, even in exile, showed human dignity—Napoleon is the object of admiration and enthusiasm; he is "grand." But Kutuzov—the man who from beginning to end of his activity in 1812 never once wavered by word or deed from Borodino to Vilna, who presented an example of self-sacrifice unmatched in history and a living awareness of the future significance of what was happening—Kutuzov seems to them something vague and pathetic, and when they speak of him and of the year 1812, they always seem a little embarrassed.

And yet it is hard to imagine a historical figure whose actions were so unwaveringly directed toward a single aim. And it would be hard to imagine any aim more worthy or more in harmony with the will of the entire people. Still harder would it be to find another instance in history where the aim of a historical figure was so completely accomplished as the aim to which all of Kutuzov's efforts were directed in 1812.

Kutuzov never spoke of "forty centuries looking down from the Pyramids," of the sacrifices he was making for the fatherland, or of what he intended or had accomplished. In general he said nothing about himself, struck no poses, always appeared to be the simplest and most ordinary of men, and said the simplest and most ordinary things. He wrote letters to his daughters and to Madame de Stael, read novels, enjoyed the company of pretty women, joked with generals, officers, and soldiers, and never contradicted anyone who tried to prove anything to him. When Count Rostopchin galloped up to Kutuzov at the Yauza bridge and personally accused him of causing Moscow's destruction, saying: "How could you promise not to abandon Moscow without a battle?" Kutuzov replied: "And I shall not abandon Moscow without a battle"—though Moscow was already abandoned. When Arakcheev, coming from the Emperor, told him that Ermolov ought to be appointed chief of artillery, Kutuzov replied: "Yes, I was just saying so myself"—though a moment before he had said the exact opposite. What did it matter to him—the only man amid a senseless crowd who understood the tremendous significance of what was happening—whether Rostopchin blamed him or himself for Moscow's destruction? Still less could it matter who was named chief of artillery.

Not only in these cases but constantly, that old man—who through long experience had reached the conviction that thoughts and the words expressing them are not what move people—used perfectly meaningless words that simply came into his head.

But that man, so careless with his words, never once during his entire period of activity uttered a single word inconsistent with the one aim toward which he worked throughout the whole war. Obviously, despite himself, in the most diverse circumstances, he repeatedly expressed his true convictions with the bitter certainty that he would not be understood. Beginning with the battle of Borodino, from which point his disagreement with those around him began, he alone said that Borodino was a victory, and he repeated this both verbally and in his dispatches and reports until his death. He alone said that the loss of Moscow did not mean the loss of Russia. In reply to Lauriston's proposal of peace, he said: There can be no peace, for such is the people's will. He alone, during the French retreat, said that all their maneuvers were useless, that everything was working out better than they could wish without them, that the enemy must be offered a "golden bridge," that the battles at Tarutino, Vyazma, and Krasnoe were unnecessary, that they needed to keep enough strength to reach the border, and that he would not sacrifice a single Russian for ten Frenchmen.

And this courtier, as he is portrayed—who lies to Arakcheev to please the Emperor—he alone, at the cost of the Emperor's displeasure, said in Vilna that to carry the war beyond the frontier was useless and harmful.

Nor do his words alone prove that he understood the meaning of events. His actions—without the slightest deviation—were all directed toward one and the same threefold end: (1) to concentrate all his strength for the conflict with the French, (2) to defeat them, and (3) to drive them out of Russia, while minimizing as far as possible the suffering of his people and his army.

This supposed procrastinator Kutuzov, whose motto was "Patience and Time," this supposed enemy of decisive action, gave battle at Borodino and invested the preparations for it with unparalleled solemnity. This Kutuzov, who before the battle of Austerlitz said it would be lost, he alone, contradicting everyone else, declared to his dying day that Borodino was a victory—despite the assurance of generals that the battle was lost and the unprecedented fact that an army had to retreat after winning. He alone, throughout the entire retreat, insisted that further battles were useless, that a new war should not be begun, and that the Russian frontier should not be crossed.

It is easy now to understand the significance of these events—if only we refrain from attributing to the actions of the masses aims that existed only in the heads of a dozen people—for the events and their results now lie before us.
But how did that old man, alone, in opposition to the general opinion, so accurately perceive the importance of the people's view of events that in all his actions he was never once untrue to it?
The source of that extraordinary power of insight lay in the national feeling that he possessed in full purity and strength.

Only the recognition that he possessed this feeling caused the people, in such a strange manner and contrary to the Tsar's wish, to choose him—an old man in disfavor—as their representative in the national war. And only that feeling placed him on the highest pedestal from which he, the commander in chief, devoted all his powers not to slaying and destroying men but to saving them and showing them pity.
That simple, modest, and therefore truly great figure could not be forced into the false mold of a European hero—the supposed ruler of men—that history has fabricated.
To a servant, no man can be great, because a servant has his own idea of what greatness means.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: November fifth was the first day of what is called the battle of Krasnoe. Toward evening—after much arguing and many mistakes by generals who went to the wrong places, after adjutants had been sent racing about with counter-orders—when it became clear that the enemy was in full flight everywhere and that there could be no battle, Kutuzov left Krasnoe and went to Dobroe, where his headquarters had been transferred that day.

The day was clear and frosty. Kutuzov rode to Dobroe on his plump little white horse, followed by an enormous retinue of discontented generals who whispered among themselves behind his back. All along the road, groups of French prisoners captured that day—there were seven thousand of them—crowded around campfires to warm themselves. Near Dobroe, an immense crowd of tattered prisoners, buzzing with talk and wrapped and bandaged in whatever they could find, stood in the road beside a long row of unharnessed French guns. At the approach of the commander in chief, the buzz of talk ceased and all eyes turned to Kutuzov, who wore a white cap with a red band and a padded overcoat that bulged on his round shoulders as he moved slowly along the road on his white horse. One of the generals was reporting where the guns and prisoners had been captured.

Kutuzov seemed distracted and wasn't listening. He squinted with a dissatisfied expression as he studied the prisoners, who presented an especially wretched sight. Most of them were disfigured by frostbitten noses and cheeks, and nearly all had red, swollen, and festering eyes.

One group of Frenchmen stood close to the road, and two of them—one with his face covered in sores—were tearing at a piece of raw flesh with their hands. There was something horrible and animal-like in the fleeting glance they cast at the riders and in the hostile expression with which the soldier with the sores immediately turned away and went back to what he was doing.

Kutuzov looked long and hard at these two soldiers. He puckered his face, squinted, and pensively nodded his head. At another spot, he noticed a Russian soldier laughingly patting a Frenchman on the shoulder and saying something to him in a friendly way, and Kutuzov nodded his head again with the same expression.

"What were you saying?" he asked the general, who was continuing his report and directing the commander in chief's attention to some captured French standards standing before the Preobrazhensky regiment.
"Ah, the standards!" said Kutuzov, clearly pulling himself back with difficulty from the thoughts that preoccupied him.
He looked around absently. Thousands of eyes were watching him from all sides, waiting for a word from him.

He stopped in front of the Preobrazhensky regiment, sighed deeply, and closed his eyes. Someone on his staff beckoned to the soldiers carrying the standards to come forward and surround the commander in chief. Kutuzov was silent for several seconds, then, submitting with obvious reluctance to the duty imposed by his position, raised his head and began to speak. A crowd of officers gathered around him. He looked carefully at the circle of officers, recognizing several of them.

"I thank you all!" he said, addressing the soldiers and then the officers again. In the stillness around him, his slowly spoken words were clearly audible. "I thank you all for your hard and faithful service. The victory is complete, and Russia will not forget you! Honor to you forever."
He paused and looked around.

"Lower its head, lower it!" he said to a soldier who had accidentally lowered the French eagle he was holding in front of the Preobrazhensky standards. "Lower, lower, that's it. Hurrah, lads!" he added, with a quick motion of his chin.
"Hur-r-rah!" roared thousands of voices.
While the soldiers were shouting, Kutuzov leaned forward in his saddle and bowed his head, and his eye lit up with a mild and seemingly ironic gleam.

"You see, brothers..." he said when the shouts had died away... and all at once his voice and the expression on his face changed. It was no longer the commander in chief speaking but an ordinary old man who wanted to tell his comrades something very important.
A stir ran through the crowd of officers and the soldiers' ranks as they pressed forward to hear better what he was going to say.

"You see, brothers, I know it's hard for you, but it can't be helped! Bear up—it won't be long now! We'll see our visitors off and then we'll rest. The Tsar won't forget your service. It's hard for you, but still you're at home, while they—you see what they've come to," he said, pointing at the prisoners. "Worse off than our poorest beggars. While they were strong, we didn't spare ourselves, but now we can even pity them. They're human beings too. Isn't that right, lads?"

He looked around, and in the direct, respectful, wondering gazes fixed on him, he read agreement with what he had said. His face grew brighter and brighter with an old man's gentle smile, drawing the corners of his lips and eyes into a web of wrinkles. He stopped speaking and bowed his head as if in thought.
"But then again, who asked them to come here? Serves them right, the bloody bastards!" he suddenly cried, raising his head.
And flourishing his whip, he rode off at a gallop for the first time during the entire campaign, leaving behind the broken ranks of soldiers who were laughing joyfully and shouting "Hurrah!"

Kutuzov's actual words were barely understood by the troops. No one could have repeated the field marshal's speech, which began solemnly and ended as an old man's simple, heartfelt talk. But the genuine sincerity of that speech, the feeling of triumphant majesty combined with pity for the enemy and an awareness of the justice of their cause—expressed so perfectly by that old man's good-natured final outburst—was not merely understood but lived in the soul of every soldier and found expression in their joyous, prolonged cheering. Afterward, when one of the generals asked Kutuzov whether he wanted his carriage sent for, Kutuzov unexpectedly gave a sob in his reply, clearly deeply moved.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: When the troops reached their night's stopping place on November eighth—the last day of the Krasnoe battles—it was already growing dark. All day it had been calm and frosty with occasional light snow, and toward evening the sky began to clear. Through the falling snow, a purple-black starry sky appeared and the frost grew sharper.

An infantry regiment that had left Tarutino three thousand strong but now numbered only nine hundred was one of the first to arrive at the halting place—a village on the highway. The quartermasters who met the regiment reported that all the huts were full of sick and dead Frenchmen, cavalrymen, and members of the staff. Only one hut was available for the regimental commander.
The commander rode up to his hut. The regiment passed through the village and stacked its arms in front of the last houses.

Like some huge, many-limbed animal, the regiment began to prepare its shelter and food. One part dispersed and waded knee-deep through snow into a birch forest to the right of the village, and immediately the sounds of axes, swords crashing through branches, and merry voices could be heard from there. Another group busied itself around the regimental wagons and horses, getting out kettles and hardtack and feeding the horses. A third section scattered through the village, arranging quarters for the staff officers, hauling out French corpses from the huts, and dragging away boards, dry wood, and thatch from the roofs for campfires, or fence panels for shelter.
About fifteen men with merry shouts were shaking down the tall wattle wall of a shed whose roof had already been removed.

"Now then, all together—push!" cried the voices, and the huge surface of the wall, sprinkled with snow and creaking with frost, swayed in the darkness of the night. The lower stakes cracked more and more, and finally the wall fell, along with the men who had been pushing it. Loud, rough laughter and joyous shouts followed.
"Now then, grab it in pairs! Hand up the lever! That's it... Where are you shoving?"
"Now, all together! But wait a moment, boys... With a song!"

Everyone fell silent, and a soft, pleasant, velvety voice began to sing. At the end of the third verse, as the last note died away, twenty voices roared out at once: "Oo-oo-oo-oo! That's it. All together! Heave away, boys!" But despite their combined efforts, the wattle hardly moved, and in the silence that followed, the heavy breathing of the men was the only sound.
"Hey, Sixth Company! You devils! Give us a hand... We might need you one of these days."

About twenty men from the Sixth Company, who were on their way into the village, joined the haulers, and the wattle wall—about thirty-five feet long and seven feet high—moved forward along the village street, swaying, pressing on and cutting into the shoulders of the gasping men.
"Get along... Falling? What are you stopping for? There now..."
Cheerful, meaningless abuse flowed freely.

"What do you think you're doing?" came the sharp, authoritative voice of a sergeant major who came upon the men hauling their load. "There are officers here! The general himself is in that hut, and you foul-mouthed brutes! I'll give it to you!" he shouted, hitting the first man he reached a swinging blow on the back. "Can't you keep it down?"
The men fell silent. The soldier who had been struck groaned and wiped his face, which had been scratched bloody when he fell against the wattle.
"There, see how that devil hits! He's made my face all bloody," he said in a frightened whisper when the sergeant major had passed.
"Don't you like it?" said a laughing voice, and lowering their tones, the men moved on.
Once they were out of the village, they began talking again just as loudly as before, larding their conversation with the same pointless profanity.

In the hut the men had passed, the senior officers had gathered and were in animated discussion over tea about the day's events and the maneuvers proposed for the next day. The plan was to make a flanking march to the left, cut off the Viceroy (Murat), and capture him.

By the time the soldiers had dragged the wattle fence into place, campfires were blazing on all sides. Wood crackled, snow melted, and black shadows of soldiers moved back and forth across the trampled area.

Axes and hatchets rang out everywhere. Everything was done without any orders being given. Firewood was gathered for the night, shelters were put up for the officers, kettles were boiling, and muskets and equipment were put in order.

The wattle wall the men had brought was set up in a semicircle by the Eighth Company as a windbreak against the north, propped up by musket rests, with a campfire built in front of it. They beat the evening drum, called the roll, had supper, and settled around the fires for the night—some mending their footwear, some smoking pipes, and some stripping naked to steam the lice out of their shirts.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: You would have thought that under the almost incredibly wretched conditions the Russian soldiers endured—lacking warm boots and sheepskin coats, with no roof over their heads, camping in the snow at eighteen below zero, without even full rations (the supply wagons didn't always keep up with the troops)—they would have presented a sad and depressing sight.

On the contrary, the army had never appeared more cheerful and spirited, not even under the best material conditions. This was because all who began to grow depressed or who lost strength were sifted out of the army day by day. All the physically or mentally weak had long since been left behind; only the best of the army—physically and mentally—remained.

More men gathered behind the wattle fence of the Eighth Company than anywhere else. Two sergeants major sat with them and their campfire blazed brighter than the others. For permission to sit by their wattle, they demanded contributions of firewood.

"Hey, Makeev! Where've you gone, you son of a gun? Are you lost, or have the wolves eaten you? Bring more wood!" shouted a red-haired, red-faced man, squinting and blinking from the smoke but not moving away from the fire. "And you, Jackdaw, go get some wood too!" he said to another soldier.

This red-haired man was neither a sergeant nor a corporal, but being robust, he ordered around those weaker than himself. The soldier they called "Jackdaw," a thin little fellow with a sharp nose, got up obediently and was about to go when the slender, handsome figure of a young soldier carrying a load of wood appeared in the firelight.
"Bring it here—that's the stuff!"

They split up the wood, pressed it down on the fire, blew on it with their mouths, and fanned it with the skirts of their greatcoats, making the flames hiss and crackle. The men drew closer and lit their pipes. The handsome young soldier who had brought the wood set his arms akimbo and began stamping his cold feet rapidly and nimbly on the spot.
"Mother! The dew is cold but clear... It's good that I'm a musketeer..." he sang, pretending to hiccup after each line.
"Watch it, your soles will fly off!" shouted the red-haired man, noticing that the dancer's boot sole was hanging loose. "What a fellow you are for dancing!"
The dancer stopped, pulled off the loose piece of leather, and threw it on the fire.

"Right you are, friend," he said, and having sat down, took a scrap of blue French cloth from his knapsack and wrapped it around his foot. "It's the steam that ruins them," he added, stretching out his feet toward the fire.
"They'll be issuing us new ones soon. They say once we've finished hammering them, we'll get double kits!"
"And that rascal Petrov has fallen behind after all, it seems," said one sergeant major.
"I've had my eye on him for a while," said the other.
"Well, he's a sorry excuse for a soldier..."
"But in the Third Company, they say nine men went missing yesterday."
"Sure, but when a man's feet are frozen, how can he walk?"
"Come on, don't talk nonsense!" said the sergeant major.
"Do you want the same thing to happen to you?" said an old soldier, turning reproachfully to the man who had spoken about frozen feet.

"Well, you know," said the sharp-nosed man they called Jackdaw, in a squeaky, unsteady voice, raising himself on the other side of the fire, "a fat man gets thin, but a thin man—it's death. Take me, for instance! I've got no strength left," he added with sudden determination, turning to the sergeant major. "Tell them to send me to the hospital. I'm aching all over. I won't be able to keep up anyway."
"That'll do, that'll do!" the sergeant major replied quietly.
The soldier said no more and the conversation moved on.
"What a lot of those Frenchies they took today, and the fact is that not one of them had what you'd call real boots," said a soldier, starting a new topic. "They were nothing but fakes."
