"The Cossacks took their boots. They were clearing the hut for the colonel and carried them out. It was pitiful to see, boys," the dancer put in. "As they turned them over, one seemed still alive, and would you believe it, he was jabbering something in their language."
"But they're a clean lot, lads," the first man went on. "He was white—white as birchbark—and some of them are such fine-looking fellows, you'd think they were noblemen."
"Well, what do you expect? They make soldiers of all classes over there."
"But they can't understand our language at all," said the dancer with a puzzled smile. "I asked him who his master was, and he just jabbered away in his own way. A strange lot!"

"But here's what's odd, friends," continued the man who had marveled at their whiteness, "the peasants at Mozhaysk were saying that when they started burying the dead—where the battle was, you know—well, the dead had been lying there nearly a month, and the peasant says, 'They lie as white as paper, clean, and not so much smell as a puff of gunpowder.'"
"Was it from the cold?" someone asked.

"Clever fellow! From the cold indeed! It was hot then. If it had been from the cold, ours wouldn't have rotted either. 'But,' he says, 'go up to ours, and they're all rotten and full of maggots. So,' he says, 'we tie cloths over our faces and turn our heads away as we drag them off—we can barely manage it. But theirs,' he says, 'are white as paper and don't smell any more than a whiff of gunpowder.'"
Everyone was silent.
"Must be from their food," said the sergeant major. "They ate the same food as the gentry."
No one disagreed.

"That peasant near Mozhaysk where the battle was said they called up men from ten villages around and carted for twenty days and still didn't finish clearing away the dead. And as for the wolves, he says..."
"That was a real battle," said an old soldier. "It's the only one worth remembering. Everything since then has just been tormenting people."

"And you know what, Daddy—the day before yesterday we charged at them, and my word, they didn't let us get close before they just threw down their muskets and dropped to their knees. 'Pardon!' they say. That's just one example. They say Platov captured Napoleon himself twice. But he didn't know the right magic word. He catches him and catches him—no good! He turns into a bird in his hands and flies away. And there's no way to kill him either."
"You're a first-class liar, Kiselev, I can see that!"
"Liar, nothing! It's the honest truth."
"If he fell into my hands—once I caught him, I'd bury him in the ground with an aspen stake to pin him down. What a lot of people he's destroyed!"
"Well, either way, we're going to finish it. He won't be coming here again," said the old soldier, yawning.
The conversation died down and the soldiers began settling in to sleep.
"Look at the stars. Amazing how they shine! You'd think the women had laid out their linen to dry," said one of the men, gazing admiringly at the Milky Way.
"That's a sign of a good harvest next year."
"We'll need more wood."
"You warm your back and your belly freezes. That's a strange thing."
"Oh Lord!"
"What are you pushing for? Is the fire only for you? Look how he's sprawling!"

In the silence that followed, the snoring of those who had fallen asleep could be heard. Others turned over and warmed themselves, occasionally exchanging a few words. From a campfire a hundred paces away came the sound of loud, merry laughter.
"Listen to them roaring over there in the Fifth Company!" said one of the soldiers. "And what a crowd of them there are!"
One of the men got up and went over to the Fifth Company.
"They're having a great time," he said, coming back. "Two Frenchies have turned up. One's practically frozen, and the other's a real show-off. He's singing songs..."
"Oh, I'll go over and have a look..."
And several of the men went over to the Fifth Company.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: The Fifth Company was camped at the very edge of the forest. A huge campfire blazed brightly in the middle of the snow, lighting up the branches of trees heavy with frost.
Around midnight they heard footsteps in the snow and the cracking of dry branches in the forest.
"A bear, lads," said one of the men.
They all raised their heads to listen, and out of the forest into the bright firelight stepped two strangely dressed human figures clinging to each other.

They were two Frenchmen who had been hiding in the forest. They came up to the fire, hoarsely saying something in a language the Russian soldiers didn't understand. One was taller than the other; he wore an officer's hat and seemed completely exhausted. As he approached the fire and tried to sit down, he fell. The other, a short, sturdy soldier with a shawl tied around his head, was stronger. He lifted his companion and said something, pointing to his mouth. The Russian soldiers gathered around the Frenchmen, spread a greatcoat on the ground for the sick man, and brought buckwheat porridge and vodka for both of them.
The exhausted French officer was Ramballe, and the man with the shawl around his head was Morel, his orderly.

When Morel had drunk some vodka and finished his bowl of porridge, he suddenly became unnaturally cheerful and chattered nonstop to the soldiers, who couldn't understand him. Ramballe refused food and, resting his head on his elbow, lay silent beside the campfire, staring at the Russian soldiers with red, vacant eyes. Occasionally he let out a long groan, then fell silent again. Morel, pointing to his shoulders, tried to convey that Ramballe was an officer and ought to be warmed. A Russian officer who had approached the fire sent to ask his colonel whether he would take a French officer into his hut, and when the messenger returned saying the colonel agreed, Ramballe was told to go. He rose and tried to walk but staggered and would have fallen if a nearby soldier hadn't caught him.
"You won't try that again, eh?" said one of the soldiers, winking and turning mockingly to Ramballe.
"Oh, you fool! Why talk rubbish, you oaf—a real peasant!" came rebukes from every side at the joking soldier.
They surrounded Ramballe, lifted him onto the crossed arms of two soldiers, and carried him to the hut. Ramballe put his arms around their necks as they carried him and began wailing plaintively:
"Oh, you fine fellows, my kind, kind friends! These are real men! Oh, my brave, kind friends!" And he rested his head on one soldier's shoulder like a child.
Meanwhile, Morel was sitting in the best spot by the fire, surrounded by soldiers.

Morel, a short, sturdy Frenchman with inflamed, streaming eyes, wore a woman's cloak and had a shawl tied around his head over his cap, babushka-style. He was clearly tipsy and was singing a French song in a hoarse, broken voice with one arm thrown around the nearest soldier. The soldiers simply held their sides watching him.
"Come on, come on, teach us how it goes! I'll pick it up quick. How does it go?" said a man who was both a singer and a comedian, the one Morel was embracing.
"Long live Henry the Fourth! Long live that brave king!" sang Morel, winking. "That rowdy devil..."
("Long live Henry the Fourth, that valiant king! That rowdy devil.")
"Vivarika! Vif-seruvaru! Sedyablyaka!" the soldier repeated, waving his arm and actually catching the tune.
"Bravo! Ha, ha, ha!" Rough, joyful laughter burst from all sides.
Morel, wrinkling up his face, laughed too.
"Well, go on, go on!"
"Who had a triple talent—for drinking, for fighting, and for being a charming fellow..."
(Who had a triple talent—for drinking, for fighting, and for being a gallant old boy...)
"Smooth, that is. Come on now, Zaletaev!"
"Ke..." Zaletaev brought out with effort: "ke-e-e-e," he drawled, laboriously pursing his lips, "le-trip-ta-la-de-bu-de-ba, e de-tra-va-ga-la," he sang.
"Fine! Just like the Frenchman! Ho ho ho! Want some more to eat?"
"Give him some porridge—it takes a long time to fill up after you've been starving."

They gave him more porridge and Morel, laughing, set to work on his third bowl. All the young soldiers watched him with beaming smiles. The older men, who considered it beneath their dignity to amuse themselves with such nonsense, continued lying on the other side of the fire, but one would occasionally prop himself up on an elbow and glance at Morel with a smile.
"They're human beings too," said one of them as he wrapped himself in his coat. "Even weeds grow from their own roots."
"Oh Lord, oh Lord! How starry it is! Incredible! That means a hard frost..."

They all fell quiet. The stars, as if knowing that no one was watching them, began to play in the dark sky: now flaring up, now vanishing, now trembling, they whispered among themselves something joyful and mysterious.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: The French army melted away at the steady rate of a mathematical progression, and the crossing of the Berezina—about which so much has been written—was only one intermediate stage in its destruction, not at all the decisive episode of the campaign. If so much has been and still is written about the Berezina, on the French side this is only because at the broken bridge across that river, the calamities the army had been enduring were suddenly concentrated into a single tragic spectacle that seared itself into every memory. On the Russian side, it's simply because in Petersburg—far from the actual fighting—yet another plan (one of Pfuel's) had been devised to trap Napoleon at the Berezina River. Everyone was certain that everything would go according to plan, and therefore insisted that it was the Berezina crossing that destroyed the French army. In reality, the results of the crossing were far less disastrous to the French—in guns and men lost—than Krasnoe had been, as the numbers show.

The sole importance of the Berezina crossing lies in the fact that it plainly and undeniably proved the bankruptcy of all the plans to cut off the enemy's retreat, and confirmed the soundness of the only possible course of action—the one Kutuzov and the mass of the army demanded—which was simply to follow the enemy. The French mob fled at ever-increasing speed, all its energy directed toward reaching its goal. It fled like a wounded animal, and it was impossible to block its path. This was shown not so much by its arrangements for crossing as by what happened at the bridges. When the bridges collapsed, unarmed soldiers, civilians from Moscow, and women with children who were traveling with the French—all carried forward by sheer momentum—piled into boats and onto the ice-covered water and refused to surrender.

That impulse was entirely rational. The condition of both fugitives and pursuers was equally miserable. As long as they stayed with their own people, each could hope for help from comrades and hold a defined place among them. But those who surrendered, while remaining in the same wretched state, would drop to a lower level in any claim on the necessities of life. The French didn't need to be told that half the prisoners—whom the Russians didn't know what to do with—perished of cold and hunger despite their captors' desire to save them. They sensed it could not be otherwise. The most compassionate Russian commanders, those favorably disposed toward the French—even Frenchmen serving in the Russian army—could do nothing for the prisoners. The French perished from the very conditions to which the Russian army itself was exposed. It was impossible to take bread and clothing from starving, essential Russian soldiers to give to Frenchmen who, though not threatening or hated or guilty, were simply unnecessary. Some Russians even did that, but they were exceptions.

Certain destruction lay behind the French, but ahead lay hope. Their bridges had been burned; there was no salvation except in collective flight, and on that the whole strength of the French was concentrated.

The farther they fled, the more wretched became the plight of the remnant—especially after the Berezina, on which (thanks to the Petersburg plan) the Russians had placed such high hopes—and the more heated grew the passions of the Russian commanders, who blamed one another and above all Kutuzov. Anticipating that the failure of the Petersburg Berezina plan would be blamed on Kutuzov led to increasing dissatisfaction, contempt, and ridicule. The ridicule and contempt were expressed, of course, in respectful form, making it impossible for him to ask what exactly he was being accused of. They didn't talk seriously to him; when reporting or asking for his approval, they appeared to be fulfilling an unpleasant formality while winking behind his back and trying to undermine him at every turn.

Because they couldn't understand him, all these people assumed it was useless to talk to the old man; that he would never grasp the profundity of their plans; that he would answer with his stock phrases about a "golden bridge," the impossibility of crossing the frontier with a mob of ragged men, and so on. They had heard all that before. And everything he said—that they needed to wait for supplies, that the men had no boots—was so simple, while what they proposed was so complex and clever, that it was obvious he was a stupid old man while they, though not in command, were military geniuses.

After the junction with the army of the brilliant admiral and Petersburg hero Wittgenstein, this mood and staff gossip reached a peak. Kutuzov saw this and merely sighed and shrugged. Only once, after the affair at the Berezina, did he get angry and write the following letter to Bennigsen (who reported separately to the Emperor):

"On account of your frequent bouts of ill health, would Your Excellency kindly be so good as to proceed to Kaluga upon receipt of this, there to await further commands and appointments from His Imperial Majesty."

But after Bennigsen's departure, the Grand Duke Constantine Pavlovich joined the army. He had participated at the beginning of the campaign but had been removed by Kutuzov. Now, returning to the army, he informed Kutuzov of the Emperor's displeasure at the slow progress and poor results. The Emperor intended to join the army personally in a few days.

The old man, experienced in both court and military affairs—this same Kutuzov who in August had been chosen commander in chief against the sovereign's wishes, who had removed the Grand Duke and heir apparent from the army, who on his own authority and contrary to the Emperor's will had decided to abandon Moscow—now instantly understood that his day was over, his role played out, and the power he supposedly held was no longer his. And he understood this not merely from the court's attitude. He saw, on the one hand, that the military campaign in which he had played his part was finished, and he felt his mission was accomplished. At the same time, he began to feel the physical weariness of his aged body and the need for rest.

On November twenty-ninth, Kutuzov entered Vilna—his "dear Vilna," as he called it. Twice during his career he had been governor of Vilna. In that wealthy city, which had not been damaged, he found old friends and associations as well as the comforts of life he had so long been deprived of. And he suddenly turned from the cares of army and state, and as far as the passions seething around him allowed, immersed himself in the quiet life he had once known, as if everything happening in the world of history no longer concerned him at all.

Chichagov—one of the most zealous proponents of "cutting off" and "breaking through," who had first wanted to operate in Greece, then in Warsaw, but never wished to go where he was actually sent; Chichagov, noted for his bold manner of speaking to the Emperor, and who considered Kutuzov indebted to him (because when he was sent to conclude peace with Turkey in 1811, independently of Kutuzov, he found the peace already made and acknowledged to the Emperor that the credit belonged to Kutuzov)—this Chichagov was the first to meet Kutuzov at the castle where the latter was to stay. In undress naval uniform, carrying a dirk with his cap under his arm, he handed Kutuzov a garrison report and the keys to the city. The contemptuous-yet-respectful attitude of the younger generation toward the old man in his dotage was expressed to the highest degree in Chichagov's behavior, as he was well aware of the accusations being leveled at Kutuzov.
In conversation with Chichagov, Kutuzov happened to mention that the vehicles packed with china captured from him at Borisov had been recovered and would be returned.

"You mean to imply that I have nothing to eat from? On the contrary, I can supply you with everything, even if you want to throw dinner parties," Chichagov replied warmly, trying with every word to prove his own integrity and therefore imagining Kutuzov was driven by the same concern.
Kutuzov, shrugging his shoulders, replied with his subtle, knowing smile: "I merely meant what I said."

Contrary to the Emperor's wishes, Kutuzov kept the greater part of the army in Vilna. Those around him said he became extraordinarily slack and physically feeble during his stay. He attended to army business reluctantly, left everything to his generals, and while waiting for the Emperor to arrive led a leisurely life.

The Emperor left Petersburg on December seventh with his retinue—Count Tolstoy, Prince Volkonsky, Arakcheev, and others—and reached Vilna on the eleventh. In his traveling sleigh, he drove straight to the castle. Despite the severe frost, about a hundred generals and staff officers in full dress uniform stood before the castle, along with a guard of honor from the Semenov regiment.
A courier galloping ahead in a troika with three foam-flecked horses shouted "Coming!" and Konovnitsyn rushed into the vestibule to inform Kutuzov, who was waiting in the porter's lodge.

A minute later, the old man's large, heavy figure in full-dress uniform—his chest covered with medals and a sash wrapped around his stomach—waddled out onto the porch. He put on his two-pointed hat, and holding his gloves in one hand, walked with effort sideways down the steps to street level, taking in his other hand the report he had prepared for the Emperor.

There was running to and fro and whispering; another troika flew up at great speed, and then all eyes turned to an approaching sleigh in which the figures of the Emperor and Volkonsky could already be seen.

From the force of fifty years' habit, all this had a physically exciting effect on the old general. He carefully felt himself all over, adjusted his hat, and pulling himself together, drew himself upright. At the very moment the Emperor stepped down from the sleigh and looked up at him, Kutuzov handed over the report and began speaking in his smooth, ingratiating voice.

The Emperor swept a rapid glance over Kutuzov from head to foot, frowned for an instant, but immediately composed himself, stepped forward, extended his arms, and embraced the old man. This embrace too, because of a deep-seated emotional association, had its usual effect on Kutuzov, and he gave a sob.
The Emperor greeted the officers and the Semenov guard, then pressed the old man's hand again and went into the castle with him.

When alone with the field marshal, the Emperor expressed his dissatisfaction at the slowness of the pursuit and the mistakes made at Krasnoe and the Berezina, and outlined his plans for a future campaign abroad. Kutuzov made no objection or comment. The same submissive, expressionless look with which he had listened to the Emperor's orders on the field of Austerlitz seven years before settled on his face.
When Kutuzov came out of the study and was crossing the ballroom with his heavy, waddling gait, head bowed, someone's voice stopped him:
"Your Serene Highness!"

Kutuzov raised his head and looked for a long time into the eyes of Count Tolstoy, who stood before him holding a silver tray on which lay a small object. Kutuzov seemed not to understand what was expected of him.

Suddenly he appeared to remember. A barely perceptible smile flickered across his puffy face, and bowing low and respectfully, he took the object from the tray. It was the Order of St. George, First Class.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The next day the field marshal gave a dinner and ball that the Emperor honored with his presence. Kutuzov had received the Order of St. George, First Class, and the Emperor showed him the highest honors, but everyone knew of the imperial displeasure. The forms were observed and the Emperor was the first to set the example, yet everybody understood that the old man was considered at fault and good for nothing. When Kutuzov, following an old tradition from Catherine's day, ordered the captured standards lowered at the Emperor's feet as he entered the ballroom, the Emperor made a face and muttered something in which some people caught the words "the old comedian."
The Emperor's displeasure with Kutuzov was especially heightened at Vilna by the fact that Kutuzov clearly could not or would not understand the importance of the coming campaign.
When the Emperor told the assembled officers the following morning: "You have not only saved Russia, you have saved Europe!" they all understood that the war was not over.

Kutuzov alone refused to see this and openly stated that no new war could improve Russia's position or add to her glory, but could only diminish the glorious standing Russia had won. He tried to demonstrate to the Emperor the impossibility of raising fresh troops, spoke of the hardships the people had already endured, of the possibility of failure, and so on.
Given the field marshal's frame of mind, he was naturally regarded as nothing more than a hindrance and obstacle to the impending war.

To avoid unpleasant confrontations with the old man, the natural solution was to do what had been done with him at Austerlitz and with Barclay at the start of the Russian campaign: transfer authority to the Emperor himself, thus pulling the rug from under the commander in chief without upsetting the old man by telling him directly.

To this end, his staff was gradually restructured and its real power removed and transferred to the Emperor. Toll, Konovnitsyn, and Ermolov received new appointments. Everyone spoke openly of the field marshal's great weakness and failing health.
His health had to be bad for his position to be taken from him and given to another. And indeed his health was poor.

So naturally, simply, and gradually—just as he had come from Turkey to Petersburg to recruit the militia, and then to the army when he was needed—now that his part was played, Kutuzov's place was taken by a new and necessary performer.
The war of 1812, besides its national significance dear to every Russian heart, was now to take on another, European significance.

The movement of peoples from west to east was to be followed by a movement from east to west, and for this new war another leader was needed—one with different qualities and views, driven by different motives.
Alexander I was as necessary for the movement of peoples from east to west and for the redrawing of national boundaries as Kutuzov had been for the salvation and glory of Russia.

Kutuzov did not understand what Europe, the balance of power, or Napoleon meant. He could not understand it. For the representative of the Russian people, after the enemy had been destroyed and Russia had been liberated and raised to the summit of her glory, there was nothing left to do as a Russian. Nothing remained for the representative of the national war but to die. And Kutuzov died.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: As generally happens, Pierre did not feel the full effects of the physical privation and strain he had endured as a prisoner until after they were over. After his liberation, he reached Orel, and on the third day there, when preparing to continue to Kiev, he fell ill and was bedridden for three months. He had what the doctors called "bilious fever." But despite the fact that they treated him, bled him, and gave him medicine, he recovered.

Very little impression was left on Pierre's mind by everything that happened from his rescue to his illness. He remembered only the dull gray weather, now rainy and now snowy, internal physical distress, and pains in his feet and side. He recalled a general impression of people's misfortunes and suffering, of being pestered by the curiosity of officers and generals who questioned him, and the difficulty of finding a carriage and horses. Above all, he remembered his inability to think and feel during that time. On the day of his rescue, he had seen Petya Rostov's body. That same day, he learned that Prince Andrew, after surviving the battle of Borodino by more than a month, had recently died at the Rostovs' house in Yaroslavl, and Denisov, who told him this, also mentioned Helene's death, assuming Pierre had heard about it long ago. All of this seemed merely strange to Pierre at the time—he felt unable to grasp its significance. Just then, his only desire was to get away as quickly as possible from places where people were killing one another, to some peaceful refuge where he could recover, rest, and make sense of all the strange new things he had learned. But upon reaching Orel, he immediately fell ill. When he came to after his illness, he saw two of his servants attending him—Terenty and Vaska, who had come from Moscow—as well as his cousin the eldest princess, who had been living on his estate at Yelets and, hearing of his rescue and illness, had come to look after him.

It was only gradually during his recovery that Pierre shed the impressions he had grown accustomed to over the past months and got used to the idea that no one would force him to go anywhere tomorrow, that no one would take away his warm bed, and that he would certainly get his dinner, tea, and supper. But for a long time he still dreamed of captivity. In the same gradual way, he came to absorb the news he had been told after his rescue: the death of Prince Andrew, the death of his wife, and the destruction of the French.

A joyous feeling of freedom—that complete, innate freedom natural to every person, which he had first experienced at the initial halt outside Moscow—filled Pierre's soul during his recovery. He was surprised to find that this inner freedom, which was independent of external circumstances, now came with the added bonus of external liberty. He was alone in a strange town, without acquaintances. No one demanded anything of him or sent him anywhere. He had everything he wanted; the thought of his wife, which had been a constant torment, was gone now that she was no more.

"Oh, how wonderful! How splendid!" he said to himself when a neatly set table was brought to him with savory broth, or when he lay down at night in a soft, clean bed, or when he remembered that the French were gone and his wife was no more. "Oh, how wonderful, how splendid!"
And from old habit he asked himself: "Well, and what next? What am I going to do?" And he immediately gave himself the answer: "Well, I shall live. Ah, how splendid!"

The very question that had formerly tormented him, the thing he had endlessly sought—the aim of life—no longer existed for him now. That search for an aim hadn't merely disappeared temporarily; he felt it no longer existed and could never arise again. And this very absence of any aim gave him the complete, joyous sense of freedom that constituted his happiness at this time.

He could not see an aim, for he now had faith—not faith in any kind of rule, or words, or ideas, but faith in an ever-living, ever-present God. Before, he had sought God through the aims he set himself. That search for an aim had been simply a search for God. And suddenly, in captivity, he had learned—not through words or reasoning but through direct feeling—what his old nurse had told him long ago: that God is here and everywhere. In captivity he had learned that in Karataev, God was greater, more infinite and unfathomable, than in the Architect of the Universe recognized by the Freemasons. He felt like a man who, after straining his eyes to see into the far distance, discovers what he sought right at his feet. All his life he had looked over the heads of the people around him, when he should have simply looked straight ahead without straining his eyes.

In the past he had never been able to find that great, inscrutable, infinite something. He had only felt that it must exist somewhere and had searched for it. In everything near and understandable, he had seen only what was limited, petty, ordinary, and meaningless. He had equipped himself with a mental telescope and peered into the distance, where the petty everyday world, hidden in mist, had seemed great and infinite simply because it wasn't clearly visible. European life, politics, Freemasonry, philosophy, philanthropy—all had seemed that way. But even then, in moments of what he had considered weakness, his mind had penetrated those distances and seen the same pettiness, worldliness, and meaninglessness there too. Now, however, he had learned to see the great, the eternal, and the infinite in everything, and so—to see it and take joy in contemplating it—he naturally threw away the telescope through which he had been gazing over people's heads, and gladly beheld the ever-changing, eternally great, unfathomable, and infinite life around him. And the closer he looked, the more at peace and happy he became. That terrible question "What for?"—which had once demolished all his mental constructions—no longer existed for him. To that question, "What for?" a simple answer now always stood ready in his soul: "Because there is a God, that God without whose will not a single hair falls from a man's head."

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: Outwardly, Pierre had barely changed at all. He looked the same as he always had. He was still absent-minded and seemed occupied not with what was in front of him but with something of his own. The difference between the old Pierre and the new was this: before, when he failed to grasp what was before him or what was being said, he would furrow his brow painfully, as if straining to make out something in the distance. Now he still forgot what people said to him and still didn't see what was right before his eyes, but he looked at everything with a barely perceptible, seemingly ironic smile, and listened to what was said while clearly seeing and hearing something entirely different. Before, he had seemed like a kindhearted but unhappy man, and people had tended to avoid him. Now a smile of pure joy played constantly around his lips, and his eyes shone with sympathy for others and a quiet question: were they as happy as he was? People felt genuinely pleased to be around him.

Before, he had talked a lot, got excited when he spoke, and rarely listened. Now he seldom got carried away in conversation and knew how to listen in a way that made people readily share their most intimate secrets with him.

The princess, who had never liked Pierre and had been especially hostile toward him since feeling indebted to him after the old count's death, had now—after staying a short time in Orel, where she had come intending to show Pierre that despite his ingratitude she felt duty-bound to nurse him—found to her surprise and irritation that she had grown fond of him. Pierre made no effort to win her approval; he simply studied her with interest. Before, she had felt that he looked at her with indifference and irony, so she had retreated into herself as she did with everyone, showing him only her combative side. But now he seemed to be reaching for the most hidden places in her heart, and—mistrustfully at first, then gratefully—she let him see the kind, gentle sides of her nature.

The most cunning person in the world couldn't have won her trust more effectively, drawing out memories of the best times of her youth and showing sympathy for them. Yet Pierre's cunning consisted simply in the pleasure he took in bringing out the human qualities of this bitter, hardened, and—in her own way—proud princess.
"Yes, he's a very, very kind man when he's not under the influence of bad people but of people like me," she thought.

His servants too—Terenty and Vaska—noticed the change in Pierre in their own way. They thought he had become much "simpler." Terenty, after helping him undress and wishing him good night, would often linger with his master's boots in his hands and clothes over his arm, hoping Pierre might start a conversation. And Pierre, noticing that Terenty wanted to chat, usually kept him there.
"Well, tell me—how did you manage to get food?" he would ask.

And Terenty would start talking about the destruction of Moscow and the old count, standing there a long time holding the clothes and talking, or sometimes listening to Pierre's stories, before going out to the hall with a pleasant feeling of closeness to his master and genuine affection for him.

The doctor who attended Pierre and visited him every day—though he felt obligated to act as if his every moment were precious to suffering humanity—would sit for hours with Pierre, telling his favorite stories and sharing observations about his patients' characters, especially the ladies.
"It's a pleasure to talk to a man like that; he's nothing like our provincial types," he would say.
There were several French prisoners of war in Orel, and the doctor brought one of them, a young Italian, to meet Pierre.
This officer began visiting Pierre regularly, and the princess liked to tease him about the Italian's open affection.
The Italian seemed happy only when he could visit Pierre, talk with him, tell him about his past life back home and his love, and pour out his outrage against the French and especially Napoleon.
"If all Russians are anything like you, it's a sin to fight such a nation," he told Pierre. "You, who suffered so much from the French, don't even feel any resentment toward them."
Pierre had won the Italian's passionate devotion simply by drawing out the best in him and taking pleasure in doing so.

During Pierre's last days in Orel, his old Masonic acquaintance Count Willarski—who had introduced him to the lodge back in 1807—came to see him. Willarski had married a Russian heiress with a large estate in Orel province and held a temporary post in the local commissariat department.

Hearing that Bezukhov was in Orel, Willarski—though they had never been close—came to him with the kind of warm declarations of friendship that people who meet in a desert tend to exchange. Willarski was bored in Orel and was glad to meet someone from his own circle who, he assumed, shared his interests.
But to his surprise, Willarski quickly noticed that Pierre had fallen far behind the times and had sunk, as he put it to himself, into apathy and self-absorption.
"You're letting yourself go, my dear fellow," he said.

But despite all that, Willarski found it more pleasant than before to spend time with Pierre, and came to see him every day. To Pierre, as he watched and listened to Willarski, it seemed strange to think that he himself had been just like that not so long ago.

Willarski was a married man with a family, busy with his family affairs, his wife's affairs, and his official duties. He saw all these occupations as obstacles to real life, and considered them contemptible because their aim was merely the welfare of himself and his family. Military, administrative, political, and Masonic concerns constantly consumed his attention. And Pierre, without trying to change his views or condemning him, but with the calm, joyful, and amused smile that was now habitual, watched this strange yet very familiar phenomenon with interest.

There was something new in Pierre's dealings with Willarski, with the princess, with the doctor, and with everyone he met—something that earned him universal goodwill. It was his acceptance of the impossibility of changing anyone's mind through words, and his recognition that everyone thinks, feels, and sees things from their own perspective. This natural uniqueness of each person, which used to excite and irritate Pierre, now became the basis for the sympathy he felt and the interest he took in other people. The differences—and sometimes outright contradictions—between what people believed and how they lived, and between one person and another, pleased him and drew from him an amused, gentle smile.

In practical matters, Pierre unexpectedly discovered a sense of inner balance he had never had before. Previously, all financial questions—especially requests for money, to which he was constantly exposed as an extremely wealthy man—had thrown him into a state of helpless anxiety and confusion. "Should I give or not?" he would ask himself. "I have it and he needs it. But someone else needs it more. Who needs it most? And maybe they're both frauds?" In the old days he had found no way out of such dilemmas and had given to everyone who asked, as long as he had anything left to give. He had been in a similar state of paralysis regarding every question about his property, when one adviser said one thing and another said the opposite.

Now, to his surprise, he found that he no longer felt any doubt or confusion about these things. There was now a judge inside him who, by some rule Pierre couldn't identify, decided what should and shouldn't be done.

He was as indifferent to money as ever, but now he felt certain about what was right and what wasn't. The first time he relied on this new inner judge was when a French prisoner, a colonel, came to him and—after talking at length about his military exploits—essentially demanded that Pierre give him four thousand francs to send to his wife and children. Pierre refused without the slightest difficulty or effort, and was amazed afterward at how simple and easy something had been that once seemed impossibly hard. At the same time that he refused the colonel, he decided he would need to find a tactful way, when leaving Orel, to get the Italian officer to accept some money he clearly needed. Another sign of Pierre's more settled practical judgment was his decision about his wife's debts and the rebuilding of his houses in and near Moscow.
His head steward came to see him in Orel, and Pierre went over his reduced income with him. According to the steward's calculations, the burning of Moscow had cost Pierre about two million rubles.

To comfort Pierre for these losses, the steward presented an estimate showing that despite everything, his income would actually increase—if he refused to pay his wife's debts, which he was under no legal obligation to pay, and didn't rebuild his Moscow house or the country estate nearby, which had cost eighty thousand rubles a year and brought in nothing.
"Yes, of course, that's true," Pierre said with a cheerful smile. "I don't need any of that at all. By being ruined, I've become much richer."

But in January, Savelich arrived from Moscow with an account of the situation there, including an architect's estimate for rebuilding the town house and country house, speaking of it as a settled matter. Around the same time, Pierre received letters from Prince Vasili and other Petersburg acquaintances about his wife's debts. And Pierre decided that the steward's proposals, which had pleased him so much, were wrong—that he needed to go to Petersburg to settle his wife's affairs, and he needed to rebuild in Moscow. Why this was necessary he couldn't say, but he knew with certainty that it had to be done. His income would be cut by three-quarters, but he felt it was right.
Willarski was heading to Moscow, and they agreed to travel together.

Throughout his recovery in Orel, Pierre had felt a sense of joy, freedom, and life; but during his journey, surrounded by the open world and hundreds of new faces, that feeling only intensified. He felt like a schoolboy on holiday. Everyone—the coach driver, the post-house overseers, the peasants on the roads and in the villages—held a fresh significance for him. Willarski's constant complaints about the ignorance and poverty of Russia and its backwardness compared to Europe only heightened Pierre's delight. Where Willarski saw stagnation, Pierre saw extraordinary strength and vitality—the strength that sustained the life of this original, distinctive, and unique people across those vast, snow-covered spaces. He didn't argue with Willarski and even seemed to agree with him—since apparent agreement was the simplest way to avoid pointless debates—and he smiled joyfully as he listened.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: It would be hard to explain why and where ants rush when their anthill has been destroyed: some hauling away bits of debris, larvae, and dead bodies, others streaming back to the hill, or why they bump into each other, chase one another, and fight. But it would be equally hard to explain what drove people to swarm back to Moscow after the French had gone. And just as when you watch ants around their ruined hill, despite the complete destruction of the colony the tenacity, energy, and sheer number of the swarming insects show that everything has been destroyed except something indestructible and immaterial—the spirit of the colony—so too Moscow in October, despite the absence of any authorities, churches, treasures, or houses, was still the same Moscow it had been in August. Everything was destroyed except something intangible yet powerful and indestructible.

The motives of those who flooded into Moscow from all directions were enormously varied and personal, and at first mostly savage and brutal. Only one motive was shared by all: the pull toward the place that had once been called Moscow, to apply their energies there.
Within a week Moscow had fifteen thousand inhabitants; in two weeks, twenty-five thousand; and so on, rising steadily. By autumn 1813 the population exceeded what it had been before 1812.

The first Russians to enter Moscow were the Cossacks of Wintzingerode's detachment, peasants from nearby villages, and residents who had fled Moscow and been hiding in the surrounding area. The Russians who returned to Moscow, finding it plundered, began plundering it themselves. They continued what the French had started. Peasant cart-drivers came from all around to steal the goods scattered throughout Moscow's ruined neighborhoods. Cossacks carried off whatever they could to their camps; homeowners took everything they found in other people's houses and moved it into their own, claiming it as their property.
But the first wave of plunderers was followed by a second and a third, and as numbers grew, the plundering became harder and took on more definite forms.

The French had found Moscow abandoned but with all the systems of an organized society intact—diverse branches of commerce and craftsmanship, luxury goods, government offices, and religious institutions. These forms were lifeless but still existed. There were markets, shops, warehouses, grain stores, and bazaars—most of them still stocked with goods. There were factories and workshops. There were palaces and wealthy mansions filled with luxury items. There were hospitals, prisons, government buildings, churches, and cathedrals. The longer the French stayed, the more these forms of city life crumbled away, and at the end nothing was left but mindless, purposeless plundering.

The longer the French plundering continued, the more both Moscow's wealth and the plunderers' strength were destroyed. But the Russian plundering that accompanied the reoccupation of the capital—since it was carried out by such vast numbers and was directed at what still remained—quickly brought Moscow back to life. And just as water seeping into a dry sponge does not flow freely anymore, neither separately nor as a pool, so the army and population flooding into Moscow simply spread through the ruined city, which soaked them up, and the process of restoration began.

Besides the plunderers, all sorts of people—some drawn by curiosity, some by official duties, some by self-interest—homeowners, clergy, officials of every kind, tradesmen, artisans, and peasants—streamed into Moscow from every direction, like blood rushing to the heart.

Within a week, the peasants who had come with empty carts to haul away plunder were stopped by the authorities and forced to cart dead bodies out of the city instead. Other peasants, hearing what had happened to their neighbors, brought in cartloads of grain, hay, and charcoal, undercutting each other's prices until they fell below what they had been before. Crews of carpenters hoping for high wages arrived daily, and on all sides new houses were going up and burned ones were being repaired. Merchants set up shop in makeshift stalls. Restaurants and inns opened in fire-damaged buildings. The clergy resumed services in many of the churches that had escaped the fire. Donors contributed looted church furnishings that had been recovered. Officials set up their small offices with writing desks and filing cabinets in small rooms. The higher authorities and the police organized the distribution of goods left behind by the French. The owners of houses in which a great deal of property from other buildings had been gathered complained of the unfairness of having everything taken to the Faceted Palace, while others argued that the French had brought things from different houses to one location, and it was therefore unfair to let the owner of that house keep everything found in it. People cursed the police and bribed them; estimates for the rebuilding of government buildings were drawn up ten times their real cost; and appeals for help were made. The old count's Rostov spirit was alive, regenerating the city.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: At the end of January, Pierre arrived in Moscow and stayed in a wing of his house that hadn't been burned. He called on Count Rostopchin and some acquaintances who had returned, and planned to leave for Petersburg in two days. Everyone was celebrating the victory; the ruined capital was buzzing with life and energy. Pierre was welcomed everywhere; everyone wanted to see him and hear about what he'd been through. He felt warmly disposed toward all the people he met, but was now instinctively on guard with everyone, careful not to tie himself down in any way. To every question put to him—whether important or trivial—such as: Where would he live? Would he rebuild? When was he going to Petersburg? Could he deliver a certain parcel?—he would answer: "Yes, perhaps," or "I think so," and so on.

He had heard that the Rostovs were in Kostroma, but thoughts of Natasha rarely came to him. When they did, it was only as a pleasant memory of the distant past. He felt free not only from social obligations but from the feeling that he had chosen to impose on himself.

On the third day after his arrival, he learned from the Drubetskoys that Princess Mary was in Moscow. The death, suffering, and final days of Prince Andrew had often occupied Pierre's thoughts and now came back to him with fresh vividness. Having heard over dinner that Princess Mary was in Moscow and living in her own house on Vozdvizhenka Street, which had survived the fire, he went to see her that same evening.
On his way to the house, Pierre kept thinking about Prince Andrew, about their friendship, their various meetings, and especially their last one at Borodino.

"Is it possible that he died in that bitter state of mind? Is it possible the meaning of life was never revealed to him before he died?" Pierre wondered. He thought of Karataev and his death, and involuntarily began comparing the two men—so different, yet somehow alike because of the love Pierre had felt for both and because both had lived and both had died.

Pierre drove up to the old prince's house in a very serious mood. The house had survived the fire; it showed signs of damage but its general appearance was unchanged. The old footman who greeted Pierre wore a stern expression, as if wanting to make the visitor feel that the absence of the old prince had not disrupted the household routine. He told Pierre that the princess had retired to her rooms and received visitors on Sundays.
"Please announce me. Perhaps she'll see me," said Pierre.
"Yes, sir," the man replied. "Please step into the portrait gallery."

A few minutes later the footman returned with Dessalles, who brought word from the princess that she would be very glad to see Pierre if he would excuse the informality and come upstairs to her rooms.

In a rather low room lit by a single candle sat the princess, and with her another person dressed in black. Pierre remembered that the princess always had lady companions, but who they were and what they were like he never knew. "This must be one of her companions," he thought, glancing at the woman in black.
The princess rose quickly to meet him and held out her hand.

"Yes," she said, looking at his changed face after he had kissed her hand, "so this is how we meet again. He spoke of you even at the very end," she went on, turning her eyes from Pierre to her companion with a shyness that surprised him.
"I was so glad to hear you were safe. It was the first good news we'd received in a long time."
Again the princess glanced at her companion with even more unease and was about to add something, but Pierre interrupted her.

"Imagine—I knew nothing about him!" he said. "I thought he'd been killed. Everything I know I heard secondhand from others. I only know that he ended up with the Rostovs... What a strange coincidence!"

Pierre spoke quickly and with animation. He glanced once at the companion's face, saw her attentive, kindly gaze fixed on him, and—as often happens when you're talking—felt somehow that this companion in the black dress was a good, kind, wonderful person who wouldn't interfere with his heartfelt conversation with Princess Mary.
But when he mentioned the Rostovs, Princess Mary's face showed still greater embarrassment. She again glanced rapidly from Pierre's face to that of the woman in the black dress and said:
"Don't you really recognize her?"

Pierre looked again at the companion's pale, delicate face with its dark eyes and distinctive mouth, and something near to him, long forgotten and more than sweet, looked back at him from those attentive eyes.

"But no, it can't be!" he thought. "This stern, thin, pale face that looks so much older! It can't be her. It just reminds me of her." But at that moment Princess Mary said, "Natasha!" And with difficulty, with effort, like a rusty door being forced open, a smile appeared on the face with the attentive eyes, and through that opening door came a fragrance from a long-forgotten world of happiness that Pierre had lost all thought of—especially now. It breathed over him, engulfed him, and swallowed him whole. When she smiled, there could be no doubt: it was Natasha, and he loved her.

In that moment, Pierre involuntarily revealed—to her, to Princess Mary, and above all to himself—a secret he hadn't even known he carried. He flushed with joy and painful emotion. He tried to hide his feelings. But the more he tried, the more clearly—more clearly than any words could have conveyed—he revealed to himself, to her, and to Princess Mary that he loved her.

"No, it's just the surprise," Pierre thought. But as soon as he tried to resume the conversation he'd been having with Princess Mary, he glanced again at Natasha, and a deeper flush spread across his face, and an even stronger wave of joy and agitation seized his heart.

Pierre had failed to notice Natasha because he hadn't expected to see her there, but he had failed to recognize her because the change in her since he'd last seen her was enormous. She had grown thin and pale. But it wasn't the thinness and pallor that made her unrecognizable—she was unrecognizable in the first moment because on that face, whose eyes had always shone with suppressed delight in life, there was now—when he first entered and glanced at her—not the slightest shadow of a smile. There were only eyes, watchful, kind, and sadly questioning.
Pierre's confusion was not mirrored by any confusion on Natasha's part—only by the pleasure that softly lit up her whole face.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: "She's come to stay with me," said Princess Mary. "The count and countess will be here in a few days. The countess is in a terrible state, but Natasha herself needed to see a doctor. They made her come with me."
"Yes, is there a single family untouched by grief right now?" said Pierre, turning to Natasha. "You know it happened the very day we were rescued. I saw him. What a wonderful boy he was!"
Natasha looked at him, and by way of answer her eyes widened and lit up.
"What can anyone say or think of as consolation?" said Pierre. "Nothing! Why did such a splendid boy, so full of life, have to die?"
"Yes, in these times it would be hard to live without faith..." remarked Princess Mary.
"Yes, yes, that's absolutely true," Pierre quickly agreed.
"Why is it true?" Natasha asked, looking intently into Pierre's eyes.
"How can you ask why?" said Princess Mary. "Just the thought of what awaits us—"
Natasha, without waiting for Princess Mary to finish, looked inquiringly at Pierre again.
"And because," Pierre continued, "only someone who believes that God is watching over us can bear a loss like hers and... yours."
Natasha had already opened her mouth to speak but suddenly stopped. Pierre quickly turned away from her and addressed Princess Mary again, asking about his friend's last days.

Pierre's confusion had now almost vanished, but at the same time he felt that his freedom had completely disappeared. He felt there was now a judge of his every word and action whose judgment mattered to him more than the judgment of all the rest of the world. As he spoke he was constantly aware of the impression his words were making on Natasha. He didn't deliberately say things to please her, but whatever he said, he judged himself through her eyes.

Princess Mary—with the reluctance usual in such cases—began describing the state in which she had found Prince Andrew. But Pierre's face, quivering with emotion, his questions and eager, restless expression, gradually compelled her to go into details she shrank from calling up in her own mind.

"Yes, yes, and so...?" Pierre kept saying, leaning toward her with his whole body, listening intently. "Yes, yes... so he found peace and grew gentle? He had always sought one thing with all his soul—to be completely good—so he couldn't have been afraid of death. His flaws—if he had any—didn't come from within himself. So he did find peace?" Pierre asked. "What a blessing that he saw you again!" he added to Natasha.
Natasha's face twitched. She frowned and lowered her eyes for a moment. She hesitated briefly over whether to speak.

"Yes, that was happiness," she said in her quiet, deep voice. "For me it certainly was happiness." She paused. "And he... he said he was hoping for exactly that at the moment I came to see him..." Her voice broke.
Natasha blushed, pressed her clasped hands against her knees, and then, with a visible effort to control herself, lifted her head and began speaking rapidly.

"We knew nothing when we left Moscow. I didn't dare ask about him. Then suddenly Sonya told me he was traveling with us. I had no idea, couldn't imagine what state he was in—all I wanted was to see him, to be near him," she said, trembling with agitation.
And without letting them interrupt, she went on to tell what she had never told anyone—everything she had lived through during those three weeks of their journey and time in Yaroslavl.

Pierre listened with parted lips and eyes brimming with tears. As he listened, he thought not of Prince Andrew or of death, not of what she was telling him. He listened to her and felt nothing but compassion for the suffering she was going through now, in the telling.
Princess Mary, frowning in her effort to hold back tears, sat beside Natasha and heard for the first time the story of those last days of her brother's love and Natasha's.
Clearly, Natasha needed to tell this painful yet somehow joyful story.
She spoke, weaving the most trivial details together with the deepest secrets of her soul, and it seemed she could never finish. Several times she repeated the same thing twice.
Dessalles' voice was heard outside the door, asking whether little Nicholas might come in to say good night.
"Well, that's all—everything," said Natasha.
She jumped up quickly, almost ran to the door hidden behind curtains, bumped her head against it, and rushed from the room with a moan of either pain or grief.
Pierre gazed at the door through which she'd disappeared and couldn't understand why he suddenly felt completely alone in the world.
Princess Mary roused him from his thoughts by drawing his attention to her nephew, who had come into the room.

At that moment of emotional tenderness, young Nicholas's face—so like his father's—moved Pierre so deeply that after kissing the boy, he quickly stood up, pulled out his handkerchief, and walked to the window.
"No, Natasha and I sometimes don't go to sleep until after two, so please don't leave. I'll have supper brought. Go downstairs—we'll be right there."
Before Pierre left the room, Princess Mary told him: "This is the first time she's spoken about him like that."

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: Pierre was shown into the large, brightly lit dining room. A few minutes later he heard footsteps, and Princess Mary entered with Natasha. Natasha was calm, though a serious, solemn expression had settled on her face again. Princess Mary, Natasha, and Pierre all equally felt that awkwardness that usually follows a serious and deeply felt conversation. To continue from where you left off is impossible; to talk about trivial things feels wrong; yet to sit in silence is unpleasant, because you want to be talking and this silence feels like pretending. They went to the table in silence. The servants pulled back their chairs and pushed them in. Pierre unfolded his cold napkin and, deciding to break the silence, glanced at Natasha and Princess Mary. Both had clearly reached the same decision at the same moment: in both their eyes shone satisfaction with life and an acknowledgment that besides grief there is also joy.
"Do you drink vodka, Count?" asked Princess Mary, and those words instantly banished the shadows of the past. "Now tell us about yourself," she said. "We hear such incredible stories about you."

"Yes," Pierre replied with the smile of mild irony that had become habitual. "People even tell me about wonders I never dreamed of! Maria Abramovna invited me over and kept telling me what had happened to me, or what should have happened. Stepan Stepanych also taught me how I ought to tell my story. In general, I've noticed that being an interesting person is very convenient"—he smiled at Natasha—"because people invite me out and then tell me everything themselves."
Natasha smiled and was about to speak.
"We've been told," Princess Mary interrupted, "that you lost two million rubles in Moscow. Is that true?"
"But I'm three times richer than before," Pierre replied.
Though his financial position had actually worsened—he'd decided to pay his wife's debts and rebuild his houses—Pierre still maintained that he was three times richer than before.
"What I've definitely gained is freedom," he began seriously, but stopped, sensing this was too self-centered a topic.
"And are you rebuilding?"
"Yes. Savelich says I have to!"

"Tell me—you didn't know about the countess's death when you decided to stay in Moscow?" asked Princess Mary, and immediately blushed, realizing that her question, coming right after his mention of freedom, seemed to attribute motives to him that perhaps he didn't deserve.

"No," Pierre answered, clearly not finding the implied meaning of Princess Mary's words at all awkward. "I heard about it in Orel, and you can't imagine how it shook me. We weren't a model couple," he said quickly, glancing at Natasha and sensing in her curious look a question about what his attitude toward his wife had been. "But that death hit me terribly hard. When two people quarrel, both are always at fault, and your own guilt suddenly becomes unbearably heavy when the other person is no longer alive. And then, such a death... without friends, without comfort. I felt very, very sorry for her," he finished, and was pleased to notice an expression of glad approval on Natasha's face.
"Yes, and so you're an eligible bachelor again," said Princess Mary.
Pierre suddenly flushed crimson and for a long time tried not to look at Natasha. When he ventured a glance her way, her face was cold, stern, and—he thought—even contemptuous.
"And did you really see and speak to Napoleon, as we've been told?" asked Princess Mary.
Pierre laughed.
"No, not once! Everyone seems to think that being a prisoner of war means being Napoleon's guest. I not only never saw him, I never even heard anything about him—I was in much lower company!"
Supper was over, and Pierre, who had at first declined to talk about his captivity, was gradually drawn into doing so.
"But is it true that you stayed in Moscow to kill Napoleon?" Natasha asked with a slight smile. "I guessed it back then, when we met at the Sukharev Tower. Do you remember?"
Pierre admitted it was true, and from there Princess Mary's questions and especially Natasha's gradually led him into giving a detailed account of his adventures.

At first he spoke with the amused, gentle irony that had become his usual manner toward everyone and especially toward himself. But when he came to the horrors and sufferings he'd witnessed, he was carried away without realizing it and began speaking with the restrained emotion of someone reliving painful memories.

Princess Mary looked from Pierre to Natasha with a gentle smile. In the whole story she saw only Pierre and his goodness. Natasha, leaning on her elbow, her expression constantly changing with the story, watched Pierre without taking her eyes off him for a single moment, clearly living through everything he described along with him.
"You're not telling us everything—I'm sure you did something..." Natasha said, then paused and added, "something fine?"
Pierre continued. When he reached the execution, he tried to skip over the horrible details, but Natasha insisted that he leave nothing out.
Pierre began to speak about Karataev, then stopped. By this time he had risen from the table and was pacing the room, Natasha following him with her eyes. Then he added:
"No, you can't understand what I learned from that uneducated man—that simple fellow."
"Yes, yes, go on!" said Natasha. "Where is he?"
"They killed him almost before my eyes."
And Pierre, his voice trembling the whole time, went on to tell about the last days of their retreat, Karataev's illness, and his death.

He told his story as he had never recalled it before. He now seemed to see a new meaning in everything he'd been through. And now, telling it all to Natasha, he experienced that pleasure a man feels when women listen to him—not clever women who, when they listen, try to either memorize what they hear in order to enrich their own minds and then repeat it, or to fit what they're told into their own framework and contribute their own clever comments worked out in their own little mental world—but the pleasure that comes from real women, gifted with the ability to select and absorb all that is best in what a man reveals of himself. Natasha, without knowing it, was all attention: she didn't miss a word, a tremor in his voice, a glance, a twitch of his facial muscles, or a gesture. She caught each word on the fly and carried it straight to her open heart, intuiting the mysterious meaning of Pierre's entire spiritual journey.

Princess Mary understood his story and felt for him, but she saw something else now that absorbed all her attention. She saw the possibility of love and happiness between Natasha and Pierre, and this thought, occurring to her for the first time, filled her heart with joy.
It was three in the morning. The servants came in with sad, stern faces to change the candles, but nobody noticed them.

Pierre finished his story. Natasha continued to look at him intently with bright, attentive, animated eyes, as if trying to understand something more that he had perhaps left untold. Pierre, in shy, happy confusion, kept glancing at her and trying to think of something to say that might shift the conversation to a different subject. He began speaking, and Princess Mary too looked at Natasha. She had often been near a woman in love and had seen that look before; she recognized it now on Natasha's face, and she understood.

"People talk about misfortunes and suffering," Pierre said, "but if right now someone asked me, 'Would you rather be what you were before you were taken prisoner, or go through it all again?'—for God's sake, let me go through captivity again and eat horseflesh! We imagine that the moment we're knocked out of our usual track, everything is lost. But that's just when something new and good begins. As long as there's life, there's happiness. There's a great deal, a great deal ahead of us. I'm saying this to you," he added, turning to Natasha.
"Yes, yes," she said, answering something quite different. "I too would wish for nothing but to live it all over from the beginning."
Pierre looked at her intently.
"Yes, and nothing more," said Natasha.
"It's not true, not true!" Pierre cried. "I'm not to blame for being alive and wanting to live—and neither are you!"
Suddenly Natasha bent her head, covered her face with her hands, and began to cry.
"What is it, Natasha?" said Princess Mary.
"Nothing, nothing." She smiled at Pierre through her tears. "Good night! It's time for bed."
Pierre got up and said goodbye.
Princess Mary and Natasha met as usual in the bedroom. They talked about what Pierre had told them. Princess Mary didn't say what she thought of Pierre, and Natasha didn't mention him either.
"Well, good night, Mary!" said Natasha. "Do you know, I'm often afraid that by not talking about him"—she meant Prince Andrew—"for fear of not doing justice to our feelings, we're forgetting him."
Princess Mary sighed deeply, acknowledging the justice of Natasha's remark, but didn't say so in words.
"Is it possible to forget?" she said.

"It did me so much good to tell everything today. It was hard and painful, but good—very good!" said Natasha. "I'm sure he truly loved him. That's why I told him... Was it all right?" she added, suddenly blushing.
"You mean telling Pierre? Oh yes. What a wonderful man he is!" said Princess Mary.

"Do you know, Mary..." Natasha suddenly said with a mischievous smile—the kind Princess Mary hadn't seen on her face for a long time—"he's somehow grown so clean, smooth, and fresh—as if he'd just come out of a bath. Don't you think? Out of a moral bath. Right?"
"Yes," Princess Mary replied. "He's improved enormously."
"With a short coat and his hair cropped; just as if—well, just as if he'd come straight from the bath... Papa used to—"
"I understand why he"—meaning Prince Andrew—"loved no one so much as him," said Princess Mary.
"Yes, and yet he's completely different from him. People say men become friends when they're very different. That must be true. He really is nothing like him—in anything."
"Yes, but he's wonderful."
"Well, good night," said Natasha.
And the same mischievous smile lingered on her face for a long time, as if it had been forgotten there.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: It was a long time before Pierre could fall asleep that night. He paced up and down his room, now frowning over a difficult problem, now suddenly shrugging his shoulders and wincing, now smiling happily.

He was thinking about Prince Andrew, about Natasha, about their love—one moment jealous of her past, the next reproaching himself for that feeling. It was already six in the morning and he still paced the room.

"Well, what's to be done if there's no way around it? What can I do? Obviously this is how it has to be," he told himself, and hastily undressing, he got into bed—happy and agitated, but free of hesitation or indecision.
"Strange and impossible as such happiness seems, I must do everything I can so that she and I may become husband and wife," he told himself.
A few days earlier Pierre had decided to leave for Petersburg on Friday. When he woke on Thursday, Savelich came to ask about packing for the trip.

"What—Petersburg? What is Petersburg? Who's in Petersburg?" he asked, though only of himself. "Oh yes, a long time ago—before all this happened—I did mean to go to Petersburg for some reason," he reflected. "Why? But maybe I will go... What a good, considerate fellow he is!" he thought, looking at Savelich. "And what a nice smile!"
"Well, Savelich, do you still not want to accept your freedom?" Pierre asked him.
"What good is freedom to me, your excellency? We lived under the late count—God rest his soul!—and we've lived under you too, and never been mistreated."
"And your children?"
"The children will be fine just the same. With masters like you, anyone can get along."
"But what about my heirs?" said Pierre. "Suppose I suddenly get married... it could happen," he added with an involuntary smile.
"If I may say so, your excellency, that would be a very good thing."
"He thinks it's so easy," Pierre thought. "He doesn't know how terrifying it is, how dangerous. Too soon or too late... it's terrifying!"
"So what are your orders? Are you leaving tomorrow?" asked Savelich.

"No, I'll put it off a bit. I'll tell you later. Forgive me for the trouble I've put you through," said Pierre, and seeing Savelich smile, he thought: "How strange it is that he doesn't know there is no Petersburg for me now, and that this has to be settled first. But he probably does know and is just pretending. Should I talk to him about it? No, some other time."
At breakfast, Pierre told the princess—his cousin—that he'd been to see Princess Mary the day before and had met there—"Guess who? Natasha Rostova!"
The princess seemed to find this no more remarkable than if he'd seen some Anna Semyonovna.
"Do you know her?" Pierre asked.
"I've seen the princess," she replied. "I heard they were arranging a match for her with young Rostov. That would be very good for the Rostovs—they're said to be completely ruined."
"No—I mean, do you know Natasha Rostova?"
"I heard about that business of hers at the time. It was very unfortunate."
"She either doesn't understand or she's pretending," Pierre thought. "Better not say anything to her either."
The princess had also prepared provisions for Pierre's journey.
"How kind they all are," Pierre thought. "What's amazing is that they bother with these things now, when none of it could matter to them anymore. And all for me!"
That same day the Chief of Police came to Pierre, inviting him to send a representative to the Faceted Palace to collect property that was being returned to its owners.

"And this man too," thought Pierre, studying the Chief of Police's face. "What a fine, good-looking officer, and how kind. Think of him bothering with such trifles right now! And people actually say he's dishonest and takes bribes. What nonsense! And besides, why shouldn't he take bribes? That's how he was raised. Everyone does it. But what a pleasant, kind face, and how he smiles as he looks at me!"
Pierre went to Princess Mary's for dinner.

As he drove through the streets past burned-out houses, he was struck by the beauty of those ruins. The chimney stacks and crumbling walls, stretching out to conceal one another, reminded him of the Rhine and the Colosseum. The cab drivers and passengers he passed, the carpenters working on frames for new buildings, the women selling goods at the street corners—all looked at him with cheerful, beaming faces that seemed to say: "Ah, here he is! Let's see what comes of this!"

At the entrance to Princess Mary's house, Pierre felt unsure whether he had really been there the night before, really seen Natasha and talked with her. "Maybe I imagined it. Maybe I'll go in and find no one." But he had barely entered the room when he felt her presence—felt it through the sudden loss of his freedom. She was wearing the same black dress with soft folds, and her hair was arranged the same way as the evening before, but she was completely different. If she had looked like this the night before when he entered the room, he couldn't have failed to recognize her for a single instant.
She was as he had known her almost as a child and later as Prince Andrew's fiancée. A bright, questioning light shone in her eyes, and her face wore a friendly and strangely playful expression.
Pierre stayed for dinner and would have spent the whole evening there, but Princess Mary was going to vespers and Pierre left with her.

The next day he came early, stayed for dinner, and spent the whole evening. Though Princess Mary and Natasha were clearly glad to see their visitor, and though all of Pierre's interest was now centered on that house, by evening they had talked over everything and the conversation kept moving between those insignificant topics that arise when people want to keep talking but can't find new subjects. Pierre stayed so late that Princess Mary and Natasha kept exchanging glances, obviously waiting for him to leave. Pierre saw this but couldn't bring himself to go. He felt heavy and awkward, but still sat on because he simply couldn't get up and leave.
Princess Mary, foreseeing no end to it, was the first to rise and, complaining of a headache, began to say good night.
"So you're going to Petersburg tomorrow?" she asked.

"No, I'm not going," Pierre replied hastily, in a surprised, almost offended tone. "Yes... no... to Petersburg? Tomorrow—but I won't say goodbye yet. I'll come by in case you have any errands for me," he said, standing before Princess Mary, flushing and fidgeting, not leaving.

Natasha gave him her hand and left the room. Princess Mary, instead of going, sank into an armchair and fixed her deep, radiant eyes on him with a look that was both stern and intent. The weariness she'd plainly shown before had completely vanished. With a deep, heavy sigh she seemed to be preparing herself for a long conversation.
The instant Natasha left, Pierre's awkwardness and confusion disappeared and were replaced by eager excitement. He quickly pulled a chair up to Princess Mary.

"Yes, I wanted to tell you," he said, responding to her look as if she had spoken. "Princess, help me! What should I do? Can I hope? Princess, my dear friend, listen! I know everything. I know I'm not worthy of her, I know it's impossible to talk about it now. But I want to be her brother. No, I don't... I can't..."
He paused and rubbed his face and eyes with his hands.

"Well," he went on, clearly struggling for self-control and coherence. "I don't know when I first began to love her, but I've loved her and her alone all my life, and I love her so much that I can't imagine life without her. I can't ask for her hand right now, but the thought that maybe she could be mine, and that I might miss that chance... that chance... is terrible. Tell me—can I hope? Tell me, what should I do? Dear princess!" he said after a brief pause, touching her hand when she didn't reply.
"I'm thinking about what you've told me," Princess Mary answered. "This is what I'll say. You're right that to speak to her of love at present—"

Princess Mary stopped. She'd been about to say that speaking of love was impossible, but she stopped because she had seen from the sudden change in Natasha two days ago that Natasha would not only not be hurt if Pierre spoke of his love, but that it was the one thing she wanted.
"To speak to her now wouldn't do," the princess said all the same.
"But what am I to do?"
"Leave it to me," said Princess Mary. "I know..."
Pierre was looking into Princess Mary's eyes.
"Well?... Well?..." he said.
"I know that she loves... will love you," Princess Mary corrected herself.
Before the words were out, Pierre had sprung up and seized Princess Mary's hand with a frightened expression.
"What makes you think so? You think I can hope? You think—?"
"Yes, I think so," said Princess Mary with a smile. "Write to her parents, and leave it to me. I'll tell her when the time is right. I want this to happen, and my heart tells me it will."
"No, it can't be! How happy I am! But it can't be... How happy I am! No, it can't be!" Pierre kept saying as he kissed Princess Mary's hands.
"Go to Petersburg—that would be best. And I'll write to you," she said.
"To Petersburg? Go there? Very well, I'll go. But may I come again tomorrow?"

The next day Pierre came to say goodbye. Natasha was less animated than the day before; but as he looked at her, Pierre sometimes felt as if he were vanishing, as if neither he nor she existed anymore, that nothing existed but happiness. "Can this be real? No, it can't," he told himself at every glance, every gesture, every word that filled his heart with joy.
When, saying goodbye, he took her thin, slender hand, he couldn't help holding it a little longer in his.

"Is it possible that this hand, this face, those eyes—all this treasure of feminine charm, so strange to me now—is it possible that one day it will be mine forever, as familiar as I am to myself?... No, that's impossible!"
"Goodbye, Count," she said aloud. "I'll very much look forward to your return," she added in a whisper.

And these simple words, her look, and the expression on her face that accompanied them formed, for two months, the subject of inexhaustible memories, interpretations, and happy meditations for Pierre. "'I'll very much look forward to your return.' How did she say it? How did she look? What did she mean? What was the look in her eyes?" And his recalled impression was so vivid that it seemed to happen right then, and he would smile all over again.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: There was nothing in Pierre's soul now that resembled what had troubled him during his courtship of Helene.

He did not repeat to himself with a sickening feeling of shame the words he had spoken, or think: "Oh, why didn't I say that?" and "Whatever made me say 'I love you'?" On the contrary, he now replayed in his mind every word he or Natasha had said, down to the smallest detail of her face and smile, and wanted to add nothing and take nothing away. He only wished he could say it all again. "Was it right when she said, 'Leave it to me'? Did she really see into my soul? Yes, she did," Pierre told himself. "And she's wonderful! 'Something fine!'—how she said it! And her eyes. And how she blushed when she said: 'I'll very much look forward to your return'... She loves me. Yes, she loves me." That was the only worry that often troubled Pierre. He made no plans now. The happiness before him seemed so inconceivable that if only he could reach it, there would be nothing beyond. Everything ended there.

That was the only doubt that often troubled Pierre. He made no plans now. The happiness before him seemed so inconceivable that if only he could reach it, it would be the end of everything. Nothing would come after.

A joyful, unexpected frenzy—which he had thought himself incapable of—possessed him.
