The whole meaning of life, not for him alone but for the whole world, seemed to him centered in his love and the possibility of being loved by her. At times everyone seemed to him to be occupied with one thing only—his future happiness. Sometimes it seemed to him that everyone was as happy as he was, and merely tried to hide that happiness by pretending to be busy with other things. In every word and gesture he saw hints of his own happiness. He often startled people who met him by his meaningful, joyful looks and smiles, which seemed to express a secret understanding between them. But when he realized that people might not know about his happiness, he pitied them with all his heart and felt the urge to somehow explain to them that everything they were occupied with was absolute nonsense and trivialities not worth thinking about.

When people suggested he enter the civil service, or when the war or general political affairs were discussed on the assumption that everyone's well-being depended on some particular turn of events, he would listen with his mild, compassionate smile, and startle everyone with his strange comments. But those who thought they understood Pierre, as well as those who didn't, all felt at this time that he was a delightful and extraordinary person—generous, gentle, clever, cheerful, and magnanimous.

When dealing with the affairs and papers of his dead wife, her memory stirred in him nothing but pity that she had never known the joy he now knew. Prince Vasili, who had gotten a new post and some fresh decorations and was especially proud of himself just then, struck Pierre as a touching, kind, and pitiable old man.

Often in later life Pierre recalled this period of blissful madness. All the views he formed of people and situations during this time remained true for him always. He not only never renounced them later, but when he was in doubt or felt conflicted, he would ask himself what he would have thought at that time, and that perspective never failed him.

"I may have seemed strange and eccentric then," he thought, "but I wasn't as crazy as it looked. On the contrary, I was wiser and had more insight then than at any other time, and I understood everything worth understanding in life, because... because I was happy."

Pierre's madness consisted in this: he no longer waited, as he once did, to discover personal qualities—what he called "good qualities"—in people before loving them. His heart was now overflowing with love, and by loving people without cause, he discovered undeniable reasons to love them.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: After Pierre's departure that first evening, when Natasha had said to Princess Mary with a mischievous, mocking smile: "He looks just—yes, just as if he'd come out of a Russian bath, in a short coat and with his hair cropped"—from that moment something hidden and unknown to her but irresistible awoke in Natasha's soul.

Everything about her—her face, her walk, her look, her voice—was suddenly changed. To her own surprise, a force of life and a hope of happiness rose to the surface and demanded to be satisfied. From that evening she seemed to have forgotten everything that had happened to her. She never again complained about her situation, never said a word about the past, and was no longer afraid to make cheerful plans for the future. She spoke little of Pierre, but when Princess Mary mentioned him, a long-extinguished light flickered in her eyes and her lips curved in a strange smile.

The change that took place in Natasha at first surprised Princess Mary, but when she understood what it meant, it grieved her. "Can she have loved my brother so little that she could forget him so quickly?" she thought when she reflected on the change. But when she was with Natasha, she wasn't angry with her and didn't reproach her. The awakened force of life that had taken hold of Natasha was clearly so powerful and beyond her control that Princess Mary felt she had no right to reproach her, even in her own heart.
Natasha gave herself up so fully and openly to this new feeling that she didn't even try to hide the fact that she was no longer sad but bright and cheerful.
When Princess Mary returned to her room after her late-night conversation with Pierre, Natasha met her at the door.
"He's spoken? Yes? He has spoken?" she repeated.
And a joyful yet pitiful expression—which seemed to beg forgiveness for her joy—settled on Natasha's face.
"I wanted to listen at the door, but I knew you'd tell me."
However touching the look Natasha gave her seemed to Princess Mary, and however sorry she felt seeing her excitement, these words pained her for a moment. She remembered her brother and his love.
"But what can be done? She can't help it," the princess thought.
And with a sad, somewhat stern expression she told Natasha everything Pierre had said. Hearing that he was going to Petersburg, Natasha was stunned.
"To Petersburg!" she repeated, as if unable to understand.
But noticing the grieved look on Princess Mary's face, she guessed the reason for that sadness and suddenly began to cry.
"Mary," she said, "tell me what I should do! I'm afraid of being bad. Whatever you tell me, I'll do. Tell me..."
"You love him?"
"Yes," Natasha whispered.
"Then why are you crying? I'm happy for you," said Princess Mary, who—because of those tears—had already quite forgiven Natasha's joy.
"It won't be right away—someday. Just think how wonderful it will be when I'm his wife and you marry Nicholas!"
"Natasha, I've asked you not to talk about that. Let's talk about you."
They were silent for a while.
"But why go to Petersburg?" Natasha suddenly asked, and quickly answered her own question. "No, no—he has to... Yes, Mary, he has to."

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Seven years had passed. The storm-tossed sea of European history had subsided within its shores and seemed to have grown calm. But the mysterious forces that move humanity—mysterious because the laws governing them are unknown to us—continued to operate.

Though the surface of the sea of history appeared motionless, the movement of humanity went on as ceaselessly as the flow of time. Various groups of people formed and dissolved, the formation and dissolution of kingdoms and displacements of peoples were in preparation.

The sea of history was no longer driven violently from shore to shore as before. It was churning in its depths. Historical figures were no longer carried by the waves from one shore to another. They now seemed to spin in place. Historical figures who had formerly commanded armies and directed the movement of masses through wars, campaigns, and battles now guided the surging masses through political and diplomatic maneuvers, laws, and treaties.
Historians call this activity of historical figures "the reaction."

In describing this period, they sternly condemn the historical figures who, in their view, caused what they call the reaction. All the prominent people of that era—from Alexander and Napoleon to Madame de Stael, Photius, Schelling, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others—are arraigned before their stern tribunal and acquitted or condemned according to whether they promoted progress or reaction.

According to these accounts, a reaction took place in Russia too at this time, and the chief culprit was Alexander I—the same man who, according to these same historians, was the chief cause of the liberal reforms at the start of his reign, the savior of Russia, and the hero of Europe. Yet in present-day Russian literature, from schoolboy essayists to serious historians, there is no one who does not criticize Alexander for the things he supposedly did wrong during this period.
There is no one in Russian literature now, from schoolboy essayists to learned historians, who does not take a shot at Alexander for his mistakes during this phase of his reign.

"He should have acted this way, not that way. In this case he did well; in that case, badly. He was admirable at the start of his reign and during 1812, but was wrong to give a constitution to Poland, create the Holy Alliance, empower Arakcheyev, encourage Golitsyn and mysticism, and then encourage Shishkov and Photius. He was wrong to interfere with the army's front-line administration; he was wrong to disband the Semyonovsky regiment, and so on and so on."
It would take a dozen pages to list all the criticisms historians make of him, based on their knowledge of what is good for humanity.
What do these criticisms mean?

Don't the very actions for which historians praise Alexander I—the liberal reforms at the start of his reign, the struggle with Napoleon, the firmness he showed in 1812, and the campaign of 1813—flow from the same sources, the same conditions of birth, education, and life that shaped Alexander's personality and produced the actions for which historians blame him, such as the Holy Alliance, the restoration of Poland, and the reaction of the 1820s?
What is the real substance of these criticisms?

It lies in the fact that a historical figure like Alexander I, standing at the highest possible pinnacle of human power, in the blinding light of history focused upon him—exposed to the strongest influences imaginable: the intrigues, flattery, and self-deception inseparable from power, and feeling a responsibility for everything happening in Europe at every moment of his life—proved to be, not fifty years ago but today, not a person of particularly virtuous character. That is what the historians' criticisms amount to.

But even if we assume that Alexander was mistaken fifty years ago in his idea of what was good for the people, we must also assume that the historian who judges him will, after some time, also turn out to be wrong in his understanding of what is good for humanity. This assumption is all the more natural and inevitable because the development of history shows us that every year, with every new writer, what we consider good for humanity changes. What once seemed good—giving Poland a constitution and forming the Holy Alliance—is later regarded as harmful. What seems harmful—the Napoleonic wars, the spread of revolutionary ideas—is later recognized as good.

Alexander's activity, or Napoleon's, cannot be called useful or harmful, because we cannot say what it was useful or harmful for. If someone dislikes it, that is only because it doesn't match their limited understanding of what is good. Whether I see the preservation of my father's house in Moscow in 1812 as good, or the glory of the Russian army, or the prosperity of Petersburg's university or Poland's freedom, or Russia's greatness, or Europe's balance of power, or a certain kind of European civilization called "progress"—I must acknowledge that the activity of any historical figure had, besides these aims, other aims more broadly and universally human that are beyond my grasp.

But let us suppose that what is called science can reconcile all contradictions and possesses an unchanging standard of good and bad by which to judge historical characters and events; let us say that Alexander could have done everything differently; let us even say that—guided by those who criticize him, who claim to know the ultimate goal of humanity's movement—he could have followed the program of nationalism, freedom, equality, and progress (for there seems to be no other) that his present-day critics would prescribe for him. Let us assume all that was possible. What then would have become of the activity of all the people who opposed the direction that the government was taking at that time? Their activity would not have existed; there would have been no life; there would have been nothing.
If we accept that human life can be governed by reason, then the very possibility of life is destroyed.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: If we assume, as historians do, that great men lead humanity toward the attainment of certain goals—the greatness of Russia or of France, the balance of power in Europe, the spread of revolutionary ideas, general progress, or anything else—then it is impossible to explain the facts of history without resorting to the concepts of "chance" and "genius."

If the goal of the European wars at the start of the nineteenth century had been the expansion of Russia, that goal could have been achieved without all the preceding wars and without the invasion. If the goal had been the expansion of France, that goal could have been reached without the Revolution and without the Empire. If the goal had been the spread of ideas, the printing press would have accomplished that far better than soldiers. If the goal had been the progress of civilization, one can easily imagine that there were other paths to spreading civilization besides the destruction of people and their wealth.
Why did it happen this way and not some other?
Because it just happened that way! "Chance created the situation; genius made use of it," says history.
But what is chance? What is genius?

The words "chance" and "genius" do not refer to anything that actually exists, and therefore cannot be defined. They only indicate a certain stage in our understanding of events. I don't know why a certain event occurs; I think I cannot know; so I don't try to know, and I say: "chance." I see a force producing effects beyond the scope of ordinary human powers; I don't understand why this happens, and I say: "genius."

To a flock of sheep, the ram that the shepherd drives each evening into a special pen to be fattened—growing twice as fat as the rest—must seem like a genius. And it must appear an astonishing combination of genius with a whole series of extraordinary coincidences that this ram, instead of entering the common pen each evening, ends up in a special one where he gets extra oats, and that this particular ram, swelling with fat, is eventually killed for mutton.

But the sheep only need to stop assuming that everything happening to them is designed for their sheepish purposes; they only need to admit that what happens to them may serve purposes beyond their understanding—and they will immediately see a unity and coherence in what is being done to the fattened ram. Even if they don't know why he's being fattened, at least they'll know that everything that happens to the ram doesn't happen by accident, and they'll have no need for the concepts of "chance" or "genius."

Only by giving up our claim to understand some immediately obvious purpose, and accepting that the ultimate purpose is beyond our grasp, can we see the chain of experiences in the lives of historical figures and perceive the cause of the effect they produce, which is disproportionate to their ordinary human abilities. Only then will we have no need for the words "chance" and "genius."

We need only acknowledge that we do not know the purpose of the European upheavals, and that we only know the facts—that is, the killings, first in France, then in Italy, Africa, Prussia, Austria, Spain, and Russia—and that the movements from west to east and from east to west form the essential substance of those events. Only then will we no longer need to see something exceptional—some stroke of genius—in the characters of Napoleon and Alexander, and will no longer need to attribute the event to some individual's specific quality.

By abandoning any claim to knowledge of the ultimate purpose, we will clearly see that just as it's impossible to imagine a blossom or seed better suited to a plant than the one it actually produces, so too it's impossible to imagine any two people more perfectly adapted, down to the smallest detail, to fulfill the roles that Napoleon and Alexander played.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The fundamental significance of the European events at the start of the nineteenth century lies in the mass movement of European peoples from west to east and then from east to west. The initial impulse for the westward movement came from France. For the French to unite into a military force capable of invading the East, they first needed to combine into a sufficiently large group, renounce their established customs and traditions, and—through the process of war and campaigning—develop a leader who could stand at the head of the coming military movement.

And beginning with the French Revolution, the old, inadequately large group was destroyed along with its old customs and traditions. Step by step, a larger group was formed with new customs and traditions, and a man was produced who would stand at the head of that group and of the coming westward-to-eastward movement.

A man without convictions, without habits, without traditions, without a name, and not even a Frenchman emerges—by what seem the strangest coincidences—from the turmoil of French political parties. Without joining any of them, he is carried forward to a prominent position.

His colleagues' incompetence, his opponents' weakness and insignificance, the brazenness of his lies, and his dazzling, self-confident narrow-mindedness raise him to the head of the army. The brilliant quality of the soldiers in the Italian campaign, his opponents' reluctance to fight, and his own childish boldness and self-assurance win him military glory. Countless so-called coincidences accompany him everywhere. The disfavor into which he falls with the rulers of France works in his favor. His attempts to change his career path fail: he isn't accepted into the Russian army, and his appointment to Turkey comes to nothing.

On his return from Italy he finds the government in Paris dissolving; everyone in it is being inevitably swept aside and destroyed. And by coincidence, an escape from this dangerous position presents itself in the form of a pointless, purposeless expedition to Africa. Again, the same so-called coincidences attend him. The impregnable island of Malta surrenders without a shot; his most reckless orders are crowned with success. The enemy fleet, which later won't let a single boat slip past, now lets an entire army through. In Africa, a series of crimes are committed against the practically defenseless inhabitants. And the men who commit these crimes, especially their leader, convince themselves that this is wonderful, that this is glory, that it resembles Caesar and Alexander the Great, and that it is fine.

This ideal of glory and greatness—which consists not merely in considering nothing you do to be wrong but in taking pride in every crime you commit, attributing to it an incomprehensible supernatural significance—this ideal, destined to guide this man and all who follow him, takes full shape in Africa. Whatever he does succeeds. The plague doesn't touch him. The cruelty of massacring prisoners isn't held against him. His childishly reckless, unprovoked, and ignoble departure from Africa—abandoning his comrades in misfortune—is counted in his favor, and again the enemy fleet twice lets him slip through. When, completely intoxicated by the crimes he has so successfully committed, he arrives in Paris with no plan at all, the dissolution of the Republican government, which could have swept him away a year earlier, has now gone so far that his mere presence there, standing outside any party, can only elevate him.
He had no plan; he was afraid of everything; but the parties seized upon him and demanded his participation.
He alone—with his ideal of glory and greatness forged in Italy and Egypt, his insane self-worship, his boldness in crime and frankness in lying—he alone could justify what had to be done.

He is needed for the role that awaits him, and so—almost against his will, despite his indecision, his lack of a plan, and all his mistakes—he is drawn into a conspiracy to seize power, and the conspiracy succeeds.

He is pushed into a session of the legislature. In a panic, he tries to flee, thinking himself finished. He pretends to faint and says senseless things that should have ruined him. But the once proud and shrewd rulers of France—feeling that their role is played out—are even more confused than he is, and fail to say the words they need to say to maintain their power and destroy him.

Chance—millions of chances—give him power, and all people, as if by common agreement, work to confirm that power. Chance shapes the characters of France's rulers, who submit to him; chance shapes the character of Russia's Paul I, who recognizes his authority; chance produces a plot against him that not only fails to harm him but strengthens his power. Chance throws the Duke of Enghien into his hands and accidentally compels him to kill him, thereby convincing the crowd more effectively than any other means that he has the right to rule, since he possesses the power and the will to use it. Chance arranges it so that though he strains every nerve to prepare an expedition against England—which would certainly have destroyed him—he never carries out that plan, and instead falls upon Mack and the Austrians, who surrender without a battle. Chance and genius give him victory after victory. Everything serves him. He is invincible.

Like probing movements before a battle, the western forces push eastward several times—in 1805, 1806, 1807, and 1809—gathering strength and growing. In 1811, the group of people formed in France fuses into one enormous mass with the peoples of central Europe. As this group grows, the man who stands at its head gains more and more justification for his power. During those ten years of preparation, this man forms connections with all the crowned heads of Europe. The rulers of the world, stripped naked by this man, try to oppose him with the ideals of reason and justice. But these seem weak and ridiculous before his ideal of glory and greatness, which makes no sense yet still exerts its force. In their efforts to show him that his plans are wrong, these rulers eagerly humiliate themselves before him. The King of Prussia sends his wife to seek the great man's mercy; the Emperor of Austria considers it a favor that this man accepts the daughter of the Kaisers into his bed. The Pope, guardian of all that the nations hold sacred, uses religion to promote the great man's power. It is not so much Napoleon who prepares himself for the fulfillment of his role as everyone around him who prepares him for the immense responsibility he is about to bear. There is no act, no crime or petty deception, that he commits which is not immediately reflected in the mouths of those around him as a great deed.

The invasion pushes east and reaches its ultimate goal—Moscow. The city is taken; the Russian army suffers heavier losses than the enemy had suffered in any previous war from Austerlitz to Wagram. But suddenly, instead of those strokes of chance and genius that had accompanied him so consistently through an unbroken series of successes toward his intended goal, an endless series of reverse chances occurs—from the cold he catches at Borodino to the sparks that set Moscow ablaze. And instead of genius, stupidity and cowardice appear, without parallel.
The invaders flee, turn back, flee again, and now all the chances work not for Napoleon but always against him.

A counter-movement then takes place from east to west, remarkably resembling the earlier movement from west to east. There are preliminary drives from east to west—similar to the probing movements of 1805, 1807, and 1809—before the great westward surge. There is the same fusion of smaller groups into an enormous one; the same rallying of the peoples of central Europe to the movement; the same hesitation midway; and the same increasing velocity as the goal is approached.

Paris, the final destination, is reached. Napoleon's government and army are destroyed. Napoleon himself no longer matters; all his actions are clearly pitiful and contemptible. But once again an inexplicable stroke of chance occurs. The allies detest Napoleon, in whom they see the cause of their suffering. Stripped of power and authority, exposed as a schemer and villain, he should have seemed to them what he had seemed ten years before and would seem a year later—an outlaw beyond the law. But by some strange coincidence, no one sees this. His role is not yet over. The man who ten years earlier, and one year later, was considered a brigand beyond the law is sent to an island two days' sail from France, which is given to him as his personal domain, with guards and millions that are paid to him for some unknown reason.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: The flood of nations begins to subside into its normal channels. The waves of the great movement settle, and on the calm surface eddies form in which the diplomats float, imagining that it was they who caused the flood to recede.

But the smooth sea suddenly becomes turbulent again. The diplomats think their disagreements are causing this new surge; they expect war between their sovereigns; the situation seems unsolvable. But the wave they feel rising is not coming from where they expect. It rises again from the same source—from Paris. The last backwash of the movement from the west occurs: a backwash that will resolve the apparently insoluble diplomatic difficulties and put an end to the military movement of that era.

The man who had devastated France returns to France alone, without any conspiracy and without soldiers. Any guard could arrest him, but by some strange chance no one does, and everyone rapturously greets the man they had cursed the day before and would curse again within a month.
This man is still needed to justify the final collective act.
That act is performed.
The last role is played. The actor is told to take off his costume and wash off his makeup: he won't be needed anymore.

And some years pass during which this man plays a pitiful comedy alone on his island, scheming and lying to justify his actions when justification is no longer needed, and showing the whole world what it was that people had mistaken for strength when an unseen hand was guiding him.
The stage manager, having brought the drama to its close and stripped the actor, shows him to us.
"See what you believed in! This is he! Do you see now that it was not he but I who moved you?"
But dazed by the force of the movement, it was a long time before people understood this.
Still greater coherence and inevitability can be seen in the life of Alexander I, the man who stood at the head of the counter-movement from east to west.
What qualities were needed in the man who was to stand at the head of that movement from east to west, overshadowing all others?

What was needed was a sense of justice and sympathy with European affairs—but a broad sympathy, not dulled by petty interests; a moral superiority over the other sovereigns of the day; a mild and attractive personality; and a personal grievance against Napoleon. And all of this was present in Alexander I; all of it had been prepared by countless so-called coincidences throughout his earlier life: his upbringing, his liberal beginnings, the advisors who surrounded him, Austerlitz, Tilsit, and Erfurt.

During the national war he was inactive because he was not needed. But as soon as the necessity for a general European war arose, he appeared in his place at the right moment and—uniting the nations of Europe—led them to the goal.
The goal is reached. After the final war of 1815, Alexander possesses all possible power. How does he use it?

Alexander I—the peacemaker of Europe, the man who from his youth had striven only for his people's welfare, the originator of liberal reforms in his own country—now that he seemed to possess the power and therefore the ability to bring about the welfare of his people, while Napoleon in exile was making plans that would infallibly have made nations happy had he been able to carry them out—Alexander, having fulfilled his mission and feeling the hand of God upon him, suddenly recognizes the insignificance of that apparent power, turns away from it, hands it over to despicable men, and says only:
"Not unto us, not unto us, but unto Thy name!... I too am just a man like the rest of you. Let me live like a man and think of my soul and of God."

Just as the sun and each atom of light is a sphere complete in itself, yet at the same time only a part of a whole too vast for man to comprehend, so each individual carries within himself his own aims while serving a larger purpose that lies beyond human understanding.

A bee landing on a flower stings a child. And the child is afraid of bees and declares that bees exist to sting people. A poet admires the bee drinking nectar from the flower and says bees exist to gather the fragrance of flowers. A beekeeper, noticing that the bee collects pollen and brings it to the hive, says that the bee's purpose is to gather honey. Another beekeeper, who has studied the life of the swarm more closely, says the bee gathers pollen to feed the young and rear a queen—that its purpose is the continuation of the species. A botanist notices that the pollen-dusted bee fertilizes the pistil of a flower, and he sees this as the bee's purpose. Another, observing the migration of plants, sees that the bee helps in this process, and he may say that this is the bee's purpose. But the ultimate purpose of the bee is not limited to any single one of these things that human reason can discover. The higher the human intellect rises in the discovery of such purposes, the more obvious it becomes that the ultimate purpose is beyond our reach.
All that is accessible to us is the relationship between the life of the bee and other forms of life. And so it is with the purpose of historical figures and nations.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: Natasha's marriage to Bezukhov, which took place in 1813, was the last happy event in the old Rostov family. Count Ilya Rostov died that same year, and—as always happens—with the father's death, the family fell apart.

The events of the previous year—the burning of Moscow and the flight from it, Prince Andrew's death, Natasha's despair, Petya's death, and the old countess's grief—fell blow after blow on the old count's head. He seemed unable to understand their meaning, and bowed his old head as if expecting and inviting more blows to finish him off. He appeared now frightened and bewildered, now unnaturally animated and energetic.

Natasha's wedding kept him busy for a while. He ordered dinners and suppers and obviously tried to appear cheerful, but his cheerfulness was no longer infectious as it had once been; on the contrary, it made those who knew and loved him feel sorry for him.

When Pierre and his wife had gone, the count grew very quiet and began complaining of depression. A few days later he fell ill and took to his bed. From the start, despite the doctor's reassurances, he knew he would never get up again. The countess spent two weeks in an armchair by his bed without undressing. Every time she gave him his medicine he sobbed quietly and kissed her hand. On his last day, weeping, he begged forgiveness from his wife, and also—though his absent son was not there—from his son Nicholas, for having squandered the family's fortune, which was the main thing he felt guilty about. After receiving communion and last rites, he died quietly, and the next day a crowd of acquaintances came to pay their final respects to the deceased. All those acquaintances who had so often dined and danced in his house, and who had so often mocked him behind his back, now said with a uniform feeling of inner self-reproach and tenderness: "Well, say what you like, he was a wonderful man. You don't find people like that anymore... And who doesn't have faults?"
It was precisely when the count's financial affairs had become so tangled that no one could say what would happen if he lived another year that he unexpectedly died.

Nicholas was with the Russian army in Paris when the news of his father's death reached him. He immediately resigned his commission and, without waiting for it to be accepted, took leave of absence and went to Moscow. Within a month of the count's death, the full scale of the financial chaos became clear, astonishing everyone with the enormous total of petty debts whose existence no one had suspected. The debts were twice the value of the estate.

Friends and relatives advised Nicholas to renounce the inheritance. But he considered such a refusal an insult to his father's memory, which he held sacred, and so he would not hear of refusing. He accepted the inheritance along with the obligation to pay the debts.

The creditors, who had been silent so long—restrained by the vague but powerful influence the count's careless good nature had exerted on them while he lived—now all rushed to press their claims at once. As always happens in such cases, a rivalry sprang up over whose claims would be paid first, and the very people who—like Mitenka and others—held promissory notes they had received as gifts now proved to be the most aggressive creditors. Nicholas was given no peace and no quarter. Those who had pitied the old man—the cause of their losses, if losses there really were—now fell mercilessly on his obviously innocent young son, who had voluntarily taken on the debts.

None of Nicholas's plans succeeded. The estate was sold at auction for half its value, and half the debts still remained unpaid. Nicholas accepted thirty thousand rubles from his brother-in-law Bezukhov to pay off the debts he considered genuinely binding—real debts to real people. And to avoid going to prison for the remainder, which he couldn't pay, he entered the civil service.

Returning to the army, where he would have been made colonel at the next vacancy, was out of the question, because his mother now clung to him as her only hold on life. And so despite his reluctance to stay in Moscow among people who had known him before, despite his distaste for the civil service, he took a minor government post, removed his beloved hussar uniform, and moved with his mother and Sonya into a small apartment on the Sivtsev Vrazhek.

Natasha and Pierre were living in Petersburg at the time and had no clear idea of Nicholas's situation. Having borrowed money from his brother-in-law, Nicholas tried to hide his wretched circumstances from him. His position was all the more difficult because, on his twelve-hundred-ruble salary, he had to support not only himself, his mother, and Sonya but had to shield his mother from their poverty. The countess could not imagine living without the luxuries she had known since childhood. Without understanding the difficulty, she kept demanding a carriage she no longer had to send for a friend, expensive delicacies for herself, and wine for her son.

Sonya kept house, waited on her aunt, read to her, endured her moods and secret resentment, and helped Nicholas hide their poverty from the old countess. Nicholas felt irredeemably indebted to Sonya for everything she was doing for his mother, and he admired her patience and devotion. But he tried to keep his distance from her.

He seemed in his heart to blame her for being too perfect, because there was nothing to blame her for. She had all the qualities people are valued for, but little that could have made him love her. He felt that the more he appreciated her, the less he loved her. He had taken her at her word when she wrote giving him his freedom, and now treated her as though everything between them had been long forgotten and could never, under any circumstances, be repeated.

Nicholas's financial situation kept getting worse and worse. The idea of saving something from his salary turned out to be a fantasy. Not only did he save nothing, but he even ran up small debts to meet his mother's demands. He could see no way out of his situation. The idea of marrying a rich woman, which his female relatives suggested, disgusted him. The only other way out—his mother's death—never entered his mind. He wished for nothing, hoped for nothing, and deep down took a dark, grim pleasure in stoically enduring his position. He tried to avoid old acquaintances with their expressions of pity and their offensive offers of help, avoided all entertainment and amusement, and even at home did nothing but play patience with his mother, pace silently around the room, and smoke pipe after pipe. He seemed determined to maintain within himself that gloomy state of mind in which alone he felt capable of bearing his situation.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: At the start of winter, Princess Mary came to Moscow. From talk around town she learned of the Rostovs' situation and heard how "the son has sacrificed himself for his mother," as people were saying.

"I never expected anything less of him," Princess Mary told herself, feeling a joyful confirmation of her love for him. Remembering her close relations with the whole Rostov family, which had made her almost a member of it, she felt it her duty to visit them. But when she thought of her relations with Nicholas in Voronezh, she was afraid to do so. A few weeks after arriving in Moscow, however, she made a great effort and went to see the Rostovs.

Nicholas was the first to meet her, since the countess's room could only be reached through his. Instead of the pleased greeting she'd expected, his first glance showed a cold, stiff, proud expression she had never seen on his face before. He asked about her health, led her to his mother, and stayed for five minutes before leaving.

When the princess came out of the countess's room, Nicholas met her again and accompanied her to the front hall with marked formality and stiffness. He made no reply to her remarks about his mother's health. "What's that to you? Leave me in peace," his expression seemed to say.

"Why does she come prowling here? What does she want? I can't stand these ladies and all these social niceties!" he said aloud in Sonya's presence, clearly unable to suppress his irritation after the princess's carriage had driven away.
"Oh, Nicholas, how can you talk like that?" cried Sonya, barely hiding her delight. "She's so kind, and Mama is so fond of her!"
Nicholas didn't reply and tried to avoid any further mention of the princess. But after her visit, the old countess talked about her several times a day.
She praised her, insisted that her son must return the visit, and expressed a wish to see her often—yet always grew ill-humored whenever she actually started talking about her.
Nicholas tried to keep quiet when his mother mentioned the princess, but his silence irritated her.
"She's a very admirable and excellent young woman," said the countess, "and you must go and call on her. You'd at least be seeing someone, and I think it must be dull for you just seeing us."
"But I don't want to at all, Mama."
"You used to want to, and now you don't. Really, I don't understand you, my dear. One day you're bored, and the next you won't see anyone."
"But I never said I was bored."

"You just said yourself you don't even want to see her. She's a very admirable young woman and you always liked her, but now suddenly you've got some notion in your head. You hide everything from me."
"Not at all, Mama."

"If I were asking you to do something unpleasant—but I'm only asking you to return a visit. Simple politeness requires it... Well, I've asked you, and now I won't interfere anymore, since you have secrets from your mother."
"Fine, I'll go if you want me to."
"It doesn't matter to me. I only want it for your sake."
Nicholas sighed, bit his mustache, and laid out cards for a game of patience, trying to redirect his mother's attention to another topic.
The same conversation was repeated the next day, and the day after that, and the day after that.
After her visit to the Rostovs and the unexpectedly cold reception from Nicholas, Princess Mary told herself she had been right not to want to be the first to call.
"I expected nothing else," she told herself, summoning her pride. "I have nothing to do with him, and I only wanted to see the old lady, who was always kind to me and to whom I owe so much."

But she couldn't calm herself with these reflections. A feeling close to remorse troubled her when she thought of her visit. Though she firmly resolved never to call on the Rostovs again and to forget the whole matter, she felt herself constantly in an uncertain position. And when she asked herself what exactly was troubling her, she had to admit it was her relationship with Rostov. His cold, polite manner didn't come from his heart, she felt sure of that; it concealed something. She needed to find out what it was, and until she did, she felt she could not be at peace.

One day in midwinter, as she sat in the schoolroom supervising her nephew's lessons, she was told that Rostov had called. With a firm resolution not to betray herself or show her agitation, she sent for Mademoiselle Bourienne and went with her to the drawing room.
Her first glance at Nicholas's face told her he had come only to fulfill a social obligation, and she firmly resolved to maintain the same tone in which he addressed her.

They spoke about the countess's health, about mutual friends, about the latest war news. When the ten minutes required by propriety had elapsed—after which a visitor may rise—Nicholas stood up to say goodbye.

With Mademoiselle Bourienne's help, the princess had kept the conversation going quite well. But at the very last moment—just as he rose—she was so tired of talking about things that didn't interest her, and her mind was so full of the question why she alone was granted so little joy in life, that she suddenly fell into a reverie and sat there motionless, her shining eyes staring straight ahead, unaware that he had risen.

Nicholas glanced at her and, not wanting to seem to notice her distraction, said something to Mademoiselle Bourienne and then looked at the princess again. She still sat motionless, and a look of suffering showed on her gentle face. He suddenly felt sorry for her and had a vague sense that perhaps he was the cause of her sadness. He wanted to say something kind and comforting, but couldn't think of what to say.
"Goodbye, Princess!" he said.
She started, blushed, and sighed deeply.
"Oh, forgive me," she said, as if waking up. "You're going already, Count? Well then, goodbye! Oh—the cushion for the countess!"
"Wait a moment, I'll fetch it," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, and she left the room.
They both sat in silence, occasionally glancing at each other.

"Yes, Princess," Nicholas said at last with a sad smile, "it doesn't seem long ago since we first met at Bogucharovo, but how much has happened since then! We all seemed to be in such distress then—yet I'd give anything to bring back that time... but there's no bringing it back."
Princess Mary gazed intently into his eyes with her own luminous ones as he spoke. She seemed to be searching for the hidden meaning of his words—the meaning that would explain his feelings for her.
"Yes, yes," she said, "but you have no reason to regret the past, Count. As I understand your present life, you will always look back on it with pride, because the self-sacrifice that fills it now—"
"I can't accept your praise," he interrupted hastily. "On the contrary, I constantly reproach myself... But this isn't an interesting or cheerful topic."
His face resumed its former stiff, cold expression. But the princess had caught a glimpse of the man she had known and loved, and it was to him that she now spoke.

"I thought you would let me say this," she said. "I had grown so close to you... and to your whole family, that I thought you wouldn't consider my sympathy out of place. But I was mistaken," and suddenly her voice trembled. "I don't know why," she continued, recovering herself, "you used to be different, and—"
"There are a thousand reasons why," he said, placing heavy emphasis on the word "why." "Thank you, Princess," he added softly. "Sometimes it's hard."

"So that's why! That's why!" a voice whispered in Princess Mary's soul. "No, it wasn't only that warm, kind, open look, not only that handsome face that I loved in him. I saw his noble, resolute, self-sacrificing spirit too," she told herself. "Yes, he's poor now, and I'm rich... Yes, that's the only reason... Yes, if it weren't for that..." And remembering his former tenderness, and looking now at his kind, sorrowful face, she suddenly understood the reason for his coldness.
"But why, Count, why?" she almost cried, unconsciously moving closer to him. "Why? You must tell me!"
He was silent.

"I don't understand your 'why,' Count," she continued. "But it's hard for me... I have to be honest. For some reason you want to take away our old friendship. And that hurts me." There were tears in her eyes and her voice. "I've had so little happiness in my life that every loss is painful... Forgive me. Goodbye." And suddenly she began to cry and started toward the door.
"Princess, for God's sake!" he exclaimed, trying to stop her. "Princess!"
She turned around. For a few seconds they gazed silently into each other's eyes—and what had seemed impossible and remote suddenly became possible, inevitable, and very near.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: In the winter of 1813, Nicholas married Princess Mary and moved to Bald Hills with his wife, his mother, and Sonya.

Within four years he had paid off all his remaining debts without selling any of his wife's property, and having received a small inheritance from a deceased cousin, he repaid his debt to Pierre as well.
In another three years, by 1820, he had managed his affairs so well that he was able to buy a small estate adjoining Bald Hills and was in negotiations to buy back Otradnoe—his lifelong dream.

Having started farming out of necessity, Nicholas soon grew so devoted to it that it became his favorite—and nearly his only—occupation. He was a plain, practical farmer. He didn't like innovations, especially the English methods that were then coming into vogue. He laughed at theoretical treatises on agriculture, had no interest in factories or expensive crops, and didn't obsess over any one part of his operation to the exclusion of the rest. What he always kept in mind was the estate as a whole, not any particular component. What mattered to him was not nitrogen in the soil or oxygen in the air, not special plows or fertilizers, but the principal instrument through which nitrogen, oxygen, plows, and fertilizers all worked—that is, the laboring peasant. When Nicholas first took up farming and began to understand its various branches, it was the peasant who especially engaged his attention. He saw the peasant not merely as a tool but as an end in himself and as a judge. At first he studied the peasant closely, trying to understand what he needed and what he considered good and bad, and only pretended to give orders while in fact learning from the peasants, their methods, and their language. Only when he understood the peasants' tastes and aspirations, had learned to speak their language and grasp the hidden meaning behind their words, and felt himself one of them, did he begin to manage them boldly—that is, to fulfill toward them the duty expected of him.

Guided by some intuitive gift, on taking over the estates he immediately appointed as bailiff, village elder, and delegate the very men the serfs would have chosen themselves if they'd had the right. And these appointments never changed. Before analyzing the chemical properties of manure, before exploring the principles of debit and credit (as he liked to mock), he calculated how many carts his peasants had and tried to increase their number; he kept the peasant families as large as possible and wouldn't allow them to split up; he was strict with the lazy, the vicious, and the weak, and tried to keep them out; and at sowing and harvest time he went out to the fields himself to oversee the work, studying the peasants' crops with the same attention he gave to his own.

He was as careful about the sowing and reaping of the peasants' hay and grain as his own, and few landowners had their crops sown and harvested as early, as well, or with as good a return as Nicholas.

He didn't like dealing with household serfs—the "drones," as he called them—and everyone said he spoiled them with his leniency. When a decision had to be made about a household serf, especially one who needed to be punished, he was always uncertain and consulted everyone in the house. But when it was possible to send a serf to serve as a soldier in place of a peasant, he did so without a moment's hesitation. He never felt the slightest uncertainty in his dealings with the peasants. He knew that every decision he made would be approved by all of them, with very rare exceptions.

He never let himself be harsh with someone or reward someone merely because he felt like it. He couldn't have said by what standard he measured what he should or shouldn't do, but the standard in his heart was firm and unwavering.
He would often speak with vexation about some failure or problem and say: "What can you do with our Russian peasants?" and imagine that he couldn't stand them.
Yet he loved "our Russian peasants" and their way of life with his whole soul, and for that very reason he had understood and adopted the one method of farming that produced good results.

Countess Mary was jealous of this passion of her husband's and regretted that she couldn't share it. But she couldn't grasp the joys and frustrations he drew from that world, so alien and remote to her. She couldn't understand why he was so particularly excited and happy when, having gotten up at dawn and spent the whole morning in the fields or on the threshing floor, he came back to tea from the sowing, mowing, or harvesting. She couldn't understand what made him so delighted when he talked enthusiastically about the prosperous, hardworking peasant Matvei Ermilov who had been up all night with his family carting sheaves, or about having gotten all his grain in before anyone else.

Still less could she understand why, despite his kind heart and readiness to anticipate her wishes, he nearly lost his mind when she brought him a petition from some peasant men or women who had come to her asking to be excused from work—why he, a kind man, stubbornly refused, telling her angrily not to meddle in what was none of her business. She felt that he had a world entirely his own, which he loved passionately and which was governed by laws she did not understand.

Sometimes, when she tried to understand him and spoke of the good he was doing for his serfs, he would get annoyed and reply: "Not in the least; it never entered my head, and I wouldn't lift a finger for their good! That's all poetry and old wives' nonsense—all that doing good for one's neighbor! I don't want our children to go begging; I want to build up our family fortune while I'm alive. That's all. And to do that, you need order, you need discipline... That's the point!" he would say, clenching his large fist. "And fairness too, of course!" he would add. "Because if a peasant is naked and hungry and has only one wretched horse, he's no good to himself or to anyone else."

And probably because Nicholas allowed himself no thought of doing good for others for virtue's sake, everything he did was fruitful. His wealth grew rapidly; serfs from neighboring estates came begging him to buy them. And long after his death, the peasants preserved a devoted memory of his management. "He was a real master... The peasants' affairs first, then his own. And he didn't let you get away with anything. A real master!"

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: One thing about his management sometimes troubled Nicholas: his quick temper, combined with his old hussar habit of settling things with his fists. At first he saw nothing wrong with this, but in the second year of his marriage an incident occurred that changed his view.

One summer he had sent for the village elder from Bogucharovo, a man who had taken over when Dron died and who was accused of dishonesty and various irregularities. Nicholas went out onto the porch to question him, and immediately after the elder's first answers, the sound of shouting and blows could be heard from the porch. Returning to the house for lunch, Nicholas went up to his wife, who sat with her embroidery frame, and began telling her—as he usually did—everything that had occupied him that morning. Among other things, he mentioned the Bogucharovo village elder. Countess Mary, turning red, then pale, and pressing her lips together, sat in the same position, offering no reply to her husband.
"The insolent scoundrel!" he cried, getting heated all over again just remembering. "If he'd told me he was drunk and couldn't see straight... But what's the matter, Mary?" he suddenly asked.
Countess Mary raised her head and tried to speak, but quickly looked down again, her lips trembling.
"Why, what is it, my dearest?"
Plain Countess Mary always looked better when she cried. She never cried from pain or frustration—only from sorrow or compassion—and when she wept, her radiant eyes took on an irresistible beauty.
The moment Nicholas took her hand, she could no longer hold back and began to cry.
"Nicholas, I saw it... he was wrong, but why did you... Nicholas!" She covered her face with her hands.

Nicholas said nothing. He turned crimson, left her side, and paced up and down the room. He understood what she was crying about, but couldn't immediately agree in his heart that what he had done since childhood—what he considered perfectly normal—was wrong.
"Mary," he said softly, going up to her, "it will never happen again. I give you my word. Never," he repeated in a trembling voice, like a boy asking for forgiveness.
The tears flowed even faster from the countess's eyes. She took his hand and kissed it.
"Nicholas, when did you break your cameo?" she asked, wanting to change the subject, and looking at his finger where he wore a ring with a cameo of Laocoon's head.

"Today—the same business. Oh, Mary, don't remind me of it!" And again he flushed. "I give you my word of honor it won't happen again. And let this always be a reminder," he said, pointing to the broken ring.

After that, whenever in discussions with his village elders or stewards the blood rushed to his face and his fists began to clench, Nicholas would turn the broken ring on his finger and drop his eyes before whoever was making him angry. But he still lost his temper once or twice a year and would then go to his wife and confess, promising once again that this was really the last time.
"Mary, you must despise me!" he would say. "I deserve it."
"You should just leave—walk away at once—if you don't feel strong enough to control yourself," she would reply sadly, trying to comfort her husband.

Among the local gentry, Nicholas was respected but not liked. He didn't concern himself with the interests of his own class, and so some thought him proud and others thought him stupid. The entire summer, from spring sowing to harvest, he was busy with farming. In autumn he devoted himself to hunting with the same businesslike seriousness, going off with his dogs for a month or two at a time. In winter he visited his other villages and spent his time reading. The books he read were mainly historical. Every year he bought a set number of serious books and made it a rule to read them all. He would sit in his study with a grave expression, devoting himself to this reading—a task he had initially imposed on himself as a duty but which later became a habit providing him with a special kind of satisfaction and the awareness that he was engaged in something important. Except for occasional business trips, he spent the winter at home, entering fully into the family life and the details of his relationship with his wife and children. He was growing closer to his wife, discovering new spiritual treasures in her every day.

From the time of his marriage, Sonya had lived in his house. Before that, Nicholas had told his wife everything that had passed between himself and Sonya, blaming himself and praising her. He had asked Princess Mary to be gentle and kind to his cousin. She felt her husband's generosity; she also felt her own guilt toward Sonya; she recognized that her own wealth had influenced Nicholas's choice; she could find nothing to blame Sonya for, and wanted to love her. But she could not. She could not, and sometimes her soul harbored unkind feelings toward Sonya that she could not overcome.
Once she had a conversation with her friend Natasha about Sonya and about her own injustice toward her.
"You know," said Natasha, "you've read the Gospels a lot—there's a passage that fits Sonya exactly."
"What?" asked Countess Mary, surprised.

"'To him who has, more shall be given; and from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away.' Remember? She's the one who has not. Why? I don't know. Maybe she lacks selfishness—I don't know—but from her, things are taken away, and everything has been taken away. Sometimes I feel terribly sorry for her. I used to desperately want Nicholas to marry her, but I always had a feeling it would never happen. She's a sterile flower—you know, like in strawberry plants? Sometimes I feel sorry for her, and sometimes I think she doesn't feel it the way we would."

Though Countess Mary told Natasha that those Gospel words should be understood differently, looking at Sonya she had to agree with Natasha's explanation. It really did seem that Sonya didn't find her position difficult and had grown quite reconciled to her role as a sterile flower. She seemed to value not individual people so much as the family as a whole. Like a cat, she had attached herself not to the people but to the house. She looked after the old countess, petted and spoiled the children, and was always ready to perform the small services she was capable of. But all this was accepted with too little gratitude...
The country house at Bald Hills had been rebuilt, though not on the same scale as under the old prince.

The buildings, begun under tight finances, were more than simple. The enormous house on the old stone foundations was of wood, plastered only on the inside. It had bare pine floors and was furnished with very plain hard sofas, armchairs, tables, and chairs made by their own serf carpenters from their own birch trees. The house was spacious, with rooms for the house serfs and quarters for visitors. Whole families of Rostov and Bolkonsky relatives would sometimes come to Bald Hills with sixteen horses and dozens of servants and stay for months. And four times a year—on the name days and birthdays of the heads of the household—as many as a hundred guests would gather for a day or two. The rest of the year, life went on in its unbroken routine, with its customary round of occupations—teas, breakfasts, dinners, and suppers—all provided from the estate's own produce.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: It was the eve of St. Nicholas Day, December fifth, 1820. That year Natasha and her husband and children had been staying at her brother's since early autumn. Pierre had gone to Petersburg on business "for three weeks," as he said, but had now been away for seven. He was expected back any minute.
Besides the Bezukhov family, Nicholas's old friend the retired General Vasili Dmitrich Denisov was also staying with the Rostovs on this fifth of December.

On the sixth—his name day, when the house would be full of visitors—Nicholas knew he would have to swap his Tatar tunic for a dress coat, put on narrow boots with pointed toes, and drive to the new church he had built, then receive congratulations and offer refreshments and talk about the local elections and the year's harvest. But the day before, he considered himself entitled to spend as he usually did. Before dinnertime Nicholas went over the bailiff's accounts from the Ryazan estate belonging to his wife's nephew, wrote two business letters, and strolled through the granaries, the cattle yard, and the stables. After taking measures against the general drunkenness expected the next day because of the holiday, he came in to dinner without having had a moment alone with his wife all day. He sat down at the long table laid for twenty people, around which the whole household was assembled. This included his mother, Sonya (who lived with them), his wife, their three children, their governess, their tutor, his wife's nephew with his tutor, and several others who always dined at the house.

Countess Mary sat at the other end of the table. When her husband sat down, she could tell from the quick way he grabbed his napkin and pushed aside the glass and wineglass in front of him that he was in a bad mood—as sometimes happened, especially before soup and when he came straight from work to the table. Countess Mary knew this mood well and, when she was in a good mood herself, would wait quietly until he had his first spoonful of soup, and only then begin talking—making him admit he had been in a bad mood for no reason. But today she entirely forgot this observation of hers; she felt hurt that he was cross with her for no reason, and she felt miserable. She asked him where he had been. He told her. She then asked whether all was going well on the estate. His frown deepened at her unnatural tone, and he answered briefly.

"So I'm not mistaken," thought Countess Mary. "But why is he cross with me?" She concluded from his tone that he was annoyed with her and wanted to end the conversation. She knew her remarks sounded forced, but couldn't help asking a few more questions.

Thanks to Denisov the conversation at dinner soon became general and lively, and she stopped talking to her husband. When they rose from the table and went as usual to thank the old countess, Countess Mary held out her hand and kissed her husband, asking him why he was angry with her.
"You always have such odd ideas! I didn't even think of being angry," he replied.
But the word "always" seemed to her to mean: "Yes, I am angry, but I won't tell you why."

Nicholas and his wife lived together so happily that even Sonya and the old countess—who felt jealous and would have liked them to disagree—could find nothing to criticize. But they too had their moments of tension. Occasionally, especially right after their happiest periods, a feeling of estrangement and hostility would come over them. This feeling occurred most often when Countess Mary was pregnant. She was pregnant now.

"Well, ladies and gentlemen," Nicholas said loudly and with forced cheerfulness—or so it seemed to Countess Mary, who felt he did it on purpose to annoy her—"I've been on my feet since six this morning. Tomorrow I'll have to suffer through the celebrations, so today I'm going to rest." And without a word to his wife, he went into the little sitting room and lay down on the sofa.
And without a word to his wife he went to the little sitting room and lay down on the sofa.

"That's always the way," thought Countess Mary. "He talks to everyone except me. I can see... I can see that I repel him, especially in this condition." She looked down at her pregnant figure and into the mirror at her pale, sallow, emaciated face with its larger-looking eyes.
And everything irritated her—Denisov's loud voice and laughter, Natasha's chatter, and especially the quick glance Sonya gave her.
Sonya was always the first excuse Countess Mary found for feeling irritated.
Having sat with the visitors for a while without following a word of what they said, she quietly left the room and went to the nursery.

The children were playing "going to Moscow" in a carriage made of chairs and invited her to join them. She sat down and played with them for a little while, but the thought of her husband and his unreasonable ill temper kept nagging at her. She got up and walked on tiptoe, with difficulty, to the small sitting room.
"Maybe he's not asleep. I'll have it out with him," she told herself. Little Andrew, her eldest boy, was following her on tiptoe, imitating his mother. She didn't notice him.
"Mary, dear, I think he's asleep—he was so tired," said Sonya, meeting her in the large sitting room. (It seemed to Countess Mary that Sonya crossed her path everywhere.) "Andrew might wake him."

Countess Mary looked around, saw little Andrew following her, felt that Sonya was right, and for that very reason flushed and with obvious difficulty kept herself from saying something sharp. She said nothing, but—to avoid obeying Sonya—beckoned Andrew to follow her quietly, and went to the door. Sonya went out by the other door. From the room where Nicholas lay asleep, his wife could hear his even breathing, every note of which was familiar to her. As she listened, she could see his smooth, handsome forehead and mustache, and the whole face she had studied so often in the silence of the night when he slept. Nicholas suddenly stirred and cleared his throat. And at that moment, little Andrew shouted from outside the door: "Papa! Mama's standing here!" Countess Mary paled with fright and began signaling to the boy. He fell silent, and for a moment there was a terrible stillness that lasted about a minute. She knew how much Nicholas disliked being woken. Then behind the door she heard another throat-clearing and a movement, and his displeased voice said:
"I can't get a moment's peace... Mary, is that you? Why did you bring him here?"
"I only came to look and didn't notice... I'm sorry..."

Nicholas coughed and said no more. Countess Mary moved away from the door and took the boy back to the nursery. Five minutes later, little black-eyed three-year-old Natasha—her father's pet—having learned from her brother that Papa was asleep and Mama was in the sitting room, ran to her father unnoticed by her mother. The dark-eyed little girl boldly pushed open the creaking door, marched to the sofa with determined little steps, and—seeing that her father was asleep with his back to her—stood on tiptoe and kissed the hand he was resting his head on. Nicholas turned around with a tender smile on his face.
"Natasha, Natasha!" came Countess Mary's frightened whisper from the door. "Papa wants to sleep."
"No, Mama, he doesn't want to sleep," said little Natasha with conviction. "He's laughing."
Nicholas swung his legs down, sat up, and took his daughter in his arms.
"Come in, Mary," he said to his wife.
She came in and sat down beside her husband.
"I didn't notice him following me," she said timidly. "I just looked in."
Holding his little girl with one arm, Nicholas glanced at his wife, and seeing her guilty expression, put his other arm around her and kissed her hair.
"May I kiss Mama?" he asked Natasha.
Natasha smiled shyly.
"Again!" she commanded with a bossy gesture, pointing to the spot where Nicholas had placed the kiss.
"I don't know why you think I'm cross," said Nicholas, answering the question he knew was in his wife's mind.
"You have no idea how unhappy, how lonely I feel when you're like that. It always seems to me—"
"Mary, don't be silly. You should be ashamed of yourself!" he said cheerfully.
"It seems to me that you can't love me, that I'm so plain... always... and now... in this state—"

"Oh, how ridiculous you are! It's not beauty that makes us love—it's love that makes us see beauty. It's only the Malvinas of the world who are loved for their looks. Do I love my wife? I don't just love her—but... I don't know how to put it. Without you, or when something comes between us like today, I feel completely lost—I can't do anything. Do I love my finger? No, but just try cutting it off..."
"I'm not like that myself, but I understand. So you're not angry with me?"
"Terribly angry!" he said, smiling. And he stood up, smoothed his hair, and began pacing the room.
"Do you know, Mary, what I've been thinking?" he began, immediately thinking aloud in his wife's presence now that they had made up.
He didn't ask if she was ready to listen. He didn't care. A thought had occurred to him and so it belonged to her too. And he told her his plan to convince Pierre to stay with them until spring.
Countess Mary listened until he had finished, made a comment, and in turn began thinking aloud. Her thoughts were about the children.

"You can already see the woman in her," she said in French, pointing to little Natasha. "You men accuse us women of being illogical. Here's our logic. I say: 'Papa wants to sleep!' but she says, 'No, he's laughing.' And she was right," said Countess Mary with a happy smile.

"Yes, yes." And Nicholas, taking his little daughter in his strong hand, lifted her high, set her on his shoulder, held her by the legs, and paced the room. Father and daughter wore identical expressions of carefree happiness.
"But you know, you may be unfair. You're too fond of this one," his wife whispered in French.
"Yes, but what can I do?... I try not to show it..."
At that moment they heard the sound of the door-pull and footsteps in the hall and front room, as if someone had arrived.
"Someone's here."
"I'm sure it's Pierre. I'll go and see," said Countess Mary, and she left the room.

In her absence, Nicholas allowed himself to give his little daughter a gallop around the room. Out of breath, he quickly lifted the laughing child from his shoulder and pressed her to his heart. His capering reminded him of dancing, and looking at the child's round, happy little face, he thought of what she would be like when he was an old man, taking her to balls, and he imagined her dancing the mazurka with some lanky young man, just as his late father-in-law had once danced Daniel Cooper with his daughter.

"It's him, it's him, Nicholas!" said Countess Mary, coming back a few minutes later. "Now our Natasha has come to life. You should have seen her face light up, and how she scolded him for staying away so long. Well, come along now, quick, quick! Separate yourselves at last!" she said, smiling as she looked at the little girl pressed against her father.
Nicholas went out, holding the child by the hand.
Countess Mary stayed behind in the sitting room.

"I would never, never have believed anyone could be so happy," she whispered to herself. A smile lit up her face, but at the same time she sighed, and a quiet sadness showed in her deep eyes—as though she felt, through her happiness, that there is another kind of happiness, unattainable in this life, which she could not help thinking of at that moment.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Natasha had married in the early spring of 1813, and by 1820 she already had three daughters and a son she had longed for and was now nursing. She had grown heavier and broader, so that it was hard to recognize the slim, lively Natasha of earlier years in this robust, motherly woman. Her features had settled and wore an expression of calm softness and serenity. Her face no longer had that ever-burning fire of eagerness that had been her chief charm. Now you often saw only her face and body, and her soul was not visible at all. All that could be seen was a strong, beautiful, and fertile woman. Very rarely now did the old fire blaze up—only when her husband came home, or a sick child recovered, or when she and Countess Mary talked about Prince Andrew (she never spoke of him to her husband, assuming he was jealous of Prince Andrew's memory), and very rarely when something happened to draw her into singing, which she had entirely given up after her marriage. And at those rare moments when the old fire did kindle, she was even more attractive than before, because of her new stateliness.

Since their marriage, Natasha and her husband had lived in Moscow, in Petersburg, on their estate near Moscow, and at her mother's house—that is, at Nicholas's. The young Countess Bezukhova was not often seen in society, and those who did see her were not impressed. She was neither charming nor agreeable. Not that Natasha liked solitude—she didn't really know whether she liked it or not, and in fact rather thought she didn't—but bearing, nursing, and raising children, and sharing every moment of her husband's life, meant that she could only satisfy those needs by giving up society. Everyone who had known Natasha before her marriage was surprised at the change in her, as though it were something extraordinary. Only the old countess, who—with her mother's instinct—understood that all of Natasha's outbursts had been nothing more than the need for a family, for a husband (as Natasha herself had said, more in earnest than in jest, at Otradnoe)—only the old countess was not surprised. She would say that she had always known Natasha would make a model wife and mother.
"Only she lets her love for her husband and children overflow all bounds," the countess said, "until it actually becomes ridiculous."

Natasha did not follow the golden rule urged by clever people, especially the French, which says that a girl should not let herself go after marriage, should not neglect her accomplishments, should be even more careful of her appearance than when she was single, and should charm her husband just as she had charmed him before. Natasha, on the contrary, had immediately abandoned all her accomplishments, among which the greatest was her singing. She gave it up precisely because it was such a powerful charm. She no longer bothered with her manners or her graceful ways of speaking, or with showing herself to her husband in the most flattering positions, or with avoiding boring him. She did the exact opposite of all that. She felt that the charms instinct had taught her to use before would now seem ridiculous to her husband, to whom she had given herself completely from the very first moment—that is, with her entire soul, leaving no corner of it hidden from him. She felt that the bond between her and her husband rested not on those romantic feelings that had attracted him to her, but on something else—something indefinite but firm, like the bond between her own soul and her body.

To curl her hair, put on fashionable dresses, and sing romantic songs to captivate her husband would have struck her as absurd—like decorating herself to attract herself. To dress up for others might perhaps have been pleasant—she didn't know—but she had no time for it. The main reason she didn't attend to her singing, her appearance, or even to the way she spoke was that she genuinely had no time for any of that.

We know that people have the ability to become completely absorbed in a subject, however trivial, and that there is no subject so trivial that it won't grow to infinite proportions if you devote your full attention to it.

The subject that wholly absorbed Natasha was her family: her husband, whom she had to keep so that he belonged entirely to her and to the home, and the children she had to carry, give birth to, nurse, and raise.

And the deeper she penetrated—not just with her mind but with her whole being—into the subject that absorbed her, the larger it grew and the less adequate her powers seemed, so she focused all her energy on the one thing and still could not accomplish everything she considered necessary.

Conversations and debates about women's rights—the relations of husband and wife, their freedom and obligations—existed then just as they do now, though they weren't yet called "questions." But these topics were not merely uninteresting to Natasha; she positively did not understand them. These questions, then as now, existed only for people who saw nothing in marriage except the pleasure the couple got from each other—that is, only the beginning of marriage, not its full significance, which lies in the family.

These questions, then as now, existed only for those who see nothing in marriage but the pleasure married people get from one another—that is, only the beginning of marriage and not its whole meaning, which lies in the family.

Debates of this kind—which are like the question of how to get the most enjoyment from your dinner—did not then and do not now exist for those whose purpose at dinner is nourishment; and the purpose of marriage is the family.
If the purpose of dinner is to nourish the body, a person who eats two dinners at once may get more enjoyment but won't achieve his purpose, because his stomach can't digest two dinners.
If the purpose of marriage is the family, then a person who wants many wives or husbands may get a great deal of pleasure, but will never have a real family.

If the purpose of food is nourishment and the purpose of marriage is the family, then the whole question comes down to: don't eat more than you can digest, and don't have more wives or husbands than you need for a family—that is, one wife or one husband. Natasha needed a husband. A husband was given to her. And the husband gave her a family. She not only saw no need for another, better husband, but since all the powers of her soul were devoted to serving that husband and family, she couldn't even imagine—and saw no point in imagining—what it would be like if things were different.

Natasha didn't care for society in general but valued all the more the company of her relatives—Countess Mary, her brother, her mother, and Sonya. She prized the company of people she could visit in her dressing gown, striding disheveled from the nursery with a joyful face to show a diaper with a yellow stain instead of a green one, and to hear reassuring words that the baby was now much better.

Natasha had let herself go to such an extent that her clothes, her badly chosen words, and her jealousy—she was jealous of Sonya, of the governess, of every woman, pretty or plain—were habitual subjects of jokes among those around her. The general opinion was that Pierre was under his wife's thumb, and this was indeed the case. From the very first days of their marriage, Natasha had made her demands known. Pierre was quite astonished by his wife's view—so completely new to him—that every moment of his life belonged to her and the family. His wife's demands astonished him, but they also flattered him, and he submitted.

Pierre's submission meant that he dared not only not flirt with but not even speak with a smile to any other woman, dared not dine at the club just for amusement, dared not spend money on a whim, and dared not be away for any length of time except on business—in which his wife included his intellectual pursuits, which she understood nothing about but attributed great importance to. In return, Pierre had the full right to run the whole household according to his wishes. In their own home Natasha made herself Pierre's slave, and the whole household had to go on tiptoe when Pierre was reading or writing in his study. Pierre had only to show a preference and the thing he wished was done. He had only to express a wish and Natasha jumped up to carry it out.

The entire household was governed according to Pierre's supposed wishes—that is, by his preferences, which Natasha tried to guess. Their way of life, their place of residence, their acquaintances and social connections, Natasha's occupations, the children's upbringing—all followed not only Pierre's expressed wishes but Natasha's attempts to deduce what those wishes were from ideas he had expressed in conversation. And she quite accurately identified his real wishes, and once she had found them she held to them firmly. When Pierre himself wanted to change his mind, she fought him with his own weapons.
